0009 | +++
0010 | 
0011 | We ended the last chapter by changing one number.
0012 | 
0013 | ```python
0014 | rule = 22
0015 | ```
0016 | 
0017 | became:
0018 | 
0019 | ```python
0020 | rule = 30
0021 | ```
0022 | 
0023 | Nothing else changed.
0024 | 
0025 | Same world size.
0026 | 
0027 | Same single active cell.
0028 | 
0029 | Same three-cell neighborhood.
0030 | 
0031 | Same synchronous update.
0032 | 
0033 | Same periodic boundary.
0034 | 
0035 | Same implementation.
0036 | 
0037 | Only the eight-bit local rule changed.
0038 | 
0039 | And the spacetime diagram changed dramatically.
0040 | 
0041 | ![Rule 30 from a single active cell](/images/books/digital-life/ch03-rule30-hero.png)
0042 | 
0043 | There is visible structure on the left.
0044 | 
0045 | Irregularity on the right.
0046 | 
0047 | Repeating fragments.
0048 | 
0049 | Regions that look patterned for a while and then break apart.
0050 | 
0051 | And every pixel in that history is determined completely by the previous row.
0052 | 
0053 | No random numbers are involved.
0054 | 
0055 | That is our first real surprise.
0056 | 
0057 | ---
0058 | 
0059 | # Nothing random happened
0060 | 
0061 | Rule 30 does not roll dice.
0062 | 
0063 | Its transition table is fixed:
0064 | 
0065 | ```text
0066 | 111 → 0
0067 | 110 → 0
0068 | 101 → 0
0069 | 100 → 1
0070 | 011 → 1
0071 | 010 → 1
0072 | 001 → 1
0073 | 000 → 0
0074 | ```
0075 | 
0076 | Those outputs give:
0077 | 
0078 | ```text
0079 | 00011110
0080 | ```
0081 | 
0082 | which is:
0083 | 
0084 | ```text
0085 | 30
0086 | ```
0087 | 
0088 | Every future state follows from:
0089 | 
0090 | ```text
0091 | current state
0092 | +
0093 | rule
0094 | ```
0095 | 
0096 | under the experimental setup we defined.
0097 | 
0098 | If we start from exactly the same state again, we get exactly the same history.
0099 | 
0100 | Every time.
0101 | 
0102 | So the irregularity cannot be explained by saying:
0103 | 
0104 | > randomness was injected.
0105 | 
0106 | It was not.
0107 | 
0108 | ---
0109 | 
0110 | # Deterministic does not mean obvious
0111 | 
0112 | This distinction matters.
0113 | 
0114 | A deterministic system means:
0115 | 
0116 | > given the current state, the next state is fixed.
0117 | 
0118 | It does **not** mean:
0119 | 
0120 | > the long-term trajectory is easy to predict without running the system.
0121 | 
0122 | Those are different claims.
0123 | 
0124 | Each individual update is tiny:
0125 | 
0126 | ```python
0127 | next_state = step(state, rule=30)
0128 | ```
0129 | 
0130 | One cell.
0131 | 
0132 | Three inputs.
0133 | 
0134 | One output bit.
0135 | 
0136 | But after repeated updates, a large history unfolds.
0137 | 
0138 | So we need to separate:
0139 | 
0140 | ```text
0141 | local mechanism
0142 | ```
0143 | 
0144 | from:
0145 | 
0146 | ```text
0147 | global consequence
0148 | ```
0149 | 
0150 | Locally, Rule 30 is trivial to inspect.
0151 | 
0152 | Globally, its trajectory is not.
0153 | 
0154 | That distinction is going to matter throughout this book.
0155 | 
0156 | ---
0157 | 
0158 | # Where is the complexity?
0159 | 
0160 | This is a useful question.
0161 | 
0162 | Is the apparent complexity stored in the rule?
0163 | 
0164 | Not in any obvious sense.
0165 | 
0166 | The rule is only eight bits.
0167 | 
0168 | Is it stored in the initial condition?
0169 | 
0170 | We started with one active cell.
0171 | 
0172 | Is it stored inside each cell?
0173 | 
0174 | Each cell contains one bit.
0175 | 
0176 | So the interesting structure seems to arise from:
0177 | 
0178 | ```text
0179 | simple rule
0180 | +
0181 | simple state
0182 | +
0183 | repeated local interaction
0184 | +
0185 | time
0186 | ```
0187 | 
0188 | The structure lives in the unfolding.
0189 | 
0190 | That is why the word:
0191 | 
0192 | ```text
0193 | emergence
0194 | ```
0195 | 
0196 | is tempting.
0197 | 
0198 | But we should still be careful.
0199 | 
0200 | ---
0201 | 
0202 | # Do not use "emergence" as a synonym for surprise
0203 | 
0204 | A weak definition of emergence would be:
0205 | 
0206 | > Something happened that I did not expect.
0207 | 
0208 | That is not enough.
0209 | 
0210 | Surprise depends partly on the observer.
0211 | 
0212 | A better working description is:
0213 | 
0214 | > **A macroscopic pattern or behavior arises from local interactions without being explicitly represented in the individual components.**
0215 | 
0216 | Under that definition, Rule 30 is a useful example.
0217 | 
0218 | The cells do not contain:
0219 | 
0220 | ```text
0221 | triangle
0222 | left edge
0223 | irregular right side
0224 | long-range structure
0225 | ```
0226 | 
0227 | The rule does not contain a stored spacetime diagram.
0228 | 
0229 | Yet those structures appear when the local interactions repeat.
0230 | 
0231 | That supports a modest claim:
0232 | 
0233 | > **Simple local mechanics can generate nontrivial global organization.**
0234 | 
0235 | Not life.
0236 | 
0237 | Not intelligence.
0238 | 
0239 | Not even necessarily deep complexity.
0240 | 
0241 | But enough to keep investigating.
0242 | 
0243 | ---
0244 | 
0245 | # A controlled comparison
0246 | 
0247 | Now compare Rule 22 and Rule 30 directly.
0248 | 
0249 | Same initial condition:
0250 | 
0251 | ```text
0252 | 000000000010000000000
0253 | ```
0254 | 
0255 | Run Rule 22.
0256 | 
0257 | Then run Rule 30.
0258 | 
0259 | ![Rule 22 compared with Rule 30](/images/books/digital-life/ch03-rule22-vs-rule30.png)
0260 | 
0261 | Everything except the local rule remains fixed.
0262 | 
0263 | Conceptually:
0264 | 
0265 | ```text
0266 | Experiment A
0267 | rule = 22
0268 | 
0269 | Experiment B
0270 | rule = 30
0271 | ```
0272 | 
0273 | Same:
0274 | 
0275 | ```text
0276 | initial state
0277 | boundary condition
0278 | world size
0279 | generation count
0280 | update semantics
0281 | ```
0282 | 
0283 | Only the rule changes.
0284 | 
0285 | So under this fixed experimental configuration, the change in trajectory is attributable to the change in rule.
0286 | 
0287 | That sounds obvious.
0288 | 
0289 | Later, when our systems contain hundreds of interacting mechanisms, it will not be obvious at all.
0290 | 
0291 | This is why we are learning the discipline here.
0292 | 
0293 | ---
0294 | 
0295 | # Change one bit in the rule
0296 | 
0297 | Rule 30 is:
0298 | 
0299 | ```text
0300 | 00011110
0301 | ```
0302 | 
0303 | Flip one output bit and we move to a neighboring rule.
0304 | 
0305 | For example:
0306 | 
0307 | ```text
0308 | 00011111
0309 | ```
0310 | 
0311 | or:
0312 | 
0313 | ```text
0314 | 00010110
0315 | ```
0316 | 
0317 | The representation changes only slightly.
0318 | 
0319 | The resulting trajectory may not.
0320 | 
0321 | That creates another question:
0322 | 
0323 | > **How stable is a system's global behavior under small changes to its local mechanism?**
0324 | 
0325 | This is a much better question than:
0326 | 
0327 | > What does Rule 30 do?
0328 | 
0329 | Because eventually we will care about:
0330 | 
0331 | ```text
0332 | mutation
0333 | variation
0334 | robustness
0335 | search
0336 | evolution
0337 | ```
0338 | 
0339 | A tiny change in representation can have a large change in consequence.
0340 | 
0341 | We should remember that.
0342 | 
0343 | ---
0344 | 
0345 | # Change one bit in the world
0346 | 
0347 | Now keep the rule fixed and perturb the initial condition.
0348 | 
0349 | Start with:
0350 | 
0351 | ```text
0352 | 000000000010000000000
0353 | ```
0354 | 
0355 | Then compare:
0356 | 
0357 | ```text
0358 | 000000000011000000000
0359 | ```
0360 | 
0361 | One extra active cell.
0362 | 
0363 | Everything else remains identical.
0364 | 
0365 | Run both under Rule 30.
0366 | 
0367 | ![A one-cell perturbation spreading under Rule 30](/images/books/digital-life/ch03-rule30-perturbation.png)
0368 | 
0369 | At first the difference is tiny.
0370 | 
0371 | Then it spreads.
0372 | 
0373 | One changed cell alters several local neighborhoods.
0374 | 
0375 | Those changed neighborhoods alter later neighborhoods.
0376 | 
0377 | The perturbation propagates.
0378 | 
0379 | Now we have something measurable.
0380 | 
0381 | ---
0382 | 
0383 | # Track the difference, not just the worlds
0384 | 
0385 | Suppose we have:
0386 | 
0387 | ```text
0388 | A
0389 | 00000100000
0390 | 
0391 | B
0392 | 00000110000
0393 | ```
0394 | 
0395 | Their difference is:
0396 | 
0397 | ```text
0398 | 00000010000
0399 | ```
0400 | 
0401 | One cell.
0402 | 
0403 | After one generation, the worlds may differ in several cells.
0404 | 
0405 | Then more.
0406 | 
0407 | Instead of only studying:
0408 | 
0409 | ```text
0410 | world A
0411 | world B
0412 | ```
0413 | 
0414 | we can construct:
0415 | 
0416 | ```text
0417 | difference(A, B)
0418 | ```
0419 | 
0420 | That difference field is useful because it converts:
0421 | 
0422 | > these two runs look different
0423 | 
0424 | into something we can measure.
0425 | 
0426 | We can track:
0427 | 
0428 | ```text
0429 | number of differing cells
0430 | fraction of differing cells
0431 | spatial width of the difference
0432 | rate of divergence
0433 | ```
0434 | 
0435 | This is an important step.
0436 | 
0437 | The animation gives us the hypothesis.
0438 | 
0439 | The difference field gives us an instrument.
0440 | 
0441 | ---
0442 | 
0443 | # Measure the spread
0444 | 
0445 | A simple quantity is the Hamming distance between two binary states.
0446 | 
0447 | For states:
0448 | 
0449 | $$
0450 | A_t
0451 | $$
0452 | 
0453 | and:
0454 | 
0455 | $$
0456 | B_t
0457 | $$
0458 | 
0459 | define:
0460 | 
0461 | $$
0462 | D(t)
0463 | =
0464 | \sum_i
0465 | \mathbf{1}
0466 | \left[
0467 | A_t(i) \neq B_t(i)
0468 | \right]
0469 | $$
0470 | 
0471 | In code:
0472 | 
0473 | ```python
0474 | def difference_count(a, b):
0475 |     return sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b))
0476 | ```
0477 | 
0478 | Now run the two initial conditions forward and record:
0479 | 
0480 | ```python
0481 | difference = []
0482 | 
0483 | for _ in range(generations):
0484 |     difference.append(
0485 |         difference_count(state_a, state_b)
0486 |     )
0487 | 
0488 |     state_a = step(state_a, rule=30)
0489 |     state_b = step(state_b, rule=30)
0490 | ```
0491 | 
0492 | Plot that over time.
0493 | 
0494 | ![Measured growth of the perturbation](/images/books/digital-life/ch03-rule30-difference-growth.png)
0495 | 
0496 | Now we are no longer saying:
0497 | 
0498 | > the disturbance seems to spread.
0499 | 
0500 | We are asking:
0501 | 
0502 | > **how much of the world becomes different, and how quickly?**
0503 | 
0504 | That is a better question.
0505 | 
0506 | ---
0507 | 
0508 | # Sensitivity is not yet chaos
0509 | 
0510 | At this point it is tempting to say:
0511 | 
0512 | > Rule 30 is chaotic.
0513 | 
0514 | Maybe.
0515 | 
0516 | But we should not use that word casually.
0517 | 
0518 | In dynamical systems, chaos has technical meanings.
0519 | 
0520 | Likewise:
0521 | 
0522 | ```text
0523 | irregular
0524 | random
0525 | chaotic
0526 | complex
0527 | emergent
0528 | ```
0529 | 
0530 | are not synonyms.
0531 | 
0532 | For this chapter, we can safely say:
0533 | 
0534 | ```text
0535 | Rule 30 is deterministic.
0536 | 
0537 | Its spacetime diagram contains visually irregular regions.
0538 | 
0539 | Small changes to the initial state can spread through later states.
0540 | 
0541 | The divergence can be measured.
0542 | ```
0543 | 
0544 | That is enough.
0545 | 
0546 | If a stronger word requires a stronger definition, we should earn it later.
0547 | 
0548 | ---
0549 | 
0550 | # The first control is not enough
0551 | 
0552 | Suppose our difference count grows rapidly.
0553 | 
0554 | Can we immediately claim that Rule 30 is unusually sensitive?
0555 | 
0556 | No.
0557 | 
0558 | Compared with what?
0559 | 
0560 | We should also run:
0561 | 
0562 | ```text
0563 | Rule 22
0564 | Rule 30
0565 | other neighboring rules
0566 | ```
0567 | 
0568 | with the same perturbation protocol.
0569 | 
0570 | Then we can ask:
0571 | 
0572 | ```text
0573 | Which rules amplify a one-bit perturbation?
0574 | 
0575 | How quickly?
0576 | 
0577 | Does the perturbation saturate?
0578 | 
0579 | Does it disappear?
0580 | 
0581 | Does it remain localized?
0582 | ```
0583 | 
0584 | That is where a visual example becomes a comparative experiment.
0585 | 
0586 | We do not have to complete that whole survey here.
0587 | 
0588 | But the experimental direction is now clear.
0589 | 
0590 | ---
0591 | 
0592 | # The danger of the screenshot
0593 | 
0594 | A single Rule 30 image is seductive.
0595 | 
0596 | But a screenshot is weak evidence.
0597 | 
0598 | I chose:
0599 | 
0600 | ```text
0601 | the rule
0602 | the initial condition
0603 | the world size
0604 | the crop
0605 | the number of generations
0606 | the rendering
0607 | ```
0608 | 
0609 | I could show only the most dramatic part.
0610 | 
0611 | That is exactly the same problem we encountered with Lenia.
0612 | 
0613 | A spectacular example is useful for finding a phenomenon.
0614 | 
0615 | It tells us much less about how general that phenomenon is.
0616 | 
0617 | Eventually we will need to ask:
0618 | 
0619 | ```text
0620 | How often does this happen?
0621 | 
0622 | Across which rules?
0623 | 
0624 | Across which initial conditions?
0625 | 
0626 | How sensitive is it?
0627 | 
0628 | How persistent is it?
0629 | 
0630 | Can we detect it automatically?
0631 | ```
0632 | 
0633 | That is where enumeration and measurement become more important than screenshots.
0634 | 
0635 | ---
0636 | 
0637 | # One system, several observables
0638 | 
0639 | There is another useful lesson here.
0640 | 
0641 | We can look at Rule 30 as:
0642 | 
0643 | ```text
0644 | a whole spatial state at one time
0645 | ```
0646 | 
0647 | or:
0648 | 
0649 | ```text
0650 | a complete spacetime diagram
0651 | ```
0652 | 
0653 | or:
0654 | 
0655 | ```text
0656 | one cell observed across many times
0657 | ```
0658 | 
0659 | or:
0660 | 
0661 | ```text
0662 | a difference field between two runs
0663 | ```
0664 | 
0665 | or:
0666 | 
0667 | ```text
0668 | a trajectory through global state space
0669 | ```
0670 | 
0671 | These are different observables of the same underlying system.
0672 | 
0673 | That matters because what we notice depends strongly on what we measure.
0674 | 
0675 | A system may look simple under one observable and complicated under another.
0676 | 
0677 | This will become important later when we study:
0678 | 
0679 | ```text
0680 | density
0681 | activity
0682 | movement
0683 | causality
0684 | lineage
0685 | repair
0686 | ```
0687 | 
0688 | The system does not come with one privileged measurement.
0689 | 
0690 | We have to choose observables that match the question.
0691 | 
0692 | ---
0693 | 
0694 | # A tiny rule can create a large causal footprint
0695 | 
0696 | There is something almost insulting about how small Rule 30 is.
0697 | 
0698 | Its entire local behavior fits in eight lines:
0699 | 
0700 | ```python
0701 | rule = {
0702 |     (1, 1, 1): 0,
0703 |     (1, 1, 0): 0,
0704 |     (1, 0, 1): 0,
0705 |     (1, 0, 0): 1,
0706 |     (0, 1, 1): 1,
0707 |     (0, 1, 0): 1,
0708 |     (0, 0, 1): 1,
0709 |     (0, 0, 0): 0,
0710 | }
0711 | ```
0712 | 
0713 | There is no hidden controller below it.
0714 | 
0715 | Yet one changed bit can influence a growing region of future states.
0716 | 
0717 | That gives us the first major result of the book:
0718 | 
0719 | > **A globally nontrivial trajectory does not require a globally complicated controller.**
0720 | 
0721 | And now we can add something stronger:
0722 | 
0723 | > **A local perturbation can acquire a large future footprint through repeated interaction.**
0724 | 
0725 | That is more than a pretty pattern.
0726 | 
0727 | It is the beginning of causal structure.
0728 | 
0729 | ---
0730 | 
0731 | # But we still do not have a thing
0732 | 
0733 | Rule 30 gives us:
0734 | 
0735 | ```text
0736 | structure
0737 | propagation
0738 | divergence
0739 | history
0740 | ```
0741 | 
0742 | But does it give us an entity?
0743 | 
0744 | Something we can point to and say:
0745 | 
0746 | > that thing persisted.
0747 | 
0748 | Not obviously.
0749 | 
0750 | The pattern expands.
0751 | 
0752 | Regions change.
0753 | 
0754 | Differences propagate.
0755 | 
0756 | But identifying one localized organization through time is difficult.
0757 | 
0758 | So the next chapter changes the question.
0759 | 
0760 | We need a system where a pattern can appear here:
0761 | 
0762 | ```text
0763 | .##.
0764 | ##..
0765 | ....
0766 | ```
0767 | 
0768 | and later appear somewhere else while remaining recognizably the same organization.
0769 | 
0770 | That takes us to Conway's Game of Life.
0771 | 
0772 | And to a harder question:
0773 | 
0774 | > **When does a pattern become a thing?**
0775 | 
0776 | Next: **When Does a Pattern Become a Thing?**
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "04: When Does a Pattern Become a Thing?"
0003 | date = "2026-08-11T01:26:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "Use Conway's Game of Life to ask when a recurring localized pattern becomes useful to treat as an entity."
0006 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Cellular Automata", "Conway's Game of Life", "Glider", "Emergence", "Pattern Identity"]
0009 | +++
0010 | 
0011 | Rule 30 gave us structure.
0012 | 
0013 | It gave us propagation.
0014 | 
0015 | It gave us sensitivity to perturbation.
0016 | 
0017 | But it did not obviously give us a **thing**.
0018 | 
0019 | The pattern expanded.  
0020 | Regions changed.  
0021 | Differences spread.
0022 | 
0023 | Interesting global behavior appeared.
0024 | 
0025 | But if I pointed at one region and asked:
0026 | 
0027 | > Is that the same object ten generations later?
0028 | 
0029 | the answer was not obvious.
0030 | 
0031 | So let's change systems.
0032 | 
0033 | Not because Conway's Game of Life is more complicated.  
0034 | It isn't.
0035 | 
0036 | But because it gives us something Rule 30 does not give us so cleanly:
0037 | 
0038 | > **a localized pattern that appears to persist while moving through space**
0039 | 
0040 | That creates a harder question.
0041 | 
0042 | Not:
0043 | 
0044 | > Is it alive?
0045 | 
0046 | Much earlier than that:
0047 | 
0048 | > **When does it become useful to treat a pattern as a continuing thing?**
0049 | 
0050 | ---
0051 | 
0052 | ## Start With Five Cells
0053 | 
0054 | Consider this pattern:
0055 | 
0056 | ```text
0057 | .#.
0058 | ..#
0059 | ###
0060 | ```
0061 | 
0062 | Five active cells.  
0063 | Everything else is empty.
0064 | 
0065 | Nothing in those five cells says:
0066 | 
0067 | ```text
0068 | move diagonally
0069 | ```
0070 | 
0071 | There is no velocity.  
0072 | No direction variable.  
0073 | No object controller.  
0074 | No instruction such as:
0075 | 
0076 | ```python
0077 | glider.x += 1
0078 | glider.y += 1
0079 | ```
0080 | 
0081 | And yet if we run Conway's Game of Life, something remarkable happens.
0082 | 
0083 | ![A Game of Life glider moving across a fixed lattice](/images/books/digital-life/ch04-glider.gif)
0084 | 
0085 | A recognizable organization appears to travel diagonally through the grid.
0086 | 
0087 | We normally say:
0088 | 
0089 | > the glider moved.
0090 | 
0091 | But before we accept that sentence, we should ask what actually moved.
0092 | 
0093 | ---
0094 | 
0095 | ## The Cells Did Not Move
0096 | 
0097 | Game of Life cells occupy fixed coordinates.
0098 | 
0099 | A cell does not travel across the lattice.
0100 | 
0101 | Instead, cells become active and inactive according to their neighborhoods.
0102 | 
0103 | So the underlying process is closer to:
0104 | 
0105 | ```text
0106 | activity in one region
0107 |         ↓
0108 | changes nearby neighborhoods
0109 |         ↓
0110 | different cells become active
0111 |         ↓
0112 | earlier cells become inactive
0113 |         ↓
0114 | a similar organization appears nearby
0115 | ```
0116 | 
0117 | ```mermaid
0118 | flowchart LR
0119 |     A[Active cells<br/>in region R] --> B[Change nearby<br/>neighborhoods]
0120 |     B --> C[Different cells<br/>become active]
0121 |     C --> D[Earlier cells<br/>become inactive]
0122 |     D --> E[Similar organization<br/>appears shifted]
0123 | ```
0124 | 
0125 | No material object crosses the grid.  
0126 | The **organization** does.
0127 | 
0128 | This is the same conceptual problem we encountered with Lenia.  
0129 | But Game of Life gives us a much cleaner laboratory.
0130 | 
0131 | ---
0132 | 
0133 | ## The Game of Life Rule
0134 | 
0135 | Game of Life uses a two-dimensional binary lattice.
0136 | 
0137 | Every cell examines its eight immediate neighbors.
0138 | 
0139 | An active cell survives if it has:
0140 | 
0141 | ```text
0142 | 2 or 3
0143 | ```
0144 | 
0145 | active neighbors.
0146 | 
0147 | An inactive cell becomes active if it has:
0148 | 
0149 | ```text
0150 | exactly 3
0151 | ```
0152 | 
0153 | active neighbors.
0154 | 
0155 | Usually written:
0156 | 
0157 | ```text
0158 | B3/S23
0159 | ```
0160 | 
0161 | That is the entire rule.
0162 | 
0163 | There is no special rule for:
0164 | 
0165 | ```text
0166 | glider
0167 | block
0168 | blinker
0169 | spaceship
0170 | ```
0171 | 
0172 | There is only:
0173 | 
0174 | ```text
0175 | local binary state
0176 | +
0177 | eight-cell neighborhood
0178 | +
0179 | B3/S23
0180 | +
0181 | synchronous update
0182 | ```
0183 | 
0184 | The larger structures are descriptions we introduce after observing what the local dynamics produce.
0185 | 
0186 | ---
0187 | 
0188 | ## Build the Rule
0189 | 
0190 | A clear implementation is small:
0191 | 
0192 | ```python
0193 | import numpy as np
0194 | 
0195 | 
0196 | def life_step(state):
0197 |     neighbors = (
0198 |         np.roll(np.roll(state,  1, axis=0),  1, axis=1)
0199 |         + np.roll(state,  1, axis=0)
0200 |         + np.roll(np.roll(state,  1, axis=0), -1, axis=1)
0201 |         + np.roll(state,  1, axis=1)
0202 |         + np.roll(state, -1, axis=1)
0203 |         + np.roll(np.roll(state, -1, axis=0),  1, axis=1)
0204 |         + np.roll(state, -1, axis=0)
0205 |         + np.roll(np.roll(state, -1, axis=0), -1, axis=1)
0206 |     )
0207 | 
0208 |     born = (state == 0) & (neighbors == 3)
0209 |     survive = (state == 1) & ((neighbors == 2) | (neighbors == 3))
0210 | 
0211 |     return (born | survive).astype(np.uint8)
0212 | ```
0213 | 
0214 | Again:
0215 | 
0216 | ```text
0217 | local state
0218 | +
0219 | local interaction
0220 | +
0221 | same rule everywhere
0222 | ```
0223 | 
0224 | No global object model.
0225 | 
0226 | ---
0227 | 
0228 | ## Put a Glider Into the World
0229 | 
0230 | ```python
0231 | state = np.zeros((20, 20), dtype=np.uint8)
0232 | 
0233 | glider = np.array([
0234 |     [0, 1, 0],
0235 |     [0, 0, 1],
0236 |     [1, 1, 1],
0237 | ], dtype=np.uint8)
0238 | 
0239 | state[2:5, 2:5] = glider
0240 | ```
0241 | 
0242 | Now update four times:
0243 | 
0244 | ```python
0245 | for _ in range(4):
0246 |     state = life_step(state)
0247 | ```
0248 | 
0249 | After four generations, the same local configuration returns one cell diagonally away.
0250 | 
0251 | So we can measure:
0252 | 
0253 | ```text
0254 | period = 4 generations
0255 | displacement = (+1, +1)
0256 | ```
0257 | 
0258 | That is already stronger than:
0259 | 
0260 | > it looks like it moved.
0261 | 
0262 | We have a repeatable relationship.
0263 | 
0264 | ---
0265 | 
0266 | ## What Persisted?
0267 | 
0268 | Suppose we label the five active cells at the start:
0269 | 
0270 | ```text
0271 | A
0272 | B
0273 | C
0274 | D
0275 | E
0276 | ```
0277 | 
0278 | Four generations later, the original active coordinates are mostly no longer active.
0279 | 
0280 | The pattern is made from different cells.  
0281 | Its coordinates changed.  
0282 | Its intermediate shape changed.
0283 | 
0284 | Yet we still naturally say:
0285 | 
0286 | > the glider is over there now.
0287 | 
0288 | So what persisted?
0289 | 
0290 | Not:
0291 | 
0292 | ```text
0293 | the same cells
0294 | ```
0295 | 
0296 | Not:
0297 | 
0298 | ```text
0299 | the same coordinates
0300 | ```
0301 | 
0302 | Not even:
0303 | 
0304 | ```text
0305 | the same exact shape at every generation
0306 | ```
0307 | 
0308 | What persisted was something more like:
0309 | 
0310 | ```text
0311 | a recurring sequence of local configurations
0312 | +
0313 | a stable transformation through time
0314 | +
0315 | a fixed displacement
0316 | ```
0317 | 
0318 | That is already a much richer notion of identity than material continuity.
0319 | 
0320 | ---
0321 | 
0322 | ## Material Identity and Organizational Identity
0323 | 
0324 | We can distinguish two rough notions of sameness.
0325 | 
0326 | ### Material identity
0327 | 
0328 | ```text
0329 | same components
0330 | =
0331 | same thing
0332 | ```
0333 | 
0334 | That works well for some physical objects.  
0335 | But it is a poor description of a glider.
0336 | 
0337 | ### Organizational identity
0338 | 
0339 | ```text
0340 | same organization
0341 | through an allowed transformation
0342 | =
0343 | usefully treated as the same thing
0344 | ```
0345 | 
0346 | The glider strongly invites this second description.
0347 | 
0348 | But there is an important qualification.  
0349 | We have not proved:
0350 | 
0351 | > every persistent pattern is an entity.
0352 | 
0353 | We have shown something narrower:
0354 | 
0355 | > **Material continuity is not necessary for a useful operational notion of identity in this system.**
0356 | 
0357 | That is enough.
0358 | 
0359 | ```mermaid
0360 | flowchart TD
0361 |     A[Identity Criteria] --> B[Material Identity]
0362 |     A --> C[Organizational Identity]
0363 |     B --> B1["Same cells<br/>(fails for glider)"]
0364 |     C --> C1["Same configuration<br/>+ transformation"]
0365 |     C1 --> C2["Recurrence after period<br/>+ translation"]
0366 | ```
0367 | 
0368 | ---
0369 | 
0370 | ## Measure the Motion
0371 | 
0372 | We can make this less philosophical.
0373 | 
0374 | Take the active coordinates:
0375 | 
0376 | ```python
0377 | positions = np.argwhere(state == 1)
0378 | ```
0379 | 
0380 | and compute their centroid:
0381 | 
0382 | ```python
0383 | centroid = positions.mean(axis=0)
0384 | ```
0385 | 
0386 | Track that through time.
0387 | 
0388 | ![The measured centroid trajectory of a glider](/images/books/digital-life/ch04-glider-centroid.png)
0389 | 
0390 | Now:
0391 | 
0392 | > the glider moved
0393 | 
0394 | can become:
0395 | 
0396 | > the centroid of this localized pattern changes systematically through time.
0397 | 
0398 | That gives us:
0399 | 
0400 | ```text
0401 | position
0402 | displacement
0403 | velocity
0404 | trajectory
0405 | ```
0406 | 
0407 | as observables.
0408 | 
0409 | The noun:
0410 | 
0411 | ```text
0412 | glider
0413 | ```
0414 | 
0415 | starts becoming experimentally useful because several measurable quantities remain coherent through its transformations.
0416 | 
0417 | ---
0418 | 
0419 | ## Localization Matters
0420 | 
0421 | Why is the glider easier to treat as a thing than Rule 30's expanding history?
0422 | 
0423 | One major reason is:
0424 | 
0425 | > **localization**
0426 | 
0427 | Most of the world is not part of the glider.  
0428 | Activity is concentrated in a bounded region.
0429 | 
0430 | We can measure:
0431 | 
0432 | ```python
0433 | positions = np.argwhere(state == 1)
0434 | 
0435 | minimum = positions.min(axis=0)
0436 | maximum = positions.max(axis=0)
0437 | ```
0438 | 
0439 | That gives us a bounding box.
0440 | 
0441 | We can define properties such as:
0442 | 
0443 | ```text
0444 | area
0445 | active-cell count
0446 | centroid
0447 | velocity
0448 | shape
0449 | orientation
0450 | period
0451 | ```
0452 | 
0453 | Now we have a candidate operational boundary.
0454 | 
0455 | But we should already mark that word:
0456 | 
0457 | > candidate.
0458 | 
0459 | Later we will encounter systems where connected geometry may not be the correct boundary of the continuing organization.
0460 | 
0461 | For now, localization is a useful first approximation.
0462 | 
0463 | ---
0464 | 
0465 | ## A Block Persists Differently
0466 | 
0467 | Consider:
0468 | 
0469 | ```text
0470 | ##
0471 | ##
0472 | ```
0473 | 
0474 | This is a block.
0475 | 
0476 | Under Game of Life it remains unchanged.
0477 | 
0478 | ![Fixed, periodic and translating persistence](/images/books/digital-life/ch04-persistence-types.png)
0479 | 
0480 | It is:
0481 | 
0482 | ```text
0483 | localized
0484 | persistent
0485 | stationary
0486 | ```
0487 | 
0488 | The glider is:
0489 | 
0490 | ```text
0491 | localized
0492 | persistent
0493 | translating
0494 | periodically transforming internally
0495 | ```
0496 | 
0497 | So:
0498 | 
0499 | ```text
0500 | persistence
0501 | ```
0502 | 
0503 | and:
0504 | 
0505 | ```text
0506 | movement
0507 | ```
0508 | 
0509 | are already separate properties.
0510 | 
0511 | ---
0512 | 
0513 | ## A Blinker Persists by Changing
0514 | 
0515 | Now consider:
0516 | 
0517 | ```text
0518 | ###
0519 | ```
0520 | 
0521 | One generation later:
0522 | 
0523 | ```text
0524 | #
0525 | #
0526 | #
0527 | ```
0528 | 
0529 | Then back again.
0530 | 
0531 | This is a blinker.
0532 | 
0533 | Its exact state does not persist.  
0534 | Its behavior does.
0535 | 
0536 | So persistence itself has several forms.
0537 | 
0538 | ---
0539 | 
0540 | ## Three Forms of Persistence
0541 | 
0542 | ### Fixed persistence
0543 | 
0544 | ```text
0545 | state(t + 1) = state(t)
0546 | ```
0547 | 
0548 | Example: block
0549 | 
0550 | ### Periodic persistence
0551 | 
0552 | ```text
0553 | state(t + p) = state(t)
0554 | ```
0555 | 
0556 | for some period `p`.
0557 | 
0558 | Example: blinker (p=2)
0559 | 
0560 | ### Translating persistence
0561 | 
0562 | For some period `p` and spatial translation Δ:
0563 | 
0564 | ```text
0565 | state(t + p) = translate(state(t), Δ)
0566 | ```
0567 | 
0568 | Example: glider (p=4, Δ=(+1,+1))
0569 | 
0570 | ```mermaid
0571 | graph TD
0572 |     Persistence[Persistence Types] --> Fixed[Fixed<br/>state unchanged]
0573 |     Persistence --> Periodic[Periodic<br/>returns after p steps]
0574 |     Persistence --> Translating[Translating<br/>returns shifted after p steps]
0575 |     Fixed --> Block["Example: Block"]
0576 |     Periodic --> Blinker["Example: Blinker (p=2)"]
0577 |     Translating --> Glider["Example: Glider (p=4, Δ=+1,+1)"]
0578 | ```
0579 | 
0580 | That is much better than one vague word.  
0581 | We can now specify what kind of persistence we mean.
0582 | 
0583 | ---
0584 | 
0585 | ## Identity Depends on Which Changes We Ignore
0586 | 
0587 | Suppose the glider at `t = 0` occupies one location.  
0588 | At `t = 4`, it occupies the same local configuration shifted by (+1,+1).
0589 | 
0590 | A raw whole-grid comparison gives:
0591 | 
0592 | ```python
0593 | np.array_equal(state_t0, state_t4)
0594 | ```
0595 | 
0596 | which returns `False`.
0597 | 
0598 | But if we compensate for translation:
0599 | 
0600 | ```python
0601 | shifted = np.roll(
0602 |     np.roll(state_t0, 1, axis=0),
0603 |     1,
0604 |     axis=1,
0605 | )
0606 | ```
0607 | 
0608 | the patterns match.
0609 | 
0610 | So identity depends partly on what transformations we decide are irrelevant.
0611 | 
0612 | Do we care about:
0613 | 
0614 | ```text
0615 | position?
0616 | orientation?
0617 | scale?
0618 | phase?
0619 | exact constituent cells?
0620 | ```
0621 | 
0622 | Different choices imply different identity criteria.
0623 | 
0624 | This is not merely philosophy.  
0625 | It determines the algorithm we use to detect persistent entities.
0626 | 
0627 | ---
0628 | 
0629 | ## Identity Requires Invariants
0630 | 
0631 | One useful way to think about identity is:
0632 | 
0633 | > What survives the transformations we allow?
0634 | 
0635 | For the glider:
0636 | 
0637 | ```text
0638 | position          changes
0639 | active cells      change
0640 | intermediate form changes
0641 | ```
0642 | 
0643 | But after four generations:
0644 | 
0645 | ```text
0646 | local configuration recurs
0647 | +
0648 | displacement is predictable
0649 | ```
0650 | 
0651 | That relationship is invariant.
0652 | 
0653 | So an operational definition might be:
0654 | 
0655 | > **A glider is a localized dynamical pattern whose local state recurs after a fixed period up to spatial translation.**
0656 | 
0657 | That is testable.
0658 | 
0659 | ---
0660 | 
0661 | ## But This Is Only Our First Definition of a Thing
0662 | 
0663 | This is important.
0664 | 
0665 | Right now we are using:
0666 | 
0667 | ```text
0668 | localized connected geometry
0669 | +
0670 | recurrence
0671 | +
0672 | coherent trajectory
0673 | ```
0674 | 
0675 | as evidence that treating something as an entity is useful.
0676 | 
0677 | That works beautifully for a glider.
0678 | 
0679 | It does not follow that this is the universal definition of a digital individual.
0680 | 
0681 | Later we may find:
0682 | 
0683 | ```text
0684 | disconnected components
0685 | ```
0686 | 
0687 | that participate in:
0688 | 
0689 | ```text
0690 | one continuing causal process
0691 | ```
0692 | 
0693 | or:
0694 | 
0695 | ```text
0696 | identical geometries
0697 | ```
0698 | 
0699 | that belong to:
0700 | 
0701 | ```text
0702 | completely different causal histories
0703 | ```
0704 | 
0705 | If that happens, geometry will stop being enough.
0706 | 
0707 | So the glider gives us a **working definition**, not a final ontology.
0708 | 
0709 | That distinction is going to become important.
0710 | 
0711 | ---
0712 | 
0713 | ## The Danger of Naming Things
0714 | 
0715 | Game of Life contains named patterns such as:
0716 | 
0717 | ```text
0718 | block
0719 | blinker
0720 | beacon
0721 | glider
0722 | lightweight spaceship
0723 | pulsar
0724 | gun
0725 | ```
0726 | 
0727 | Names are useful.  
0728 | Instead of listing coordinates, we can say:
0729 | 
0730 | > glider
0731 | 
0732 | and reason at a higher level.
0733 | 
0734 | But naming has a side effect.  
0735 | Once something has a noun, the mind starts treating it as an object automatically.
0736 | 
0737 | The noun does not prove the ontology.
0738 | 
0739 | Calling a pattern:
0740 | 
0741 | ```text
0742 | spaceship
0743 | ```
0744 | 
0745 | does not make it an engineered vehicle.  
0746 | Calling something:
0747 | 
0748 | ```text
0749 | gun
0750 | ```
0751 | 
0752 | does not make it analogous to a physical gun in every meaningful respect.
0753 | 
0754 | We will use names.  
0755 | But we should remember:
0756 | 
0757 | > **Naming compresses description. It does not establish mechanism.**
0758 | 
0759 | ---
0760 | 
0761 | ## Can Two Apparent Things Interact?
0762 | 
0763 | Now put two localized patterns in the same world.
0764 | 
0765 | Depending on their geometry and timing, they may:
0766 | 
0767 | ```text
0768 | pass
0769 | collide
0770 | destroy one another
0771 | produce debris
0772 | produce another recognizable pattern
0773 | ```
0774 | 
0775 | ![Two localized Game of Life patterns interacting](/images/books/digital-life/ch04-collision.gif)
0776 | 
0777 | Now the entity-level description becomes even more useful.
0778 | 
0779 | We can ask:
0780 | 
0781 | ```text
0782 | Did pattern A alter pattern B?
0783 | 
0784 | Did either persist?
0785 | 
0786 | Was a new localized pattern produced?
0787 | 
0788 | Was the collision outcome reproducible?
0789 | 
0790 | Would the same outcome occur if one input were removed?
0791 | ```
0792 | 
0793 | That final question is especially important.  
0794 | It begins moving us from:
0795 | 
0796 | ```text
0797 | pattern description
0798 | ```
0799 | 
0800 | toward:
0801 | 
0802 | ```text
0803 | causal analysis
0804 | ```
0805 | 
0806 | We will need that later.
0807 | 
0808 | ---
0809 | 
0810 | ## Does a Glider Carry Information?
0811 | 
0812 | A glider begins in one region.  
0813 | Later, a correlated structured state exists somewhere else.
0814 | 
0815 | So something about the earlier configuration constrains a later distant configuration.
0816 | 
0817 | Operationally:
0818 | 
0819 | ```text
0820 | localized state
0821 |       ↓
0822 | repeated local transformations
0823 |       ↓
0824 | correlated localized state elsewhere
0825 | ```
0826 | 
0827 | ```mermaid
0828 | flowchart LR
0829 |     A[Localized pattern<br/>at t=0, pos x] --> B[Repeated local<br/>transformations]
0830 |     B --> C[Correlated localized<br/>pattern at t=4, pos x+Δ]
0831 | ```
0832 | 
0833 | This is why gliders can be used as signals in computational constructions inside Game of Life.
0834 | 
0835 | But we should again avoid saying too much.
0836 | 
0837 | We do not need:
0838 | 
0839 | > the glider understands information.
0840 | 
0841 | We only need:
0842 | 
0843 | > **a structured local state can propagate through space while preserving relationships that another mechanism can respond to.**
0844 | 
0845 | That is enough to make it useful as a signal.
0846 | 
0847 | ---
0848 | 
0849 | ## So Is the Glider a Thing?
0850 | 
0851 | Biologically?  
0852 | We have shown nothing close to enough.
0853 | 
0854 | Philosophically?  
0855 | We can argue indefinitely.
0856 | 
0857 | Experimentally?  
0858 | We can be precise.
0859 | 
0860 | The glider is:
0861 | 
0862 | ```text
0863 | localized
0864 | dynamically persistent
0865 | periodic
0866 | translating
0867 | reproducible from the same initial condition
0868 | describable independently of the exact cells currently active
0869 | ```
0870 | 
0871 | That makes it useful to treat the glider as:
0872 | 
0873 | > **a pattern-level entity under a defined persistence criterion**
0874 | 
0875 | Notice the wording.
0876 | 
0877 | Not:
0878 | 
0879 | > the glider is alive.
0880 | 
0881 | Not:
0882 | 
0883 | > the glider is objectively an organism.
0884 | 
0885 | Not even:
0886 | 
0887 | > connected glider geometry is the universal meaning of individuality.
0888 | 
0889 | Only:
0890 | 
0891 | > treating it as a continuing entity is useful because measurable relationships remain coherent across its transformations.
0892 | 
0893 | That is the bounded claim.
0894 | 
0895 | ---
0896 | 
0897 | ## Now We Have Something We Can Hurt
0898 | 
0899 | Rule 30 gave us spreading structure.  
0900 | The glider gives us a localized persistent pattern.
0901 | 
0902 | That means we can finally perform a stronger experiment.
0903 | 
0904 | We can:
0905 | 
0906 | ```text
0907 | remove one cell
0908 | remove several cells
0909 | alter its phase
0910 | collide it with another pattern
0911 | ```
0912 | 
0913 | and ask:
0914 | 
0915 | ```text
0916 | Does the organization continue?
0917 | 
0918 | Does it remain recognizable?
0919 | 
0920 | Does it return toward its previous form?
0921 | 
0922 | Does it become another persistent structure?
0923 | 
0924 | Does it disappear?
0925 | ```
0926 | 
0927 | That leads to three ideas that are easy to confuse:
0928 | 
0929 | ```text
0930 | persistence
0931 | ≠
0932 | robustness
0933 | ≠
0934 | regeneration
0935 | ```
0936 | 
0937 | A pattern surviving forever in an undisturbed world tells us much less than a pattern surviving disturbance.
0938 | 
0939 | So next, we stop admiring it.  
0940 | We damage it.
0941 | 
0942 | Next: **Kill It.**
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "05: Kill It"
0003 | date = "2026-08-11T01:34:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "Damage persistent digital patterns and separate survival, robustness and regeneration into experimentally distinct claims."
0006 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Cellular Automata", "Robustness", "Regeneration", "Perturbation", "Game of Life"]
0009 | +++
0010 | 
0011 | We have been too kind to our systems.
0012 | 
0013 | So far we have:
0014 | 
0015 | - initialized them carefully,
0016 | - placed them in clean environments,
0017 | - watched them evolve,
0018 | - selected examples that behave interestingly,
0019 | - and mostly left them alone.
0020 | 
0021 | That is a dangerous way to understand a mechanism.
0022 | 
0023 | A structure that persists under exactly the conditions that produce it tells us something.
0024 | 
0025 | But not enough.
0026 | 
0027 | If we want to know what is actually maintaining that structure, we need to interfere.
0028 | 
0029 | So let's interfere.
0030 | 
0031 | ---
0032 | 
0033 | ## Start With the Glider
0034 | 
0035 | Our glider:
0036 | 
0037 | ```text
0038 | .#.
0039 | ..#
0040 | ###
0041 | ```
0042 | 
0043 | is a dynamically persistent localized pattern.
0044 | 
0045 | Under undisturbed Game of Life dynamics, it repeats its local configuration every four generations while translating one cell diagonally.
0046 | 
0047 | That gave us a useful operational definition of persistence.
0048 | 
0049 | Now remove one cell.
0050 | 
0051 | For example:
0052 | 
0053 | ```text
0054 | .#.
0055 | ...
0056 | ###
0057 | ```
0058 | 
0059 | One bit changed.  
0060 | Same rule.  
0061 | Same world.  
0062 | Same boundary condition.  
0063 | Same update semantics.
0064 | 
0065 | Only the state has been perturbed.
0066 | 
0067 | Run it.
0068 | 
0069 | ![Survival as damage severity increases](/images/books/digital-life/ch05-damage-survival-curve.png)
0070 | 
0071 | Several outcomes are possible.
0072 | 
0073 | The structure may disappear.  
0074 | It may become another Life pattern.  
0075 | Some activity may survive.  
0076 | Debris may spread.
0077 | 
0078 | But one possibility is especially important:
0079 | 
0080 | > **the original glider may fail to reconstruct itself**
0081 | 
0082 | That immediately separates two claims:
0083 | 
0084 | ```text
0085 | persists when undisturbed
0086 | ```
0087 | 
0088 | from:
0089 | 
0090 | ```text
0091 | returns after disturbance
0092 | ```
0093 | 
0094 | Those are not the same property.
0095 | 
0096 | ---
0097 | 
0098 | ## Three Different Claims
0099 | 
0100 | We need separate words for separate phenomena.
0101 | 
0102 | ### Persistence
0103 | 
0104 | A structure continues under its ordinary dynamics.
0105 | 
0106 | ```text
0107 | undisturbed state
0108 |       ↓
0109 | ordinary dynamics
0110 |       ↓
0111 | organization continues
0112 | ```
0113 | 
0114 | ### Robustness
0115 | 
0116 | A perturbation occurs, but some defined property continues to hold.
0117 | 
0118 | ```text
0119 | organization
0120 |       ↓
0121 | perturbation
0122 |       ↓
0123 | property still holds
0124 | ```
0125 | 
0126 | ### Regeneration
0127 | 
0128 | A perturbation substantially changes the structure, and subsequent dynamics return it toward a defined previous organization.
0129 | 
0130 | ```text
0131 | organization
0132 |       ↓
0133 | damage
0134 |       ↓
0135 | organization disrupted
0136 |       ↓
0137 | continued dynamics
0138 |       ↓
0139 | defined organization returns
0140 | ```
0141 | 
0142 | ```mermaid
0143 | flowchart TD
0144 |     A[Original Organization] --> B[Perturbation]
0145 |     B --> C[Outcome?]
0146 |     C --> D[Property still holds<br/><i>Robustness</i>]
0147 |     C --> E[Organization disrupted]
0148 |     E --> F[Dynamics continue]
0149 |     F --> G[Previous organization returns<br/><i>Regeneration</i>]
0150 |     C --> H[Organization lost<br/><i>No recovery</i>]
0151 | ```
0152 | 
0153 | So:
0154 | 
0155 | ```text
0156 | persistence
0157 | ≠
0158 | robustness
0159 | ≠
0160 | regeneration
0161 | ```
0162 | 
0163 | A system can possess one without possessing the others.  
0164 | This distinction will matter repeatedly.
0165 | 
0166 | ---
0167 | 
0168 | ## A Block Persists Perfectly
0169 | 
0170 | Take the Game of Life block:
0171 | 
0172 | ```text
0173 | ##
0174 | ##
0175 | ```
0176 | 
0177 | Under ordinary Life evolution:
0178 | 
0179 | ```text
0180 | t = 0
0181 | 
0182 | ##
0183 | ##
0184 | 
0185 | t = 1
0186 | 
0187 | ##
0188 | ##
0189 | 
0190 | t = 2
0191 | 
0192 | ##
0193 | ##
0194 | ```
0195 | 
0196 | Perfect persistence.
0197 | 
0198 | Now delete one cell:
0199 | 
0200 | ```text
0201 | #.
0202 | ##
0203 | ```
0204 | 
0205 | Run the dynamics.
0206 | 
0207 | The pattern collapses.
0208 | 
0209 | So the block has excellent:
0210 | 
0211 | ```text
0212 | undisturbed persistence
0213 | ```
0214 | 
0215 | and poor tolerance to this particular intervention.
0216 | 
0217 | The perturbation has exposed something that observation alone did not.
0218 | 
0219 | ---
0220 | 
0221 | ## The Perturbation Is the Experiment
0222 | 
0223 | Before this chapter, many of our experiments looked like:
0224 | 
0225 | ```text
0226 | initial state
0227 |       ↓
0228 | evolution
0229 |       ↓
0230 | observation
0231 | ```
0232 | 
0233 | Now the structure changes:
0234 | 
0235 | ```text
0236 | initial state
0237 |       ↓
0238 | ordinary behavior
0239 |       ↓
0240 | controlled intervention
0241 |       ↓
0242 | response
0243 |       ↓
0244 | measurement
0245 | ```
0246 | 
0247 | The perturbation is not unwanted noise around the experiment.
0248 | 
0249 | > **The perturbation is the experiment.**
0250 | 
0251 | We deliberately change something because the response can reveal which mechanisms matter.
0252 | 
0253 | This is the beginning of causal experimentation.
0254 | 
0255 | ---
0256 | 
0257 | ## Damage Must Be Defined
0258 | 
0259 | “Damage the pattern” sounds intuitive.
0260 | 
0261 | It is useless experimentally until we specify what we changed.
0262 | 
0263 | For a binary cellular automaton, damage could mean:
0264 | 
0265 | ```text
0266 | turn one active cell off
0267 | ```
0268 | 
0269 | or:
0270 | 
0271 | ```text
0272 | flip N randomly selected cells
0273 | ```
0274 | 
0275 | or:
0276 | 
0277 | ```text
0278 | erase everything inside a region
0279 | ```
0280 | 
0281 | or:
0282 | 
0283 | ```text
0284 | replace part of the pattern with random state
0285 | ```
0286 | 
0287 | These are different interventions.
0288 | 
0289 | A reproducible protocol might be:
0290 | 
0291 | ```text
0292 | pattern: glider
0293 | damage time: t = 20
0294 | damage operation: active → inactive
0295 | damage amount: one cell
0296 | damage positions: every active cell in turn
0297 | repetitions: all possible deletions
0298 | observation window: 50 generations
0299 | ```
0300 | 
0301 | Now another person can repeat the experiment.  
0302 | And now we can meaningfully compare systems.
0303 | 
0304 | ---
0305 | 
0306 | ## One Lucky Recovery Proves Very Little
0307 | 
0308 | Imagine a structure containing ten active cells.
0309 | 
0310 | Delete one particular cell.  
0311 | It returns to its previous pattern.
0312 | 
0313 | Interesting.
0314 | 
0315 | Now delete one of the other nine cells.  
0316 | It collapses.
0317 | 
0318 | Then the statement:
0319 | 
0320 | > the system regenerates after damage
0321 | 
0322 | would be far too broad.
0323 | 
0324 | A better experiment systematically tests perturbations.
0325 | 
0326 | For example:
0327 | 
0328 | ```python
0329 | for cell in active_cells:
0330 |     damaged = state.copy()
0331 |     damaged[cell] = 0
0332 | 
0333 |     result = run(damaged)
0334 | 
0335 |     measure_response(result)
0336 | ```
0337 | 
0338 | Now we can ask:
0339 | 
0340 | ```text
0341 | Which perturbations were tolerated?
0342 | 
0343 | Which positions were critical?
0344 | 
0345 | How much organization remained?
0346 | 
0347 | Did the original organization return?
0348 | 
0349 | How long did that take?
0350 | ```
0351 | 
0352 | Instead of one anecdote, we obtain a:
0353 | 
0354 | > **damage-response profile**
0355 | 
0356 | ---
0357 | 
0358 | ## Survival Is Not Recovery
0359 | 
0360 | Suppose we damage a structure and some activity remains.
0361 | 
0362 | That does not mean the structure regenerated.
0363 | 
0364 | Imagine:
0365 | 
0366 | ```text
0367 | before
0368 | 
0369 | .###.
0370 | ##.##
0371 | .###.
0372 | ```
0373 | 
0374 | After damage:
0375 | 
0376 | ```text
0377 | .#...
0378 | ##...
0379 | .....
0380 | ```
0381 | 
0382 | Twenty generations later:
0383 | 
0384 | ```text
0385 | ##...
0386 | ##...
0387 | .....
0388 | ```
0389 | 
0390 | Something survived.  
0391 | But the previous organization did not return.
0392 | 
0393 | So:
0394 | 
0395 | ```text
0396 | nonzero activity
0397 | ```
0398 | 
0399 | is not recovery.
0400 | 
0401 | Neither is:
0402 | 
0403 | ```text
0404 | localized activity
0405 | ```
0406 | 
0407 | To make a regeneration claim, we need a defined relationship between:
0408 | 
0409 | ```text
0410 | organization before perturbation
0411 | ```
0412 | 
0413 | and:
0414 | 
0415 | ```text
0416 | organization after continued evolution
0417 | ```
0418 | 
0419 | ---
0420 | 
0421 | ## Recovery Forces Us to Define Identity
0422 | 
0423 | This connects directly to the previous chapter.
0424 | 
0425 | Suppose our target pattern is `T` and the later pattern is `R`.
0426 | 
0427 | For a stationary discrete pattern, we might compare them directly:
0428 | 
0429 | ```python
0430 | np.array_equal(T, R)
0431 | ```
0432 | 
0433 | But that fails for a glider.  
0434 | A glider could return while shifted in space.
0435 | 
0436 | So perhaps recovery means:
0437 | 
0438 | ```text
0439 | same organization
0440 | up to translation
0441 | ```
0442 | 
0443 | For an oscillator:
0444 | 
0445 | ```text
0446 | same organization
0447 | up to phase
0448 | ```
0449 | 
0450 | For more complicated systems we may need invariance under:
0451 | 
0452 | ```text
0453 | translation
0454 | rotation
0455 | phase
0456 | scale
0457 | internal deformation
0458 | ```
0459 | 
0460 | The moment we ask:
0461 | 
0462 | > Did it regenerate?
0463 | 
0464 | we are forced to answer:
0465 | 
0466 | > **What counts as the same entity?**
0467 | 
0468 | The philosophical problem has become an engineering requirement.
0469 | 
0470 | ---
0471 | 
0472 | ## Exact Equality Is Usually the Wrong Metric
0473 | 
0474 | Suppose we compare two whole worlds using:
0475 | 
0476 | ```python
0477 | def similarity(a, b):
0478 |     return np.mean(a == b)
0479 | ```
0480 | 
0481 | There is an immediate problem.
0482 | 
0483 | If almost every cell is zero, two completely different tiny structures may still score close to 1.0 because the empty background dominates the metric.
0484 | 
0485 | So our measurement must focus on the structure we care about.
0486 | 
0487 | One simple choice is intersection-over-union.
0488 | 
0489 | For active-cell sets A and B:
0490 | 
0491 | $$
0492 | IoU(A,B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}
0493 | $$
0494 | 
0495 | Identical active regions produce 1.0.  
0496 | Disjoint regions produce 0.0.
0497 | 
0498 | In code:
0499 | 
0500 | ```python
0501 | def iou(a, b):
0502 |     intersection = np.logical_and(a, b).sum()
0503 |     union = np.logical_or(a, b).sum()
0504 | 
0505 |     if union == 0:
0506 |         return 1.0
0507 | 
0508 |     return intersection / union
0509 | ```
0510 | 
0511 | For moving structures, we would first align them under the transformations our identity criterion allows.
0512 | 
0513 | Still imperfect.  
0514 | But explicit.
0515 | 
0516 | ---
0517 | 
0518 | ## Metrics Create Claims
0519 | 
0520 | Suppose we define:
0521 | 
0522 | ```text
0523 | recovered =
0524 |     IoU >= 0.90
0525 |     within 50 generations
0526 |     after optimal translation alignment
0527 | ```
0528 | 
0529 | Now we can report:
0530 | 
0531 | > Under this perturbation protocol, the pattern returned to at least 0.90 IoU with its pre-damage morphology within 50 updates after translation alignment.
0532 | 
0533 | That is much uglier than:
0534 | 
0535 | > It healed itself.
0536 | 
0537 | Good.
0538 | 
0539 | The ugly statement tells us what was actually demonstrated.  
0540 | We can always summarize later.  
0541 | But the experiment should preserve the operational claim.
0542 | 
0543 | ---
0544 | 
0545 | ## Robustness Does Not Require Regeneration
0546 | 
0547 | A system may fail to restore its previous shape while preserving something else.
0548 | 
0549 | Imagine a future digital system whose behavior is:
0550 | 
0551 | ```text
0552 | move toward a signal source
0553 | ```
0554 | 
0555 | Damage changes its morphology.  
0556 | Its shape similarity falls dramatically.  
0557 | Yet it continues moving toward the signal.
0558 | 
0559 | Then:
0560 | 
0561 | ```text
0562 | morphology failed
0563 | ```
0564 | 
0565 | while:
0566 | 
0567 | ```text
0568 | capability survived
0569 | ```
0570 | 
0571 | So there are at least two questions:
0572 | 
0573 | ```text
0574 | Did the structure recover?
0575 | ```
0576 | 
0577 | and:
0578 | 
0579 | ```text
0580 | Did the capability survive or recover?
0581 | ```
0582 | 
0583 | These are different measurements.
0584 | 
0585 | And this is a broader lesson:
0586 | 
0587 | > **Robustness always needs an object: robust with respect to what?**
0588 | 
0589 | Shape?  
0590 | Movement?  
0591 | Computation?  
0592 | Replication?  
0593 | Memory?
0594 | 
0595 | A system is not simply “robust.”  
0596 | It is robust with respect to some property under some class of perturbations.
0597 | 
0598 | ---
0599 | 
0600 | ## Build a Damage Curve
0601 | 
0602 | One perturbation gives one data point.
0603 | 
0604 | Increase the intervention systematically.
0605 | 
0606 | For example:
0607 | 
0608 | ```text
0609 | 0% removed
0610 | 5% removed
0611 | 10% removed
0612 | 20% removed
0613 | 40% removed
0614 | 60% removed
0615 | ```
0616 | 
0617 | At each level:
0618 | 
0619 | 1. perturb the pattern,
0620 | 2. evolve it,
0621 | 3. measure survival,
0622 | 4. measure structural similarity,
0623 | 5. repeat across positions or random seeds.
0624 | 
0625 | Then plot:
0626 | 
0627 | ```text
0628 | damage severity
0629 |       ↓
0630 | response
0631 | ```
0632 | 
0633 | ![A Game of Life glider undergoing a controlled perturbation](/images/books/digital-life/ch05-glider-damage.gif)
0634 | 
0635 | Now we can ask whether degradation is:
0636 | 
0637 | ```text
0638 | gradual
0639 | abrupt
0640 | threshold-like
0641 | position-dependent
0642 | ```
0643 | 
0644 | That tells us much more than one impressive animation.
0645 | 
0646 | ---
0647 | 
0648 | ## Damage Location Matters
0649 | 
0650 | Suppose a structure contains one hundred active cells.
0651 | 
0652 | Removing ten cells from one region might do almost nothing.  
0653 | Removing ten elsewhere might destroy the pattern completely.
0654 | 
0655 | So:
0656 | 
0657 | ```text
0658 | amount of damage
0659 | ```
0660 | 
0661 | is not enough.
0662 | 
0663 | We also need:
0664 | 
0665 | ```text
0666 | location of damage
0667 | ```
0668 | 
0669 | This allows us to search for:
0670 | 
0671 | ```text
0672 | fragile regions
0673 | redundant regions
0674 | critical structures
0675 | distributed organization
0676 | ```
0677 | 
0678 | Eventually this becomes a question about where the system's causal organization actually lives.
0679 | 
0680 | Is function concentrated?  
0681 | Distributed?  
0682 | Redundant?  
0683 | Does there even exist a clean spatial location corresponding to the mechanism?
0684 | 
0685 | We should not assume the answer in advance.
0686 | 
0687 | ---
0688 | 
0689 | ## Repeated Perturbation Is a Stronger Test
0690 | 
0691 | Suppose a system survives one intervention.
0692 | 
0693 | Damage it again.  
0694 | Then again.
0695 | 
0696 | ```text
0697 | damage
0698 |   ↓
0699 | response
0700 |   ↓
0701 | damage
0702 |   ↓
0703 | response
0704 |   ↓
0705 | damage
0706 |   ↓
0707 | response
0708 | ```
0709 | 
0710 | A system might survive one perturbation by consuming redundancy that never returns.  
0711 | Another might repeatedly reconstruct the lost organization.
0712 | 
0713 | Those are different mechanisms.
0714 | 
0715 | So repeated intervention lets us distinguish:
0716 | 
0717 | ```text
0718 | one-time tolerance
0719 | ```
0720 | 
0721 | from:
0722 | 
0723 | ```text
0724 | sustained recovery capacity
0725 | ```
0726 | 
0727 | Again, the perturbation reveals structure that clean observation hides.
0728 | 
0729 | ---
0730 | 
0731 | ## Damage Does Not Have to Mean Deleting Cells
0732 | 
0733 | The deeper idea is not “injury.”  
0734 | It is intervention.
0735 | 
0736 | We could alter:
0737 | 
0738 | ```text
0739 | state
0740 | parameters
0741 | environment
0742 | resource access
0743 | boundary conditions
0744 | noise level
0745 | update timing
0746 | other interacting structures
0747 | ```
0748 | 
0749 | The common pattern is:
0750 | 
0751 | ```text
0752 | hold most things fixed
0753 |       ↓
0754 | change one defined condition
0755 |       ↓
0756 | measure the response
0757 | ```
0758 | 
0759 | This matters because a capability becomes much more informative when we know where it fails.
0760 | 
0761 | A system that works only under one carefully selected setup may still be interesting.  
0762 | But the boundary of the claim is narrow.  
0763 | Perturbation helps us find that boundary.
0764 | 
0765 | ---
0766 | 
0767 | ## The Glider Fails the Stronger Test
0768 | 
0769 | Return to the glider.
0770 | 
0771 | It is:
0772 | 
0773 | ```text
0774 | localized
0775 | periodic
0776 | translating
0777 | dynamically persistent
0778 | ```
0779 | 
0780 | But perturb the wrong cell and its characteristic trajectory disappears.
0781 | 
0782 | That does not make the glider less interesting.  
0783 | It makes our description more precise.
0784 | 
0785 | We can say:
0786 | 
0787 | > **The glider exhibits translating dynamic persistence under undisturbed Game of Life dynamics.**
0788 | 
0789 | We should not infer:
0790 | 
0791 | > The glider exhibits robust self-maintenance under damage.
0792 | 
0793 | Those are different achievements.  
0794 | And now we have an experiment that separates them.
0795 | 
0796 | ---
0797 | 
0798 | ## Could Local Dynamics Regenerate Structure?
0799 | 
0800 | Now the stronger question becomes interesting.
0801 | 
0802 | Can we build a system where:
0803 | 
0804 | ```text
0805 | organized state
0806 |       ↓
0807 | perturbation
0808 |       ↓
0809 | organization disrupted
0810 |       ↓
0811 | local dynamics continue
0812 |       ↓
0813 | organization returns
0814 | ```
0815 | 
0816 | without a central controller simply storing the desired image and repainting it?
0817 | 
0818 | That would be a more interesting mechanism.
0819 | 
0820 | If we eventually encounter or construct such a system, the protocol is already waiting for it:
0821 | 
0822 | ```text
0823 | How much perturbation?
0824 | 
0825 | Where?
0826 | 
0827 | How many trials?
0828 | 
0829 | How similar was the recovered organization?
0830 | 
0831 | How long did recovery take?
0832 | 
0833 | What baseline are we comparing against?
0834 | 
0835 | Does recovery generalize to perturbations not used to construct the system?
0836 | ```
0837 | 
0838 | The measurement rules come before the spectacular GIF.
0839 | 
0840 | ---
0841 | 
0842 | ## Intervention Is Becoming Part of Our Method
0843 | 
0844 | We started the book with:
0845 | 
0846 | ```text
0847 | state
0848 | +
0849 | local interaction
0850 | +
0851 | time
0852 | ```
0853 | 
0854 | Then we added observation.  
0855 | Now we have added intervention.
0856 | 
0857 | Our laboratory increasingly looks like:
0858 | 
0859 | ```mermaid
0860 | flowchart TD
0861 |     A[System] --> B[Observation]
0862 |     B --> C[Hypothesis]
0863 |     C --> D[Controlled Intervention]
0864 |     D --> E[Response]
0865 |     E --> F[Measurement]
0866 |     F --> G[Bounded Claim]
0867 |     G -.->|refine| C
0868 | ```
0869 | 
0870 | This is a major step.
0871 | 
0872 | We are no longer merely asking:
0873 | 
0874 | > What does the system do?
0875 | 
0876 | We can ask:
0877 | 
0878 | > **What makes the system able to do it?**
0879 | 
0880 | ---
0881 | 
0882 | ## Attack the Capability
0883 | 
0884 | This gives us a general rule for the rest of the book.
0885 | 
0886 | If a system appears to possess:
0887 | 
0888 | ```text
0889 | memory
0890 | persistence
0891 | regeneration
0892 | adaptation
0893 | inheritance
0894 | coordination
0895 | ```
0896 | 
0897 | do not only observe the condition in which the capability appears.  
0898 | Intervene on the mechanism that supposedly supports it.
0899 | 
0900 | For memory:
0901 | 
0902 | ```text
0903 | remove or corrupt candidate stored state
0904 | ```
0905 | 
0906 | For regeneration:
0907 | 
0908 | ```text
0909 | damage the organization
0910 | ```
0911 | 
0912 | For adaptation:
0913 | 
0914 | ```text
0915 | change the environment
0916 | ```
0917 | 
0918 | For inheritance:
0919 | 
0920 | ```text
0921 | compare successors with and without inherited information
0922 | ```
0923 | 
0924 | For coordination:
0925 | 
0926 | ```text
0927 | break communication or alter neighbors
0928 | ```
0929 | 
0930 | Then ask whether the capability survives.
0931 | 
0932 | That moves us from association toward mechanism.
0933 | 
0934 | ---
0935 | 
0936 | ## And Now Reproduction Enters — Carefully
0937 | 
0938 | Damage raises another possibility.
0939 | 
0940 | Instead of requiring one organization to persist indefinitely, a system might produce another organization resembling itself.
0941 | 
0942 | That would move persistence from:
0943 | 
0944 | ```text
0945 | one continuing instance
0946 | ```
0947 | 
0948 | to something like:
0949 | 
0950 | ```text
0951 | information or organization
0952 | continuing across instances
0953 | ```
0954 | 
0955 | Biology uses this strategy extensively.
0956 | 
0957 | But we should not therefore assume that digital life must.
0958 | 
0959 | A digital system might:
0960 | 
0961 | ```text
0962 | persist indefinitely
0963 | repair itself
0964 | grow continuously
0965 | fork
0966 | copy
0967 | checkpoint
0968 | restore
0969 | merge
0970 | ```
0971 | 
0972 | Reproduction is only one possible mechanism among several.
0973 | 
0974 | So the next chapter is not asking:
0975 | 
0976 | > What must life do next?
0977 | 
0978 | It is asking a narrower experimental question:
0979 | 
0980 | > **What changes when one persistent pattern can produce another?**
0981 | 
0982 | That question brings new traps.
0983 | 
0984 | A duplicate is not automatically offspring.  
0985 | Similarity is not automatically causal reproduction.  
0986 | Variation is not automatically inheritance.  
0987 | Mutation is not automatically evolution.
0988 | 
0989 | Before we can use any of those words, we need mechanisms and tests.
0990 | 
0991 | So next we ask:
0992 | 
0993 | > **Can It Make Another One?**
```
