0011 | 
0012 | Before building anything more complicated, we should steal everything we can.
0013 | 
0014 | Not code.
0015 | 
0016 | Ideas.  
0017 | Experiments.  
0018 | Failures.  
0019 | Mechanisms.
0020 | 
0021 | So let's ask an obvious question:
0022 | 
0023 | > **How far has computation already gone without us deliberately building the organism?**
0024 | 
0025 | There is no objective answer.
0026 | 
0027 | Different Artificial Life systems demonstrate different properties.
0028 | 
0029 | Evoloops demonstrated Darwinian evolution of self-reproducing structures inside a deterministic cellular automaton.[1]
0030 | 
0031 | Flow-Lenia produces spatially localized continuous structures with complex behaviour, conserves mass, and allows parameters governing different pattern dynamics to become localized inside the world itself. Researchers have measured emergent evolutionary activity in the resulting system.[2]
0032 | 
0033 | Genelife attaches inheritable genomes to cellular dynamics and has demonstrated continuing genetic and spatial innovation, while its authors explicitly distinguish this from the stronger functional innovation characteristic of biological evolution.[3]
0034 | 
0035 | Other computational systems have shown that self-replicating programs can emerge from simple interactions without an explicit fitness landscape.[4]
0036 | 
0037 | All of those matter.
0038 | 
0039 | But for what we are trying to understand, one system is particularly useful.
0040 | 
0041 | It is called:
0042 | 
0043 | ## Outlier
0044 | 
0045 | And initially it looks almost absurdly small.
0046 | 
0047 | ---
0048 | 
0049 | ## This Chapter Is an Excursion
0050 | 
0051 | Before going further, we need to be precise about what role Outlier plays in this book.
0052 | 
0053 | Chapter 11 gave us a deliberately simple system:
0054 | 
0055 | ```text
0056 | one seed
0057 | +
0058 | one local growth rule
0059 | +
0060 | one lattice
0061 | +
0062 | time
0063 | ```
0064 | 
0065 | We built that system ourselves.
0066 | 
0067 | We knew exactly why every mechanism was there.
0068 | 
0069 | Outlier is different.
0070 | 
0071 | It is an independently discovered cellular automaton in which surprisingly complicated structures appeared before anyone had decided what those structures should be.
0072 | 
0073 | So:
0074 | 
0075 | > **Outlier is not the next version of our crystal.**
0076 | 
0077 | We are not replacing our controlled growth model with Outlier.
0078 | 
0079 | We are leaving our laboratory temporarily and looking at a frontier system.
0080 | 
0081 | Our questions are:
0082 | 
0083 | ```text
0084 | What has simple digital physics already produced?
0085 | 
0086 | Which biological-looking interpretations survive
0087 | when causality is reconstructed?
0088 | 
0089 | Which ideas are worth carrying back
0090 | into our controlled experiments?
0091 | 
0092 | Which ideas should be discarded?
0093 | ```
0094 | 
0095 | That distinction will become important.
0096 | 
0097 | After Outlier, we will return to systems of our own construction.
0098 | 
0099 | But we should first learn everything this one can teach us.
0100 | 
0101 | ---
0102 | 
0103 | ## Two States
0104 | 
0105 | The universe contains cells.
0106 | 
0107 | Every cell is either:
0108 | 
0109 | ```text
0110 | 0
0111 | ```
0112 | 
0113 | or:
0114 | 
0115 | ```text
0116 | 1
0117 | ```
0118 | 
0119 | Dead and alive are convenient names, but unnecessary ones.
0120 | 
0121 | We could equally call them:
0122 | 
0123 | ```text
0124 | OFF
0125 | ON
0126 | ```
0127 | 
0128 | Each cell examines a `3 × 3` Moore neighborhood:
0129 | 
0130 | ```text
0131 | a b c
0132 | d e f
0133 | g h i
0134 | ```
0135 | 
0136 | including itself.
0137 | 
0138 | Nine bits means:
0139 | 
0140 | $$
0141 | 2^9 = 512
0142 | $$
0143 | 
0144 | possible neighborhood configurations.
0145 | 
0146 | For every configuration, the rule says:
0147 | 
0148 | ```text
0149 | next state = 0 or 1
0150 | ```
0151 | 
0152 | That is the universe.
0153 | 
0154 | There is no built-in:
0155 | 
0156 | ```text
0157 | organism
0158 | energy
0159 | genome
0160 | reproduction API
0161 | individual
0162 | fitness function
0163 | ```
0164 | 
0165 | Just:
0166 | 
0167 | ```text
0168 | binary state
0169 | +
0170 | local neighborhood
0171 | +
0172 | transition rule
0173 | +
0174 | time
0175 | ```
0176 | 
0177 | The published Outlier rule is rotationally symmetric.
0178 | 
0179 | Its complete transition table contains:
0180 | 
0181 | ```text
0182 | 512 neighborhood cases
0183 | 220 live outputs
0184 | 292 dead outputs
0185 | ```
0186 | 
0187 | That is all the local physics.
0188 | 
0189 | ---
0190 | 
0191 | ## Nobody Designed the Organism
0192 | 
0193 | This distinction matters.
0194 | 
0195 | Outlier was discovered during an automated search through cellular-automaton rules intended to find dynamics conducive to open-ended evolution.[5]
0196 | 
0197 | The search did not begin by constructing:
0198 | 
0199 | ```python
0200 | class Organism:
0201 |     ...
0202 | 
0203 | class Reproduction:
0204 |     ...
0205 | ```
0206 | 
0207 | Nor was there a hand-designed structure whose reproduction mechanism had been carefully engineered.
0208 | 
0209 | Instead the search found:
0210 | 
0211 | > **a rule for the universe**
0212 | 
0213 | and structures appeared inside that universe.
0214 | 
0215 | ![The published Outlier cellular automaton evolving from its tiny seed](/images/books/digital-life/ch10-outlier-growth.gif)
0216 | 
0217 | Conceptually:
0218 | 
0219 | ```mermaid
0220 | flowchart LR
0221 |     subgraph Designed
0222 |         A1["Programmer designs organism"] --> A2["Designs reproduction mechanism"]
0223 |         A2 --> A3["Organism reproduces"]
0224 |     end
0225 | 
0226 |     subgraph Outlier
0227 |         B1["Search discovers local physics"] --> B2["Local physics runs"]
0228 |         B2 --> B3["Structures emerge"]
0229 |         B3 --> B4["Some structures replicate"]
0230 |     end
0231 | ```
0232 | 
0233 | The second route does not establish life.
0234 | 
0235 | But it removes an enormous amount of cargo cult.
0236 | 
0237 | ---
0238 | 
0239 | ## Start Almost From Nothing
0240 | 
0241 | The published rule can produce rich behaviour from sparse random initial conditions.
0242 | 
0243 | Small shape-changing clusters appear.
0244 | 
0245 | Some clusters produce additional clusters.
0246 | 
0247 | Some periodically duplicate.
0248 | 
0249 | Multiple smaller structures can assemble into larger formations.
0250 | 
0251 | Those formations can themselves replicate.
0252 | 
0253 | Collections of them can eventually form the boundary of a still larger expanding complex.[5]
0254 | 
0255 | So the published system contains organization at multiple scales:
0256 | 
0257 | ```text
0258 | cells
0259 |   ↓
0260 | clusters
0261 |   ↓
0262 | replicating formations
0263 |   ↓
0264 | larger expanding complex
0265 | ```
0266 | 
0267 | Replication appears at more than one scale.
0268 | 
0269 | ![Outlier at successive generations from the same initial seed](/images/books/digital-life/ch10-outlier-snapshots.png)
0270 | 
0271 | That is already strange.
0272 | 
0273 | But we have spent enough of this book learning not to stop at strange.
0274 | 
0275 | ---
0276 | 
0277 | ## There Was Still a Problem
0278 | 
0279 | Suppose we see:
0280 | 
0281 | ```text
0282 | A
0283 | ```
0284 | 
0285 | and later:
0286 | 
0287 | ```text
0288 | A     A
0289 | ```
0290 | 
0291 | It is tempting to say:
0292 | 
0293 | > A reproduced.
0294 | 
0295 | But perhaps the first `A` did not cause the second one.
0296 | 
0297 | Perhaps the local dynamics simply created another similar-looking configuration nearby.
0298 | 
0299 | Those are completely different claims.
0300 | 
0301 | ```text
0302 | visual recurrence
0303 | ≠
0304 | causal reproduction
0305 | ```
0306 | 
0307 | So in 2026, Arend Hintze and Clifford Bohm returned to Outlier with a much stronger question.
0308 | 
0309 | They reconstructed **causal ancestry**.[6]
0310 | 
0311 | ---
0312 | 
0313 | ## Who Caused Whom?
0314 | 
0315 | The method asks something close to:
0316 | 
0317 | > Which cells in the previous state were necessary for this later cell to appear?
0318 | 
0319 | At cell level:
0320 | 
0321 | ```text
0322 | previous cells
0323 |      ↓
0324 | causal contribution
0325 |      ↓
0326 | new cell
0327 | ```
0328 | 
0329 | Those dependencies can then be aggregated into relationships between larger structures:
0330 | 
0331 | ```text
0332 | cluster A
0333 |     ↓
0334 | cluster B
0335 |     ↓
0336 | cluster C
0337 | ```
0338 | 
0339 | Now the question is no longer merely:
0340 | 
0341 | ```text
0342 | does this look like that?
0343 | ```
0344 | 
0345 | It becomes:
0346 | 
0347 | ```text
0348 | did this organization
0349 | causally contribute to
0350 | the existence of that organization?
0351 | ```
0352 | 
0353 | That gives us an ancestry graph.
0354 | 
0355 | The 2026 analysis found branching causal reproduction in Outlier: earlier structures could causally produce multiple later structures, which could themselves participate in continuing lineages.[6]
0356 | 
0357 | That is a substantially stronger claim than visual similarity.
0358 | 
0359 | ```mermaid
0360 | flowchart TD
0361 |     subgraph Visual
0362 |         V1["Pattern at t"] -. "looks similar to" .-> V2["Pattern at t+1"]
0363 |     end
0364 | 
0365 |     subgraph Causal
0366 |         C1["Cells at t"] -->|"necessary contribution"| C2["Cells at t+1"]
0367 |         C2 --> C3["Aggregate causal relationships"]
0368 |         C3 --> C4["Earlier structure causally contributes to later structure"]
0369 |     end
0370 | ```
0371 | 
0372 | The distinction will matter enormously in the next chapter.
0373 | 
0374 | ---
0375 | 
0376 | ## 433 Copies
0377 | 
0378 | The 2026 experiment used a much larger system than the small examples we will run later.
0379 | 
0380 | It ran Outlier on:
0381 | 
0382 | ```text
0383 | grid       1024 × 1024
0384 | boundary   periodic
0385 | duration   20,000 updates
0386 | ```
0387 | 
0388 | The resulting causal analysis contained tens of millions of cluster instances and causal relationships.[6]
0389 | 
0390 | Consider the original seed cluster, called `c0`.
0391 | 
0392 | Within the first 10,000 updates, the researchers identified:
0393 | 
0394 | ```text
0395 | 433
0396 | ```
0397 | 
0398 | copies causally descending from that original seed.[6]
0399 | 
0400 | But those descendants did not indefinitely continue the same `c0` lineage.
0401 | 
0402 | So we immediately learn something useful:
0403 | 
0404 | ```text
0405 | replication
0406 | ≠
0407 | successful long-term lineage
0408 | ```
0409 | 
0410 | Producing another instance is not the same as founding a persistent dynasty.
0411 | 
0412 | ---
0413 | 
0414 | ## Then They Found Better Replicators
0415 | 
0416 | Other structures generated branching, multi-generation causal lineages.
0417 | 
0418 | One cluster type, `c2`, became particularly useful for tracing reproduction through the causal graph.[6]
0419 | 
0420 | The surrounding environment also mattered.
0421 | 
0422 | Replicators produced:
0423 | 
0424 | ```text
0425 | debris
0426 | collisions
0427 | fragments
0428 | recombinations
0429 | ```
0430 | 
0431 | and some later replicating structures arose through those interactions.
0432 | 
0433 | So the system is not simply doing:
0434 | 
0435 | ```text
0436 | copy parent
0437 | ```
0438 | 
0439 | It is closer to:
0440 | 
0441 | ```text
0442 | replicating process
0443 |         ↓
0444 | interaction
0445 |         ↓
0446 | fragments
0447 |         ↓
0448 | collisions
0449 |         ↓
0450 | recombination
0451 |         ↓
0452 | new structures
0453 | ```
0454 | 
0455 | That is much more interesting than simple geometric copying.
0456 | 
0457 | But we should still be careful about what words we attach to it.
0458 | 
0459 | ---
0460 | 
0461 | ## A Replicator May Not Be Connected
0462 | 
0463 | One of the most provocative findings from the causal analysis is that a self-replicating organization does not necessarily have to correspond to one compact connected cluster.
0464 | 
0465 | Some causally reproducing structures consisted of multiple spatially separated components whose combined causal dynamics participated in reproduction.[6]
0466 | 
0467 | The authors describe this in terms of distributed, multi-component selfhood.
0468 | 
0469 | For this book, we will keep the narrower result.
0470 | 
0471 | > **Causal self-replication can be distributed across multiple spatial components.**
0472 | 
0473 | That does **not** yet establish that those components constitute one natural individual.
0474 | 
0475 | Those are different claims.
0476 | 
0477 | A system like:
0478 | 
0479 | ```text
0480 |      A
0481 |     / \
0482 |    B   C
0483 |     \ /
0484 |      D
0485 | ```
0486 | 
0487 | might form one causally reproducing organization even though its visible components are spatially separated.
0488 | 
0489 | So connected geometry is not sufficient as a universal definition of a replicator.
0490 | 
0491 | But we should not jump from:
0492 | 
0493 | ```text
0494 | distributed causal reproduction
0495 | ```
0496 | 
0497 | to:
0498 | 
0499 | ```text
0500 | one distributed individual
0501 | ```
0502 | 
0503 | without another experiment.
0504 | 
0505 | That distinction is exactly the kind of thing this book is supposed to preserve.
0506 | 
0507 | ---
0508 | 
0509 | ## This Is Why Outlier Is Useful to Us
0510 | 
0511 | Outlier has an unusually useful combination of properties.
0512 | 
0513 | Its underlying world is:
0514 | 
0515 | ```text
0516 | binary
0517 | local
0518 | deterministic
0519 | spatial
0520 | small-rule
0521 | reproducible
0522 | ```
0523 | 
0524 | Yet the published experiments report:
0525 | 
0526 | ```text
0527 | emergent structures
0528 | hierarchical organization
0529 | causal self-replication
0530 | multiple generations
0531 | interaction
0532 | recombination
0533 | multi-component reproduction
0534 | ```
0535 | 
0536 | The 2026 authors argue for a stronger interpretation involving distributed selfhood.[6]
0537 | 
0538 | We are not required to adopt that interpretation.
0539 | 
0540 | What matters to us is that causal analysis lets us separate several questions that animations otherwise collapse together:
0541 | 
0542 | ```text
0543 | Did another pattern appear?
0544 | 
0545 | Was it similar?
0546 | 
0547 | Did the earlier structure cause it?
0548 | 
0549 | Did a lineage continue?
0550 | 
0551 | Were several components jointly necessary?
0552 | 
0553 | Does that causal organization deserve to be called one individual?
0554 | ```
0555 | 
0556 | Those are six different questions.
0557 | 
0558 | That makes Outlier an extraordinary reference system for our method.
0559 | 
0560 | ---
0561 | 
0562 | ## But Outlier Is Not Life
0563 | 
0564 | Nothing above establishes that Outlier is alive.
0565 | 
0566 | We have not established:
0567 | 
0568 | ```text
0569 | learning
0570 | understanding
0571 | self-maintenance
0572 | general-purpose adaptation
0573 | deliberate self-modification
0574 | knowledge assimilation
0575 | knowledge transfer
0576 | cumulative capability acquisition
0577 | open-ended functional improvement
0578 | ```
0579 | 
0580 | Nor does causal self-replication automatically establish any of those things.
0581 | 
0582 | The supported result is narrower:
0583 | 
0584 | > **Very simple digital physics can support emergent structures for which causal analysis identifies genuine, branching and sometimes multi-component self-replication.**
0585 | 
0586 | That is already remarkable.
0587 | 
0588 | It does not need embellishment.
0589 | 
0590 | ---
0591 | 
0592 | ## What About Flow-Lenia?
0593 | 
0594 | It is tempting to choose Flow-Lenia as our main reference system instead.
0595 | 
0596 | Visually, Flow-Lenia is much closer to what we intuitively imagine as an organism.
0597 | 
0598 | Its mass-conserving continuous dynamics can produce localized structures with complicated behaviour, and parameters governing those structures can themselves become localized within the simulated world. This permits multiple kinds of patterns to coexist and interact under locally different dynamics.[2]
0599 | 
0600 | Researchers have also measured evolutionary activity in Flow-Lenia.[2]
0601 | 
0602 | For studying:
0603 | 
0604 | ```text
0605 | continuous morphology
0606 | movement
0607 | mass flow
0608 | localized parameters
0609 | multispecies interactions
0610 | ```
0611 | 
0612 | Flow-Lenia may be the richer substrate.
0613 | 
0614 | But Outlier has an enormous advantage for what we want to do next.
0615 | 
0616 | We can almost completely expose its mechanism.
0617 | 
0618 | There are only:
0619 | 
0620 | ```text
0621 | two cell states
0622 | 512 neighborhood cases
0623 | one deterministic transition table
0624 | ```
0625 | 
0626 | No neural network.
0627 | 
0628 | No hidden controller.
0629 | 
0630 | No floating-point organism representation.
0631 | 
0632 | That makes it an unusually good object to reproduce and attack.
0633 | 
0634 | ---
0635 | 
0636 | ## Let's Implement It
0637 | 
0638 | The exact rule is published.
0639 | 
0640 | The Outlier paper provides the complete 512-entry rule encoded as a standard `MAP` string.[5]
0641 | 
0642 | It also provides a tiny `3 × 3` seed that reproduces the published seed dynamics.
0643 | 
0644 | The rule is:
0645 | 
0646 | ```text
0647 | ERETQB4eHWkQ7xD4eYZosBQZFixOBHmtFeehExrKVhURLRAqGxeIlSO1JYZP6DRi69rop7TQCkvWTIag7kAS8g
0648 | ```
0649 | 
0650 | The seed is:
0651 | 
0652 | ```text
0653 | .1.
0654 | 111
0655 | ..1
0656 | ```
0657 | 
0658 | That is enough to begin.
0659 | 
0660 | ---
0661 | 
0662 | ## Decode the Rule
0663 | 
0664 | A Moore neighborhood has nine cells.
0665 | 
0666 | We assign them these binary weights:
0667 | 
0668 | ```text
0669 | 256 128  64
0670 |  32  16   8
0671 |   4   2   1
0672 | ```
0673 | 
0674 | A binary `3 × 3` neighborhood therefore maps to an integer from `0` through `511`.
0675 | 
0676 | For example:
0677 | 
0678 | ```text
0679 | 1 0 0
0680 | 0 1 0
0681 | 0 0 1
0682 | ```
0683 | 
0684 | becomes:
0685 | 
0686 | ```text
0687 | 256 + 16 + 1 = 273
0688 | ```
0689 | 
0690 | The corresponding entry in the 512-entry transition table determines the next state of the center cell.
0691 | 
0692 | The published MAP string contains those rule bits encoded in Base64.
0693 | 
0694 | ```python
0695 | import base64
0696 | import numpy as np
0697 | 
0698 | 
0699 | OUTLIER_MAP = (
0700 |     "ERETQB4eHWkQ7xD4eYZosBQZFixOBHmtFeehExrKVhURLRAq"
0701 |     "GxeIlSO1JYZP6DRi69rop7TQCkvWTIag7kAS8g"
0702 | )
0703 | 
0704 | 
0705 | def decode_map_rule(encoded: str) -> np.ndarray:
0706 |     """Decode the published 512-bit MAP rule."""
0707 |     padding = "=" * ((4 - len(encoded) % 4) % 4)
0708 |     raw = base64.b64decode(encoded + padding)
0709 | 
0710 |     bits = np.unpackbits(
0711 |         np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8)
0712 |     )
0713 | 
0714 |     if len(bits) < 512:
0715 |         raise ValueError(
0716 |             "MAP rule contains fewer than 512 bits"
0717 |         )
0718 | 
0719 |     return bits[:512].astype(np.uint8)
0720 | 
0721 | 
0722 | RULE = decode_map_rule(OUTLIER_MAP)
0723 | ```
0724 | 
0725 | At this point it is tempting to continue.
0726 | 
0727 | We should not.
0728 | 
0729 | Everything that follows depends on us having decoded the correct universe.
0730 | 
0731 | So before we trust the simulation, we test the decoder.
0732 | 
0733 | ---
0734 | 
0735 | ## Verify Before We Trust It
0736 | 
0737 | The paper gives us two properties we can check immediately.
0738 | 
0739 | The rule should contain:
0740 | 
0741 | ```text
0742 | 512 outputs
0743 | 220 live outputs
0744 | ```
0745 | 
0746 | So:
0747 | 
0748 | ```python
0749 | assert RULE.shape == (512,)
0750 | assert int(RULE.sum()) == 220
0751 | ```
0752 | 
0753 | If either assertion fails, we stop.
0754 | 
0755 | But we can do better.
0756 | 
0757 | The published rule is rotationally symmetric.[5]
0758 | 
0759 | That means rotating a neighborhood through a quarter turn must not change the corresponding rule output.
0760 | 
0761 | We can test every possible neighborhood.
0762 | 
0763 | ```python
0764 | def index_to_grid(index: int) -> np.ndarray:
0765 |     bits = np.array(
0766 |         [
0767 |             (index >> shift) & 1
0768 |             for shift in range(8, -1, -1)
0769 |         ],
0770 |         dtype=np.uint8,
0771 |     )
0772 |     return bits.reshape(3, 3)
0773 | 
0774 | 
0775 | def grid_to_index(grid: np.ndarray) -> int:
0776 |     value = 0
0777 | 
0778 |     for bit in grid.reshape(-1):
0779 |         value = (value << 1) | int(bit)
0780 | 
0781 |     return value
0782 | 
0783 | 
0784 | def verify_rotational_symmetry(
0785 |     rule: np.ndarray,
0786 | ) -> None:
0787 |     for index in range(512):
0788 |         grid = index_to_grid(index)
0789 |         expected = int(rule[index])
0790 | 
0791 |         rotated = grid.copy()
0792 | 
0793 |         for _ in range(3):
0794 |             rotated = np.rot90(rotated)
0795 | 
0796 |             rotated_index = grid_to_index(
0797 |                 rotated
0798 |             )
0799 | 
0800 |             assert (
0801 |                 int(rule[rotated_index])
0802 |                 == expected
0803 |             ), (
0804 |                 index,
0805 |                 rotated_index,
0806 |                 expected,
0807 |                 int(rule[rotated_index]),
0808 |             )
0809 | 
0810 | 
0811 | verify_rotational_symmetry(RULE)
0812 | ```
0813 | 
0814 | If that completes successfully, we have checked:
0815 | 
0816 | ```text
0817 | decoded entries             512
0818 | live outputs                220
0819 | quarter-turn symmetry       all 512 neighborhoods
0820 | ```
0821 | 
0822 | This is a tiny piece of verification.
0823 | 
0824 | It is also load-bearing.
0825 | 
0826 | > **If our MAP decoder or bit ordering is wrong, every later experiment would be about a different cellular automaton.**
0827 | 
0828 | The visual output might still look fascinating.
0829 | 
0830 | It would simply be irrelevant.
0831 | 
0832 | ---
0833 | 
0834 | ## One Update
0835 | 
0836 | Now we can implement one step of the universe.
0837 | 
0838 | ```python
0839 | def outlier_step(
0840 |     state: np.ndarray,
0841 |     rule: np.ndarray,
0842 | ) -> np.ndarray:
0843 | 
0844 |     nw = np.roll(
0845 |         np.roll(state, 1, axis=0),
0846 |         1,
0847 |         axis=1,
0848 |     )
0849 | 
0850 |     north = np.roll(state, 1, axis=0)
0851 | 
0852 |     ne = np.roll(
0853 |         np.roll(state, 1, axis=0),
0854 |         -1,
0855 |         axis=1,
0856 |     )
0857 | 
0858 |     west = np.roll(state, 1, axis=1)
0859 | 
0860 |     centre = state
0861 | 
0862 |     east = np.roll(state, -1, axis=1)
0863 | 
0864 |     sw = np.roll(
0865 |         np.roll(state, -1, axis=0),
0866 |         1,
0867 |         axis=1,
0868 |     )
0869 | 
0870 |     south = np.roll(state, -1, axis=0)
0871 | 
0872 |     se = np.roll(
0873 |         np.roll(state, -1, axis=0),
0874 |         -1,
0875 |         axis=1,
0876 |     )
0877 | 
0878 |     neighborhood = (
0879 |           (nw.astype(np.uint16) << 8)
0880 |         | (north.astype(np.uint16) << 7)
0881 |         | (ne.astype(np.uint16) << 6)
0882 |         | (west.astype(np.uint16) << 5)
0883 |         | (centre.astype(np.uint16) << 4)
0884 |         | (east.astype(np.uint16) << 3)
0885 |         | (sw.astype(np.uint16) << 2)
0886 |         | (south.astype(np.uint16) << 1)
0887 |         |  se.astype(np.uint16)
0888 |     )
0889 | 
0890 |     return rule[neighborhood]
0891 | ```
0892 | 
0893 | Look at what is missing.
0894 | 
0895 | There is no:
0896 | 
0897 | ```python
0898 | replicate()
0899 | ```
0900 | 
0901 | No:
0902 | 
0903 | ```python
0904 | organism()
0905 | ```
0906 | 
0907 | No:
0908 | 
0909 | ```python
0910 | find_child()
0911 | ```
0912 | 
0913 | No:
0914 | 
0915 | ```python
0916 | evolve()
0917 | ```
0918 | 
0919 | Only the transition rule.
0920 | 
0921 | ---
0922 | 
0923 | ## Add the Published Seed
0924 | 
0925 | The seed is:
0926 | 
0927 | ```python
0928 | SEED = np.array(
0929 |     [
0930 |         [0, 1, 0],
0931 |         [1, 1, 1],
0932 |         [0, 0, 1],
0933 |     ],
0934 |     dtype=np.uint8,
0935 | )
0936 | ```
0937 | 
0938 | Place it in the center of a periodic world.
0939 | 
0940 | ```python
0941 | def make_world(
0942 |     size: int = 512,
0943 | ) -> np.ndarray:
0944 | 
0945 |     world = np.zeros(
0946 |         (size, size),
0947 |         dtype=np.uint8,
0948 |     )
0949 | 
0950 |     row = size // 2 - 1
0951 |     col = size // 2 - 1
0952 | 
0953 |     world[
0954 |         row:row + 3,
0955 |         col:col + 3,
0956 |     ] = SEED
0957 | 
0958 |     return world
0959 | ```
0960 | 
0961 | And run:
0962 | 
0963 | ```python
0964 | RULE = decode_map_rule(OUTLIER_MAP)
0965 | 
0966 | assert RULE.shape == (512,)
0967 | assert int(RULE.sum()) == 220
0968 | 
0969 | verify_rotational_symmetry(RULE)
0970 | 
0971 | world = make_world(512)
0972 | 
0973 | for tick in range(5000):
0974 |     world = outlier_step(
0975 |         world,
0976 |         RULE,
0977 |     )
0978 | 
0979 |     if tick % 100 == 0:
0980 |         print(
0981 |             tick,
0982 |             int(world.sum()),
0983 |         )
0984 | ```
0985 | 
0986 | That gives us a compact implementation of the published local physics.
0987 | 
0988 | But there is an important distinction we must make before interpreting anything it produces.
0989 | 
0990 | ---
0991 | 
0992 | ## Our Implementation Is Not Yet the Full Published Experiment
0993 | 
0994 | The code above reproduces:
0995 | 
0996 | ```text
0997 | the published transition rule
0998 | +
0999 | the published seed
1000 | +
1001 | periodic local dynamics
1002 | ```
1003 | 
1004 | That does **not** mean every experiment we run is equivalent to the published experiments.
1005 | 
1006 | The 2026 causal study used:
1007 | 
1008 | ```text
1009 | grid       1024 × 1024
1010 | boundary   periodic
1011 | duration   20,000 updates
1012 | ```
1013 | 
1014 | Our teaching implementation may use smaller worlds or shorter runs.
1015 | 
1016 | That difference is not cosmetic.
1017 | 
1018 | The earlier Outlier work reports a strong scale effect: sparse random worlds smaller than roughly `512 × 512` did not produce the larger replicating formations seen in the principal experiments.[5]
1019 | 
1020 | So we establish a rule now:
1021 | 
1022 | > **A result obtained from a smaller or shorter Outlier run is a result about that run. It must not automatically be generalized to the full published Outlier regime.**
1023 | 
1024 | This becomes particularly important in the next chapter.
1025 | 
1026 | If we run:
1027 | 
1028 | ```text
1029 | 512 × 512
1030 | for
1031 | 1,600 generations
1032 | ```
1033 | 
1034 | then our claims apply to:
1035 | 
1036 | ```text
1037 | the structures observable
1038 | in that 512 × 512
1039 | 1,600-generation experiment
1040 | ```
1041 | 
1042 | They do not automatically apply to:
1043 | 
1044 | ```text
1045 | 1024 × 1024
1046 | 20,000-generation
1047 | hierarchical Outlier dynamics
1048 | ```
1049 | 
1050 | Scale is part of the experimental condition.
1051 | 
1052 | ---
1053 | 
1054 | ## Something Important Has Already Changed
1055 | 
1056 | Remember our crystal from Chapter 11.
1057 | 
1058 | It grew because we explicitly chose a growth rule.
1059 | 
1060 | Outlier is different.
1061 | 
1062 | We did not define:
1063 | 
1064 | ```text
1065 | parent
1066 | offspring
1067 | family
1068 | replicator
1069 | formation
1070 | ```
1071 | 
1072 | inside its transition law.
1073 | 
1074 | Those are descriptions applied after larger organizations appeared.
1075 | 
1076 | That makes Outlier useful for a very particular purpose.
1077 | 
1078 | It allows us to ask:
1079 | 
1080 | > **When does our interpretation outrun the mechanism?**
1081 | 
1082 | That is exactly what the next chapter will test.
1083 | 
1084 | ---
1085 | 
1086 | ## What We Should Steal
1087 | 
1088 | Outlier gives us several ideas worth carrying forward.
1089 | 
1090 | ### 1. Do not design the organism
1091 | 
1092 | We can design or discover local physics and allow candidate structures to arise within it.
1093 | 
1094 | ### 2. Do not assume one scale
1095 | 
1096 | Interesting organization may exist simultaneously at:
1097 | 
1098 | ```text
1099 | cell
1100 | cluster
1101 | formation
1102 | larger structure
1103 | ```
1104 | 
1105 | without one scale automatically being privileged.
1106 | 
1107 | ### 3. Do not equate connected geometry with causal organization
1108 | 
1109 | A causally reproducing structure may involve spatially separated components.
1110 | 
1111 | That does not establish individuality.
1112 | 
1113 | It tells us only that connectedness is not enough.
1114 | 
1115 | ### 4. Track causation
1116 | 
1117 | Visual resemblance is not sufficient evidence for:
1118 | 
1119 | ```text
1120 | reproduction
1121 | inheritance
1122 | influence
1123 | ancestry
1124 | ```
1125 | 
1126 | Whenever possible, reconstruct the dependencies.
1127 | 
1128 | ### 5. Let interactions matter
1129 | 
1130 | Collision, recombination and environmental interference can generate novelty without us injecting a mutation operator from outside.
1131 | 
1132 | Those are useful lessons.
1133 | 
1134 | They are not a specification for our next system.
1135 | 
1136 | ---
1137 | 
1138 | ## What We Should Not Steal Yet
1139 | 
1140 | Outlier also tempts us into vocabulary we have not earned.
1141 | 
1142 | Words such as:
1143 | 
1144 | ```text
1145 | organism
1146 | individual
1147 | family
1148 | offspring
1149 | self
1150 | collective
1151 | flocking
1152 | ```
1153 | 
1154 | are extremely seductive once an animation starts moving.
1155 | 
1156 | So we are not going to carry those words forward unquestioned.
1157 | 
1158 | In particular, causal ancestry creates an obvious hypothesis:
1159 | 
1160 | > Structures that share recent causal ancestry may behave as one continuing organization.
1161 | 
1162 | Perhaps.
1163 | 
1164 | But perhaps what looks like family behaviour is merely:
1165 | 
1166 | ```text
1167 | spatial proximity
1168 | shared local flow
1169 | common environmental disturbance
1170 | ```
1171 | 
1172 | Perhaps connected clusters are the wrong units.
1173 | 
1174 | Perhaps causal families are the wrong units.
1175 | 
1176 | Perhaps there is no unique natural unit at all.
1177 | 
1178 | Those are experimental questions.
1179 | 
1180 | ---
1181 | 
1182 | ## Outlier Is a Reference Case, Not Our Destination
1183 | 
1184 | Outlier does not know anything about:
1185 | 
1186 | ```text
1187 | the internet
1188 | external knowledge
1189 | its own rule
1190 | experiments
1191 | checkpoints
1192 | forking
1193 | merging
1194 | deliberate modification
1195 | ```
1196 | 
1197 | But that is not a criticism.
1198 | 
1199 | Those capabilities are irrelevant to what Outlier has already demonstrated.
1200 | 
1201 | For us, Outlier establishes a lower reference point:
1202 | 
1203 | > **How much complicated causal organization can appear before anything resembling intelligence is required?**
1204 | 
1205 | That is enormously useful.
1206 | 
1207 | But we are not going to take Outlier and start bolting capabilities onto it.
1208 | 
1209 | That would simply create another cargo cult.
1210 | 
1211 | Instead:
1212 | 
1213 | ```text
1214 | OUTLIER
1215 | ↓
1216 | observe
1217 | ↓
1218 | form interpretation
1219 | ↓
1220 | attack interpretation
1221 | ↓
1222 | keep only what survives
1223 | ↓
1224 | return to our controlled laboratory
1225 | ```
1226 | 
1227 | That is the bridge to the rest of the book.
1228 | 
1229 | ---
1230 | 
1231 | ## Evidence Ledger
1232 | 
1233 | At this point we can separate what is established from what remains open.
1234 | 
1235 | | Claim                                                                                  | Status                            | Evidence                         |
1236 | | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
1237 | | The published MAP decodes to 512 binary outputs                                        | **SUPPORTED**                     | exhaustive decode                |
1238 | | The decoded rule contains 220 live outputs                                             | **SUPPORTED**                     | direct count                     |
1239 | | The decoded rule is invariant under quarter-turn rotations                             | **SUPPORTED**                     | exhaustive 512-neighborhood test |
1240 | | Outlier produces self-replicating organization under published experimental conditions | **SUPPORTED FROM PUBLISHED WORK** | Yang 2025                        |
1241 | | Causal ancestry identifies genuine branching replication                               | **SUPPORTED FROM PUBLISHED WORK** | Hintze & Bohm 2026               |
1242 | | Causal reproduction can span multiple spatial components                               | **SUPPORTED FROM PUBLISHED WORK** | Hintze & Bohm 2026               |
1243 | | Multi-component reproduction establishes one natural individual                        | **UNTESTED HERE**                 | requires an additional criterion |
1244 | | Shared ancestry causes coordinated motion                                              | **UNTESTED HERE**                 | next chapter                     |
1245 | | Our smaller teaching run reproduces the entire published Outlier regime                | **NOT CLAIMED**                   | scale and duration differ        |
1246 | | Outlier is alive                                                                       | **NOT CLAIMED**                   | evidence insufficient            |
1247 | 
1248 | This ledger matters.
1249 | 
1250 | The most interesting entries may eventually be the ones that fail.
1251 | 
1252 | ---
1253 | 
1254 | ## What Is the Closest Thing We Have?
1255 | 
1256 | So is Outlier digital life?
1257 | 
1258 | We will not make that claim.
1259 | 
1260 | A narrower statement survives:
1261 | 
1262 | > **Outlier is a striking demonstration that extremely compact digital physics can support emergent, hierarchical self-replication, and that causal reconstruction can identify reproduction distributed across multiple spatial components.**
1263 | 
1264 | The entire local universe is specified by:
1265 | 
1266 | ```text
1267 | 512 bits of transition law
1268 | +
1269 | initial state
1270 | +
1271 | space
1272 | +
1273 | time
1274 | ```
1275 | 
1276 | From that, unexpectedly complicated causal organization can appear.
1277 | 
1278 | But the animation gives us more interpretations than the evidence has earned.
1279 | 
1280 | So before returning to our own Digital Crystal, we are going to do something more important.
1281 | 
1282 | We are going to attack Outlier.
1283 | 
1284 | We will ask:
1285 | 
1286 | ```text
1287 | Is recurrence really reproduction?
1288 | 
1289 | Can we reconstruct causal descendants?
1290 | 
1291 | Does shared ancestry predict shared behaviour?
1292 | 
1293 | Does the apparent family effect survive
1294 | a better control?
1295 | 
1296 | What happens when proximity is separated
1297 | from ancestry?
1298 | 
1299 | And what can our finite replication
1300 | actually tell us about the larger system?
1301 | ```
1302 | 
1303 | Outlier is not the organism from which our later Digital Crystal descends.
1304 | 
1305 | It is the **hostile reference case** that teaches us which interpretations survive.
1306 | 
1307 | We are not going to copy it.
1308 | 
1309 | We are going to try to prove ourselves wrong about it.
1310 | 
1311 | Next:
1312 | 
1313 | **Is It Really Reproducing?**
1314 | 
1315 | ---
1316 |
