0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | We are leaving Outlier.
0013 | 
0014 | Not because it failed.
0015 | 
0016 | Quite the opposite.
0017 | 
0018 | Outlier did exactly what we needed an external reference system to do.
0019 | 
0020 | It showed us that very simple digital physics can support structures that recur, move, interact and participate in measurable causal lineages.
0021 | 
0022 | Then we attacked our own interpretations.
0023 | 
0024 | Some survived.
0025 | 
0026 | Some did not.
0027 | 
0028 | The causal reproduction result survived.
0029 | 
0030 | One of our strongest explanations for the apparent coordinated motion did not.
0031 | 
0032 | That is useful.
0033 | 
0034 | But Outlier is not the next version of our crystal.
0035 | 
0036 | We are not going to copy it.
0037 | 
0038 | We are not going to take its structures and start bolting biological capabilities onto them.
0039 | 
0040 | We are going back to the laboratory.
0041 | 
0042 | There is one idea worth carrying with us:
0043 | 
0044 | ```text
0045 | local computation
0046 | ↓
0047 | repeated interaction
0048 | ↓
0049 | characteristic larger-scale structure
0050 | ```
0051 | 
0052 | That idea is much smaller than an organism.
0053 | 
0054 | It is much smaller than reproduction.
0055 | 
0056 | It does not require individuality.
0057 | 
0058 | And it brings us back to something we encountered earlier.
0059 | 
0060 | The crystal.
0061 | 
0062 | ---
0063 | 
0064 | ## Back to the Laboratory
0065 | 
0066 | In Chapter 11 we built an intentionally trivial growth system.
0067 | 
0068 | One seed.
0069 | 
0070 | A hexagonal lattice.
0071 | 
0072 | A local rule.
0073 | 
0074 | Occupied cells remained occupied.
0075 | 
0076 | Empty cells could become occupied through local contact.
0077 | 
0078 | No target morphology.
0079 | 
0080 | No stored radius.
0081 | 
0082 | No global shape.
0083 | 
0084 | And yet a characteristic large-scale structure appeared.
0085 | 
0086 | That experiment established something small but important:
0087 | 
0088 | > **A repeated local computational process can generate persistent global structure without containing an explicit representation of that structure.**
0089 | 
0090 | Then we left our laboratory.
0091 | 
0092 | Outlier was an excursion into a system we did not design.
0093 | 
0094 | Now we return.
0095 | 
0096 | But we are not simply continuing the Chapter 11 model unchanged.
0097 | 
0098 | We are going to ask it a new question.
0099 | 
0100 | > Can the environment leave a measurable mark on the structure that grows inside it?
0101 | 
0102 | That requires a new experimental model.
0103 | 
0104 | ---
0105 | 
0106 | ## What Changed Since Chapter 11?
0107 | 
0108 | This matters enough to state explicitly.
0109 | 
0110 | Chapter 14 does **not** use exactly the same growth rule as Chapter 11.
0111 | 
0112 | The Chapter 11 crystal was deliberately minimal:
0113 | 
0114 | ```text
0115 | CHAPTER 11
0116 | 
0117 | binary occupancy
0118 | +
0119 | hexagonal neighborhood
0120 | +
0121 | irreversible growth
0122 | +
0123 | deterministic local attachment
0124 | ```
0125 | 
0126 | Its purpose was to ask what continued structured growth requires.
0127 | 
0128 | The model in this chapter adds several mechanisms:
0129 | 
0130 | ```text
0131 | CHAPTER 14
0132 | 
0133 | binary occupancy
0134 | +
0135 | hexagonal neighborhood
0136 | +
0137 | irreversible growth
0138 | +
0139 | stochastic attachment
0140 | +
0141 | environmental forcing
0142 | +
0143 | fixed lattice anisotropy
0144 | +
0145 | crowding penalty
0146 | ```
0147 | 
0148 | Why introduce them?
0149 | 
0150 | Because our new question is different.
0151 | 
0152 | Chapter 11 asked:
0153 | 
0154 | > Can simple local growth generate characteristic persistent form?
0155 | 
0156 | Chapter 14 asks:
0157 | 
0158 | > Can changing external conditions influence that growth strongly enough to leave a persistent measurable signature?
0159 | 
0160 | To ask that question, the environment needs some way to modulate local attachment.
0161 | 
0162 | Stochastic attachment gives the forcing room to influence which locally available events actually happen.
0163 | 
0164 | Anisotropy gives the lattice persistent directional structure.
0165 | 
0166 | Crowding prevents attachment probability from increasing without bound simply because a location has many occupied neighbours.
0167 | 
0168 | These mechanisms are introduced for this experiment.
0169 | 
0170 | They are not discoveries from Chapter 11.
0171 | 
0172 | And this has an important consequence:
0173 | 
0174 | > **Results from the Chapter 11 crystal do not automatically transfer to Digital Crystal v1.**
0175 | 
0176 | For example, Chapter 11's hole-filling experiment does not prove that this stochastic model has the same damage response.
0177 | 
0178 | This is a new model.
0179 | 
0180 | It must earn its own claims.
0181 | 
0182 | ---
0183 | 
0184 | ## We Gave It a Name
0185 | 
0186 | We gave it a name.
0187 | 
0188 | That was the easy part.
0189 | 
0190 | ```text
0191 | DIGITAL CRYSTAL
0192 | ```
0193 | 
0194 | The harder question is whether the name means anything.
0195 | 
0196 | A digital crystal cannot mean:
0197 | 
0198 | > a thing that looks like quartz
0199 | 
0200 | Nor can it mean:
0201 | 
0202 | > anything arranged on a hexagonal grid
0203 | 
0204 | Those would be visual definitions.
0205 | 
0206 | And we already know what happens when we allow appearance to substitute for mechanism.
0207 | 
0208 | So we need a computational definition.
0209 | 
0210 | A physical crystal acquires structure through repeated local interactions during formation.
0211 | 
0212 | The large-scale structure follows from those interactions.
0213 | 
0214 | Let us try the analogous idea digitally.
0215 | 
0216 | Our first working definition is:
0217 | 
0218 | > **A Digital Crystal is a local computational growth process in which characteristics of an external input become expressed as persistent, measurable morphology.**
0219 | 
0220 | That is deliberately narrow.
0221 | 
0222 | It says nothing about:
0223 | 
0224 | ```text
0225 | life
0226 | memory
0227 | learning
0228 | adaptation
0229 | reproduction
0230 | intelligence
0231 | agency
0232 | ```
0233 | 
0234 | Good.
0235 | 
0236 | We have a definition that gives us an experiment.
0237 | 
0238 | ---
0239 | 
0240 | ## Give the Crystal an Environment
0241 | 
0242 | Our earlier crystal could be written approximately as:
0243 | 
0244 | $$
0245 | C_{t+1}=G(C_t)
0246 | $$
0247 | 
0248 | where (C_t) is the current crystal and (G) is the local growth rule.
0249 | 
0250 | Now we introduce an environmental forcing signal (E_t):
0251 | 
0252 | $$
0253 | C_{t+1}=G(C_t,E_t)
0254 | $$
0255 | 
0256 | The signal does not draw the crystal.
0257 | 
0258 | It does not say:
0259 | 
0260 | ```python
0261 | if signal == "sine":
0262 |     draw_sine_shape()
0263 | ```
0264 | 
0265 | That would merely be a strange plotting library.
0266 | 
0267 | The same growth mechanism must operate under every source.
0268 | 
0269 | The external signal only changes the conditions under which individual local attachment events occur.
0270 | 
0271 | ```mermaid
0272 | flowchart LR
0273 |     E["Environmental signal E(t)"] --> G["Local growth dynamics G(C,E)"]
0274 |     C["Current crystal state C(t)"] --> G
0275 |     G --> C2["Next crystal state C(t+1)"]
0276 |     C2 --> M["Final morphology"]
0277 | ```
0278 | 
0279 | Different input.
0280 | 
0281 | Same growth rule.
0282 | 
0283 | Different result?
0284 | 
0285 | That is our first question.
0286 | 
0287 | ---
0288 | 
0289 | ## The Local Rule
0290 | 
0291 | We retain the axial hexagonal lattice.
0292 | 
0293 | Every cell has six immediate neighbors.
0294 | 
0295 | ```python
0296 | HEX_DIRECTIONS = (
0297 |     (1, 0),
0298 |     (1, -1),
0299 |     (0, -1),
0300 |     (-1, 0),
0301 |     (-1, 1),
0302 |     (0, 1),
0303 | )
0304 | ```
0305 | 
0306 | Growth remains local.
0307 | 
0308 | For every candidate frontier cell, attachment depends on several quantities:
0309 | 
0310 | ```text
0311 | occupied-neighbour count
0312 | fixed lattice anisotropy
0313 | current environmental signal
0314 | local crowding
0315 | stochastic attachment
0316 | ```
0317 | 
0318 | There is no target morphology.
0319 | 
0320 | No global drawing routine.
0321 | 
0322 | No stored answer describing what the crystal should become.
0323 | 
0324 | The signal only affects attachment probability.
0325 | 
0326 | One convenient form is:
0327 | 
0328 | $$
0329 | P(\text{attach})
0330 | =
0331 | \sigma\left(
0332 | a + bn + cE_t + dA - q
0333 | \right)
0334 | $$
0335 | 
0336 | where:
0337 | - \(n\) is occupied-neighbor count,
0338 | - \(E_t\) is the current signal,
0339 | - \(A\) is a fixed local anisotropy term,
0340 | - \(q\) is a crowding penalty,
0341 | - \(\sigma\) maps the result into a probability.
0342 | 
0343 | For Digital Crystal v1 the growth parameters are frozen during the experiment.
0344 | 
0345 | The important experimental constraint is:
0346 | 
0347 | > **The growth mechanism remains fixed while the source changes.**
0348 | 
0349 | Otherwise source recovery would tell us nothing.
0350 | 
0351 | ---
0352 | 
0353 | ## First Make Sure It Still Grows
0354 | 
0355 | Before giving the system interesting signals, give it the least interesting signal possible:
0356 | 
0357 | $$
0358 | E(t)=0
0359 | $$
0360 | 
0361 | Constant.
0362 | 
0363 | No oscillation.
0364 | 
0365 | No changing environment.
0366 | 
0367 | The generalized model should still produce a growing structure.
0368 | 
0369 | It did.
0370 | 
0371 | In the full baseline run the crystal reached approximately:
0372 | 
0373 | ```text
0374 | occupied cells        5,924
0375 | maximum hex radius       44
0376 | boundary edges          552
0377 | ```
0378 | 
0379 | {{< figure
0380 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-01-baseline.png"
0381 | alt="Baseline Digital Crystal grown under a constant zero-valued environmental signal, shown alongside its input signal and population growth."
0382 | caption="Digital Crystal v1 produces a growing structure under constant forcing. This establishes only that the generalized model grows."
0383 | 
0384 | >}}
0385 | 
0386 | This proves very little.
0387 | 
0388 | It does **not** prove that Chapter 11's properties survived.
0389 | 
0390 | It does not establish robustness.
0391 | 
0392 | It does not establish anything resembling life.
0393 | 
0394 | It merely establishes that our generalized model remains a growth process.
0395 | 
0396 | That is enough to continue.
0397 | 
0398 | ---
0399 | 
0400 | ## Six Environments
0401 | 
0402 | Now give exactly the same growth rule six different types of forcing:
0403 | 
0404 | ```text
0405 | constant
0406 | sine
0407 | square
0408 | sawtooth
0409 | white noise
0410 | random walk
0411 | ```
0412 | 
0413 | The individual source instances vary.
0414 | 
0415 | Periods vary.
0416 | 
0417 | Phases vary.
0418 | 
0419 | Noise realizations vary.
0420 | 
0421 | Random walks vary.
0422 | 
0423 | At each growth step the crystal receives only the scalar value currently presented to it.
0424 | 
0425 | For one run:
0426 | 
0427 | $$
0428 | E_t=\sin(\omega t+\phi)
0429 | $$
0430 | 
0431 | Another receives a square wave.
0432 | 
0433 | Another receives white noise.
0434 | 
0435 | Another receives a random walk.
0436 | 
0437 | {{< figure
0438 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-02-source-signals.png"
0439 | alt="Example environmental signals used to drive Digital Crystal growth: constant, sine, square, sawtooth, white noise and random walk."
0440 | caption="Six forcing-process families. Digital Crystal v1 receives only the current scalar environmental value."
0441 | 
0442 | >}}
0443 | 
0444 | Then we let the crystals grow.
0445 | 
0446 | Same model.
0447 | 
0448 | Different environment.
0449 | 
0450 | {{< figure
0451 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-02-source-gallery.png"
0452 | alt="Six Digital Crystals grown using the same local rule but driven by constant, sine, square, sawtooth, white-noise and random-walk signals."
0453 | caption="Same local growth mechanism, different forcing processes. The morphologies appear different, but appearance is only the start of the experiment."
0454 | 
0455 | >}}
0456 | 
0457 | And immediately we encounter the problem that has followed us through this entire book.
0458 | 
0459 | They look different.
0460 | 
0461 | So what?
0462 | 
0463 | ---
0464 | 
0465 | ## Pretty Pictures Are Cheap
0466 | 
0467 | It would be very easy to stop here.
0468 | 
0469 | We could write:
0470 | 
0471 | > Look. Different signals generate different crystals.
0472 | 
0473 | And the chapter would make an attractive demonstration.
0474 | 
0475 | But thirteen chapters have taught us not to do that.
0476 | 
0477 | A picture can suggest a hypothesis.
0478 | 
0479 | It cannot establish the explanation.
0480 | 
0481 | Perhaps one random seed generated a larger structure by chance.
0482 | 
0483 | Perhaps square waves merely produce a larger mean attachment probability.
0484 | 
0485 | Perhaps our eyes are categorizing noise.
0486 | 
0487 | Perhaps the source classes differ in some trivial statistic that becomes encoded as total area.
0488 | 
0489 | We need populations.
0490 | 
0491 | Not examples.
0492 | 
0493 | ---
0494 | 
0495 | ## Six Hundred Crystals
0496 | 
0497 | For the main source-family experiment we generated:
0498 | 
0499 | ```text
0500 | 100 constant
0501 | 100 sine
0502 | 100 square
0503 | 100 sawtooth
0504 | 100 white noise
0505 | 100 random walk
0506 | ```
0507 | 
0508 | A total of:
0509 | 
0510 | ```text
0511 | 600 crystals
0512 | ```
0513 | 
0514 | Each experiment uses:
0515 | 
0516 | ```text
0517 | same Digital Crystal rule
0518 | same experimental horizon
0519 | same measurement system
0520 | different source instance
0521 | different stochastic growth realization
0522 | ```
0523 | 
0524 | Now we stop looking at individual pictures.
0525 | 
0526 | We measure them.
0527 | 
0528 | ```mermaid
0529 | flowchart TD
0530 |     S1["Constant ×100"] --> G["Same fixed growth rule"]
0531 |     S2["Sine ×100"] --> G
0532 |     S3["Square ×100"] --> G
0533 |     S4["Sawtooth ×100"] --> G
0534 |     S5["White noise ×100"] --> G
0535 |     S6["Random walk ×100"] --> G
0536 |     G --> M["Morphology: 42 measured features"]
0537 |     M --> H["Hide source labels"]
0538 |     H --> C["Train on one subset"]
0539 |     C --> T["Test on unseen crystals"]
0540 | ```
0541 | 
0542 | ---
0543 | 
0544 | ## Measure the Morphology
0545 | 
0546 | For every final crystal we extracted 42 morphological measurements.
0547 | 
0548 | They included quantities such as:
0549 | 
0550 | ```text
0551 | area
0552 | perimeter
0553 | maximum radius
0554 | compactness
0555 | boundary roughness
0556 | bounding-box aspect
0557 | centroid displacement
0558 | radial distribution
0559 | angular distribution
0560 | six-fold angular structure
0561 | boundary-radius variation
0562 | ```
0563 | 
0564 | The source signal itself is **not** included.
0565 | 
0566 | The classifier gets:
0567 | 
0568 | ```text
0569 | the final measured crystal
0570 | ```
0571 | 
0572 | not:
0573 | 
0574 | ```text
0575 | the final crystal
0576 | +
0577 | the answer
0578 | ```
0579 | 
0580 | {{< figure
0581 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-05-morphology-metrics.png"
0582 | alt="Distributions of several measured Digital Crystal morphology features across the six source-process families."
0583 | caption="Some measured morphological characteristics differ systematically across forcing-process families."
0584 | 
0585 | >}}
0586 | 
0587 | Already this is more useful than looking at the gallery.
0588 | 
0589 | There are measurable differences.
0590 | 
0591 | But measurable differences still do not tell us how much source information survives.
0592 | 
0593 | ---
0594 | 
0595 | ## Hide the Source
0596 | 
0597 | Imagine I hand you one finished crystal.
0598 | 
0599 | I do not tell you whether it grew under:
0600 | 
0601 | ```text
0602 | sine
0603 | square
0604 | noise
0605 | random walk
0606 | ...
0607 | ```
0608 | 
0609 | Can the forcing family be recovered from morphology alone?
0610 | 
0611 | There are six classes.
0612 | 
0613 | Random guessing succeeds at:
0614 | 
0615 | $$
0616 | \frac{1}{6}\approx16.7%
0617 | $$
0618 | 
0619 | That gives us a clean baseline.
0620 | 
0621 | Train on one part of the crystal population.
0622 | 
0623 | Test on crystals the model has never seen.
0624 | 
0625 | ---
0626 | 
0627 | ## Can We Recover the Source?
0628 | 
0629 | The held-out result was:
0630 | 
0631 | ```text
0632 | chance                 16.7%
0633 | 
0634 | random forest           52.2%
0635 | logistic regression     53.9%
0636 | ```
0637 | 
0638 | {{< figure
0639 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-06-source-accuracy.png"
0640 | alt="Held-out classification accuracy for recovering the source process from Digital Crystal morphology compared with the six-way chance baseline."
0641 | caption="Source-process family can be recovered from held-out Digital Crystal morphology substantially above the 16.7% chance baseline."
0642 | 
0643 | >}}
0644 | 
0645 | Two very different classifier families produce broadly similar performance.
0646 | 
0647 | That matters.
0648 | 
0649 | We are not relying on one unusual model discovering one unusual boundary.
0650 | 
0651 | The confusion matrix shows that the retained information is uneven.
0652 | 
0653 | {{< figure
0654 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-06-source-confusion.png"
0655 | alt="Confusion matrix showing predictions of source-process family from final Digital Crystal morphology."
0656 | caption="Source recovery is substantial but incomplete. Some forcing families leave more distinctive morphological signatures than others."
0657 | 
0658 | >}}
0659 | 
0660 | Now we have a result worth keeping.
0661 | 
0662 | Not:
0663 | 
0664 | > The crystal remembers its history.
0665 | 
0666 | Not:
0667 | 
0668 | > The crystal understands the environment.
0669 | 
0670 | Something much smaller:
0671 | 
0672 | > **The final morphology contains information that makes forcing-process family recoverable substantially above chance.**
0673 | 
0674 | The relationship is:
0675 | 
0676 | ```text
0677 | source process
0678 | ↓
0679 | local stochastic growth
0680 | ↓
0681 | persistent morphology
0682 | ↓
0683 | source family partly recoverable
0684 | ```
0685 | 
0686 | That is evidence for the Digital Crystal definition.
0687 | 
0688 | ---
0689 | 
0690 | ## But What Exactly Was Recovered?
0691 | 
0692 | This is where the experiment becomes interesting.
0693 | 
0694 | Consider sine and square forcing.
0695 | 
0696 | They differ in temporal ordering.
0697 | 
0698 | But they also differ in:
0699 | 
0700 | ```text
0701 | value distribution
0702 | time spent near extrema
0703 | autocorrelation
0704 | transition structure
0705 | possibly other simple statistics
0706 | ```
0707 | 
0708 | So perhaps the classifier is not recovering the temporal process.
0709 | 
0710 | Perhaps it is recovering some broad statistical property of the values experienced during growth.
0711 | 
0712 | That would still be a result.
0713 | 
0714 | But it would be a different result.
0715 | 
0716 | So now we try to destroy the stronger interpretation.
0717 | 
0718 | ---
0719 | 
0720 | ## The Same-Mean Control
0721 | 
0722 | The varying signals were normalized to approximately the same mean.
0723 | 
0724 | The constant control remained zero.
0725 | 
0726 | Yet morphology-class centroids still differed substantially.
0727 | 
0728 | Standardized distances from the constant population were approximately:
0729 | 
0730 | ```text
0731 | sine          4.45
0732 | square       13.82
0733 | saw           2.44
0734 | white noise   2.40
0735 | random walk   1.40
0736 | ```
0737 | 
0738 | So mean forcing alone cannot explain the source-family result.
0739 | 
0740 | Variation matters.
0741 | 
0742 | But this still does not establish that **temporal order** matters.
0743 | 
0744 | ---
0745 | 
0746 | ## Destroy Time
0747 | 
0748 | Take a source sequence:
0749 | 
0750 | ```text
0751 | 0.7
0752 | 0.2
0753 | -0.3
0754 | 0.9
0755 | -0.8
0756 | ...
0757 | ```
0758 | 
0759 | Shuffle it:
0760 | 
0761 | ```text
0762 | -0.3
0763 | 0.9
0764 | 0.7
0765 | -0.8
0766 | 0.2
0767 | ...
0768 | ```
0769 | 
0770 | The shuffled signal preserves:
0771 | 
0772 | ```text
0773 | same values
0774 | same mean
0775 | same variance
0776 | same minimum
0777 | same maximum
0778 | same histogram
0779 | ```
0780 | 
0781 | But its temporal ordering is destroyed.
0782 | 
0783 | So now the hypothesis becomes much cleaner.
0784 | 
0785 | If the final crystal retains recoverable information about chronology, crystals grown from the ordered and shuffled sequences should be distinguishable.
0786 | 
0787 | ```mermaid
0788 | flowchart LR
0789 |     O["Ordered signal"] --> G1["Same growth rule"]
0790 |     S["Shuffled signal\<br/>same values"] --> G2["Same growth rule"]
0791 |     G1 --> M1["Final morphology"]
0792 |     G2 --> M2["Final morphology"]
0793 |     M1 --> C["Can morphology reveal order condition?"]
0794 |     M2 --> C
0795 | ```
0796 | 
0797 | ---
0798 | 
0799 | ## Ordered or Shuffled?
0800 | 
0801 | Binary chance is:
0802 | 
0803 | ```text
0804 | 50%
0805 | ```
0806 | 
0807 | The result:
0808 | 
0809 | ```text
0810 | chance                 50.0%
0811 | 
0812 | random forest           51.3%
0813 | logistic regression     51.7%
0814 | ```
0815 | 
0816 | {{< figure
0817 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-07-order-accuracy.png"
0818 | alt="Classification accuracy for distinguishing crystals grown from ordered signals versus shuffled versions containing the same signal values."
0819 | caption="Ordered-versus-shuffled source histories cannot be recovered above chance in this experiment."
0820 | 
0821 | >}}
0822 | 
0823 | The confusion matrix tells the same story.
0824 | 
0825 | {{< figure
0826 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-07-order-confusion.png"
0827 | alt="Confusion matrix for classifying ordered versus shuffled signal histories from final Digital Crystal morphology."
0828 | caption="The morphology provides no useful separation between ordered and shuffled histories under this protocol."
0829 | 
0830 | >}}
0831 | 
0832 | Under this experiment, neither classifier recovered temporal order above roughly:
0833 | 
0834 | ```text
0835 | 52%
0836 | ```
0837 | 
0838 | That is not evidence of useful sequence recovery.
0839 | 
0840 | And we need to be precise about what this means.
0841 | 
0842 | It does **not** prove that no conceivable measurement could ever recover any temporal information from this model.
0843 | 
0844 | It does establish:
0845 | 
0846 | > **Our morphology representation and classifiers do not recover ordered-versus-shuffled history above chance under this protocol.**
0847 | 
0848 | That is already enough to kill the stronger claim we were drifting toward.
0849 | 
0850 | ---
0851 | 
0852 | ## Maybe the Control Is Still Too Weak
0853 | 
0854 | There is another problem.
0855 | 
0856 | A sine wave and a square wave do not merely differ in ordering.
0857 | 
0858 | Their distributions differ.
0859 | 
0860 | So perhaps the successful source-family classifier is relying primarily on distributional differences.
0861 | 
0862 | We can remove even that possibility.
0863 | 
0864 | Construct a single value multiset:
0865 | 
0866 | $$
0867 | V={v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_{72}}
0868 | $$
0869 | 
0870 | Now every source receives **exactly the same values**.
0871 | 
0872 | Not approximately the same distribution.
0873 | 
0874 | Not merely the same mean and variance.
0875 | 
0876 | Exactly the same multiset.
0877 | 
0878 | Only the temporal arrangement changes.
0879 | 
0880 | ---
0881 | 
0882 | ## Six Ways to Arrange the Same World
0883 | 
0884 | Using one fixed set of values, create several temporal organizations:
0885 | 
0886 | ```text
0887 | RANDOM
0888 | random permutation
0889 | 
0890 | BLOCK
0891 | low values grouped, then high values grouped
0892 | 
0893 | ALTERNATING
0894 | low, high, low, high...
0895 | 
0896 | SMOOTH
0897 | neighboring values change gradually
0898 | 
0899 | BURST
0900 | quiet periods interrupted by concentrated excursions
0901 | 
0902 | PERIODIC
0903 | values arranged into a repeating temporal motif
0904 | ```
0905 | 
0906 | Every source contains exactly the same samples.
0907 | 
0908 | {{< figure
0909 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-09-matched-temporal-signals.png"
0910 | alt="Six temporal organizations built from exactly the same set of input values: random, block, alternating, smooth, burst and periodic."
0911 | caption="Exactly the same values, reorganized in time. Distribution is held fixed; temporal organization changes."
0912 | 
0913 | >}}
0914 | 
0915 | Then grow crystals again.
0916 | 
0917 | Frozen model.
0918 | 
0919 | No parameter tuning.
0920 | 
0921 | No attempt to rescue the hypothesis.
0922 | 
0923 | {{< figure
0924 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-09-matched-temporal-crystals.png"
0925 | alt="Digital Crystals grown from six differently ordered signals containing exactly the same input values."
0926 | caption="The temporal forcing histories differ radically, but their final morphologies are much harder to distinguish."
0927 | 
0928 | >}}
0929 | 
0930 | There is another important safeguard.
0931 | 
0932 | All temporal arrangements created from one value set remain together during train/test splitting.
0933 | 
0934 | The classifier cannot train on one ordering of value set A and then be tested on another ordering of that same value set.
0935 | 
0936 | Held-out value sets are genuinely unseen.
0937 | 
0938 | That prevents a subtle leakage path.
0939 | 
0940 | ---
0941 | 
0942 | ## The Stronger Temporal Experiment Fails Too
0943 | 
0944 | When the value multiset is held exactly constant, temporal organization is not recoverable above chance under the tested classifiers.
0945 | 
0946 | This is the sharper negative result.
0947 | 
0948 | The positive source-family result is therefore **not evidence that Digital Crystal v1 is a chronological recorder**.
0949 | 
0950 | Whatever source information survives is much more compatible with:
0951 | 
0952 | ```text
0953 | distributional characteristics
0954 | +
0955 | aggregate forcing statistics
0956 | +
0957 | interaction with stochastic growth
0958 | ```
0959 | 
0960 | than with:
0961 | 
0962 | ```text
0963 | recoverable temporal sequence
0964 | ```
0965 | 
0966 | The crystal had a state.
0967 | 
0968 | It did not have a recoverable history.
0969 | 
0970 | ---
0971 | 
0972 | ## A Crystal Is Not a Tape Recorder
0973 | 
0974 | This is where the result becomes better than the idea we started with.
0975 | 
0976 | We initially imagined:
0977 | 
0978 | ```text
0979 | environmental history
0980 | ↓
0981 | crystal
0982 | ↓
0983 | history written into morphology
0984 | ```
0985 | 
0986 | That was too strong.
0987 | 
0988 | What the experiment supports is closer to:
0989 | 
0990 | ```text
0991 | environmental statistics
0992 | ↓
0993 | local dynamics
0994 | ↓
0995 | persistent morphology
0996 | ```
0997 | 
0998 | The exact sequence is largely lost under the measurements and classifiers we tested.
0999 | 
1000 | Some broader characteristics survive.
1001 | 
1002 | That is strangely crystal-like.
1003 | 
1004 | Inspect a physical crystal and its structure may reveal something about the conditions under which it formed.
1005 | 
1006 | It does not necessarily contain a frame-by-frame movie of formation.
1007 | 
1008 | Our Digital Crystal appears closer to that.
1009 | 
1010 | A morphological statistic.
1011 | 
1012 | Not a tape recorder.
1013 | 
1014 | ---
1015 | 
1016 | ## Robustness
1017 | 
1018 | There is still another danger.
1019 | 
1020 | Perhaps source recovery occurs only at one carefully selected environmental forcing strength.
1021 | 
1022 | So we varied the forcing strength while leaving the rest of the local growth mechanism unchanged.
1023 | 
1024 | Held-out random-forest source-classification accuracy was:
1025 | 
1026 | ```text
1027 | forcing         accuracy
1028 | 
1029 | 0.75             34.1%
1030 | 0.85             43.2%
1031 | 0.95             50.0%
1032 | 1.00             52.3%
1033 | 1.05             52.3%
1034 | 1.15             63.6%
1035 | 1.25             43.2%
1036 | ```
1037 | 
1038 | Chance remains:
1039 | 
1040 | ```text
1041 | 16.7%
1042 | ```
1043 | 
1044 | {{< figure
1045 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch14-08-robustness.png"
1046 | alt="Held-out source classification accuracy across several Digital Crystal forcing strengths."
1047 | caption="Source-family recovery remains above chance across the tested forcing-strength sweep, although the small sweep is noisy and should not be interpreted as a smooth response curve."
1048 | 
1049 | >}}
1050 | 
1051 | We need to be disciplined here.
1052 | 
1053 | The sweep is noisy.
1054 | 
1055 | There is no clean monotonic trend.
1056 | 
1057 | `1.15` happens to perform much better than `1.25`.
1058 | 
1059 | So we should **not** say:
1060 | 
1061 | > Increasing forcing predictably increases recoverability.
1062 | 
1063 | We have not shown that.
1064 | 
1065 | The surviving claim is narrower:
1066 | 
1067 | > **Source-family information remains recoverable above chance at every tested forcing strength in this sweep.**
1068 | 
1069 | That suggests the phenomenon is not confined to exactly one parameter value.
1070 | 
1071 | It does **not** establish a scaling law.
1072 | 
1073 | It does not tell us what the optimal forcing strength is.
1074 | 
1075 | And this experiment is too small to infer the shape of the response curve.
1076 | 
1077 | That is enough.
1078 | 
1079 | ---
1080 | 
1081 | ## What Have We Actually Built?
1082 | 
1083 | We began with a metaphor:
1084 | 
1085 | ```text
1086 | DIGITAL CRYSTAL
1087 | ```
1088 | 
1089 | Then gave it a provisional operational definition:
1090 | 
1091 | > **A local computational growth process in which characteristics of an external input become expressed as persistent, measurable morphology.**
1092 | 
1093 | That definition survives.
1094 | 
1095 | A stronger version does not.
1096 | 
1097 | We cannot say:
1098 | 
1099 | > The crystal records its temporal history.
1100 | 
1101 | We tried.
1102 | 
1103 | The evidence did not support it.
1104 | 
1105 | That failure makes the definition cleaner.
1106 | 
1107 | ---
1108 | 
1109 | ## A Better Computational Definition
1110 | 
1111 | Let (C_t) denote the complete crystal state.
1112 | 
1113 | Let (E_t) denote environmental forcing.
1114 | 
1115 | Let (G) denote the fixed local stochastic growth dynamics.
1116 | 
1117 | Then:
1118 | 
1119 | $$
1120 | C_{t+1}=G(C_t,E_t)
1121 | $$
1122 | 
1123 | At experimental horizon (T), morphology is measured through:
1124 | 
1125 | $$
1126 | M_T=\Phi(C_T)
1127 | $$
1128 | 
1129 | where (\Phi) extracts the morphological measurements.
1130 | 
1131 | Our source-family experiment establishes:
1132 | 
1133 | $$
1134 | M_T
1135 | \rightarrow
1136 | \text{recoverable information about source family}
1137 | $$
1138 | 
1139 | substantially above chance.
1140 | 
1141 | But the matched-value temporal experiment does **not** establish:
1142 | 
1143 | $$
1144 | M_T
1145 | \rightarrow
1146 | \text{recoverable temporal ordering}
1147 | $$
1148 | 
1149 | So our current evidence supports:
1150 | 
1151 | ```text
1152 | SOURCE CHARACTERISTICS
1153 |        ↓
1154 | LOCAL DYNAMICS
1155 |        ↓
1156 | MORPHOLOGY
1157 |        ↓
1158 | PARTIAL SOURCE RECOVERY
1159 | ```
1160 | 
1161 | but not:
1162 | 
1163 | ```text
1164 | COMPLETE TEMPORAL HISTORY
1165 |        ↓
1166 | MORPHOLOGY
1167 |        ↓
1168 | HISTORY RECOVERABLE
1169 | ```
1170 | 
1171 | That distinction matters enormously.
1172 | 
1173 | Because it tells us what the crystal is missing.
1174 | 
1175 | ---
1176 | 
1177 | ## A Picture Made by a Process
1178 | 
1179 | There is also a practical implication.
1180 | 
1181 | A Digital Crystal can function as a generative visualization.
1182 | 
1183 | Feed it:
1184 | 
1185 | ```text
1186 | software metrics
1187 | network traffic
1188 | model activity
1189 | market data
1190 | music
1191 | weather
1192 | sensor data
1193 | mathematical functions
1194 | ```
1195 | 
1196 | and let those signals influence formation.
1197 | 
1198 | A conventional graph usually performs something like:
1199 | 
1200 | ```text
1201 | value
1202 | ↓
1203 | coordinate
1204 | ↓
1205 | pixel
1206 | ```
1207 | 
1208 | The Digital Crystal instead performs:
1209 | 
1210 | ```text
1211 | value
1212 | ↓
1213 | local attachment conditions
1214 | ↓
1215 | many stochastic local interactions
1216 | ↓
1217 | persistent morphology
1218 | ```
1219 | 
1220 | The result is not directly drawn from the signal.
1221 | 
1222 | It is **grown under its influence**.
1223 | 
1224 | That may make it useful as art.
1225 | 
1226 | It may make it useful as telemetry.
1227 | 
1228 | It may make it useful as a regime visualization.
1229 | 
1230 | But those are possible applications.
1231 | 
1232 | They are not the scientific claim of this chapter.
1233 | 
1234 | ---
1235 | 
1236 | ## Could a Software System Grow a Crystal?
1237 | 
1238 | Imagine a running service emits measurements every few seconds:
1239 | 
1240 | ```text
1241 | latency
1242 | errors
1243 | test state
1244 | queue depth
1245 | memory pressure
1246 | ```
1247 | 
1248 | Instead of drawing another conventional dashboard, allow those signals to influence a Digital Crystal.
1249 | 
1250 | At the end of the day we have:
1251 | 
1252 | > **the day's crystal**
1253 | 
1254 | Days with different statistical regimes may produce different morphologies.
1255 | 
1256 | A healthy system may produce a different morphological distribution from a noisy or persistently degraded one.
1257 | 
1258 | We now have experimental reason to think this kind of mapping is plausible.
1259 | 
1260 | But we also know an important limitation.
1261 | 
1262 | Suppose two days contain approximately the same set of values in different temporal order.
1263 | 
1264 | Digital Crystal v1 may not distinguish them.
1265 | 
1266 | That is not an inconvenience to hide.
1267 | 
1268 | It is a property of the model we have measured.
1269 | 
1270 | ---
1271 | 
1272 | ## The Crystal Has State
1273 | 
1274 | There is a subtle point here.
1275 | 
1276 | The crystal obviously has state.
1277 | 
1278 | At time (t), (C_t) depends on earlier attachment events.
1279 | 
1280 | A cell added at step 10 may still exist at step 70.
1281 | 
1282 | Past events contributed causally to the present.
1283 | 
1284 | But that does not imply that the present is a useful record of the past.
1285 | 
1286 | This experiment gives us a distinction we are going to need:
1287 | 
1288 | > **Past contributed to present does not imply present preserves the order of the past.**
1289 | 
1290 | Those are different properties.
1291 | 
1292 | We now have evidence separating them.
1293 | 
1294 | ---
1295 | 
1296 | ## State Is Not History
1297 | 
1298 | Consider two sequences:
1299 | 
1300 | ```text
1301 | A B C D
1302 | ```
1303 | 
1304 | and:
1305 | 
1306 | ```text
1307 | D B A C
1308 | ```
1309 | 
1310 | Both can influence a process.
1311 | 
1312 | Both can alter its final state.
1313 | 
1314 | But suppose the final state contains no recoverable information allowing us to distinguish which ordering occurred.
1315 | 
1316 | Then the process accumulated consequences without retaining recoverable chronology.
1317 | 
1318 | That is approximately where Digital Crystal v1 stands.
1319 | 
1320 | It has a **state**.
1321 | 
1322 | We have not yet demonstrated a **history**.
1323 | 
1324 | ```mermaid
1325 | flowchart LR
1326 |     P["Past events"] -->|causal influence| S["Current state"]
1327 |     S --> Q{"Can temporal order\<br/>be reconstructed?"}
1328 |     Q -- Yes --> H["History retained"]
1329 |     Q -- No --> N["State without demonstrated history"]
1330 | ```
1331 | 
1332 | That gives us the next experimental problem.
1333 | 
1334 | ---
1335 | 
1336 | ## Evidence Ledger
1337 | 
1338 | ### SUPPORTED — Source Information in Morphology
1339 | 
1340 | Across 600 crystals, forcing-process family could be recovered from morphology substantially above six-way chance:
1341 | 
1342 | ```text
1343 | random forest           52.2%
1344 | logistic regression     53.9%
1345 | chance                   16.7%
1346 | ```
1347 | 
1348 | So we can support:
1349 | 
1350 | > **A fixed local computational growth process can transform differences in forcing environment into persistent morphological differences containing recoverable source-family information.**
1351 | 
1352 | ---
1353 | 
1354 | ### SUPPORTED — Mean Alone Does Not Explain the Effect
1355 | 
1356 | The varying source processes were approximately mean-normalized, while their morphology populations remained measurably distinct.
1357 | 
1358 | So:
1359 | 
1360 | > **The source-family result is not explained solely by average forcing value.**
1361 | 
1362 | ---
1363 | 
1364 | ### SUPPORTED — Effect Is Not Confined to One Tested Forcing Strength
1365 | 
1366 | Source-family recovery remained above chance at every tested value in the seven-point forcing-strength sweep.
1367 | 
1368 | But the sweep is noisy.
1369 | 
1370 | So we can claim:
1371 | 
1372 | > **The effect survives moderate parameter variation in the tested sweep.**
1373 | 
1374 | We cannot claim:
1375 | 
1376 | ```text
1377 | a monotonic relationship
1378 | an optimum forcing strength
1379 | a scaling law
1380 | ```
1381 | 
1382 | ---
1383 | 
1384 | ### FAILED — Final Morphology Recovers Temporal Order
1385 | 
1386 | Ordered-versus-shuffled classification gave:
1387 | 
1388 | ```text
1389 | random forest           51.3%
1390 | logistic regression     51.7%
1391 | chance                   50.0%
1392 | ```
1393 | 
1394 | A stronger experiment in which every condition contained exactly the same input multiset also failed to establish recoverable temporal organization.
1395 | 
1396 | So:
1397 | 
1398 | > **We do not find evidence that final morphology preserves temporal order in a form recoverable by the tested feature representation and classifiers.**
1399 | 
1400 | ---
1401 | 
1402 | ### NOT ESTABLISHED — History
1403 | 
1404 | The crystal's present state depends causally on previous events.
1405 | 
1406 | That alone does not establish a recoverable history.
1407 | 
1408 | So:
1409 | 
1410 | ```text
1411 | state                 SUPPORTED
1412 | recoverable chronology NOT SUPPORTED
1413 | history               NOT YET ESTABLISHED
1414 | ```
1415 | 
1416 | ---
1417 | 
1418 | ### NOT CLAIMED
1419 | 
1420 | We cannot claim that the crystal:
1421 | 
1422 | ```text
1423 | learns
1424 | adapts
1425 | understands
1426 | has goals
1427 | has memory in the strong sense
1428 | reproduces
1429 | is an organism
1430 | is alive
1431 | ```
1432 | 
1433 | Nor can we claim that Digital Crystal v1 inherits every property of the Chapter 11 crystal.
1434 | 
1435 | Different model.
1436 | 
1437 | Different experiment.
1438 | 
1439 | Different claims.
1440 | 
1441 | ---
1442 | 
1443 | ## What Survived?
1444 | 
1445 | At the beginning of this chapter we proposed:
1446 | 
1447 | > **A Digital Crystal is a local computational growth process in which characteristics of an external input become expressed as persistent, measurable morphology.**
1448 | 
1449 | That survives.
1450 | 
1451 | The experiment supports:
1452 | 
1453 | ```text
1454 | environment
1455 | ↓
1456 | local computation
1457 | ↓
1458 | persistent form
1459 | ↓
1460 | some information about environment remains
1461 | ```
1462 | 
1463 | The stronger idea:
1464 | 
1465 | ```text
1466 | environmental sequence
1467 | ↓
1468 | persistent form
1469 | ↓
1470 | chronology recoverable
1471 | ```
1472 | 
1473 | did not survive.
1474 | 
1475 | That distinction is now part of the definition.
1476 | 
1477 | ---
1478 | 
1479 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
1480 | 
1481 | The stronger hypothesis in this chapter failed.
1482 | 
1483 | We began with an idea close to:
1484 | 
1485 | ```text
1486 | environmental history
1487 | ↓
1488 | growth
1489 | ↓
1490 | final morphology
1491 | ↓
1492 | history recoverable
1493 | ```
1494 | 
1495 | That was too strong.
1496 | 
1497 | The source-family experiment succeeded:
1498 | 
1499 | ```text
1500 | random forest          52.2%
1501 | logistic regression    53.9%
1502 | chance                  16.7%
1503 | ```
1504 | 
1505 | So the final morphology retained substantial information about the **kind of forcing process** under which the crystal formed.
1506 | 
1507 | But when temporal order was isolated, the signal disappeared.
1508 | 
1509 | For ordered-versus-shuffled histories:
1510 | 
1511 | ```text
1512 | random forest          51.3%
1513 | logistic regression    51.7%
1514 | chance                  50.0%
1515 | ```
1516 | 
1517 | And when every condition received exactly the same value multiset and only temporal organization changed, the stronger temporal experiment failed as well.
1518 | 
1519 | So Chapter 14 leaves us with a sharper distinction:
1520 | 
1521 | ```text
1522 | COARSE SOURCE CHARACTERISTICS
1523 | RECOVERABLE
1524 | 
1525 | EXACT TEMPORAL ORDER
1526 | NOT RECOVERED
1527 | ```
1528 | 
1529 | The failed chronology claim does not erase the source-family result.
1530 | 
1531 | It tells us what kind of information the substrate preferentially preserves.
1532 | 
1533 | ### Phenomenon record
1534 | 
1535 | **Phenomenon:** Lossy history integration
1536 | 
1537 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
1538 | 
1539 | **Current bounded description:**
1540 | 
1541 | > Digital Crystal v1 transforms external forcing into persistent morphology that preserves enough information for source-family recovery substantially above chance, while the tested final-state representation does not preserve temporal order in a recoverable form.
1542 | 
1543 | The simplest mechanistic picture is:
1544 | 
1545 | ```text
1546 | external forcing
1547 | ↓
1548 | many irreversible local attachment events
1549 | ↓
1550 | aggregate structural bias
1551 | ↓
1552 | persistent morphology
1553 | ```
1554 | 
1555 | The process integrates consequences of the past.
1556 | 
1557 | But integration is lossy.
1558 | 
1559 | It appears to preserve some broad statistics of the forcing process more readily than exact chronology.
1560 | 
1561 | That gives us a provisional cross-chapter principle:
1562 | 
1563 | > **Irreversible growth can preserve coarse historical structure while discarding fine temporal identity.**
1564 | 
1565 | We should not yet treat this as a universal law of Digital Crystals.
1566 | 
1567 | For now it is a substrate-level principle supported by this chapter and available for comparison with later experiments.
1568 | 
1569 | ### Information hierarchy exposed by this chapter
1570 | 
1571 | Chapter 14 separates several different levels of historical information:
1572 | 
1573 | ```text
1574 | past affected present
1575 |         SUPPORTED
1576 | 
1577 | source family recoverable
1578 |         SUPPORTED
1579 | 
1580 | mean alone explains source effect
1581 |         FAILED
1582 | 
1583 | exact temporal order recoverable
1584 |         NOT SUPPORTED
1585 | 
1586 | complete chronology retained
1587 |         NOT ESTABLISHED
1588 | ```
1589 | 
1590 | That hierarchy matters.
1591 | 
1592 | A process can be history-dependent without being a history recorder.
1593 | 
1594 | A final state can contain information about past conditions without preserving the sequence in which those conditions occurred.
1595 | 
1596 | So:
1597 | 
1598 | ```text
1599 | HISTORY-DEPENDENT
1600 | ≠
1601 | HISTORY-READABLE
1602 | ```
1603 | 
1604 | and:
1605 | 
1606 | ```text
1607 | STATE
1608 | ≠
1609 | CHRONOLOGY
1610 | ```
1611 | 
1612 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
1613 | 
1614 | The surviving phenomenon does **not** establish:
1615 | 
1616 | - memory in the strong sense,
1617 | - learning,
1618 | - adaptation,
1619 | - interpretation of the environment,
1620 | - a stored event log,
1621 | - sender identity,
1622 | - exact chronology,
1623 | - or life.
1624 | 
1625 | It establishes something narrower:
1626 | 
1627 | > **The substrate behaves as a lossy integrator of environmental history: broad characteristics of forcing can survive in morphology even when exact temporal ordering does not.**
1628 | 
1629 | This phenomenon should now be tracked independently of the chapter's failed chronology hypothesis.
1630 | 
1631 | ---
1632 | 
1633 | ## The Useful Failure
1634 | 
1635 | This may be the most important result in the chapter.
1636 | 
1637 | We wanted to ask the crystal:
1638 | 
1639 | > What happened to you?
1640 | 
1641 | The crystal could answer something weaker:
1642 | 
1643 | > I can tell you something about the kind of conditions under which I formed.
1644 | 
1645 | Then we asked:
1646 | 
1647 | > Fine. What happened first?
1648 | 
1649 | And under the experiments we performed, the answer was effectively:
1650 | 
1651 | > I don't know.
1652 | 
1653 | That is not the end of the Digital Crystal.
1654 | 
1655 | It identifies the next missing capability.
1656 | 
1657 | The crystal has a present.
1658 | 
1659 | It does not yet have a usable past.
1660 | 
1661 | So perhaps the next step is not to make it intelligent.
1662 | 
1663 | Not to give it goals.
1664 | 
1665 | Not to give it reproduction.
1666 | 
1667 | Not to give it learning.
1668 | 
1669 | Something much smaller.
1670 | 
1671 | Give it a way to **keep what happened**.
1672 | 
1673 | Not interpret it.
1674 | 
1675 | Not learn from it.
1676 | 
1677 | Not decide what it means.
1678 | 
1679 | Just preserve enough information that the past can still be distinguished from another possible past.
1680 | 
1681 | Because before a process can do anything with history, there must be some history left.
1682 | 
1683 | ---
1684 | 
1685 | ## The Digital Crystal
1686 | 
1687 | We began this chapter with a name.
1688 | 
1689 | Now the name has earned a little more weight.
1690 | 
1691 | A Digital Crystal is not a crystalline picture.
1692 | 
1693 | It is not a cellular automaton merely because it grows on a lattice.
1694 | 
1695 | It is not a primitive animal.
1696 | 
1697 | It is not our attempt to recreate biological life.
1698 | 
1699 | For now:
1700 | 
1701 | > **A Digital Crystal is a local computational growth process in which characteristics of an external input become expressed as persistent, measurable morphology.**
1702 | 
1703 | The definition is small.
1704 | 
1705 | That is intentional.
1706 | 
1707 | The experiments support it.
1708 | 
1709 | The stronger claims failed.
1710 | 
1711 | ```mermaid
1712 | flowchart TD
1713 |     A["ENVIRONMENTAL INPUT"] --> B["FIXED LOCAL DYNAMICS"]
1714 |     B --> C["DIGITAL CRYSTAL"]
1715 |     C --> D["PERSISTENT MORPHOLOGY"]
1716 |     D --> E["SOURCE-FAMILY INFORMATION RECOVERABLE"]
1717 |     D --> F["TEMPORAL ORDER NOT RECOVERED"]
1718 | ```
1719 | 
1720 | The crystal can tell us something about the world that formed it.
1721 | 
1722 | It cannot yet tell us what happened first.
1723 | 
1724 | **So next, we give the crystal a past.**
```

```markdown

0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | At the end of the last chapter, our Digital Crystal could tell us something about the world that formed it.
0013 | 
0014 | But not enough.
0015 | 
0016 | Different forcing processes produced different morphologies.
0017 | 
0018 | We could hide the source and recover its family substantially better than chance.
0019 | 
0020 | Then we asked a harder question:
0021 | 
0022 | > What happened first?
0023 | 
0024 | We took exactly the same environmental values and rearranged them in time.
0025 | 
0026 | Smooth.
0027 | 
0028 | Bursting.
0029 | 
0030 | Periodic.
0031 | 
0032 | Alternating.
0033 | 
0034 | Random.
0035 | 
0036 | The final morphology could not reliably tell them apart.
0037 | 
0038 | ```text
0039 | SAME VALUES
0040 | +
0041 | DIFFERENT ORDER
0042 | ↓
0043 | NO RECOVERABLE TEMPORAL SIGNATURE
0044 | ```
0045 | 
0046 | The crystal had accumulated a state.
0047 | 
0048 | It had not preserved a usable history.
0049 | 
0050 | That gives us the next experiment.
0051 | 
0052 | Not intelligence.
0053 | 
0054 | Not learning.
0055 | 
0056 | Not adaptation.
0057 | 
0058 | Something much smaller.
0059 | 
0060 | > **What must a digital process preserve if we want its past to survive?**
0061 | 
0062 | ---
0063 | 
0064 | ## The Present Is Not the Past
0065 | 
0066 | Our Digital Crystal already has a present state.
0067 | 
0068 | At any moment, (C_t) contains the cells that currently exist.
0069 | 
0070 | Those cells are consequences of earlier growth.
0071 | 
0072 | So the past clearly mattered.
0073 | 
0074 | But Chapter 14 taught us an important distinction:
0075 | 
0076 | > **Past contributed to present does not imply present contains a recoverable record of the past.**
0077 | 
0078 | A footprint exists because someone walked there.
0079 | 
0080 | The footprint is not the walk.
0081 | 
0082 | A crater exists because something struck the ground.
0083 | 
0084 | The crater is not the complete trajectory of the object that made it.
0085 | 
0086 | Our crystal is similar.
0087 | 
0088 | Its current shape contains consequences.
0089 | 
0090 | That does not mean it contains the sequence that produced them.
0091 | 
0092 | So we need to separate two ideas:
0093 | 
0094 | ```text
0095 | STATE
0096 | and
0097 | HISTORY
0098 | ```
0099 | 
0100 | ---
0101 | 
0102 | ## State
0103 | 
0104 | We begin with an operational definition:
0105 | 
0106 | > **A state representation is sufficient if it contains enough information to continue the process faithfully from here.**
0107 | 
0108 | That wording matters.
0109 | 
0110 | We are **not** claiming that we already know the mathematically smallest possible state.
0111 | 
0112 | We are asking whether a particular stored representation is sufficient.
0113 | 
0114 | Perhaps the picture itself is enough.
0115 | 
0116 | Perhaps:
0117 | 
0118 | ```text
0119 | occupied cells
0120 | ```
0121 | 
0122 | is the complete state.
0123 | 
0124 | We can test that.
0125 | 
0126 | Digital Crystal v1 is stochastic.
0127 | 
0128 | Its continuation depends on random attachment decisions.
0129 | 
0130 | Its continuation also depends on where the process currently is in the environmental input.
0131 | 
0132 | So a candidate checkpoint might contain:
0133 | 
0134 | ```text
0135 | occupied cells
0136 | birth-time metadata
0137 | current timestep
0138 | current signal position
0139 | random-number-generator state
0140 | model parameters
0141 | ```
0142 | 
0143 | But we should not declare all of those necessary merely because they sound plausible.
0144 | 
0145 | We should remove them.
0146 | 
0147 | One at a time.
0148 | 
0149 | ---
0150 | 
0151 | ## Run the Crystal Continuously
0152 | 
0153 | We take frozen Digital Crystal v1 from Chapter 14.
0154 | 
0155 | The local growth rule does not change.
0156 | 
0157 | The experiment runs for:
0158 | 
0159 | ```text
0160 | 96 steps
0161 | ```
0162 | 
0163 | with a checkpoint halfway through:
0164 | 
0165 | ```text
0166 | t = 48
0167 | ```
0168 | 
0169 | In the full v3 experiment:
0170 | 
0171 | ```text
0172 | population at checkpoint    2,702
0173 | final population            9,574
0174 | ```
0175 | 
0176 | The final morphology receives a hash:
0177 | 
0178 | ```text
0179 | bc8e6d8c9783431f1459bf17
0180 | ```
0181 | 
0182 | and the full process state receives another:
0183 | 
0184 | ```text
0185 | bd33c9aa0a510803be6ce6bf
0186 | ```
0187 | 
0188 | {{< figure
0189 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-01-reference-and-checkpoint.png"
0190 | alt="The Chapter 15 Digital Crystal input signal with a checkpoint at step 48, together with the crystal at the checkpoint and its final state at step 96."
0191 | caption="The continuous reference trajectory. The midpoint checkpoint will be restored, damaged and replayed in later experiments."
0192 | 
0193 | >}}
0194 | 
0195 | Now we can demand something much stronger than visual similarity.
0196 | 
0197 | If the checkpoint is sufficient, then restoring it should produce:
0198 | 
0199 | > **exactly the same future.**
0200 | 
0201 | ---
0202 | 
0203 | ## Before We Could Save the State, We Found a Hidden One
0204 | 
0205 | Our first implementation failed this experiment.
0206 | 
0207 | The checkpoint appeared complete.
0208 | 
0209 | We saved:
0210 | 
0211 | ```text
0212 | occupied cells
0213 | birth metadata
0214 | timestep
0215 | signal cursor
0216 | RNG state
0217 | ```
0218 | 
0219 | Then we restored it.
0220 | 
0221 | The future changed.
0222 | 
0223 | At first that looked like evidence that something important was missing from our checkpoint.
0224 | 
0225 | But another result contradicted that interpretation.
0226 | 
0227 | When we reconstructed the same checkpoint **without passing through serialization**, continuation was exact.
0228 | 
0229 | So something was happening at the implementation boundary.
0230 | 
0231 | The culprit was surprisingly mundane.
0232 | 
0233 | Candidate attachment sites were held in a Python `set`.
0234 | 
0235 | The growth loop effectively did:
0236 | 
0237 | ```python
0238 | for cell in frontier:
0239 |     ...
0240 |     rng.random()
0241 | ```
0242 | 
0243 | A set has no scientific ordering.
0244 | 
0245 | Its internal iteration order is an implementation detail.
0246 | 
0247 | Two sets can contain exactly the same cells but iterate them in different orders after reconstruction.
0248 | 
0249 | That meant:
0250 | 
0251 | ```text
0252 | same mathematical cells
0253 | +
0254 | same RNG state
0255 | +
0256 | same signal
0257 | ```
0258 | 
0259 | could still become:
0260 | 
0261 | ```text
0262 | RNG draw #1 → different candidate
0263 | RNG draw #2 → different candidate
0264 | ...
0265 | ```
0266 | 
0267 | The simulation had accidentally acquired an undeclared state variable:
0268 | 
0269 | ```text
0270 | PYTHON CONTAINER LAYOUT
0271 | ```
0272 | 
0273 | That is not a property of the Digital Crystal.
0274 | 
0275 | It is a property of the implementation.
0276 | 
0277 | So we removed it.
0278 | 
0279 | The growth rule now consumes stochastic decisions in a canonical order:
0280 | 
0281 | ```python
0282 | for cell in sorted(frontier):
0283 | ```
0284 | 
0285 | Then we reran the experiment.
0286 | 
0287 | ---
0288 | 
0289 | ## State Belonging to the Model vs State Belonging to the Program
0290 | 
0291 | Before trusting checkpointing again, we added a stronger invariant.
0292 | 
0293 | Take a checkpoint.
0294 | 
0295 | Serialize and deserialize:
0296 | 
0297 | ```text
0298 | occupied cells
0299 | birth metadata
0300 | RNG state
0301 | ```
0302 | 
0303 | into fresh Python objects.
0304 | 
0305 | Then compare the original state and reconstructed state.
0306 | 
0307 | They must produce:
0308 | 
0309 | ```text
0310 | same one-step continuation
0311 | and
0312 | same complete remaining continuation
0313 | ```
0314 | 
0315 | The v3 reproducibility invariant passed:
0316 | 
0317 | ```text
0318 | occupied state equal                   True
0319 | birth metadata equal                   True
0320 | signal cursor equal                    True
0321 | RNG state equal                        True
0322 | process hash equal                     True
0323 | 
0324 | one-step continuation exact            True
0325 | full remaining horizon exact           True
0326 | remaining steps checked                48
0327 | ```
0328 | 
0329 | The implementation no longer depends on accidental set layout.
0330 | 
0331 | That gives us a methodological rule worth keeping:
0332 | 
0333 | > **An experimental model must distinguish state belonging to the phenomenon from state accidentally belonging to its implementation.**
0334 | 
0335 | Only after that did checkpointing become a meaningful experiment.
0336 | 
0337 | ---
0338 | 
0339 | ## Stop It
0340 | 
0341 | At step `48` we serialize the operating state.
0342 | 
0343 | Not a screenshot.
0344 | 
0345 | Not a rendered image.
0346 | 
0347 | The actual continuation representation.
0348 | 
0349 | Then we terminate that runtime state.
0350 | 
0351 | Load the checkpoint from SQLite.
0352 | 
0353 | Continue.
0354 | 
0355 | If our checkpoint representation is sufficient, the restored process should not merely resemble the uninterrupted one.
0356 | 
0357 | It should become:
0358 | 
0359 | ```text
0360 | the same cells
0361 | the same attachment decisions
0362 | the same population trajectory
0363 | the same final process state
0364 | ```
0365 | 
0366 | ---
0367 | 
0368 | ## Save, Restore, Continue
0369 | 
0370 | After the reproducibility fix:
0371 | 
0372 | ```text
0373 | exact final morphology            True
0374 | exact final process state         True
0375 | population trajectory identical   True
0376 | attachment trajectory identical   True
0377 | symmetric-difference cells        0
0378 | ```
0379 | 
0380 | The morphology hashes match:
0381 | 
0382 | ```text
0383 | REFERENCE   bc8e6d8c9783431f1459bf17
0384 | RESTORED    bc8e6d8c9783431f1459bf17
0385 | ```
0386 | 
0387 | The complete process hashes match too.
0388 | 
0389 | {{< figure
0390 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-02-exact-restore.png"
0391 | alt="The final continuously run Digital Crystal beside the final crystal produced after checkpoint, SQLite restore and continuation."
0392 | caption="After canonicalizing stochastic candidate traversal, continuous execution and checkpoint → restore → continue produce the exact same trajectory."
0393 | 
0394 | >}}
0395 | 
0396 | And this was not a one-run accident.
0397 | 
0398 | We repeated the checkpoint experiment across:
0399 | 
0400 | ```text
0401 | 30 independent runs
0402 | ```
0403 | 
0404 | Result:
0405 | 
0406 | ```text
0407 | 30 / 30 exact
0408 | ```
0409 | 
0410 | So we have earned the first major claim:
0411 | 
0412 | > **The stored Digital Crystal checkpoint representation is sufficient for exact continuation of the stochastic process.**
0413 | 
0414 | Notice what we have **not** claimed.
0415 | 
0416 | We have not proven that this is the smallest possible state representation.
0417 | 
0418 | That question remains open.
0419 | 
0420 | ---
0421 | 
0422 | ## What Actually Matters for Continuation?
0423 | 
0424 | Now we deliberately damage the checkpoint.
0425 | 
0426 | But this time the experiments are carefully isolated.
0427 | 
0428 | Every variant receives exactly:
0429 | 
0430 | ```text
0431 | 48 continuation updates
0432 | ```
0433 | 
0434 | So altering the environmental cursor does not accidentally alter the length of the experiment.
0435 | 
0436 | ---
0437 | 
0438 | ## Remove the Random State
0439 | 
0440 | First:
0441 | 
0442 | ```text
0443 | same morphology
0444 | same birth metadata
0445 | same timestep
0446 | same signal position
0447 | different RNG continuation state
0448 | ```
0449 | 
0450 | The final result becomes:
0451 | 
0452 | ```text
0453 | final population                 9,550
0454 | symmetric-difference cells          28
0455 | normalized difference          0.002924
0456 | ```
0457 | 
0458 | The difference is small.
0459 | 
0460 | But it is not zero.
0461 | 
0462 | Exact continuation fails.
0463 | 
0464 | So:
0465 | 
0466 | > **RNG continuation state matters for exact continuation of Digital Crystal v1.**
0467 | 
0468 | That is not philosophical speculation.
0469 | 
0470 | We removed it.
0471 | 
0472 | The future changed.
0473 | 
0474 | ---
0475 | 
0476 | ## Move the Environmental Cursor
0477 | 
0478 | Next:
0479 | 
0480 | ```text
0481 | same morphology
0482 | same RNG state
0483 | same timestep
0484 | same continuation horizon
0485 | ```
0486 | 
0487 | but move the signal cursor:
0488 | 
0489 | ```text
0490 | 48 → 45
0491 | ```
0492 | 
0493 | Both conditions still execute exactly `48` future updates.
0494 | 
0495 | The result:
0496 | 
0497 | ```text
0498 | final population                 9,549
0499 | symmetric-difference cells          27
0500 | normalized difference          0.002820
0501 | ```
0502 | 
0503 | So we can now say:
0504 | 
0505 | > **Where the process currently sits in the environmental sequence affects exact continuation.**
0506 | 
0507 | The environment is not merely historical context.
0508 | 
0509 | Its current position is part of the continuation conditions.
0510 | 
0511 | ---
0512 | 
0513 | ## Remove the Birth Times
0514 | 
0515 | Now we perform a cleaner test.
0516 | 
0517 | Preserve:
0518 | 
0519 | ```text
0520 | occupied cells
0521 | RNG state
0522 | signal cursor
0523 | timestep
0524 | ```
0525 | 
0526 | but replace the birth-time metadata.
0527 | 
0528 | What happens?
0529 | 
0530 | ```text
0531 | final population                 9,574
0532 | symmetric-difference cells           0
0533 | normalized difference          0.000000
0534 | ```
0535 | 
0536 | The final occupied set is exact.
0537 | 
0538 | Only the birth-time metadata differs.
0539 | 
0540 | That gives us an extremely useful distinction.
0541 | 
0542 | Under the current Digital Crystal v1 growth rule:
0543 | 
0544 | > **Birth times are part of the historical record, but they are not required for the same geometric continuation.**
0545 | 
0546 | This is the first place where state and history begin to separate experimentally.
0547 | 
0548 | Birth time tells us:
0549 | 
0550 | ```text
0551 | how the current structure formed
0552 | ```
0553 | 
0554 | but the growth mechanism does not consult it when deciding the next attachment.
0555 | 
0556 | So birth time can matter to history without mattering to future growth.
0557 | 
0558 | ---
0559 | 
0560 | ## Save Only the Morphology
0561 | 
0562 | Now perform the brutal test.
0563 | 
0564 | Preserve only the visible occupied structure.
0565 | 
0566 | Reconstruct other process details incorrectly.
0567 | 
0568 | Continue.
0569 | 
0570 | The result:
0571 | 
0572 | ```text
0573 | final population                 9,548
0574 | symmetric-difference cells          30
0575 | normalized difference          0.003133
0576 | ```
0577 | 
0578 | The visible shape at the checkpoint was identical.
0579 | 
0580 | The future was not.
0581 | 
0582 | {{< figure
0583 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-03-state-omission.png"
0584 | alt="Comparison of final-state divergence after restoring the full checkpoint, changing RNG state, shifting the signal cursor, changing birth metadata, or restoring morphology only."
0585 | caption="Visible morphology is insufficient for exact continuation. RNG state and environmental sequence position affect future growth, while birth-time metadata does not affect the occupied-set continuation under Digital Crystal v1."
0586 | 
0587 | >}}
0588 | 
0589 | This gives us another version of a lesson that has followed us through the book:
0590 |
