0594 | 
0595 | ---
0596 | 
0597 | ## What We Have Actually Identified
0598 | 
0599 | We need to be careful here.
0600 | 
0601 | We have not discovered:
0602 | 
0603 | > the unique minimal state of Digital Crystal v1.
0604 | 
0605 | We have discovered something narrower.
0606 | 
0607 | The experiments establish:
0608 | 
0609 | ```text
0610 | FULL CHECKPOINT
0611 | → sufficient
0612 | 
0613 | VISIBLE MORPHOLOGY ALONE
0614 | → insufficient
0615 | 
0616 | RNG CONTINUATION STATE
0617 | → causally relevant to exact continuation
0618 | 
0619 | SIGNAL POSITION
0620 | → causally relevant to exact continuation
0621 | 
0622 | BIRTH-TIME METADATA
0623 | → not required for geometric continuation
0624 | ```
0625 | 
0626 | That is enough.
0627 | 
0628 | The useful operational idea is:
0629 | 
0630 | > **State is whatever information the future actually needs.**
0631 | 
0632 | Not whatever information happens to exist in our data structures.
0633 | 
0634 | And not whatever information sounds philosophically important.
0635 | 
0636 | ---
0637 | 
0638 | ## Now Give It History
0639 | 
0640 | Checkpointing solves one problem:
0641 | 
0642 | > Where are we now, and what do we need to continue?
0643 | 
0644 | It does not answer:
0645 | 
0646 | > How did we get here?
0647 | 
0648 | For that, we create an explicit event history.
0649 | 
0650 | At every growth step we preserve:
0651 | 
0652 | ```text
0653 | step
0654 | input value
0655 | cells added
0656 | population
0657 | resulting morphology hash
0658 | ```
0659 | 
0660 | So the history becomes:
0661 | 
0662 | ```text
0663 | STEP 1
0664 | input = ...
0665 | added = [...]
0666 | state hash = ...
0667 | 
0668 | STEP 2
0669 | input = ...
0670 | added = [...]
0671 | state hash = ...
0672 | 
0673 | STEP 3
0674 | ...
0675 | ```
0676 | 
0677 | This is not memory in any cognitive sense.
0678 | 
0679 | The crystal does not inspect this record.
0680 | 
0681 | It does not learn from it.
0682 | 
0683 | It does not use it to make decisions.
0684 | 
0685 | It is an explicit formation history.
0686 | 
0687 | Now we ask whether the record is sufficient to reconstruct what happened.
0688 | 
0689 | ---
0690 | 
0691 | ## Replay the Process
0692 | 
0693 | There are two different ways to replay a past.
0694 | 
0695 | The distinction matters.
0696 | 
0697 | ---
0698 | 
0699 | ## Procedural Replay
0700 | 
0701 | First:
0702 | 
0703 | ```text
0704 | same initial seed
0705 | +
0706 | same environmental signal
0707 | +
0708 | same frozen growth rule
0709 | +
0710 | same stochastic initialization
0711 | ↓
0712 | run again
0713 | ```
0714 | 
0715 | The result:
0716 | 
0717 | ```text
0718 | exact final morphology     True
0719 | exact final process state  True
0720 | ```
0721 | 
0722 | That establishes reproducibility of the computational procedure.
0723 | 
0724 | But it does not yet establish that the **stored event history** is sufficient.
0725 | 
0726 | So we perform a stronger test.
0727 | 
0728 | ---
0729 | 
0730 | ## Replay the Events
0731 | 
0732 | This time we do **not** rerun the stochastic growth rule.
0733 | 
0734 | Instead, take the recorded event stream.
0735 | 
0736 | At every step:
0737 | 
0738 | ```text
0739 | read cells that appeared
0740 | ↓
0741 | apply those additions
0742 | ↓
0743 | recompute morphology hash
0744 | ↓
0745 | compare with original recorded hash
0746 | ```
0747 | 
0748 | There are:
0749 | 
0750 | ```text
0751 | 96 recorded steps
0752 | ```
0753 | 
0754 | Result:
0755 | 
0756 | ```text
0757 | 96 / 96 morphology hashes match
0758 | ```
0759 | 
0760 | Final morphology:
0761 | 
0762 | ```text
0763 | exact
0764 | ```
0765 | 
0766 | {{< figure
0767 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-04-history-replay.png"
0768 | alt="Step-by-step comparison showing that every morphology hash produced by replaying the Digital Crystal event log matches the recorded original trajectory."
0769 | caption="The event history reconstructs the recorded morphology trajectory exactly: 96 matching hashes out of 96."
0770 | 
0771 | >}}
0772 | 
0773 | Now we have earned a second claim:
0774 | 
0775 | > **The explicit event history is sufficient to reconstruct the exact recorded morphology trajectory.**
0776 | 
0777 | Not the hidden historical RNG state.
0778 | 
0779 | Not every internal implementation detail.
0780 | 
0781 | The formation trajectory.
0782 | 
0783 | That is the correct scope.
0784 | 
0785 | ---
0786 | 
0787 | ## State Is Not History
0788 | 
0789 | We can now make the distinction operational.
0790 | 
0791 | A checkpoint and an event history both describe the same process.
0792 | 
0793 | But they answer different questions.
0794 | 
0795 | ```text
0796 | STATE
0797 | =
0798 | enough information for faithful continuation
0799 | 
0800 | HISTORY
0801 | =
0802 | enough information to reconstruct how the present morphology was formed
0803 | ```
0804 | 
0805 | A checkpoint can continue forward exactly.
0806 | 
0807 | An event log can reconstruct backward through the morphology trajectory.
0808 | 
0809 | But those capabilities are not interchangeable.
0810 | 
0811 | The history reconstructed from cell additions does **not** restore the historical RNG state.
0812 | 
0813 | And if we take reconstructed geometry without the correct stochastic continuation state, exact future continuation fails.
0814 | 
0815 | In the full experiment:
0816 | 
0817 | ```text
0818 | history reconstructs checkpoint morphology    True
0819 | checkpoint continues exactly                  True
0820 | 
0821 | history-derived geometry without RNG
0822 | continues exactly                             False
0823 | ```
0824 | 
0825 | The final difference in that last condition was:
0826 | 
0827 | ```text
0828 | 0.003133
0829 | ```
0830 | 
0831 | So:
0832 | 
0833 | ```text
0834 | CHECKPOINT
0835 | → FUTURE
0836 | 
0837 | EVENT HISTORY
0838 | → PAST MORPHOLOGY
0839 | ```
0840 | 
0841 | They overlap.
0842 | 
0843 | But they are different mechanisms.
0844 | 
0845 | ---
0846 | 
0847 | ## The Digital Answer Was Not Biological
0848 | 
0849 | There is something important about how we solved this.
0850 | 
0851 | We could have tried to build a special region inside the crystal whose geometry somehow encoded its entire formation history.
0852 | 
0853 | A biological analogy might tempt us toward:
0854 | 
0855 | ```text
0856 | memory organ
0857 | genome-like store
0858 | special history structure
0859 | ```
0860 | 
0861 | But computation gives us another possibility.
0862 | 
0863 | ```text
0864 | serialization
0865 | checkpoint
0866 | event log
0867 | replay
0868 | branch
0869 | ```
0870 | 
0871 | These are native computational affordances.
0872 | 
0873 | We do not need to imitate a biological storage mechanism if the substrate gives us a different way to preserve the same capability.
0874 | 
0875 | This is exactly the rule we established earlier:
0876 | 
0877 | > **Do not import a biological mechanism unless the digital substrate actually requires it.**
0878 | 
0879 | The crystal's past does not need to look biological.
0880 | 
0881 | It only needs to be recoverable.
0882 | 
0883 | ---
0884 | 
0885 | ## A Digital Advantage
0886 | 
0887 | Biological systems generally do not offer us cheap, exact, executable copies of an earlier complete physical state.
0888 | 
0889 | Digital systems often can.
0890 | 
0891 | Our checkpoint is executable.
0892 | 
0893 | That changes what a saved past can be.
0894 | 
0895 | It is not merely evidence that something happened.
0896 | 
0897 | It can become:
0898 | 
0899 | ```text
0900 | an experimental starting point
0901 | ```
0902 | 
0903 | from which alternative futures are generated.
0904 | 
0905 | ---
0906 | 
0907 | ## Restore the Same Past Twice
0908 | 
0909 | Take the exact checkpoint at step `48`.
0910 | 
0911 | Restore it twice.
0912 | 
0913 | Both copies begin with:
0914 | 
0915 | ```text
0916 | same occupied cells
0917 | same timestep
0918 | same signal cursor
0919 | same RNG state
0920 | same continuation state
0921 | ```
0922 | 
0923 | Nothing differs.
0924 | 
0925 | Then deliberately provide different future environments.
0926 | 
0927 | ```text
0928 |               ┌── FUTURE A
0929 | SAVED PAST ───┤
0930 |               └── FUTURE B
0931 | ```
0932 | 
0933 | The resulting morphologies diverge.
0934 | 
0935 | In one illustrative branch:
0936 | 
0937 | ```text
0938 | final symmetric difference    35 cells
0939 | normalized difference         0.003655
0940 | ```
0941 | 
0942 | {{< figure
0943 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-06-counterfactual-branches.png"
0944 | alt="One saved Digital Crystal checkpoint shown beside two different final morphologies generated from different prescribed future forcing."
0945 | caption="One exact checkpoint serves as a shared executable starting condition for two controlled future environments."
0946 | 
0947 | >}}
0948 | 
0949 | And we can watch that divergence develop.
0950 | 
0951 | {{< figure
0952 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-06-counterfactual-divergence.png"
0953 | alt="A line plot showing morphology divergence through time between two Digital Crystal futures starting from the same checkpoint."
0954 | caption="Alternative prescribed futures starting from the same saved state generate measurable divergence."
0955 | 
0956 | >}}
0957 | 
0958 | So one capability is clearly established:
0959 | 
0960 | > **A complete digital checkpoint can act as an executable counterfactual branch point.**
0961 | 
0962 | But there is a trap here.
0963 | 
0964 | ---
0965 | 
0966 | ## Different Futures Always Diverge — But Why?
0967 | 
0968 | Suppose two continuations end differently.
0969 | 
0970 | It is tempting to say:
0971 | 
0972 | > The different environments caused the divergence.
0973 | 
0974 | But Digital Crystal v1 is stochastic.
0975 | 
0976 | Different random continuation states also produce different futures.
0977 | 
0978 | So the number:
0979 | 
0980 | ```text
0981 | 35 different cells
0982 | ```
0983 | 
0984 | means nothing by itself.
0985 | 
0986 | We need a null.
0987 | 
0988 | ---
0989 | 
0990 | ## The Stochastic Null
0991 | 
0992 | We compare two experiments.
0993 | 
0994 | ### Environmental treatment
0995 | 
0996 | ```text
0997 | same checkpoint
0998 | same RNG state
0999 | different future forcing
1000 | ```
1001 | 
1002 | ### Stochastic null
1003 | 
1004 | ```text
1005 | same checkpoint
1006 | same future forcing
1007 | different valid RNG states
1008 | ```
1009 | 
1010 | We run:
1011 | 
1012 | ```text
1013 | 60 replicates
1014 | ```
1015 | 
1016 | for each condition.
1017 | 
1018 | Now compare final normalized morphology divergence.
1019 | 
1020 | ---
1021 | 
1022 | ## The Environment Did Not Win
1023 | 
1024 | Different future environments produced:
1025 | 
1026 | ```text
1027 | mean divergence      0.003815
1028 | median               0.003655
1029 | ```
1030 | 
1031 | The stochastic null produced:
1032 | 
1033 | ```text
1034 | mean divergence      0.005290
1035 | median               0.004812
1036 | ```
1037 | 
1038 | So:
1039 | 
1040 | ```text
1041 | treatment - null mean    -0.001475
1042 | ```
1043 | 
1044 | The environmental treatment was not larger.
1045 | 
1046 | The pairwise superiority probability was:
1047 | 
1048 | ```text
1049 | 0.1975
1050 | ```
1051 | 
1052 | and the treatment median did not exceed the stochastic-null 95th percentile.
1053 | 
1054 | {{< figure
1055 | src="/images/books/digital-life/ch15-06-counterfactual-null.png"
1056 | alt="Comparison of final Digital Crystal divergence under different future environments versus divergence produced by ordinary stochastic continuation variation."
1057 | caption="Changing future forcing produces alternative futures, but the resulting divergence is not larger than ordinary stochastic continuation divergence under this experiment."
1058 | 
1059 | >}}
1060 | 
1061 | This kills a stronger interpretation.
1062 | 
1063 | We cannot say:
1064 | 
1065 | > **Environmental differences dominate future divergence.**
1066 | 
1067 | They did not.
1068 | 
1069 | In fact, under this protocol ordinary stochastic variation produced somewhat greater divergence on average.
1070 | 
1071 | That leaves a smaller, cleaner result:
1072 | 
1073 | > **The checkpoint is an executable branch point, but branchability does not imply that one chosen environmental manipulation dominates the system's intrinsic stochastic variation.**
1074 | 
1075 | That is exactly why the null matters.
1076 | 
1077 | ---
1078 | 
1079 | ## This Is Not Reproduction
1080 | 
1081 | We should resist that word.
1082 | 
1083 | We can restore the same checkpoint many times.
1084 | 
1085 | That resembles copying.
1086 | 
1087 | But the copying is performed by our experimental infrastructure.
1088 | 
1089 | Nothing here establishes autonomous reproduction.
1090 | 
1091 | The useful property is narrower:
1092 | 
1093 | > **Digital state can be duplicated as an exact starting condition for controlled counterfactual experiments.**
1094 | 
1095 | That is already powerful enough.
1096 | 
1097 | ---
1098 | 
1099 | ## The Crystal Now Has a Recoverable Past
1100 | 
1101 | Chapter 14 ended with:
1102 | 
1103 | ```text
1104 | PRESENT MORPHOLOGY
1105 | → SOME SOURCE INFORMATION SURVIVES
1106 | 
1107 | TEMPORAL ORDER
1108 | → NOT RECOVERABLE
1109 | ```
1110 | 
1111 | We did not solve that by forcing more temporal information into morphology.
1112 | 
1113 | We introduced a separate historical mechanism.
1114 | 
1115 | Now we have:
1116 | 
1117 | ```text
1118 | CURRENT PROCESS STATE
1119 | +
1120 | EVENT HISTORY
1121 | ```
1122 | 
1123 | which provides two complementary capabilities:
1124 | 
1125 | ```text
1126 | STATE
1127 | → CONTINUE
1128 | 
1129 | HISTORY
1130 | → RECONSTRUCT
1131 | ```
1132 | 
1133 | Together:
1134 | 
1135 | ```text
1136 | PAST
1137 | ↓
1138 | PRESENT
1139 | ↓
1140 | POSSIBLE FUTURES
1141 | ```
1142 | 
1143 | But those arrows mean different things.
1144 | 
1145 | The past can be reconstructed.
1146 | 
1147 | The present can be resumed.
1148 | 
1149 | The future can be branched.
1150 | 
1151 | That is something Digital Crystal v1 did not possess in Chapter 14.
1152 | 
1153 | ---
1154 | 
1155 | ## A Past Without Memory
1156 | 
1157 | It is tempting to call this memory.
1158 | 
1159 | I do not think we have earned that yet.
1160 | 
1161 | We have built:
1162 | 
1163 | ```text
1164 | storage
1165 | checkpointing
1166 | history
1167 | replay
1168 | restore
1169 | branching
1170 | ```
1171 | 
1172 | But the crystal itself does not inspect the record.
1173 | 
1174 | It does not ask:
1175 | 
1176 | > What happened before?
1177 | 
1178 | It does not change its behavior because of an earlier event stored in the log.
1179 | 
1180 | The history exists.
1181 | 
1182 | The process does not yet consult it.
1183 | 
1184 | So for now:
1185 | 
1186 | > **The Digital Crystal has a recoverable past.**
1187 | 
1188 | Not memory.
1189 | 
1190 | Not learning.
1191 | 
1192 | A past.
1193 | 
1194 | That is enough.
1195 | 
1196 | ---
1197 | 
1198 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
1199 | 
1200 | The chapter began with a simple problem:
1201 | 
1202 | ```text
1203 | the crystal has a present
1204 | but
1205 | the present does not preserve chronology
1206 | ```
1207 | 
1208 | Chapter 14 had already shown that final morphology contains some information about the conditions under which the crystal formed, but not enough to reconstruct temporal ordering.
1209 | 
1210 | Chapter 15 asked a different question:
1211 | 
1212 | > What information must survive if the process is to continue exactly, and what information must survive if its formation history is to be reconstructed?
1213 | 
1214 | The answer turned out to contain two distinct mechanisms.
1215 | 
1216 | ### The checkpoint phenomenon
1217 | 
1218 | A complete checkpoint can be serialized, restored and continued exactly.
1219 | 
1220 | Across the validation runs:
1221 | 
1222 | ```text
1223 | 30 / 30 exact restores
1224 | ```
1225 | 
1226 | The restored process reproduced:
1227 | 
1228 | ```text
1229 | the same cells
1230 | the same attachment decisions
1231 | the same population trajectory
1232 | the same final process state
1233 | ```
1234 | 
1235 | But visible morphology alone was not sufficient.
1236 | 
1237 | The same occupied structure could lead to a different future when hidden continuation variables differed.
1238 | 
1239 | So:
1240 | 
1241 | ```text
1242 | VISIBLE FORM
1243 | ≠
1244 | EXECUTABLE STATE
1245 | ```
1246 | 
1247 | This is not merely an implementation lesson.
1248 | 
1249 | It tells us that the future of the Digital Crystal depends on information that is not necessarily visible in the current morphology.
1250 | 
1251 | ### Phenomenon record
1252 | 
1253 | **Phenomenon:** Executable hidden state
1254 | 
1255 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
1256 | 
1257 | **Current bounded description:**
1258 | 
1259 | > Digital Crystal v1 requires continuation-relevant state beyond visible morphology for exact future replay. A complete checkpoint is sufficient for exact continuation, while morphology alone is not.
1260 | 
1261 | The experimentally identified continuation-relevant components include:
1262 | 
1263 | ```text
1264 | occupied structure
1265 | RNG continuation state
1266 | environmental sequence position
1267 | ```
1268 | 
1269 | while birth-time metadata behaves differently:
1270 | 
1271 | ```text
1272 | birth time
1273 | → historical information
1274 | 
1275 | birth time
1276 | → not required for same occupied-set continuation
1277 | ```
1278 | 
1279 | That gives us another important distinction:
1280 | 
1281 | ```text
1282 | HISTORICAL INFORMATION
1283 | ≠
1284 | CAUSALLY ACTIVE CONTINUATION STATE
1285 | ```
1286 | 
1287 | ### State and history are different computational objects
1288 | 
1289 | The event-log experiment exposes the other half of the chapter.
1290 | 
1291 | The stored history reconstructs:
1292 | 
1293 | ```text
1294 | 96 / 96 morphology states exactly
1295 | ```
1296 | 
1297 | but that event history does not restore the historical RNG state required for exact stochastic continuation.
1298 | 
1299 | So the two representations answer different questions:
1300 | 
1301 | ```text
1302 | CHECKPOINT
1303 | → what is required to continue from here?
1304 | 
1305 | EVENT HISTORY
1306 | → how did the present morphology arise?
1307 | ```
1308 | 
1309 | or more compactly:
1310 | 
1311 | ```text
1312 | STATE
1313 | → FUTURE
1314 | 
1315 | HISTORY
1316 | → PAST
1317 | ```
1318 | 
1319 | They overlap, but they are not interchangeable.
1320 | 
1321 | This gives us a second project-wide distinction:
1322 | 
1323 | > **A process can preserve enough information to reconstruct its past without preserving the continuation state required to regenerate its exact future from that reconstruction alone.**
1324 | 
1325 | ### The implementation failure revealed a deeper rule
1326 | 
1327 | The accidental dependence on Python `set` iteration order matters here too.
1328 | 
1329 | Before canonicalization, the simulation contained an undeclared continuation variable:
1330 | 
1331 | ```text
1332 | Python container traversal order
1333 | ```
1334 | 
1335 | Two mathematically equivalent reconstructed states could consume the same random draws in different orders and diverge.
1336 | 
1337 | That was not Digital Crystal physics.
1338 | 
1339 | It was implementation state leaking into the experiment.
1340 | 
1341 | Once frontier traversal was canonicalized, exact restore became reproducible.
1342 | 
1343 | This gives us a methodological phenomenon worth carrying across the project:
1344 | 
1345 | > **Scientific state must be separated from implementation state.**
1346 | 
1347 | If hidden program details influence outcomes, they must either be promoted into the declared model or eliminated.
1348 | 
1349 | ### Connection to the Lossy-History Principle
1350 | 
1351 | Chapter 15 also sharpens the result from Chapter 14.
1352 | 
1353 | Chapter 14 showed:
1354 | 
1355 | ```text
1356 | coarse source characteristics
1357 | survive in morphology
1358 | 
1359 | exact temporal order
1360 | does not
1361 | ```
1362 | 
1363 | Chapter 15 shows that this loss is not inevitable to the digital substrate as a whole.
1364 | 
1365 | The chronology can be preserved perfectly if we use an explicit event history.
1366 | 
1367 | So the stronger cross-chapter picture becomes:
1368 | 
1369 | ```text
1370 | MORPHOLOGY
1371 | → lossy historical integration
1372 | 
1373 | EVENT LOG
1374 | → exact formation-history reconstruction
1375 | 
1376 | CHECKPOINT
1377 | → exact continuation
1378 | ```
1379 | 
1380 | That matters because it tells us that different representations preserve different slices of the past.
1381 | 
1382 | The substrate gives us several native computational affordances:
1383 | 
1384 | ```text
1385 | serialization
1386 | checkpointing
1387 | event logging
1388 | replay
1389 | branching
1390 | ```
1391 | 
1392 | We do not need to force all historical information into visible form.
1393 | 
1394 | ### Counterfactual branchability survives, dominance does not
1395 | 
1396 | The checkpoint also provides an executable branch point.
1397 | 
1398 | One exact saved state can be restored into multiple controlled futures.
1399 | 
1400 | That property survives.
1401 | 
1402 | But the stronger environmental-divergence interpretation does not.
1403 | 
1404 | Different prescribed future environments produced measurable divergence, yet that divergence did not exceed ordinary stochastic continuation variation under the frozen comparison.
1405 | 
1406 | So:
1407 | 
1408 | ```text
1409 | EXECUTABLE BRANCHABILITY
1410 | SUPPORTED
1411 | 
1412 | ENVIRONMENTAL MANIPULATION
1413 | DOMINATES STOCHASTIC DIVERGENCE
1414 | NOT SUPPORTED
1415 | ```
1416 | 
1417 | Again, the failed interpretation does not erase the underlying capability.
1418 | 
1419 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
1420 | 
1421 | The surviving phenomena do **not** establish:
1422 | 
1423 | - cognitive memory,
1424 | - learning,
1425 | - adaptation,
1426 | - autonomous reproduction,
1427 | - a mathematically minimal state representation,
1428 | - a biological genome analogue,
1429 | - or life.
1430 | 
1431 | They establish something narrower and more computationally native:
1432 | 
1433 | > **A Digital Crystal can possess hidden executable state sufficient for exact continuation, an explicit history sufficient for exact morphology reconstruction, and a checkpoint that functions as a reusable counterfactual branch point. These are distinct capabilities carried by distinct representations.**
1434 | 
1435 | This phenomenon should now be tracked independently of the chapter's stronger historical or environmental interpretations.
1436 | 
1437 | ---
1438 | 
1439 | ## Evidence Ledger
1440 | 
1441 | | Claim                                                             | Status            | Evidence                                              |
1442 | | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
1443 | | Canonicalized model survives state serialization/reconstruction   | **SUPPORTED**     | one-step and 48-step invariant pass                   |
1444 | | Complete checkpoint resumes exact trajectory                      | **SUPPORTED**     | identical process and morphology hashes               |
1445 | | Exact restore generalizes across tested seeds                     | **SUPPORTED**     | `30/30` exact                                         |
1446 | | Visible morphology alone is sufficient continuation state         | **FAILED**        | 30-cell divergence                                    |
1447 | | RNG state matters for exact continuation                          | **SUPPORTED**     | 28-cell divergence                                    |
1448 | | Signal cursor matters at fixed horizon                            | **SUPPORTED**     | 27-cell divergence                                    |
1449 | | Birth-time metadata affects future occupied-set growth            | **FAILED**        | 0 differing occupied cells                            |
1450 | | Birth times function as historical metadata in v1                 | **SUPPORTED**     | history differs while geometric continuation does not |
1451 | | Event log reconstructs morphology trajectory                      | **SUPPORTED**     | `96/96` trajectory hashes                             |
1452 | | Event log reconstructs historical RNG state                       | **NOT SUPPORTED** | additions alone do not contain RNG history            |
1453 | | State and history are operationally distinct                      | **SUPPORTED**     | one continues; one reconstructs                       |
1454 | | Checkpoint is an executable branch point                          | **SUPPORTED**     | controlled alternative continuations                  |
1455 | | Different forcing produces divergence beyond stochastic variation | **NOT SUPPORTED** | treatment mean `<` stochastic-null mean               |
1456 | | Checkpoint representation is mathematically minimal               | **UNTESTED**      | only sufficiency/ablations tested                     |
1457 | | Stored history is cognitive memory                                | **NOT CLAIMED**   | process does not consult history                      |
1458 | | Crystal learns or adapts from history                             | **NOT CLAIMED**   | no such mechanism                                     |
1459 | | Crystal is alive                                                  | **NOT CLAIMED**   | evidence insufficient                                 |
1460 | 
1461 | ---
1462 | 
1463 | ## Bounded Claims
1464 | 
1465 | From this chapter we can reasonably claim:
1466 | 
1467 | 1. **Exact continuation** — A complete Digital Crystal v1 checkpoint can be serialized, restored and continued without altering the stochastic trajectory.
1468 | 
1469 | 2. **Reproducibility across runs** — Exact restore succeeded in `30/30` independent validation runs.
1470 | 
1471 | 3. **Morphology is not complete state** — Identical visible structure can produce a different future if relevant hidden continuation variables differ.
1472 | 
1473 | 4. **RNG state matters** — Stochastic continuation state affects exact future growth.
1474 | 
1475 | 5. **Environmental position matters** — Signal position affects exact continuation even when the number of future updates is held fixed.
1476 | 
1477 | 6. **Birth time is history, not growth state in v1** — Changing birth metadata alone does not alter the future occupied-cell trajectory.
1478 | 
1479 | 7. **History can reconstruct morphology** — The explicit event log reconstructs the recorded formation trajectory exactly across `96/96` states.
1480 | 
1481 | 8. **State and history are operationally distinct** — The checkpoint supports continuation; the event log supports reconstruction.
1482 | 
1483 | 9. **A checkpoint is an executable counterfactual branch point** — One saved state can be reused to generate controlled alternative continuations.
1484 | 
1485 | 10. **Environmental branching did not exceed stochastic divergence** — Under the tested protocol, changing future forcing did not produce more divergence than ordinary stochastic continuation variation.
1486 | 
1487 | That is where the evidence stops.
1488 | 
1489 | ---
1490 | 
1491 | ## Something Else Has Happened
1492 | 
1493 | There is one more consequence.
1494 | 
1495 | Our history is made from events.
1496 | 
1497 | Until now those events stay inside the experimental record.
1498 | 
1499 | ```text
1500 | CRYSTAL
1501 | ↓
1502 | EVENT
1503 | ↓
1504 | HISTORY
1505 | ```
1506 | 
1507 | But an event does not have to remain internal.
1508 | 
1509 | One process can emit one.
1510 | 
1511 | Another process can receive it.
1512 | 
1513 | The event does not need to contain language.
1514 | 
1515 | It does not need semantics.
1516 | 
1517 | It may contain almost nothing.
1518 | 
1519 | ```text
1520 | one bit
1521 | a pulse
1522 | a number
1523 | ```
1524 | 
1525 | And if one process can change the conditions experienced by another, then the environment no longer needs to come entirely from outside the system.
1526 | 
1527 | Something generated inside one process can become part of another process's world.
1528 | 
1529 | ```text
1530 | CRYSTAL A
1531 | ↓
1532 | EVENT
1533 | ↓
1534 | CRYSTAL B
1535 | ```
1536 | 
1537 | But Chapter 13 taught us to be careful with correlation.
1538 | 
1539 | Chapter 14 taught us that state is not history.
1540 | 
1541 | And this chapter taught us that a branch can diverge without the environment being the dominant cause.
1542 | 
1543 | So we should not call the next thing communication merely because we connect two systems.
1544 | 
1545 | The next question has to be smaller:
1546 | 
1547 | > **Can an event emitted by one Digital Crystal reliably change another?**
1548 | 
1549 | The crystal has a past.
1550 | 
1551 | **Next, we let the crystals hear each other.**
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "16: Before There Are Messages"
0003 | date = "2026-08-12T02:38:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "A Digital Crystal can causally alter another through a one-bit event, but causal transmission is not yet sender-specific signalling."
0006 | weight = 16
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Digital Crystal", "Signalling", "Causality", "Information", "Experiments"]
0009 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | In the last chapter, the crystal acquired a past.  
0013 | Not memory in the biological sense.  
0014 | Not recollection.  
0015 | Not understanding.  
0016 | A recoverable past.
0017 | 
0018 | We learned that a complete checkpoint could continue the process exactly, that an event history could reconstruct the route by which the present morphology had formed, and that the same checkpoint could be used as a branch point for controlled alternative futures.
0019 | 
0020 | That gave us something new:
0021 | 
0022 | - A present that could be resumed.
0023 | - A past that could be reconstructed.
0024 | - A future that could be forked.
0025 | 
0026 | The next temptation was obvious.  
0027 | If one Digital Crystal can preserve state and history, perhaps two crystals can communicate.
0028 | 
0029 | That word is dangerous.  
0030 | “Communication” arrives carrying far more assumptions than we have earned.
0031 | 
0032 | A sender.  
0033 | A receiver.  
0034 | A message.  
0035 | A channel.  
0036 | Meaning.  
0037 | Perhaps even intention.
0038 | 
0039 | We have established none of those things.  
0040 | So we begin with something smaller.  
0041 | Not a message.  
0042 | A pulse.
0043 | 
0044 | > **Before there are messages, there are events that can alter another process.**
0045 | 
0046 | That is the whole experiment.  
0047 | Can one Digital Crystal produce a one‑bit event that changes another Digital Crystal?  
0048 | If the answer is no, there is no reason to discuss communication.  
0049 | If the answer is yes, we still have a long way to go.
0050 | 
0051 | ---
0052 | 
0053 | ## The Smallest Possible Channel
0054 | 
0055 | We keep the Digital Crystal itself unchanged.  
0056 | Its growth rule remains the frozen Digital Crystal v1 model from the previous chapters.  
0057 | A crystal grows locally across a hexagonal lattice. Its attachment probability depends on its local neighbourhood and on an external scalar input.
0058 | 
0059 | We add only one new mechanism: a sender crystal can emit a bit.
0060 | 
0061 | The bit is either `0` or `1`.
0062 | 
0063 | The receiver does not receive a sentence.  
0064 | It does not receive a symbol.  
0065 | It does not receive an identifier saying who sent the event.
0066 | 
0067 | The bit simply perturbs the scalar environmental input used by the receiver’s existing growth rule.
0068 | 
0069 | ```mermaid
0070 | flowchart LR
0071 |     S[Sender Growth] --> E[Endogenous Event\<br/>one bit]
0072 |     E --> R[Receiver Forcing\<br/>perturbation]
0073 |     R --> P[Receiver Attachment\<br/>probabilities change]
0074 |     P --> M[Receiver Morphology\<br/>may diverge]
0075 | ```
0076 | 
0077 | There is no separate oscillator.  
0078 | There is no artificial coordination layer.  
0079 | The pulse reaches the Digital Crystal itself.
0080 | 
0081 | That distinction matters because an earlier version of this experiment had done something weaker: it coupled auxiliary oscillators and looked for synchronization. That could have produced an interesting dynamical system while leaving the crystal’s actual growth almost untouched.
0082 | 
0083 | This experiment asks a harder question:
0084 | 
0085 | > **Does the bit reach the thing we are actually studying?**
0086 | 
0087 | ---
0088 | 
0089 | ## The Sender Does Not Fire on a Clock
0090 | 
0091 | A trivial signalling system would be easy to construct.
0092 | 
0093 | We could write:
0094 | 
0095 | ```python
0096 | if step % 10 == 0:
0097 |     send(1)
0098 | ```
0099 | 
0100 | Then every receiver could respond to a programmer‑supplied metronome.  
0101 | That would establish almost nothing.
0102 | 
0103 | Instead, the pulse must come from the sender’s own dynamics.  
0104 | At each step we count how many new cells the sender attaches.  
0105 | We compare that value with its recent attachment history.  
0106 | When current growth is unusually high relative to that recent history, the sender emits a one‑bit pulse.
0107 | 
0108 | The rule is deliberately simple.  
0109 | The pulse means only:
0110 | 
0111 | > an endogenous growth event occurred.
0112 | 
0113 | It does not mean danger.  
0114 | It does not mean food.  
0115 | It does not mean move left.  
0116 | It does not even mean “I grew.”  
0117 | Those would already be semantic claims.
0118 | 
0119 | At this stage, `1` is merely a detectable event generated by the sender’s own changing state.
0120 | 
0121 | ---
0122 | 
0123 | ## A Problem We Discovered Before the Real Experiment
0124 | 
0125 | The first versions of this experiment produced a misleading endpoint.  
0126 | The crystals eventually filled almost the entire hard‑radius region available to them.  
0127 | Once that happened, very different trajectories converged on the same final shape: a filled hexagonal disk.
0128 | 
0129 | The experiment had not discovered convergence.  
0130 | The boundary condition had erased the differences.
0131 | 
0132 | This is exactly the kind of failure the method of this book is supposed to catch.  
0133 | A final picture can become uninformative even while the process that produced it was different.
0134 | 
0135 | So the experiment now contains a saturation guard.  
0136 | For a hexagonal disk of radius (r), the maximum number of cells is:
0137 | 
0138 | $$
0139 | N(r) = 1 + 3r(r+1)
0140 | $$
0141 | 
0142 | The full experiment uses radius 56, so the hard maximum is 9,577 cells.  
0143 | We predeclare that endpoint morphology becomes invalid once a crystal reaches 85% of that capacity.
0144 | 
0145 | The experiment therefore does not blindly run for a fixed number of steps.  
0146 | Instead it finds the longest safe interval before the boundary starts dominating the result.
0147 | 
0148 | For the full sender/receiver run, 90 steps were requested.  
0149 | The common safe horizon was 76.
0150 | 
0151 | At step 76 the sender occupied 7,723 cells (~80.6% of capacity). The receiver occupied 8,026 cells (~83.8%).  
0152 | Step 77 would have crossed the guard.  
0153 | So we stop at 76.
0154 | 
0155 | That is not an inconvenience. It is part of the experiment.
0156 | 
0157 | > **The requested horizon is not necessarily the experimentally valid horizon.**
0158 | 
0159 | ---
0160 | 
0161 | ## The First Real Test: One Bit Versus No Bit
0162 | 
0163 | Before asking whether a sender’s pulse stream matters, we need to know whether a single received bit matters at all.
0164 | 
0165 | Chapter 15 gave us exactly the tool we need: checkpointing.
0166 | 
0167 | We take one receiver state and fork it.  
0168 | Both futures begin with the same morphology, birth‑time metadata, RNG state, environmental forcing, timestep, and future horizon.
0169 | 
0170 | Then we change exactly one thing: one branch receives a bit; the other does not.
0171 | 
0172 | ```mermaid
0173 | flowchart TD
0174 |     CK[Checkpoint\<br/>identical receiver state] --> BIT1[BIT = 1]
0175 |     CK --> BIT0[BIT = 0]
0176 |     BIT1 --> FUT_A[Future A]
0177 |     BIT0 --> FUT_B[Future B]
0178 |     FUT_A & FUT_B --> COMP[Compare final morphology]
0179 | ```
0180 | 
0181 | This is the strongest experiment in the chapter because it removes almost every obvious alternative explanation.  
0182 | If the two futures differ, the difference was caused by the intervention.
0183 | 
0184 | In the full run we repeated this 120 times.
0185 | 
0186 | The result was not subtle.  
0187 | In **95.8%** of interventions, the final morphologies differed.  
0188 | The mean normalized final difference was **0.1633**, with an average symmetric difference of about **158 cells**.  
0189 | The maximum observed capacity fraction in these experiments was only about 13.5%, so saturation played no role.
0190 | 
0191 | The bit did not always produce a difference; five of the 120 interventions ended with no morphology difference under the measured horizon.  
0192 | That matters.
0193 | 
0194 | The correct claim is not “every received bit necessarily changes the receiver.”  
0195 | The claim is:
0196 | 
0197 | > Under this protocol, changing one received bit while holding receiver state, stochastic state and environmental forcing fixed usually altered the receiver’s subsequent morphology.
0198 | 
0199 | That is enough to establish a primitive causal channel.
0200 | 
0201 | ---
0202 | 
0203 | ## The Pulse Has an Immediate Effect
0204 | 
0205 | We can also measure the receiver’s attachment response after the intervention.  
0206 | Across the 120 full‑profile replicates, the mean attachment difference between the bit and no‑bit branches began:
0207 | 
0208 | ```text
0209 | +1.81
0210 |  0.00
0211 | -0.34
0212 | -0.08
0213 | -0.30
0214 | -0.32
0215 | -0.39
0216 | -0.35
0217 | -0.61
0218 | -0.26
0219 | -0.25
0220 | -0.75
0221 | ```
0222 | 
0223 | The largest average effect occurs immediately.  
0224 | That is useful, but we should not turn it into a latency law.  
0225 | This is a finite‑horizon impulse response; the downstream differences depend on the crystal’s subsequent stochastic and morphological evolution.
0226 | 
0227 | We have shown that the perturbation enters the growth process and can persist through later divergence.  
0228 | We have not measured channel capacity.  
0229 | We have not identified a universal response time.  
0230 | We have not discovered a communication protocol.
0231 | 
0232 | ---
0233 | 
0234 | ## Transmission Is Not Signalling
0235 | 
0236 | At this point it would be easy to overclaim.  
0237 | One crystal emits a bit. Another crystal changes. Therefore they communicate.
0238 | 
0239 | No.
0240 | 
0241 | All we have established is causal transmission.  
0242 | A light switch also changes a circuit.  
0243 | A voltage spike changes a transistor.  
0244 | A falling rock changes whatever it hits.
0245 | 
0246 | Causal influence is necessary for signalling. It is not sufficient.
0247 | 
0248 | To move beyond transmission we need to ask a more difficult question:
0249 | 
0250 | > Does the actual sender‑generated event stream matter, or would almost any similarly structured pulse stream produce the same receiver response?
0251 | 
0252 | That question requires controls.
0253 | 
0254 | ---
0255 | 
0256 | ## Destroy the Timing
0257 | 
0258 | The first control keeps the same number of bits but shuffles when they occur.  
0259 | If exact sender timing matters, the real stream should outperform the shuffled stream.
0260 | 
0261 | It does.
0262 | 
0263 | Across 60 full‑profile replicates, the mean peak message‑to‑growth correlation for the real stream exceeded the shuffled stream by about **0.294**.  
0264 | The probability that a randomly selected real replicate exceeded a randomly selected shuffled replicate was about **0.980**.
0265 | 
0266 | So timing structure matters.  
0267 | That is already more than generic bit injection.
0268 | 
0269 | ---
0270 | 
0271 | ## Replace the Sender With Randomness
0272 | 
0273 | Next we preserve the number of pulses but place them at random times.
0274 | 
0275 | Again the real sender wins strongly.  
0276 | The real‑minus‑random difference was about **0.270**, with pairwise superiority around **0.977**.
0277 | 
0278 | So the receiver is not merely responding to message count; a burst pattern matters.
0279 | 
0280 | But this is still not enough.  
0281 | The strongest control is not randomness. It is another sender.
0282 | 
0283 | ---
0284 | 
0285 | ## The Unrelated Sender
0286 | 
0287 | We now generate a pulse stream from another Digital Crystal of the same type.  
0288 | It has its own independent environment and its own independent growth trajectory.  
0289 | Then we force its pulse count to match the real sender exactly.
0290 | 
0291 | This removes a simple explanation: perhaps the real sender looked better only because it emitted more or fewer pulses.
0292 | 
0293 | Now the receiver sees either the actual sender stream or a same‑class unrelated sender stream with the same pulse count.
0294 | 
0295 | If the actual sender carries something specific, it should win.  
0296 | It does not.
0297 | 
0298 | The real‑minus‑unrelated difference was **-0.015**.  
0299 | Pairwise superiority was **0.457**.
0300 | 
0301 | The unrelated sender was, if anything, fractionally ahead under this metric. That difference is tiny.  
0302 | The important fact is that the receiver cannot distinguish the actual sender from another crystal producing the same general class of pulse activity.
0303 | 
0304 | This is the result that stops us using the word “communication” casually.
0305 | 
0306 | > **The receiver is sensitive to a kind of event stream, but not to which same‑class crystal produced it.**
0307 | 
0308 | ---
0309 | 
0310 | ## Preserve the Pulse Intervals, Destroy Their Order
0311 | 
0312 | We can make the control harder still.  
0313 | Take the real sender’s pulse stream. Measure every gap between pulses.
0314 | 
0315 | Suppose the gaps were: `1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 1, 1, 3, …`
0316 | 
0317 | Now preserve that exact multiset of intervals but permute their order.  
0318 | The surrogate has the same number of pulses, the same collection of inter‑pulse intervals, the same coarse burst statistics — but a different chronology.
0319 | 
0320 | If the exact sequence carries important information, the real stream should outperform this surrogate.  
0321 | It does not.
0322 | 
0323 | The real‑minus‑surrogate difference was only **0.010**.  
0324 | Pairwise superiority was **0.473**.
0325 | 
0326 | Again, effectively no advantage.
0327 | 
0328 | This suggests that much of the receiver’s response is driven by coarse temporal structure rather than a uniquely informative chronology.  
0329 | That is not yet a theorem, but it is the strongest interpretation supported by this experiment.
0330 | 
0331 | > **The receiver appears to respond to the form of the pulse stream rather than the identity of its source.**
0332 | 
0333 | ```mermaid
0334 | flowchart TD
0335 |     subgraph Experiments
0336 |     A[Bit vs No Bit] --> B[Timing Shuffled]
0337 |     B --> C[Rate-Matched Random]
0338 |     C --> D[Unrelated Same-Class Sender]
0339 |     D --> E[Interval-Preserving Surrogate]
0340 |     end
0341 |     B & C --> F[Timing matters]
0342 |     D --> G[Identity of sender does not matter\<br/>under tested controls]
0343 |     E --> G
0344 |     F -.->|necessary| H[Causal Transmission Established]
0345 |     G -.->|missing| I[Sender-Specific Signalling Not Supported]
0346 | ```
0347 | 
0348 | ---
0349 | 
0350 | ## The Chain
0351 | 
0352 | Once we had a causal one‑bit channel, we tried a simple extension.  
0353 | Six crystals in a line:
0354 | 
0355 | ```mermaid
0356 | flowchart LR
0357 |     C1[C1] --> C2[C2] --> C3[C3] --> C4[C4] --> C5[C5] --> C6[C6]
0358 | ```
0359 | 
0360 | Each crystal evolves independently. A pulse from one becomes an input to the next. If that input changes the receiver enough, the receiver’s own dynamics may later generate another pulse.
0361 | 
0362 | At first glance the result looks impressive. The full run produced source‑to‑node pulse correlations of approximately:
0363 | 
0364 | ```text
0365 | C1  1.000
0366 | C2  0.537
0367 | C3  0.477
0368 | C4  0.462
0369 | C5  0.462
0370 | C6  0.458
0371 | ```
0372 | 
0373 | It would be easy to draw a picture of a signal propagating down the chain.  
0374 | So we destroy the topology.
0375 | 
0376 | The shuffled‑edge control produced:
0377 | 
0378 | ```text
0379 | C1  1.000
0380 | C2  0.498
0381 | C3  0.461
0382 | C4  0.478
0383 | C5  0.471
0384 | C6  0.461
0385 | ```
0386 | 
0387 | The mean absolute real‑versus‑shuffled difference by distance was only about **0.0164**.
0388 | 
0389 | So the chain does not establish topology‑specific propagation.  
0390 | The high correlations are real observations. The interpretation “information travelled down this particular chain” is not supported.
0391 | 
0392 | ---
0393 | 
0394 | ## The Board
0395 | 
0396 | Finally we built a 6×6 Crystal Board.  
0397 | Thirty‑six independent Digital Crystals, each connected locally to neighbouring crystals through one‑bit events.
0398 | 
0399 | ```mermaid
0400 | graph TD
0401 |     subgraph 6x6 Board
0402 |     A1---A2---A3---A4---A5---A6
0403 |     |    |    |    |    |    |
0404 |     B1---B2---B3---B4---B5---B6
0405 |     |    |    |    |    |    |
0406 |     C1---C2---C3---C4---C5---C6
0407 |     |    |    |    |    |    |
0408 |     D1---D2---D3---D4---D5---D6
0409 |     |    |    |    |    |    |
0410 |     E1---E2---E3---E4---E5---E6
0411 |     |    |    |    |    |    |
0412 |     F1---F2---F3---F4---F5---F6
0413 |     end
0414 | ```
0415 | 
0416 | No target. No game. No shape to construct. No collective objective. Just local event transmission.
0417 | 
0418 | Again, real and shuffled topologies were run from matched conditions.  
0419 | Again, both were stopped at a common safe horizon before saturation (requested horizon 90 steps, average safe horizon ~73 steps).
0420 | 
0421 | The real topology did not produce a meaningful advantage over shuffled topology.  
0422 | The final real‑minus‑shuffled neighbour‑correlation difference was only about **0.0048**.
0423 | 
0424 | So the board does not yet contain evidence of organized local signalling.  
0425 | We have created connectivity. We have not created coordination.
0426 | 
0427 | ---
0428 | 
0429 | ## What Survived
0430 | 
0431 | Chapter 16 began with a word we did not deserve: communication.  
0432 | After the experiments, most of that word has been stripped away. What survives is smaller and more precise.
0433 | 
0434 | - A one‑bit event can enter another Digital Crystal’s actual growth dynamics and alter its future morphology.
0435 | - Real pulse timing matters relative to shuffled or random timing.
0436 | - But the actual sender does not yet matter.
0437 | - An unrelated same‑class sender performs essentially as well.
0438 | - An interval‑preserving surrogate performs essentially as well.
0439 | - Local chain structure does not outperform shuffled structure convincingly.
0440 | - The 6×6 board does not outperform shuffled topology convincingly.
0441 | 
0442 | So the result is not:
0443 | 
0444 | ```text
0445 | THE CRYSTALS COMMUNICATE
0446 | ```
0447 | 
0448 | It is:
0449 | 
0450 | ```text
0451 | CAUSAL TRANSMISSION IS SUPPORTED
0452 | while
0453 | SENDER-SPECIFIC SIGNALLING IS NOT SUPPORTED
0454 | ```
0455 | 
0456 | ---
0457 | 
0458 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
0459 | 
0460 | The strongest interpretation in this chapter did not survive.
0461 | 
0462 | We began with the possibility that one Digital Crystal might do something meaningfully like communicate with another.
0463 | 
0464 | The first intervention gave us a real causal result:
0465 | 
0466 | ```text
0467 | one received bit
0468 | ↓
0469 | receiver growth dynamics change
0470 | ↓
0471 | future morphology often diverges
0472 | ```
0473 | 
0474 | Across 120 paired checkpoint interventions, `95.8%` produced a morphology difference.
0475 | 
0476 | That established something important:
0477 | 
0478 | ```text
0479 | CAUSAL TRANSMISSION
0480 | SUPPORTED
0481 | ```
0482 | 
0483 | But transmission was not the whole hypothesis.
0484 | 
0485 | The harder controls asked whether something specific about the actual sender survived into the receiver.
0486 | 
0487 | That is where the stronger interpretation failed.
0488 | 
0489 | ### The hierarchy exposed by the controls
0490 | 
0491 | The control ladder produced a very clear information hierarchy:
0492 | 
0493 | ```text
0494 | BIT VERSUS NO BIT
0495 |         strong effect
0496 | 
0497 | REAL TIMING VERSUS SHUFFLED
0498 |         real wins
0499 | 
0500 | REAL TIMING VERSUS RATE-MATCHED RANDOM
0501 |         real wins
0502 | 
0503 | REAL SENDER VERSUS COUNT-MATCHED
0504 | UNRELATED SAME-CLASS SENDER
0505 |         no meaningful advantage
0506 | 
0507 | REAL CHRONOLOGY VERSUS
0508 | IPI-PRESERVING SURROGATE
0509 |         no meaningful advantage
0510 | ```
0511 | 
0512 | So the receiver is sensitive to more than pulse count.
0513 | 
0514 | Some temporal structure matters.
0515 | 
0516 | But the information that survives is not fine enough, under these controls, to identify the sender or the exact chronology of its pulse intervals.
0517 | 
0518 | That gives us a much sharper distinction:
0519 | 
0520 | ```text
0521 | COARSE TEMPORAL STRUCTURE
0522 | MATTERS
0523 | 
0524 | SENDER IDENTITY
0525 | NOT RECOVERED
0526 | 
0527 | EXACT INTERVAL ORDER
0528 | NOT RECOVERED
0529 | ```
0530 | 
0531 | ### Phenomenon record
0532 | 
0533 | **Phenomenon:** Lossy transmission of temporal structure
0534 | 
0535 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
0536 | 
0537 | **Current bounded description:**
0538 | 
0539 | > A one-bit event can causally alter another Digital Crystal, and receiver response depends on coarse timing structure, but the tested channel does not preserve enough information for sender-specific discrimination or exact interval-order discrimination.
0540 | 
0541 | This is not merely a communication failure.
0542 | 
0543 | It tells us something about the substrate's information resolution.
0544 | 
0545 | The receiver appears sensitive to broad temporal form such as:
0546 | 
0547 | ```text
0548 | pulse density
0549 | burstiness
0550 | interval distribution
0551 | coarse timing regime
0552 | ```
0553 | 
0554 | while being comparatively insensitive to:
0555 | 
0556 | ```text
0557 | which same-class sender produced the stream
0558 | exact ordering of the same interval collection
0559 | ```
0560 | 
0561 | That pattern connects directly to Chapter 14.
0562 | 
0563 | There, final morphology preserved enough information to recover forcing-process family while exact temporal ordering failed.
0564 | 
0565 | Here, receiver response distinguishes real timing from shuffled or rate-random controls, but does not distinguish the actual sender from an unrelated same-class sender or the exact chronology from an interval-preserving surrogate.
0566 | 
0567 | Together they support a provisional cross-chapter principle:
0568 | 
0569 | > **Digital Crystal dynamics preserve coarse process structure more readily than exact chronology or source identity.**
0570 | 
0571 | This is the **Lossy-History Principle** appearing in a different experimental role.
0572 | 
0573 | Chapter 14 observed it in final morphology.
0574 | 
0575 | Chapter 16 observes it during causal transmission.
0576 | 
0577 | ### Transmission is not identity preservation
0578 | 
0579 | The distinction can be written as:
0580 | 
0581 | ```text
0582 | CAUSE
0583 | ≠
0584 | IDENTITY
0585 | 
0586 | TIMING EFFECT
0587 | ≠
0588 | CHRONOLOGY RECOVERY
0589 | 
0590 | CHANNEL
0591 | ≠
0592 | MESSAGE
0593 | 
0594 | RECEIVER RESPONSE
0595 | ≠
0596 | SENDER-SPECIFIC SIGNALLING
0597 | ```
0598 | 
0599 | The pulse absolutely reaches the receiver.
0600 | 
0601 | The receiver absolutely changes.
0602 | 
0603 | But what survives transmission is coarse.
0604 | 
0605 | The channel carries causal influence without yet carrying enough discriminating structure to make the source operationally identifiable.
0606 | 
0607 | ### The topology experiments reinforce the same lesson
0608 | 
0609 | The chain and board experiments initially looked like stronger communication results.
0610 | 
0611 | But their topology-specific interpretations failed.
0612 | 
0613 | The six-crystal chain produced high correlations, yet shuffled edges produced nearly the same pattern.
0614 | 
0615 | The 6×6 board also failed to outperform shuffled topology meaningfully.
0616 | 
0617 | So again:
0618 | 
0619 | ```text
0620 | OBSERVATION
0621 | high correlation / local influence
0622 | 
0623 | STRONG INTERPRETATION
0624 | information propagated specifically through
0625 | the intended communication topology
0626 | 
0627 | STATUS
0628 | FAILED
0629 | ```
0630 | 
0631 | The measured relationships survive.
0632 | 
0633 | The topology-specific explanation does not.
0634 | 
0635 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
0636 | 
0637 | The surviving phenomenon does **not** establish:
0638 | 
0639 | - semantic communication,
0640 | - sender recognition,
0641 | - channel capacity,
0642 | - message identity,
0643 | - coordinated behaviour,
0644 | - topology-specific information propagation,
0645 | - intention,
0646 | - agency,
0647 | - or life.
0648 | 
0649 | It establishes something narrower:
0650 | 
0651 | > **Digital Crystal dynamics can transmit causal perturbations and preserve coarse temporal structure while discarding finer information about exact chronology and source identity under the tested controls.**
0652 | 
0653 | That phenomenon now belongs in the project-wide phenomenon record independently of the chapter's failed sender-specific signalling hypothesis.
0654 | 
0655 | ---
0656 | 
0657 | ## Evidence Ledger
0658 | 
0659 | | Claim | Status | Evidence |
0660 | |---|---|---|
0661 | | A received one‑bit event can alter receiver morphology | **SUPPORTED** | 120 paired checkpoint interventions; 95.8% produced morphology divergence |
0662 | | The pulse reaches the actual Digital Crystal growth process | **SUPPORTED** | Intervention directly changes receiver forcing used by frozen growth rule |
0663 | | Real pulse timing differs from shuffled timing in receiver response | **SUPPORTED** | Real strongly outperformed shuffled control |
0664 | | Real pulse timing differs from rate‑matched random timing | **SUPPORTED** | Real strongly outperformed random timing |
0665 | | The actual sender matters more than another same‑class sender | **FAILED** | Count‑matched unrelated sender performed essentially the same |
0666 | | Exact chronology matters beyond the same inter‑pulse intervals | **FAILED** | IPI‑permutation surrogate performed essentially the same |
0667 | | Influence propagates specifically through the six‑crystal chain topology | **FAILED** | Shuffled‑edge control was nearly identical |
0668 | | Local 6×6 topology produces measurable organised signalling | **FAILED** | Real and shuffled boards were nearly identical |
0669 | | The channel carries semantics | **UNTESTED** | No semantic task was introduced |
0670 | | The crystals coordinate toward a shared objective | **UNTESTED** | No shared objective was introduced |
0671 | | Channel capacity has been measured | **UNTESTED** | No information‑theoretic capacity experiment was run |
0672 | | Digital Crystal life has been established | **UNTESTED** | This experiment addresses only primitive causal transmission |
0673 | 
0674 | ---
0675 | 
0676 | ## The Bounded Claim
0677 | 
0678 | The strongest claim supported by this chapter is:
0679 | 
0680 | > Within Digital Crystal v1, changing one received bit while holding receiver state, stochastic state and external forcing fixed can alter the receiver’s subsequent morphology. Real sender‑generated pulse timing produces stronger receiver relationships than shuffled or rate‑matched random timing, but it does not outperform count‑matched same‑class sender replay or an inter‑pulse‑interval‑preserving surrogate. This supports primitive causal transmission, not sender‑specific signalling.
0681 | 
0682 | That boundary matters.  
0683 | If we had stopped after the first positive result, we might have written “the crystals communicate.”  
0684 | After controls, the claim is much better:
0685 | 
0686 | > **The crystal can hear a pulse. It cannot yet tell who spoke.**
0687 | 
0688 | ---
0689 | 
0690 | ## The Next Question
0691 | 
0692 | Not: can we send more bits?  
0693 | But: what would make one pulse stream carry something specific about its source?
0694 | 
0695 | A channel that merely perturbs another process is not enough.  
0696 | To become signalling, something about the sender must survive transmission in a way the receiver can detect.
0697 | 
0698 | The pulse exists.  
0699 | The channel exists.  
0700 | The sender does not yet exist **in the signal**.
0701 | 
0702 | **Next, we ask how does the crystal respond to perturbation.**
