0338 | 
0339 | ## The First Design Had a Deeper Problem
0340 | 
0341 | V1 had also smuggled too much meaning into the mechanism.
0342 | 
0343 | We had created:
0344 | 
0345 | ```text
0346 | HISTORY_A
0347 | HISTORY_B
0348 | ```
0349 | 
0350 | and then explicitly told the challenge how to interpret them.
0351 | 
0352 | In other words:
0353 | 
0354 | ```text
0355 | if A:
0356 |     increase probability
0357 | 
0358 | if B:
0359 |     decrease probability
0360 | ```
0361 | 
0362 | That proved something about retained symbolic labels.
0363 | 
0364 | But our broader question was stronger.
0365 | 
0366 | We wanted to know whether:
0367 | 
0368 | > **different experiences could create different material consequences which ordinary later dynamics would respond to differently**
0369 | 
0370 | not merely whether an explicit A/B decoder could read two labels.
0371 | 
0372 | So instead of tuning V1, we redesigned the mechanism.
0373 | 
0374 | ---
0375 | 
0376 | ## Second Attempt: Remove the Symbols
0377 | 
0378 | V2 returned to one altered material state:
0379 | 
0380 | ```text
0381 | NORMAL
0382 | MODIFIED
0383 | ```
0384 | 
0385 | There was no:
0386 | 
0387 | ```text
0388 | HISTORY_A
0389 | HISTORY_B
0390 | ```
0391 | 
0392 | anywhere in the substrate.
0393 | 
0394 | The two experiences differed only in where they wrote the same modified state.
0395 | 
0396 | Experience A wrote toward one directional region of the boundary.
0397 | 
0398 | Experience B wrote toward another.
0399 | 
0400 | The initial number of modified cells was identical.
0401 | 
0402 | Then both histories continued under the same material physics.
0403 | 
0404 | Modified state propagated with the same Chapter 18 mechanism.
0405 | 
0406 | And at every propagation step we forced the two histories to copy exactly the same number of modified cells.
0407 | 
0408 | So the two histories differed in spatial organization, not in how much historical material they were allowed to create.
0409 | 
0410 | Conceptually:
0411 | 
0412 | ```mermaid
0413 | flowchart LR
0414 |     subgraph Experience A
0415 |     A1[Experience A] --> A2[Write modified cells<br/>in region A]
0416 |     A2 --> A3[Same material state<br/>same quantity]
0417 |     A3 --> A4[Spatial organization A]
0418 |     end
0419 |     subgraph Experience B
0420 |     B1[Experience B] --> B2[Write modified cells<br/>in region B]
0421 |     B2 --> B3[Same material state<br/>same quantity]
0422 |     B3 --> B4[Spatial organization B]
0423 |     end
0424 |     A4 --> C[Both receive identical later challenge]
0425 |     B4 --> C
0426 |     C --> D[Measure response difference]
0427 | ```
0428 | 
0429 | Then both received one identical later challenge.
0430 | 
0431 | No symbolic decoder.
0432 | 
0433 | No A/B-specific rule.
0434 | 
0435 | ---
0436 | 
0437 | ## But Geometry Had Become a Confound Again
0438 | 
0439 | There was one complication.
0440 | 
0441 | Because modified material affects growth, the two spatial histories might themselves create slightly different crystal geometries before the challenge.
0442 | 
0443 | That means a simple A-vs-B challenge difference would not isolate retained material.
0444 | 
0445 | Perhaps the geometry alone caused the later difference.
0446 | 
0447 | So we added a stronger control.
0448 | 
0449 | At the exact pre-challenge checkpoint, clone each history.
0450 | 
0451 | Then erase only its modified-state labels.
0452 | 
0453 | Keep the occupied geometry unchanged.
0454 | 
0455 | Now we have:
0456 | 
0457 | ```text
0458 | A retained
0459 | A erased
0460 | 
0461 | B retained
0462 | B erased
0463 | ```
0464 | 
0465 | For each history:
0466 | 
0467 | ```text
0468 | challenge
0469 | vs
0470 | no challenge
0471 | ```
0472 | 
0473 | The primary quantity becomes:
0474 | 
0475 | ```text
0476 | retained interaction
0477 | -
0478 | erased interaction
0479 | ```
0480 | 
0481 | or more explicitly:
0482 | 
0483 | ```text
0484 | [(A challenge - A no-challenge)
0485 |  -
0486 |  (B challenge - B no-challenge)]
0487 | 
0488 | MINUS
0489 | 
0490 | [(A-erased challenge - A-erased no-challenge)
0491 |  -
0492 |  (B-erased challenge - B-erased no-challenge)]
0493 | ```
0494 | 
0495 | That is a demanding test.
0496 | 
0497 | It asks:
0498 | 
0499 | > **Does retained material organization itself contribute to a history-dependent challenge response beyond whatever geometry the history already created?**
0500 | 
0501 | That is the experiment we actually wanted.
0502 |

0664 | ## A Different Kind of Failure
0665 | 
0666 | V1 and V2 failed for different reasons.
0667 | 
0668 | V1:
0669 | 
0670 | ```text
0671 | explicit symbolic readout
0672 | ↓
0673 | detectable response
0674 | ↓
0675 | too small to clear scientific threshold
0676 | ```
0677 | 
0678 | V2:
0679 | 
0680 | ```text
0681 | non-symbolic spatial history
0682 | ↓
0683 | different traces remain
0684 | ↓
0685 | traces remain causally accessible
0686 | ↓
0687 | no meaningful common-challenge readout
0688 | ```
0689 | 
0690 | V2 is the stronger result.
0691 | 
0692 | It tells us something that V1 could not.
0693 | 
0694 | The problem was not merely that the historical traces disappeared.
0695 | 
0696 | They did not.
0697 | 
0698 | The problem was not merely that A and B became spatially identical.
0699 | 
0700 | They did not.
0701 | 
0702 | And the problem was not unequal historical material quantity.
0703 | 
0704 | That was exactly controlled.
0705 | 
0706 | What failed was the next step:
0707 | 
0708 | ```text
0709 | different accessible material history
0710 | ↓
0711 | different later response
0712 | ```
0713 | 
0714 | Under this protocol, that arrow did not hold.

0716 | ---
0717 | 
0718 | ## Distinguishable Is Not Readable
0719 | 
0720 | This gives us the central distinction of Chapter 19:
0721 | 
0722 | ```mermaid
0723 | flowchart LR
0724 |     A[PERSISTENT TRACE] --> B[ACCESSIBLE TRACE]
0725 |     B --> C[DISTINGUISHABLE TRACE]
0726 |     C --> D[READABLE TRACE]
0727 |     A -.->|≠| B
0728 |     B -.->|≠| C
0729 |     C -.->|≠| D
0730 | ```
0731 | 
0732 | Chapter 18 had already separated the first two.
0733 | 
0734 | Chapter 19 adds the next separation.
0735 | 
0736 | The crystal can contain two different spatial consequences of two different pasts.
0737 | 
0738 | Those consequences can remain measurably different.
0739 | 
0740 | They can remain in contact with active construction.
0741 | 
0742 | And still:
0743 | 
0744 | > **the later dynamics may not care which trace is present.**
0745 | 
0746 | That is a stronger negative than simply losing the history.
0747 | 
0748 | A stored distinction is not automatically a functional distinction.
0749 | 
0750 | ---
0751 | 
0752 | ## The Detector Problem
0753 | 
0754 | There is another way to think about this.
0755 | 
0756 | Suppose two waves travel through a medium with different phases.
0757 | 
0758 | A detector sensitive only to total amplitude may respond identically to both.
0759 | 
0760 | The histories differ.
0761 | 
0762 | The detector is simply insensitive to the degree of freedom in which they differ.
0763 | 
0764 | We should be very careful here.
0765 | 
0766 | We have not shown that the crystal contains waves.
0767 | 
0768 | We have not shown phase.
0769 | 
0770 | We have not shown a propagating field.
0771 | 
0772 | But the analogy exposes a real experimental issue.
0773 | 
0774 | Our common challenge is one particular probe.
0775 | 
0776 | A negative result means:
0777 | 
0778 | > **this probe did not extract a scientifically meaningful history-dependent response**
0779 | 
0780 | It does not prove:
0781 | 
0782 | > **no possible later interaction could ever distinguish the histories**
0783 | 
0784 | Those are very different claims.
0785 | 
0786 | But that does not mean we should now try twenty different probes until one succeeds.
0787 | 
0788 | That would turn the experimental program into a search for significance.
0789 | 
0790 | So we stop this mechanism family here.
0791 | 
0792 | ---
0793 | 
0794 | ## Remember the Flocking Lesson
0795 | 
0796 | Earlier in the book, Outlier gave us another seductive visual impression.
0797 | 
0798 | It looked like flocking.
0799 | 
0800 | Nearby structures moved with striking local coherence.
0801 | 
0802 | At first, causal family relationships even appeared to explain some of it.
0803 | 
0804 | Then better controls removed the family effect.
0805 | 
0806 | The surviving result was narrower:
0807 | 
0808 | ```text
0809 | local geometry
0810 | +
0811 | local cellular dynamics
0812 | +
0813 | spatial organization
0814 | ↓
0815 | coherent motion
0816 | ```
0817 | 
0818 | Not flocking.
0819 | 
0820 | That episode taught us something important.
0821 | 
0822 | > **Interesting visual structure is where a question begins, not where a claim ends.**
0823 | 
0824 | The same rule applies here.
0825 | 
0826 | The directional material patterns persist.
0827 | 
0828 | They look like different histories moving through the crystal.
0829 | 
0830 | That is interesting.
0831 | 
0832 | But we do not promote:
0833 | 
0834 | ```text
0835 | wave
0836 | memory
0837 | stored message
0838 | representation
0839 | ```
0840 | 
0841 | from that appearance.
0842 | 
0843 | We retain only what the experiment earned.
0844 | 
0845 | ---
0846 | 
0847 | ## What Did Chapter 19 Actually Establish?
0848 | 
0849 | The cleanest result is not positive or negative in the ordinary sense.
0850 | 
0851 | It is a boundary.
0852 | 
0853 | We can say:
0854 | 
0855 | > **Two different directional experiences can leave persistent, spatially distinguishable organizations of the same altered material while that material remains substantially in contact with the active growth frontier. Under the frozen common-challenge protocol, those differences did not produce a scientifically meaningful difference in later response beyond a geometry-preserving erasure control.**
0856 | 
0857 | That is the technical statement.
0858 | 
0859 | In simpler language:
0860 | 
0861 | > **The crystal can carry different traces of different pasts. We have not shown that its later dynamics can use the difference.**
0862 | 
0863 | That is enough.
0864 | 
0865 | ---
0866 | 
0867 | ## Why We Are Not Building V3
0868 | 
0869 | There are many tempting next moves.
0870 | 
0871 | Change the angles.
0872 | 
0873 | Increase the material gain.
0874 | 
0875 | Move the challenge earlier.
0876 | 
0877 | Move it later.
0878 | 
0879 | Use only the first challenge step.
0880 | 
0881 | Try a different challenge shape.
0882 | 
0883 | Measure a different denominator.
0884 | 
0885 | Increase the number of groups.
0886 | 
0887 | Every one of those could produce another experiment.
0888 | 
0889 | That is exactly why we should not do them.
0890 | 
0891 | The primary result was not ambiguous.
0892 | 
0893 | It was tiny.
0894 | 
0895 | The confidence interval included zero.
0896 | 
0897 | The effect was only a few hundredths of one seed-noise standard deviation.
0898 | 
0899 | So another small tuning step would not cross a conceptual boundary.
0900 | 
0901 | It would merely search the neighbourhood of a failed mechanism.
0902 | 
0903 | We already know where that leads.
0904 | 
0905 | The book does not need V3.
0906 | 
0907 | It needs a new question.
0908 | 
0909 | ---
0910 | 
0911 | ## The New Ladder
0912 | 
0913 | At this point our historical-material ladder looks like this:
0914 | 
0915 | ```mermaid
0916 | flowchart TD
0917 |     A[EXTERNAL EVENT] --> B[LOCAL MATERIAL CHANGE]
0918 |     B --> C[PERSISTENT TRACE]
0919 |     C --> D[CAUSAL ACCESS]
0920 |     D --> E[DISTINGUISHABLE MATERIAL ORGANIZATION]
0921 |     E --> F[READOUT INTO LATER RESPONSE]
0922 |     style A fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#333
0923 |     style B fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#333
0924 |     style C fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#333
0925 |     style D fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#333
0926 |     style E fill:#ccffcc,stroke:#333
0927 |     style F fill:#ffcccc,stroke:#333,stroke-dasharray: 5 5
0928 | ```
0929 | 
0930 | The experiments support the ladder only up to:
0931 | 
0932 | ```text
0933 | DISTINGUISHABLE MATERIAL ORGANIZATION
0934 | ```
0935 | 
0936 | The final arrow remains unearned.
0937 | 
0938 | That is a useful place to stop.
0939 | 
0940 | ---
0941 | 
0942 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
0943 | 
0944 | The chapter asked whether two different pasts could become functionally distinguishable later.
0945 | 
0946 | That stronger claim failed.
0947 | 
0948 | But the failure was unusually informative because several lower rungs of the mechanism clearly survived.
0949 | 
0950 | ### What survived before readout
0951 | 
0952 | In V2, both histories wrote the same amount of modified material.
0953 | 
0954 | They propagated the same number of copies.
0955 | 
0956 | They ended with the same average quantity of altered material.
0957 | 
0958 | Yet their spatial organizations remained measurably different.
0959 | 
0960 | At the same time, roughly one fifth of the active frontier still remained in contact with modified material at the end of the retention window.
0961 | 
0962 | So the histories were not gone and not buried beyond causal reach.
0963 | 
0964 | They were still persistent, spatially distinguishable, and causally accessible.
0965 | 
0966 | Then the common challenge arrived.
0967 | 
0968 | The material-mediated history effect was `0.000431`, about `0.043%` of crystal population, with confidence interval `[-0.000380, +0.001235]` and `p ≈ 0.163`.
0969 | 
0970 | Against seed noise, the effect was only `0.033 SD`, versus the frozen requirement `0.500 SD`.
0971 | 
0972 | So the final readout arrow failed decisively.
0973 | 
0974 | ### Phenomenon record
0975 | 
0976 | **Phenomenon:** Distinguishable history without functional readout
0977 | 
0978 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
0979 | 
0980 | **Current bounded description:**
0981 | 
0982 | > Two different prior experiences can leave persistent, spatially distinguishable organizations of the same altered material while that material remains substantially coupled to the active growth interface, yet those differences need not produce a scientifically meaningful difference under a common later challenge.
0983 | 
0984 | This is stronger than merely saying history was lost.
0985 | 
0986 | The history was not lost; the distinction was still physically present and accessible.
0987 | 
0988 | What failed was the arrow from different accessible trace to different later response.
0989 | 
0990 | So Chapter 19 adds another rung to the project-wide history hierarchy:
0991 | 
0992 | ```text
0993 | PERSISTENT TRACE
0994 | ≠
0995 | ACCESSIBLE TRACE
0996 | ≠
0997 | DISTINGUISHABLE TRACE
0998 | ≠
0999 | READABLE TRACE
1000 | ```
1001 | 
1002 | ### This extends the Lossy-History Principle
1003 | 
1004 | Chapter 14 showed that broad source statistics survive more readily than exact temporal order.
1005 | 
1006 | Chapter 16 showed that coarse pulse-stream structure survives more readily than sender identity or exact interval chronology.
1007 | 
1008 | Chapter 17 showed that different histories can produce different particular futures without producing a stable population-level signature.
1009 | 
1010 | Chapter 18 showed that even persistent historical state matters only while it remains coupled to active construction.
1011 | 
1012 | Chapter 19 now shows something still stronger:
1013 | 
1014 | > **Even a persistent, accessible and measurably different historical trace can remain functionally inert with respect to a later probe.**
1015 | 
1016 | So the Lossy-History Principle is no longer only about loss of chronology; it now has several possible failure points:
1017 | 
1018 | ```mermaid
1019 | flowchart TD
1020 |     A[History] --> B{Persist?}
1021 |     B -- Yes --> C{Accessible?}
1022 |     B -- No --> X[Lost]
1023 |     C -- Yes --> D{Distinguishable?}
1024 |     C -- No --> Y[Persistent but inaccessible]
1025 |     D -- Yes --> E{Readable?}
1026 |     D -- No --> Z[Accessible but indistinguishable]
1027 |     E -- Yes --> F[Functional history]
1028 |     E -- No --> W[Distinguishable but inert]
1029 | ```
1030 | 
1031 | Those are different mechanisms.
1032 | 
1033 | ### The detector problem is real
1034 | 
1035 | The chapter's wave analogy is useful only as an analogy.
1036 | 
1037 | Two states can differ in a degree of freedom that the chosen probe does not measure.
1038 | 
1039 | So a failed challenge means this probe did not extract a meaningful history-dependent response.
1040 | 
1041 | It does not establish that no possible future interaction could ever distinguish the traces.
1042 | 
1043 | But that does not justify searching indefinitely for a probe that works.
1044 | 
1045 | The mechanism family was frozen and tested, and the primary effect was tiny.
1046 | 
1047 | So the correct action remains: **NO V3**.
1048 | 
1049 | ### Connection to the Interface Principle
1050 | 
1051 | Chapter 19 also sharpens the Interface Principle.
1052 | 
1053 | Chapter 18 showed: state must remain accessible to the active interface.
1054 | 
1055 | Chapter 19 shows: accessibility is necessary but not sufficient.
1056 | 
1057 | The active interface can still encounter a historical difference without the later dynamics producing a meaningful differential response.
1058 | 
1059 | So the revised relationship is:
1060 | 
1061 | ```text
1062 | PERSISTENCE → ACCESSIBILITY → DISTINGUISHABILITY → READOUT
1063 | ```
1064 | 
1065 | and each arrow must be earned separately.
1066 | 
1067 | This prevents us from collapsing *accessible* into *usable*.
1068 | 
1069 | ### Open propagating-field question
1070 | 
1071 | The persistent directional material organizations also resemble a moving spatial phenomenon.
1072 | 
1073 | That resemblance is worth preserving as an observation.
1074 | 
1075 | But the chapter does not establish wave, phase, propagation velocity, or dispersion.
1076 | 
1077 | So the correct status remains:
1078 | 
1079 | ```text
1080 | DIRECTIONAL SPATIAL TRACE
1081 | MEASURED
1082 | 
1083 | PROPAGATING-FIELD INTERPRETATION
1084 | OPEN
1085 | ```
1086 | 
1087 | This belongs with the Chapter 13 and Chapter 18 observations for a later spatiotemporal audit.
1088 | 
1089 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
1090 | 
1091 | The surviving phenomenon does **not** establish:
1092 | 
1093 | - memory,
1094 | - representation,
1095 | - semantic history,
1096 | - learning,
1097 | - adaptation,
1098 | - a wave mechanism,
1099 | - a general-purpose history decoder,
1100 | - or life.
1101 | 
1102 | It establishes something narrower:
1103 | 
1104 | > **The Digital Crystal can retain different, accessible material organizations corresponding to different pasts without those differences becoming functionally readable by the tested later dynamics.**
1105 | 
1106 | That phenomenon should now be tracked independently of the failed readout hypothesis.
1107 | 
1108 | ---
1109 | 
1110 | ## The Result of Chapter 19
1111 | 
1112 | The two experiments together give us one bounded conclusion.
1113 | 
1114 | V1 showed that an explicit symbolic material decoder can produce a small, reproducible history-dependent response, but the effect did not clear the predeclared scientific magnitude threshold.
1115 | 
1116 | V2 removed the symbolic decoder and allowed two experiences to create different spatial organizations of the same material state.
1117 | 
1118 | Those organizations remained measurably distinct and causally accessible, but they did not produce a meaningful difference under the common later challenge.
1119 | 
1120 | So:
1121 | 
1122 | > **Different pasts can leave different traces without those traces becoming functionally readable by later dynamics.**
1123 | 
1124 | That is the result.
1125 | 
1126 | And another distinction joins the growing list:
1127 | 
1128 | ```text
1129 | DIFFERENT HISTORY
1130 | ≠
1131 | DIFFERENT TRACE
1132 | ≠
1133 | READABLE HISTORY
1134 | ```
1135 | 
1136 | We now know that storing history is easier than using it. Again.
1137 | 
1138 | But this time the reason is not simply that the trace was buried.
1139 | 
1140 | Even an accessible difference can be inert with respect to the future probe.
1141 | 
1142 | ---
1143 | 
1144 | ## What Comes Next
1145 | 
1146 | For nine chapters, the Digital Crystal has lived inside a strange world.
1147 | 
1148 | Once material appears, it never disappears.
1149 | 
1150 | The frontier only moves outward.
1151 | 
1152 | Old cells become buried forever.
1153 | 
1154 | A trace can fall out of the causal aperture because the crystal builds over it, but nothing ever exposes it again.
1155 | 
1156 | That assumption has shaped almost every result we have obtained.
1157 | 
1158 | So rather than inventing another history reader, we are going to remove the assumption.
1159 | 
1160 | For the first time, occupied material will be allowed to vanish.
1161 | 
1162 | Nothing else.
1163 | 
1164 | No repair mechanism.
1165 | 
1166 | No energy.
1167 | 
1168 | No maintenance controller.
1169 | 
1170 | Just:
1171 | 
1172 | ```text
1173 | occupied
1174 | ↓
1175 | empty
1176 | ```
1177 | 
1178 | with some small probability.
1179 | 
1180 | That one change will make the frontier non-monotone.
1181 | 
1182 | Buried material may become exposed.
1183 | 
1184 | Construction will have to compete with loss.
1185 | 
1186 | The crystal may acquire a finite sustainable scale.
1187 | 
1188 | And properties that were impossible to distinguish under irreversible growth may finally separate.
1189 | 
1190 | ```mermaid
1191 | flowchart LR
1192 |     subgraph Irreversible
1193 |     A[Occupied] -->|grows| B[Occupied]
1194 |     B --> C[Frontier moves outward]
1195 |     C --> D[Buried state never re-exposed]
1196 |     end
1197 |     subgraph Reversible
1198 |     E[Occupied] -->|grows| F[Occupied]
1199 |     F -->|loss| G[Empty]
1200 |     G -->|regrowth| H[Occupied]
1201 |     H --> I[Buried state may become exposed]
1202 |     end
1203 |     D -.-> J[History readout constrained]
1204 |     I -.-> K[New possibilities for readout]
1205 | ```
1206 | 
1207 | Chapter 19 ends with an inaccessible word still hanging in front of us:
1208 | 
1209 | ```text
1210 | memory?
1211 | ```
1212 | 
1213 | We have not earned it.
1214 | 
1215 | Good.
1216 | 
1217 | The next experiment is not going to chase the word.
1218 | 
1219 | It is going to change the world.
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "20: What Happens When the Crystal Can Lose Material?"
0003 | date = "2026-08-12T18:49:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "The Digital Crystal had always lived in a world where occupied material lasted forever. Chapter 20 removes that assumption and discovers that loss creates new construction opportunity."
0006 | weight = 20
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Digital Crystal", "Causality", "Material Loss", "Reoccupation", "Experiments"]
0009 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | Until now, the crystal had lived in an impossible world.
0013 | 
0014 | Once a cell became occupied, it stayed occupied.
0015 | 
0016 | Forever.
0017 | 
0018 | The frontier moved outward.
0019 | 
0020 | Old material accumulated behind it.
0021 | 
0022 | Nothing eroded.
0023 | 
0024 | Nothing vanished.
0025 | 
0026 | Nothing exposed the interior again.
0027 | 
0028 | That assumption had quietly shaped almost every result since Chapter 11.
0029 | 
0030 | So Chapter 20 removed it.
0031 | 
0032 | We added one rule:
0033 | 
0034 | ```text
0035 | occupied
0036 | ↓
0037 | empty
0038 | ```
0039 | 
0040 | with some small probability.
0041 | 
0042 | Nothing else.
0043 | 
0044 | No repair mechanism.
0045 | 
0046 | No resource system.
0047 | 
0048 | No maintenance controller.
0049 | 
0050 | No energy variable.
0051 | 
0052 | No metabolism.
0053 | 
0054 | No target morphology.
0055 | 
0056 | Just loss.
0057 | 
0058 | Then we asked what broke.
0059 | 
0060 | ---
0061 | 
0062 | ## The Obvious Prediction
0063 | 
0064 | The first prediction seemed almost embarrassingly simple.
0065 | 
0066 | Suppose the crystal has an effective radius \(r\).
0067 | 
0068 | If new construction happens mainly around the outside boundary, then construction opportunity should scale roughly like perimeter:
0069 | 
0070 | $$
0071 | \text{construction} \sim r
0072 | $$
0073 | 
0074 | But if every occupied cell can disappear, then total expected loss should scale roughly like occupied area:
0075 | 
0076 | $$
0077 | \text{loss} \sim r^2
0078 | $$
0079 | 
0080 | That gives a natural prediction.
0081 | 
0082 | At small size:
0083 | 
0084 | ```text
0085 | construction > loss
0086 | ```
0087 | 
0088 | At larger size:
0089 | 
0090 | ```text
0091 | loss > construction
0092 | ```
0093 | 
0094 | So there ought to be some scale where the two balance.
0095 | 
0096 | Perhaps the crystal would stop expanding.
0097 | 
0098 | Perhaps it would hover around a finite size.
0099 | 
0100 | Perhaps above some loss rate it would collapse.
0101 | 
0102 | It was exactly the kind of candidate scaling law we wanted.
0103 | 
0104 | And because it sounded so plausible, we wrote the failure condition before running the experiment.
0105 | 
0106 | A finite dynamic regime had to satisfy all of these:
0107 | 
0108 | ```text
0109 | late population slope approximately zero
0110 | 
0111 | population still substantially above zero
0112 | 
0113 | world far from simulation capacity
0114 | 
0115 | population meaningfully smaller than decay-off baseline
0116 | ```
0117 | 
0118 | A plateau caused by extinction would not count.
0119 | 
0120 | A plateau caused by reaching the edge of the world would not count.
0121 | 
0122 | We wanted a genuine balance between construction and loss.
0123 | 
0124 | ---
0125 | 
0126 | ## First Establish the Baseline
0127 | 
0128 | With no loss, the crystal still behaved exactly as expected.
0129 | 
0130 | The decay-off baseline had a late normalized population slope around:
0131 | 
0132 | ```text
0133 | 0.037 per update
0134 | ```
0135 | 
0136 | and late net growth around:
0137 | 
0138 | ```text
0139 | 154 cells per update
0140 | ```
0141 | 
0142 | The crystal was nowhere near world capacity.
0143 | 
0144 | So we had a clean expanding reference.
0145 | 
0146 | Then we turned on loss.
0147 | 
0148 | The sweep was:
0149 | 
0150 | ```text
0151 | δ = 0.00
0152 | δ = 0.02
0153 | δ = 0.04
0154 | δ = 0.06
0155 | δ = 0.08
0156 | δ = 0.12
0157 | δ = 0.16
0158 | ```
0159 | 
0160 | The prediction was straightforward:
0161 | 
0162 | ```text
0163 | higher δ
0164 | ↓
0165 | more material removed
0166 | ↓
0167 | growth slows
0168 | ↓
0169 | eventually slope approaches zero
0170 | ```
0171 | 
0172 | That is not what happened.
0173 | 
0174 | ---
0175 | 
0176 | ## Loss Did Not Stop the Expansion
0177 | 
0178 | The late normalized population slopes stayed remarkably similar.
0179 | 
0180 | Across the entire sweep they remained close to:
0181 | 
0182 | ```text
0183 | 0.036 – 0.038
0184 | ```
0185 | 
0186 | Even at the highest tested loss rate, the crystal was still expanding.
0187 | 
0188 | The late mean population did fall.
0189 | 
0190 | At `δ = 0.16`, it was roughly one third smaller than the decay-off baseline.
0191 | 
0192 | But the slope did not flatten.
0193 | 
0194 | No non-zero loss rate met the predeclared finite-regime condition.
0195 | 
0196 | So the primary result was:
0197 | 
0198 | ```text
0199 | FAILED
0200 | ```
0201 | 
0202 | The obvious perimeter-versus-area argument had not survived contact with the substrate.
0203 | 
0204 | That failure was already useful.
0205 | 
0206 | But the reason was much more interesting.
0207 | 
0208 | ---
0209 | 
0210 | ## Look at the Gross Construction Rate
0211 | 
0212 | At first glance, increasing loss should simply subtract material from the crystal.
0213 | 
0214 | If the crystal ordinarily adds around 150 cells per update, then adding loss ought to produce something like:
0215 | 
0216 | ```text
0217 | +150 construction
0218 | -80 loss
0219 | = +70 net
0220 | ```
0221 | 
0222 | Then perhaps:
0223 | 
0224 | ```text
0225 | +150 construction
0226 | -150 loss
0227 | = 0 net
0228 | ```
0229 | 
0230 | But the construction rate itself did not remain fixed.
0231 | 
0232 | It exploded.
0233 | 
0234 | Late averages looked approximately like this:
0235 | 
0236 | | δ | attachments | losses | net growth |
0237 | |---|-------------|--------|------------|
0238 | | 0.00 | 152 | 0 | +152 |
0239 | | 0.02 | 227 | 81 | +146 |
0240 | | 0.04 | 299 | 158 | +141 |
0241 | | 0.06 | 358 | 227 | +131 |
0242 | | 0.08 | 430 | 303 | +127 |
0243 | | 0.12 | 530 | 420 | +110 |
0244 | | 0.16 | 632 | 531 | +101 |
0245 | 
0246 | At `δ = 0.16`, the crystal was losing more than five hundred cells per update.
0247 | 
0248 | But it was also attaching more than six hundred.
0249 | 
0250 | Loss had made the crystal build faster.
0251 | 
0252 | That was not in the prediction.
0253 | 
0254 | ---
0255 | 
0256 | ## The Missing Variable Was Frontier
0257 | 
0258 | The original scaling argument treated the crystal as if it had one meaningful boundary.
0259 | 
0260 | Something like:
0261 | 
0262 | ```text
0263 | solid interior
0264 | +
0265 | outer perimeter
0266 | ```
0267 | 
0268 | But random loss changes the geometry.
0269 | 
0270 | Every time an occupied site disappears, it can create a new empty location surrounded by occupied material.
0271 | 
0272 | That location becomes part of the set that ordinary growth can potentially fill.
0273 | 
0274 | ```mermaid
0275 | flowchart LR
0276 |     A[Loss removes<br/>occupied cell] --> B[New empty site<br/>in occupied region]
0277 |     B --> C[Site becomes<br/>local boundary]
0278 |     C --> D[Ordinary growth sees<br/>attachment opportunity]
0279 |     D --> E[Construction rate increases]
0280 | ```
0281 | 
0282 | So:
0283 | 
0284 | ```text
0285 | loss
0286 | ↓
0287 | new empty site
0288 | ↓
0289 | new local boundary
0290 | ↓
0291 | new attachment opportunity
0292 | ```
0293 | 
0294 | The loss process was manufacturing frontier.
0295 | 
0296 | And the boundary measurements showed it dramatically.
0297 | 
0298 | Approximate late mean boundary counts were:
0299 | 
0300 | | δ | boundary count |
0301 | |---|----------------|
0302 | | 0.00 | 372 |
0303 | | 0.02 | 807 |
0304 | | 0.04 | 1167 |
0305 | | 0.06 | 1430 |
0306 | | 0.08 | 1695 |
0307 | | 0.12 | 1940 |
0308 | | 0.16 | 2068 |
0309 | 
0310 | So our original statement:
0311 | 
0312 | ```text
0313 | construction opportunity ~ outer perimeter
0314 | ```
0315 | 
0316 | was simply the wrong geometry.
0317 | 
0318 | Once material can disappear, the crystal develops internal construction surfaces.
0319 | 
0320 | The active boundary is no longer only outside.
0321 | 
0322 | That destroys the naive scaling law.
0323 | 
0324 | ---
0325 | 
0326 | ## Where You Lose Material Matters
0327 | 
0328 | V1 contained another test.
0329 | 
0330 | Suppose the total number of removed cells is held exactly equal.
0331 | 
0332 | Does it matter whether they are removed from the surface or the interior?
0333 | 
0334 | We synchronized the loss count.
0335 | 
0336 | Every update:
0337 | 
0338 | ```text
0339 | surface branch removes K cells
0340 | interior branch removes K cells
0341 | ```
0342 | 
0343 | The total removal budget was identical.
0344 | 
0345 | The only difference was placement.
0346 | 
0347 | The result was strong.
0348 | 
0349 | Late population was about:
0350 | 
0351 | ```text
0352 | 11.1%
0353 | ```
0354 | 
0355 | higher under interior-biased loss than under surface-biased loss.
0356 | 
0357 | That cleared the predeclared 10% effect threshold.
0358 | 
0359 | And the hole counts were dramatically different:
0360 | 
0361 | ```text
0362 | surface loss      ~2.7 late holes
0363 | interior loss    ~29.8 late holes
0364 | ```
0365 | 
0366 | So equal loss did not have equal consequences.
0367 | 
0368 | Where the missing material appeared mattered.
0369 | 
0370 | At this point we had a plausible explanation.
0371 | 
0372 | Perhaps interior loss creates high-neighbour-count vacancies that ordinary growth rapidly fills.
0373 | 
0374 | But that was still only an interpretation.
0375 | 
0376 | We needed to measure it directly.
0377 | 
0378 | ---
0379 | 
0380 | ## V2: Separate New Construction from Reoccupation
0381 | 
0382 | Until loss existed, every attachment meant the same thing.
0383 | 
0384 | A cell had never been occupied before.
0385 | 
0386 | Then it became occupied.
0387 | 
0388 | So:
0389 | 
0390 | ```text
0391 | attachment = new construction
0392 | ```
0393 | 
0394 | But after material loss, that equivalence breaks.
0395 | 
0396 | A cell can now follow this path:
0397 | 
0398 | ```text
0399 | occupied
0400 | ↓
0401 | lost
0402 | ↓
0403 | empty
0404 | ↓
0405 | occupied again
0406 | ```
0407 | 
0408 | So V2 introduced an observer-only occupancy ledger.
0409 | 
0410 | It did not change the crystal.
0411 | 
0412 | It merely remembered whether each lattice position had ever been occupied before.
0413 | 
0414 | Now every attachment could be classified as one of two things:
0415 | 
0416 | ```text
0417 | FIRST OCCUPATION
0418 | a site is occupied for the first time ever
0419 | 
0420 | REOCCUPATION
0421 | a previously occupied site was lost
0422 | and later becomes occupied again
0423 | ```
0424 | 
0425 | ```mermaid
0426 | flowchart TD
0427 |     A[Attachment event] --> B{Was site ever occupied before?}
0428 |     B -- No --> C[First occupation]
0429 |     B -- Yes --> D[Reoccupation]
0430 |     D --> E[Site was previously lost]
0431 | ```
0432 | 
0433 | This distinction immediately changes how we should read the V1 numbers.
0434 | 
0435 | `632 attachments per update` does not mean:
0436 | 
0437 | ```text
0438 | 632 new places added
0439 | ```
0440 | 
0441 | It means:
0442 | 
0443 | ```text
0444 | first occupations
0445 | +
0446 | reoccupations
0447 | ```
0448 | 
0449 | The crystal may be doing enormous internal turnover while net population grows much more slowly.
0450 | 
0451 | ---
0452 | 
0453 | ## Verify the Null First
0454 | 
0455 | With no material loss, reoccupation must be impossible.
0456 | 
0457 | Nothing ever becomes empty again.
0458 | 
0459 | So V2 first ran a structural null.
0460 | 
0461 | Across 96 no-loss runs:
0462 | 
0463 | ```text
0464 | reoccupation count = 0
0465 | ```
0466 | 
0467 | exactly.
0468 | 
0469 | All attachments were first occupations.
0470 | 
0471 | Good.
0472 | 
0473 | Now we could trust the ledger.
0474 | 
0475 | ---
0476 | 
0477 | ## The Exact-Count Loss Experiment
0478 | 
0479 | We returned to the matched surface-versus-interior design.
0480 | 
0481 | Again:
0482 | 
0483 | ```text
0484 | surface loss count = interior loss count
0485 | ```
0486 | 
0487 | on every update.
0488 | 
0489 | The mean cumulative loss count in each branch was about:
0490 | 
0491 | ```text
0492 | 890 cells
0493 | ```
0494 | 
0495 | Then we asked:
0496 | 
0497 | > What fraction of those losses later became reoccupations?
0498 | 
0499 | The answer was much larger than expected.
0500 | 
0501 | ---
0502 | 
0503 | ## Almost Everything Came Back
0504 | 
0505 | For surface-biased loss:
0506 | 
0507 | ```text
0508 | reoccupation per loss ≈ 0.936
0509 | ```
0510 | 
0511 | For interior-biased loss:
0512 | 
0513 | ```text
0514 | reoccupation per loss ≈ 0.956
0515 | ```
0516 | 
0517 | Another way to measure the same phenomenon is to ask what fraction of unique lost sites were ever reoccupied.
0518 | 
0519 | Again:
0520 | 
0521 | ```text
0522 | surface     ≈ 93.6%
0523 | interior    ≈ 95.7%
0524 | ```
0525 | 
0526 | That is the central mechanistic result of Chapter 20.
0527 | 
0528 | Under these conditions, most removed sites did not remain empty.
0529 | 
0530 | They came back.
0531 | 
0532 | And usually quickly.
0533 | 
0534 | Mean reoccupation delay:
0535 | 
0536 | ```text
0537 | surface     ≈ 1.56 updates
0538 | interior    ≈ 1.09 updates
0539 | ```
0540 | 
0541 | So a typical lost site was often empty for only one or two steps.
0542 | 
0543 | ---
0544 | 
0545 | ## But the Primary V2 Hypothesis Still Failed
0546 | 
0547 | V2 had not merely predicted that reoccupation would occur.
0548 | 
0549 | It made a stronger claim.
0550 | 
0551 | We predicted that interior loss would produce a much larger reoccupation rate than surface loss.
0552 | 
0553 | The predeclared minimum difference was:
0554 | 
0555 | ```text
0556 | 0.15 additional reoccupations per loss
0557 | ```
0558 | 
0559 | The observed difference was only:
0560 | 
0561 | ```text
0562 | 0.0198
0563 | ```
0564 | 
0565 | It was statistically clear.
0566 | 
0567 | The interval was narrow.
0568 | 
0569 | The directional test was extremely small.
0570 | 
0571 | But it was nowhere near the effect size we had said would matter.
0572 | 
0573 | So the primary V2 result was:
0574 | 
0575 | ```text
0576 | FAILED
0577 | ```
0578 | 
0579 | Again.
0580 | 
0581 | And again the failure corrected the interpretation.
0582 | 
0583 | Interior loss was not special in the way we expected.
0584 | 
0585 | The much larger phenomenon was shared by both conditions.
0586 | 
0587 | ---
0588 | 
0589 | ## Almost Every Loss Creates Frontier
0590 | 
0591 | V2 also measured how much new frontier was created per removed cell.
0592 | 
0593 | The numbers were:
0594 | 
0595 | ```text
0596 | surface     ~0.995 new frontier sites per loss
0597 | interior    ~1.000 new frontier sites per loss
0598 | ```
0599 | 
0600 | That is almost one-for-one.
0601 | 
0602 | So the more general mechanism is:
0603 | 
0604 | ```text
0605 | LOCAL MATERIAL LOSS
0606 | ↓
0607 | NEW EMPTY LOCATION
0608 | ↓
0609 | NEW ATTACHMENT OPPORTUNITY
0610 | ```
0611 | 
0612 | not:
0613 | 
0614 | ```text
0615 | INTERIOR LOSS ONLY
0616 | ↓
0617 | SPECIAL ATTACHMENT OPPORTUNITY
0618 | ```
0619 | 
0620 | Interior sites were somewhat more rapidly and completely reoccupied.
0621 | 
0622 | But that was a second-order difference.
0623 | 
0624 | The major effect was universal.
0625 | 
0626 | Removing a cell almost always creates a site ordinary growth can see again.
0627 | 
0628 | ---
0629 | 
0630 | ## Reoccupation Is Not Repair
0631 | 
0632 | This is where the language matters.
0633 | 
0634 | It is tempting to say:
0635 | 
0636 | > The crystal repairs itself.
0637 | 
0638 | We have not earned that.
0639 | 
0640 | There is no:
0641 | 
0642 | ```text
0643 | damage detector
0644 | ```
0645 | 
0646 | No:
0647 | 
0648 | ```text
0649 | repair objective
0650 | ```
0651 | 
0652 | No:
0653 | 
0654 | ```text
0655 | desired target morphology
0656 | ```
0657 | 
0658 | No:
0659 | 
0660 | ```text
0661 | special reconstruction pathway
0662 | ```
0663 | 
0664 | The exact same local growth rule runs whether the empty site is:
0665 | 
0666 | ```text
0667 | new territory
0668 | ```
0669 | 
0670 | or:
0671 | 
0672 | ```text
0673 | a place that used to exist
0674 | ```
0675 | 
0676 | The crystal does not know the difference.
0677 | 
0678 | The observer does.
0679 | 
0680 | So the bounded claim is:
0681 | 
0682 | > **Material removal creates attachment opportunities that the ordinary Digital Crystal growth rule rapidly reuses.**
0683 | 
0684 | That is enough.
0685 | 
0686 | And it is more interesting than calling it repair too early.
0687 | 
0688 | ---
0689 | 
0690 | ## Population Was Hiding Turnover
0691 | 
0692 | The biggest conceptual change in this chapter is not about loss.
0693 | 
0694 | It is about measurement.
0695 | 
0696 | A population graph shows:
0697 | 
0698 | ```text
0699 | occupied cells at time t
0700 | ```
0701 | 
0702 | But that is only a net stock.
0703 | 
0704 | Once material can disappear and reappear, the same population can conceal very different underlying traffic.
0705 | 
0706 | Imagine two systems.
0707 | 
0708 | System A:
0709 | 
0710 | ```text
0711 | +100 new cells
0712 | 0 lost
0713 | ```
0714 | 
0715 | System B:
0716 | 
0717 | ```text
0718 | +600 attachments
0719 | -500 losses
0720 | ```
0721 | 
0722 | Both end the update at:
0723 | 
0724 | ```text
0725 | +100 net
0726 | ```
0727 | 
0728 | A population curve treats them as equivalent.
0729 | 
0730 | They are not.
0731 | 
0732 | System B is undergoing enormous internal turnover.
0733 | 
0734 | ```mermaid
0735 | flowchart TD
0736 |     subgraph A[System A]
0737 |     A1[+100 new cells] --> A2[Net +100]
0738 |     end
0739 |     subgraph B[System B]
0740 |     B1[+600 attachments] --> B2[-500 losses]
0741 |     B2 --> B3[Net +100]
0742 |     end
0743 |     A2 -.->|same net population| B3
0744 |     B1 -.->|huge gross turnover| B2
0745 | ```
0746 | 
0747 | So another distinction joins our evidence ladder:
0748 | 
0749 | ```text
0750 | NET POPULATION CHANGE
0751 | ≠
0752 | GROSS CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITY
0753 | ```
0754 | 
0755 | and:
0756 | 
0757 | ```text
0758 | ATTACHMENT
0759 | ≠
0760 | FIRST OCCUPATION
0761 | ```
0762 | 
0763 | Those distinctions did not exist before material could disappear.
0764 | 
0765 | Now they are essential.
0766 | 
0767 | ---
0768 | 
0769 | ## The Hole Paradox
0770 | 
0771 | There was one result that initially looked contradictory.
0772 | 
0773 | Interior-biased loss produced many more visible holes:
0774 | 
0775 | ```text
0776 | surface     ~3.2
0777 | interior    ~37.6
0778 | ```
0779 | 
0780 | Yet interior lost sites were reoccupied slightly more often and much faster.
0781 | 
0782 | How can a process with faster refill have more holes?
0783 | 
0784 | Because a snapshot counts how many holes exist now.
0785 | 
0786 | It does not tell us how long each hole survives.
0787 | 
0788 | Imagine:
0789 | 
0790 | ```text
0791 | lose A
0792 | lose B
0793 | refill A
0794 | lose C
0795 | refill B
0796 | lose D
0797 | refill C
0798 | ...
0799 | ```
0800 | 
0801 | A snapshot can show many holes even if individual holes are short-lived.
0802 | 
0803 | The process may be generating vacancies faster than any one vacancy persists.
0804 | 
0805 | Again:
0806 | 
0807 | > **State is not dynamics.**
0808 | 
0809 | A single picture of the crystal cannot reveal how much material is cycling underneath it.
0810 | 
0811 | We keep rediscovering this lesson.
0812 | 
0813 | ---
0814 | 
0815 | ## What Happened to the Scaling Law?
0816 | 
0817 | We began Chapter 20 with a candidate law:
0818 | 
0819 | ```text
0820 | growth ~ boundary
0821 | loss ~ occupied area
0822 | ```
0823 | 
0824 | therefore:
0825 | 
0826 | ```text
0827 | loss eventually wins
0828 | ```
0829 | 
0830 | The experiment rejected that reasoning under this substrate.
0831 | 
0832 | Why?
0833 | 
0834 | Because loss is not an external subtraction from a fixed geometry.
0835 | 
0836 | Loss changes the geometry that determines construction opportunity.
0837 | 
0838 | The real relationship is closer to:
0839 | 
0840 | ```text
0841 | loss
0842 | ↓
0843 | changes active boundary
0844 | ↓
0845 | changes future construction rate
0846 | ```
0847 | 
0848 | So loss and construction are dynamically coupled.
0849 | 
0850 | That means the original scaling argument treated:
0851 | 
0852 | ```text
0853 | construction rate
0854 | ```
0855 | 
0856 | as independent of:
0857 | 
0858 | ```text
0859 | loss rate
0860 | ```
0861 | 
0862 | when it is not.
0863 | 
0864 | That was the mistake.
0865 | 
0866 | And finding that mistake is more valuable than confirming the original prediction would have been.
0867 | 
0868 | ---
0869 | 
0870 | ## A Different Kind of Compensation
0871 | 
0872 | There is another tempting word here:
0873 | 
0874 | ```text
0875 | maintenance
0876 | ```
0877 | 
0878 | We should not use it yet.
0879 | 
0880 | But something important has appeared.
0881 | 
0882 | A perturbation that removes material automatically creates conditions under which the ordinary growth process tends to replace much of that material.
0883 | 
0884 | Conceptually:
0885 | 
0886 | ```text
0887 | loss
0888 | ↓
0889 | creates opportunity for the mechanism
0890 | that counteracts loss
0891 | ```
0892 | 
0893 | That is a form of **structural compensation**.
0894 | 
0895 | Not because the crystal senses damage.
0896 | 
0897 | Not because it allocates resources.
0898 | 
0899 | Not because it prefers preservation.
0900 | 
0901 | But because the geometry of removal feeds directly into the geometry of construction.
0902 | 
0903 | ```mermaid
0904 | flowchart LR
0905 |     A[Loss] --> B[Empty site]
0906 |     B --> C[New frontier]
0907 |     C --> D[Ordinary attachment]
0908 |     D --> E[Reoccupation]
0909 |     E --> F[State changes again]
0910 |     F --> A
0911 | ```
0912 | 
0913 | That is a substrate-level feedback.
0914 | 
0915 | The word `feedback` is justified here only in the mechanistic sense:
0916 | 
0917 | ```text
0918 | loss changes state
0919 | state changes future construction opportunities
0920 | construction changes state again
0921 | ```
0922 | 
0923 | We do not need to make it biological.
0924 | 
0925 | ---
0926 | 
0927 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
0928 | 
0929 | Both primary hypotheses in this chapter failed.
0930 | 
0931 | The first predicted a finite near-stationary regime in which loss would eventually balance growth.
0932 | 
0933 | That did not happen.
0934 | 
0935 | The second predicted that interior-biased loss would produce a scientifically large reoccupation advantage over surface-biased loss.
0936 | 
0937 | That also did not happen.
0938 | 
0939 | Those failures remain failures.
0940 | 
0941 | But underneath them, the experiment exposed a much broader mechanism.
0942 | 
0943 | ### Loss changed the geometry of opportunity
0944 | 
0945 | The original scaling argument treated growth and loss almost as independent processes:
0946 | 
0947 | ```text
0948 | growth
0949 | ~ outer boundary
0950 | 
0951 | loss
0952 | ~ occupied area
0953 | ```
0954 | 
0955 | That picture failed because material loss changes the very geometry that determines where growth can occur.
0956 | 
0957 | A removed cell becomes empty, and if occupied neighbours remain around it, that location becomes an ordinary attachment opportunity.
0958 | 
0959 | ```mermaid
0960 | flowchart TD
0961 |     A[LOSS] --> B[NEW EMPTY SITE]
0962 |     B --> C[NEW LOCAL FRONTIER]
0963 |     C --> D[NEW ATTACHMENT OPPORTUNITY]
0964 | ```
0965 | 
0966 | The experiment measured this almost one-for-one:
0967 | 
0968 | ```text
0969 | surface loss
0970 | ~0.995 new frontier sites per loss
0971 | 
0972 | interior loss
0973 | ~1.000 new frontier sites per loss
0974 | ```
0975 | 
0976 | The crystal did not merely suffer loss.
0977 | 
0978 | Loss manufactured frontier.
0979 | 
0980 | ### Phenomenon record
0981 | 
0982 | **Phenomenon:** Loss-generated construction opportunity
0983 | 
0984 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
0985 | 
0986 | **Current bounded description:**
0987 | 
0988 | > Under the tested Digital Crystal loss conditions, removing occupied material almost always creates a new local frontier opportunity that the ordinary frozen growth rule can potentially reuse.
0989 | 
0990 | This extends the Interface Principle from Chapter 18.
0991 | 
0992 | Chapter 18 showed that historical state matters when it remains coupled to the active construction interface.
0993 | 
0994 | Chapter 20 shows that the interface itself can be **created by loss**.
0995 | 
0996 | So the active interface is not just something the crystal carries outward.
0997 | 
0998 | It can also be regenerated internally whenever material disappears.
0999 | 
1000 | ### Reoccupation is the dominant shared phenomenon
1001 | 
1002 | Under exact-count matched loss:
1003 | 
1004 | ```text
1005 | surface unique lost sites reoccupied
1006 | ≈ 93.6%
1007 | 
1008 | interior unique lost sites reoccupied
1009 | ≈ 95.7%
1010 | ```
1011 | 
1012 | and mean reoccupation delay was approximately:
1013 | 
1014 | ```text
1015 | surface
1016 | 1.56 updates
1017 | 
1018 | interior
1019 | 1.09 updates
1020 | ```
1021 | 
1022 | The predeclared interior-minus-surface difference failed because the shared effect was already close to saturation.
1023 | 
1024 | The stronger surviving observation is therefore:
1025 | 
1026 | > **Sparse material loss is usually converted into a new attachment opportunity that ordinary growth rapidly reuses.**
1027 | 
1028 | This is not repair.
1029 | 
1030 | No damage detector exists.
1031 | 
1032 | No target state is reconstructed.
1033 | 
1034 | No special pathway distinguishes:
1035 | 
1036 | ```text
1037 | new territory
1038 | ```
1039 | 
1040 | from:
1041 | 
1042 | ```text
1043 | territory that used to be occupied
1044 | ```
1045 | 
1046 | The observer knows a site is being reoccupied.
1047 | 
1048 | The crystal does not.
1049 | 
1050 | So:
1051 | 
1052 | ```text
1053 | REOCCUPATION
1054 | ≠
1055 | REPAIR
1056 | ```
1057 | 
1058 | ### Phenomenon record
1059 | 
1060 | **Phenomenon:** Rapid reuse of lost material
1061 | 
1062 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
1063 | 
1064 | **Current bounded description:**
1065 | 
1066 | > Under the tested exact-count conditions, more than 93% of lost sites were subsequently reoccupied, typically within one or two updates, through the same local growth rule used for ordinary expansion.
1067 | 
1068 | This is a substrate-level consequence of geometry, not evidence of biological maintenance.
1069 | 
1070 | ### The Flux Principle
1071 | 
1072 | Chapter 20 also exposes a second major phenomenon.
1073 | 
1074 | Before loss existed:
1075 | 
1076 | ```text
1077 | attachment
1078 | =
1079 | first occupation
1080 | ```
1081 | 
1082 | After loss exists:
1083 | 
1084 | ```text
1085 | attachment
1086 | =
1087 | first occupation
1088 | +
1089 | reoccupation
1090 | ```
1091 | 
1092 | That means population becomes an incomplete description of the process.
1093 | 
1094 | A crystal can have modest net growth while undergoing enormous gross material traffic.
1095 | 
1096 | For example:
1097 | 
1098 | ```text
1099 | +632 attachments
1100 | -531 losses
1101 | ----------------
1102 | +101 net
1103 | ```
1104 | 
1105 | A population curve sees:
1106 | 
1107 | ```text
1108 | +101
1109 | ```
1110 | 
1111 | but the process actually executed:
1112 | 
1113 | ```text
1114 | 1163 gross material events
1115 | ```
1116 | 
1117 | So the chapter establishes:
1118 | 
1119 | ```text
1120 | NET POPULATION CHANGE
1121 | ≠
1122 | GROSS MATERIAL TURNOVER
1123 | ```
1124 | 
1125 | This gives us the **Flux Principle**:
1126 | 
1127 | > **Static population or morphology can conceal large ongoing construction, loss and reoccupation flows.**
1128 | 
1129 | The active process may be much more dynamic than its net state suggests.
1130 | 
1131 | ### State is not dynamics
1132 | 
1133 | The hole paradox reinforces the same point.
1134 | 
1135 | Interior-biased loss can show more holes in a snapshot while individual lost sites are also being reoccupied faster.
1136 | 
1137 | That is possible because:
1138 | 
1139 | ```text
1140 | number of holes now
1141 | ```
1142 | 
1143 | is not the same thing as:
1144 | 
1145 | ```text
1146 | lifetime of each hole
1147 | ```
1148 | 
1149 | A system can create and close vacancies rapidly while maintaining many vacancies at any one instant.
1150 | 
1151 | So again:
1152 | 
1153 | ```text
1154 | SNAPSHOT
1155 | ≠
1156 | PROCESS
1157 | ```
1158 | 
1159 | This is the Flux Principle in another form.
1160 | 
1161 | ### Structural compensation, not maintenance
1162 | 
1163 | The chapter also reveals a bounded feedback loop:
1164 | 
1165 | ```text
1166 | loss
1167 | ↓
1168 | changes local geometry
1169 | ↓
1170 | creates attachment opportunity
1171 | ↓
1172 | ordinary growth reoccupies sites
1173 | ↓
1174 | changes local geometry again
1175 | ```
1176 | 
1177 | That is legitimate mechanistic feedback.
1178 | 
1179 | But it is not evidence for:
1180 | 
1181 | ```text
1182 | damage sensing
1183 | goal-directed preservation
1184 | repair objective
1185 | self-maintenance
1186 | ```
1187 | 
1188 | The correct term is **structural compensation**.
1189 | 
1190 | The system counteracts some loss because the geometry of loss creates opportunities for the same process that fills empty sites.
1191 | 
1192 | ### Connection to earlier phenomena
1193 | 
1194 | The cross-chapter picture is now becoming much tighter.
1195 | 
1196 | Chapter 18:
1197 | 
1198 | ```text
1199 | causal relevance
1200 | lives at active interface
1201 | ```
1202 | 
1203 | Chapter 19:
1204 | 
1205 | ```text
1206 | accessible difference
1207 | does not guarantee readout
1208 | ```
1209 | 
1210 | Chapter 20:
1211 | 
1212 | ```text
1213 | loss creates interface
1214 | ```
1215 | 
1216 | So the interface is no longer merely:
1217 | 
1218 | ```text
1219 | the outer boundary of a growing object
1220 | ```
1221 | 
1222 | It is better understood as:
1223 | 
1224 | > **the dynamically generated set of locations where the process currently has an opportunity to change state.**
1225 | 
1226 | That definition will matter later.
1227 | 
1228 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
1229 | 
1230 | The surviving phenomena do **not** establish:
1231 | 
1232 | - repair,
1233 | - homeostasis,
1234 | - self-maintenance,
1235 | - energy use,
1236 | - metabolism,
1237 | - a finite sustainable size,
1238 | - or life.
1239 | 
1240 | They establish something narrower and more fundamental:
1241 | 
1242 | > **Material loss dynamically generates new construction opportunity, and ordinary Digital Crystal growth rapidly reuses most lost sites. At the same time, large gross turnover can remain hidden beneath relatively modest net population change.**
1243 | 
1244 | Those phenomena should now be tracked independently of the failed finite-regime and interior-superiority hypotheses.
1245 | 
1246 | ---
1247 | 
1248 | ## What Chapter 20 Established
1249 | 
1250 | The primary V1 hypothesis failed.
1251 | 
1252 | The primary V2 hypothesis failed.
1253 | 
1254 | That sounds disastrous if experiments are supposed to confirm what we hoped.
1255 | 
1256 | It is exactly what we wanted from this book.
1257 | 
1258 | V1:
1259 | 
1260 | > Background loss did **not** produce the predicted finite near-stationary regime across the tested sweep.
1261 | 
1262 | V2:
1263 | 
1264 | > Interior loss did **not** increase reoccupation over surface loss by the predeclared scientifically meaningful amount.
1265 | 
1266 | But together they exposed a stronger mechanism:
1267 | 
1268 | > **Material loss creates new attachment opportunity, and under the tested exact-count conditions more than 93% of lost sites were subsequently reoccupied, typically within one or two updates, by the ordinary frozen growth rule.**
1269 | 
1270 | That statement is measured.
1271 | 
1272 | It does not require the failed hypotheses to become true.
1273 | 
1274 | ---
1275 | 
1276 | ## The New Ladder
1277 | 
1278 | The crystal now has a new causal chain:
1279 | 
1280 | ```text
1281 | MATERIAL PRESENT
1282 | ↓
1283 | MATERIAL LOST
1284 | ↓
1285 | EMPTY SITE
1286 | ↓
1287 | NEW FRONTIER
1288 | ↓
1289 | ORDINARY ATTACHMENT
1290 | ↓
1291 | REOCCUPATION
1292 | ```
1293 | 
1294 | And we can distinguish:
1295 | 
1296 | ```text
1297 | LOSS
1298 | ≠
1299 | PERMANENT LOSS
1300 | 
1301 | ATTACHMENT
1302 | ≠
1303 | NEW CONSTRUCTION
1304 | 
1305 | REOCCUPATION
1306 | ≠
1307 | REPAIR
1308 | 
1309 | NET GROWTH
1310 | ≠
1311 | GROSS MATERIAL TURNOVER
1312 | ```
1313 | 
1314 | Those are the results of Chapter 20.
1315 | 
1316 | ---
1317 | 
1318 | ## Why We Stop Here
1319 | 
1320 | We could continue.
1321 | 
1322 | Measure exact hole lifetime distributions.
1323 | 
1324 | Sweep the placement fraction.
1325 | 
1326 | Try different loss schedules.
1327 | 
1328 | Separate one-neighbour from six-neighbour vacancies.
1329 | 
1330 | Increase the number of groups.
1331 | 
1332 | But none of those would cross a new conceptual boundary.
1333 | 
1334 | We know the essential mechanism now.
1335 | 
1336 | Loss makes reusable frontier.
1337 | 
1338 | Ordinary growth reuses it.
1339 | 
1340 | The crystal can therefore undergo large material turnover without net population collapse.
1341 | 
1342 | That is enough.
1343 | 
1344 | No V3.
1345 | 
1346 | ---
1347 | 
1348 | ## The Question We Have Now Earned
1349 | 
1350 | There is still something artificial about this world.
1351 | 
1352 | The crystal currently gets unlimited opportunities to act.
1353 | 
1354 | Every update, the growth rule can evaluate every eligible frontier site.
1355 | 
1356 | It does not have to choose between:
1357 | 
1358 | ```text
1359 | expanding outward
1360 | ```
1361 | 
1362 | and:
1363 | 
1364 | ```text
1365 | reoccupying lost material
1366 | ```
1367 | 
1368 | It can attempt both everywhere.
1369 | 
1370 | So rebuilding what vanished is almost free.
1371 | 
1372 | That is why Chapter 20 should not end with:
1373 | 
1374 | ```text
1375 | repair
1376 | ```
1377 | 
1378 | It should end with a constraint.
1379 | 
1380 | Suppose the crystal can perform only:
1381 | 
1382 | ```text
1383 | B
1384 | ```
1385 | 
1386 | construction updates per step.
1387 | 
1388 | Now every action has an opportunity cost.
1389 | 
1390 | For the first time:
1391 | 
1392 | ```text
1393 | OUTWARD CONSTRUCTION
1394 |         competes with
1395 | REOCCUPATION
1396 | ```
1397 | 
1398 | And then a genuinely new question appears:
1399 | 
1400 | > **When computational action is limited, what gets built and what gets preserved?**
1401 | 
1402 | That is no longer a question about loss alone.
1403 | 
1404 | It is a question about allocation under scarcity.
1405 | 
1406 | ```mermaid
1407 | flowchart LR
1408 |     subgraph Unlimited
1409 |     U1[Unlimited updates] --> U2[All frontier sites evaluated]
1410 |     U2 --> U3[Rebuilding lost material is almost free]
1411 |     end
1412 |     subgraph Limited
1413 |     L1[Limited construction budget B] --> L2[Must choose where to act]
1414 |     L2 --> L3[Outward growth vs reoccupation]
1415 |     L3 --> L4[Opportunity cost emerges]
1416 |     end
1417 |     U3 -.->|remove luxury| L1
1418 | ```
1419 | 
1420 | The crystal did not learn to repair itself.
1421 | 
1422 | We merely discovered that, while computation was unlimited, rebuilding what disappeared was almost free.
1423 | 
1424 | Next, we remove that luxury.

0011 | 
0012 | Chapter 20 ended with an uncomfortable fact.
0013 | 
0014 | The crystal could lose material.
0015 | 
0016 | And yet most of that material came back.
0017 | 
0018 | Not because we gave it a repair mechanism.
0019 | 
0020 | Not because it knew what had been damaged.
0021 | 
0022 | Not because it protected an intended shape.
0023 | 
0024 | The ordinary growth rule simply saw the empty sites created by loss and treated them as new attachment opportunities.
0025 | 
0026 | Under the tested exact-count conditions, more than ninety-three percent of lost sites were eventually reoccupied, usually within one or two updates.
0027 | 
0028 | That sounded impressive.
0029 | 
0030 | But there was a hidden luxury.
0031 | 
0032 | The crystal could examine essentially every available construction opportunity.
0033 | 
0034 | Every update, every eligible frontier site could receive an attachment evaluation.
0035 | 
0036 | So the crystal never really had to choose between:
0037 | 
0038 | ```text
0039 | expanding into new territory
0040 | ```
0041 | 
0042 | and:
0043 | 
0044 | ```text
0045 | reoccupying material that had disappeared
0046 | ```
0047 | 
0048 | It could attempt both.
0049 | 
0050 | Everywhere.
0051 | 
0052 | At once.
0053 | 
0054 | Rebuilding was cheap because computation was unlimited.
0055 | 
0056 | Chapter 21 removes that luxury.
0057 | 
0058 | ---
0059 | 
0060 | ## One New Constraint
0061 | 
0062 | We changed exactly one thing.
0063 | 
0064 | Instead of evaluating every eligible frontier site, the crystal could evaluate at most:
0065 | 
0066 | ```text
0067 | B
0068 | ```
0069 | 
0070 | sites per update.
0071 | 
0072 | An unevaluated site simply received no attachment draw on that step.
0073 | 
0074 | The underlying attachment probability remained unchanged.
0075 | 
0076 | The loss rule remained unchanged.
0077 | 
0078 | The crystal gained no new state.
0079 | 
0080 | No energy.
0081 | 
0082 | No resource counter.
0083 | 
0084 | No maintenance controller.
0085 | 
0086 | No memory of damage.
0087 | 
0088 | No ability to identify whether a frontier position had ever been occupied before.
0089 | 
0090 | Just:
0091 | 
0092 | ```text
0093 | many possible construction opportunities
0094 | ↓
0095 | only B can be evaluated
0096 | ```
0097 | 
0098 | For the first time, computation itself was scarce.
0099 | 
0100 | ---
0101 | 
0102 | ## Scarcity Creates Allocation
0103 | 
0104 | The new constraint introduces something the earlier crystal never experienced.
0105 | 
0106 | Competition.
0107 | 
0108 | Suppose one update contains:
0109 | 
0110 | ```text
0111 | 500 possible frontier sites
0112 | ```
0113 | 
0114 | but:
0115 | 
0116 | ```text
0117 | B = 128
0118 | ```
0119 | 
0120 | Only 128 can even be considered.
0121 | 
0122 | Now the order in which sites are selected matters.
0123 | 
0124 | That does not mean the crystal is choosing.
0125 | 
0126 | It does not mean it has priorities.
0127 | 
0128 | But different local scheduling rules can produce different material futures.
0129 | 
0130 | So V1 began with three deliberately simple policies.
0131 | 
0132 | ```text
0133 | HIGH SUPPORT
0134 | evaluate sites with more occupied neighbours first
0135 | 
0136 | NEUTRAL
0137 | evaluate frontier sites in keyed random order
0138 | 
0139 | LOW SUPPORT
0140 | evaluate sites with fewer occupied neighbours first
0141 | ```
0142 | 
0143 | The policies were allowed to see only current geometry.
0144 | 
0145 | They were not allowed to inspect occupancy history.
0146 | 
0147 | They did not know whether a site was:
0148 | 
0149 | ```text
0150 | new territory
0151 | ```
0152 | 
0153 | or:
0154 | 
0155 | ```text
0156 | a previously occupied site waiting to be reoccupied
0157 | ```
0158 | 
0159 | That distinction remained observer-only.
0160 | 
0161 | So if high-support scheduling happened to favour reoccupation, it would be an emergent consequence of local geometry rather than an explicit repair instruction.
0162 | 
0163 | ```mermaid
0164 | flowchart LR
0165 |     subgraph "Same Budget B"
0166 |     A[Many possible frontier sites] --> B{Limited evaluations}
0167 |     B --> C[Select subset]
0168 |     C --> D1[High-support scheduling]
0169 |     C --> D2[Neutral scheduling]
0170 |     C --> D3[Low-support scheduling]
0171 |     D1 --> E1[More reoccupation]
0172 |     D2 --> E2[Balanced outcome]
0173 |     D3 --> E3[More first occupation]
0174 |     end
0175 | ```
0176 | 
0177 | ---
0178 | 
0179 | ## The First Question
0180 | 
0181 | V1 asked:
0182 | 
0183 | > **At the same finite computational budget, can local scheduling change the tradeoff between reusing lost material and occupying new sites?**
0184 | 
0185 | We froze:
0186 | 
0187 | ```text
0188 | loss rate δ = 0.08
0189 | budget B = 256
0190 | ```
0191 | 
0192 | and required both sides of the predicted tradeoff to clear predeclared magnitude thresholds.
0193 | 
0194 | High-support scheduling had to produce a meaningful increase in:
0195 | 
0196 | ```text
0197 | reoccupation / loss
0198 | ```
0199 | 
0200 | while low-support scheduling had to produce a meaningful increase in:
0201 | 
0202 | ```text
0203 | first occupations / 1000 evaluations
0204 | ```
0205 | 
0206 | Both were required.
0207 | 
0208 | That mattered.
0209 | 
0210 | Because significance alone was no longer enough.
0211 | 
0212 | ---
0213 | 
0214 | ## Budget Changed Scale Immediately
0215 | 
0216 | Before looking at the policies, the neutral budget sweep already showed something striking.
0217 | 
0218 | Approximate late populations were:
0219 | 
0220 | ```text
0221 | B = 64        ~381
0222 | B = 128       ~829
0223 | B = 256      ~1717
0224 | B = 512      ~3092
0225 | B = 1024     ~3513
0226 | unlimited    ~3462
0227 | ```
0228 | 
0229 | The amount of computational opportunity strongly constrained how large the lossy crystal became.
0230 | 
0231 | At severe scarcity, late net change approached zero.
0232 | 
0233 | At larger budgets, the crystal expanded rapidly.
0234 | 
0235 | So:
0236 | 
0237 | ```text
0238 | COMPUTATIONAL OPPORTUNITY
0239 | ↓
0240 | PROCESS SCALE
0241 | ```
0242 | 
0243 | was already real.
0244 | 
0245 | That was a new property.
0246 | 
0247 | Not metabolism.
0248 | 
0249 | Not energy.
0250 | 
0251 | But the crystal could no longer be described without reference to the amount of computation available to it.
0252 | 
0253 | ---
0254 | 
0255 | ## Same Budget, Different Futures
0256 | 
0257 | Then we held the budget fixed.
0258 | 
0259 | At:
0260 | 
0261 | ```text
0262 | B = 256
0263 | ```
0264 | 
0265 | the three local scheduling rules produced very different results.
0266 | 
0267 | Approximate late behaviour:
0268 | 
0269 | ```text
0270 | HIGH SUPPORT
0271 | 
0272 | late population                  ~1923
0273 | reoccupation / loss               0.959
0274 | first occupations / 1000 evals    188
0275 | late net growth                   +24.3
0276 | ```
0277 | 
0278 | ```text
0279 | NEUTRAL
0280 | 
0281 | late population                  ~1723
0282 | reoccupation / loss               0.844
0283 | first occupations / 1000 evals    212
0284 | late net growth                   +10.0
0285 | ```
0286 | 
0287 | ```text
0288 | LOW SUPPORT
0289 | 
0290 | late population                  ~1131
0291 | reoccupation / loss               0.534
0292 | first occupations / 1000 evals    249
0293 | late net growth                    -1.5
0294 | ```
0295 | 
0296 | The differences were large.
0297 | 
0298 | High-support scheduling strongly favoured reoccupation and produced the largest persistent population.
0299 | 
0300 | Low-support scheduling favoured first occupation and left much less material behind.
0301 | 
0302 | So finite computation had created a real allocation tension:
0303 | 
0304 | ```text
0305 | REUSE LOST MATERIAL
0306 |         versus
0307 | OCCUPY NEW MATERIAL
0308 | ```
0309 | 
0310 | The crystal still did not know which was which.
0311 | 
0312 | Geometry created the bias.
0313 | 
0314 | ```mermaid
0315 | flowchart TD
0316 |     A[Same budget B=256] --> B[High support]
0317 |     A --> C[Neutral]
0318 |     A --> D[Low support]
0319 |     B --> B1[High reoccupation<br/>largest population]
0320 |     C --> C1[Moderate mix]
0321 |     D --> D1[High first occupation<br/>smallest population]
0322 |     B1 -.-> E[Allocation tension emerged]
0323 |     C1 -.-> E
0324 |     D1 -.-> E
0325 | ```
0326 | 
0327 | ---
0328 | 
0329 | ## But V1 Still Failed
0330 | 
0331 | The high-support reoccupation advantage easily cleared its threshold.
0332 | 
0333 | Observed:
0334 | 
0335 | ```text
0336 | ~0.425
0337 | ```
0338 | 
0339 | Required:
0340 | 
0341 | ```text
0342 | 0.150
0343 | ```
0344 | 
0345 | The low-support first-occupation advantage was also statistically clear.
0346 | 
0347 | Observed:
0348 | 
0349 | ```text
0350 | ~61.6 first occupations per 1000 evaluations
0351 | ```
0352 | 
0353 | But the predeclared requirement was:
0354 | 
0355 | ```text
0356 | 100
0357 | ```
0358 | 
0359 | So the formal two-arm tradeoff failed.
0360 | 
0361 | ```text
0362 | V1 STATUS: FAILED
0363 | ```
0364 | 
0365 | That failure matters.
0366 | 
0367 | We had predicted a stronger exploration-side effect than the experiment produced.
0368 | 
0369 | We do not get to reduce the threshold afterward.
0370 | 
0371 | But V1 still established several measured facts.
0372 | 
0373 | Finite computational budget strongly constrained scale.
0374 | 
0375 | Local scheduling strongly changed persistence.
0376 | 
0377 | And scarce evaluations were not neutral with respect to what kind of construction occurred.
0378 | 
0379 | That was enough to motivate a new question.
0380 | 
0381 | ---
0382 | 
0383 | ## Was There a Budget Where the Crystal Simply Stayed?
0384 | 
0385 | The neutral sweep contained one especially interesting region.
0386 | 
0387 | At low budgets, net growth approached zero.
0388 | 
0389 | That suggested a new possibility.
0390 | 
0391 | Perhaps Chapter 20 had failed to produce finite scale because material loss alone was not enough.
0392 | 
0393 | But perhaps:
0394 | 
0395 | ```text
0396 | LOSS
0397 | +
0398 | FINITE COMPUTATIONAL OPPORTUNITY
0399 | ```
0400 | 
0401 | could create something much closer to dynamic persistence.
0402 | 
0403 | So V2 dropped the scheduling-policy comparison entirely.
0404 | 
0405 | Only neutral scheduling remained.
0406 | 
0407 | The new question was:
0408 | 
0409 | > **Is there a finite budget at which the population becomes approximately stationary while material turnover continues?**
0410 | 
0411 | This was not allowed to succeed by freezing.
0412 | 
0413 | It was not allowed to succeed by dying.
0414 | 
0415 | It was not allowed to succeed by reaching the simulation boundary.
0416 | 
0417 | A qualifying regime required all of the following:
0418 | 
0419 | ```text
0420 | population remains nonzero
0421 | 
0422 | late population slope approximately zero
0423 | 
0424 | loss continues
0425 | 
0426 | reoccupation continues
0427 | 
0428 | first occupation continues
0429 | 
0430 | gross turnover remains substantial
0431 | 
0432 | world capacity is not binding
0433 | ```
0434 | 
0435 | We froze a candidate family before the fresh run:
0436 | 
0437 | ```text
0438 | B = 48, 64, 80, 96, 128
0439 | ```
0440 | 
0441 | No new candidate could be added afterward.
0442 | 
0443 | ---
0444 | 
0445 | ## V2 Came Very Close
0446 | 
0447 | The V2 result was peculiar.
0448 | 
0449 | Almost every gate passed for every budget.
0450 | 
0451 | Population survived.
0452 | 
0453 | Capacity was nowhere near binding.
0454 | 
0455 | Loss continued.
0456 | 
0457 | Reoccupation continued.
0458 | 
0459 | First occupation continued.
0460 | 
0461 | Gross turnover remained substantial.
0462 | 
0463 | Late net growth stayed small.
0464 | 
0465 | The only gate that failed was:
0466 | 
0467 | ```text
0468 | late normalized population slope
0469 | ```
0470 | 
0471 | The approximate slopes were:
0472 | 
0473 | ```text
0474 | B=48     -0.00319
0475 | B=64     -0.00271
0476 | B=80     -0.00252
0477 | B=96     -0.00268
0478 | B=128    -0.00280
0479 | ```
0480 | 
0481 | The frozen threshold was:
0482 | 
0483 | ```text
0484 | |slope| <= 0.00250
0485 | ```
0486 | 
0487 | At `B=80`, the mean missed by only a tiny amount.
0488 | 
0489 | But it missed.
0490 | 
0491 | So:
0492 | 
0493 | ```text
0494 | V2 STATUS: FAILED
0495 | ```
0496 | 
0497 | No candidate met every predeclared condition.
0498 | 
0499 | We did not search around `B=80`.
0500 | 
0501 | We did not try `78`, `79`, `81`, `82`.
0502 | 
0503 | That would have turned the experiment into threshold hunting.
0504 | 
0505 | Instead we asked why all five budgets looked so similar in proportional terms.
0506 | 
0507 | ---
0508 | 
0509 | ## The Strange Stability Underneath the Failure
0510 | 
0511 | The absolute scales were very different.
0512 | 
0513 | The approximate late populations increased from:
0514 | 
0515 | ```text
0516 | ~260 at B=48
0517 | ```
0518 | 
0519 | to:
0520 | 
0521 | ```text
0522 | ~800 at B=128
0523 | ```
0524 | 
0525 | Yet their normalized decline rates were surprisingly similar.
0526 | 
0527 | And something else was even more stable.
0528 | 
0529 | Gross turnover as a fraction of population remained close to:
0530 | 
0531 | ```text
0532 | 0.17 per update
0533 | ```
0534 | 
0535 | across the entire budget family.
0536 | 
0537 | That suggested we might have been asking the wrong kind of stability question.
0538 | 
0539 | We had been looking for:
0540 | 
0541 | ```text
0542 | stable body size
0543 | ```
0544 | 
0545 | But perhaps the substrate was offering:
0546 | 
0547 | ```text
0548 | stable process traffic
0549 | ```
0550 | 
0551 | instead.
0552 | 
0553 | That distinction became V3.
0554 | 
0555 | ---
0556 | 
0557 | ## Stable Size Is Not Stable Process
0558 | 
0559 | V3 abandoned the search for a flat population curve.
0560 | 
0561 | It did not add more budgets.
0562 | 
0563 | It did not alter the V2 slope criterion.
0564 | 
0565 | It asked a genuinely different question:
0566 | 
0567 | > **Can normalized construction and loss flows remain stable even while absolute population drifts?**
0568 | 
0569 | For each update, we measured:
0570 | 
0571 | ```text
0572 | loss / population
0573 | 
0574 | attachments / population
0575 | 
0576 | reoccupation / population
0577 | 
0578 | first occupation / population
0579 | 
0580 | gross turnover / population
0581 | ```
0582 | 
0583 | Then we changed not only computational budget, but starting size.
0584 | 
0585 | The frozen start conditions were:
0586 | 
0587 | ```text
0588 | SMALL      warmup = 8
0589 | 
0590 | MEDIUM     warmup = 14
0591 | 
0592 | LARGE      warmup = 20
0593 | ```
0594 | 
0595 | Crossed with:
0596 | 
0597 | ```text
0598 | B = 48, 64, 80, 96, 128
0599 | ```
0600 | 
0601 | If the process really had a substrate-native statistical regime, it should not depend strongly on whether we started from a smaller or larger crystal.
0602 | 
0603 | ---
0604 | 
0605 | ## What Stayed Stable
0606 | 
0607 | The most striking result was gross turnover.
0608 | 
0609 | Mean late gross turnover fractions across budgets were approximately:
0610 | 
0611 | ```text
0612 | B=48     0.17229
0613 | B=64     0.17150
0614 | B=80     0.17066
0615 | B=96     0.17147
0616 | B=128    0.17132
0617 | ```
0618 | 
0619 | The coefficient of variation across those budget means was only:
0620 | 
0621 | ```text
0622 | 0.0030
0623 | ```
0624 | 
0625 | about three tenths of one percent.
0626 | 
0627 | That is remarkably small.
0628 | 
0629 | And the temporal drift of gross turnover was also tiny.
0630 | 
0631 | The worst absolute late slope across the budget family was around:
0632 | 
0633 | ```text
0634 | 0.00024
0635 | ```
0636 | 
0637 | against a frozen tolerance of:
0638 | 
0639 | ```text
0640 | 0.0025
0641 | ```
0642 | 
0643 | So the gross material traffic was not only similar across budgets.
0644 | 
0645 | It was also approximately flat within the late observation window.
0646 | 
0647 | Meanwhile:
0648 | 
0649 | ```text
0650 | no runs collapsed
0651 | 
0652 | all population gates passed
0653 | 
0654 | all activity gates passed
0655 | 
0656 | all capacity gates passed
0657 | ```
0658 | 
0659 | The crystal continued to undergo substantial material traffic.
0660 | 
0661 | ---
0662 | 
0663 | ## Starting Size Hardly Mattered to Turnover
0664 | 
0665 | Take `B=48`.
0666 | 
0667 | Gross turnover by starting condition was roughly:
0668 | 
0669 | ```text
0670 | small     0.17330
0671 | medium    0.17267
0672 | large     0.17089
0673 | ```
0674 | 
0675 | Loss fraction was also tightly clustered.
0676 | 
0677 | Attachment fraction was tightly clustered.
0678 | 
0679 | Reoccupation fraction was tightly clustered.
0680 | 
0681 | Those metrics easily cleared the predeclared start-size invariance gate.
0682 | 
0683 | The same general pattern persisted across the other budgets.
0684 | 
0685 | At `B=96`, for example, loss, attachment, reoccupation and gross turnover all showed very low sensitivity to starting size.
0686 | 
0687 | Something in the process was genuinely stable.
0688 | 
0689 | But not everything.
0690 |

0692 | 
0693 | ## Expansion Was the Weak Point
0694 | 
0695 | The metric that broke the full V3 claim was:
0696 | 
0697 | ```text
0698 | first occupation / population
0699 | ```
0700 | 
0701 | At `B=48`:
0702 | 
0703 | ```text
0704 | small     0.01806
0705 | medium    0.01689
0706 | large     0.01356
0707 | ```
0708 | 
0709 | The coefficient of variation was:
0710 | 
0711 | ```text
0712 | 0.118
0713 | ```
0714 | 
0715 | The frozen maximum was:
0716 | 
0717 | ```text
0718 | 0.100
0719 | ```
0720 | 
0721 | So that gate failed.
0722 | 
0723 | At larger budgets, the start-size dependence weakened:
0724 | 
0725 | ```text
0726 | B=64     CV ~0.092
0727 | B=80     CV ~0.077
0728 | B=96     CV ~0.074
0729 | B=128    CV ~0.063
0730 | ```
0731 | 
0732 | Those passed.
0733 | 
0734 | But V3 required every process metric at every budget to clear the threshold.
0735 | 
0736 | So:
0737 | 
0738 | ```text
0739 | V3 STATUS: FAILED
0740 | ```
0741 | 
0742 | Again.
0743 | 
0744 | Three experiments.
0745 | 
0746 | Three formal failures.
0747 | 
0748 | And yet by now the pattern underneath those failures was much clearer than any single positive result would have been.
