0750 | ---
0751 | 
0752 | ## Two Processes Were Hiding Inside One
0753 | 
0754 | The data suggest a useful decomposition.
0755 | 
0756 | One set of flows appears remarkably stable:
0757 | 
0758 | ```text
0759 | LOSS
0760 | 
0761 | ATTACHMENT
0762 | 
0763 | REOCCUPATION
0764 | 
0765 | GROSS MATERIAL TURNOVER
0766 | ```
0767 | 
0768 | Another remains more sensitive to history and scale:
0769 | 
0770 | ```text
0771 | FIRST OCCUPATION
0772 | ```
0773 | 
0774 | That suggests a distinction between:
0775 | 
0776 | ```text
0777 | CONTINUATION
0778 | ```
0779 | 
0780 | and:
0781 | 
0782 | ```text
0783 | EXPANSION
0784 | ```
0785 | 
0786 | The crystal's ongoing material traffic is highly stable across:
0787 | 
0788 | ```text
0789 | different starting sizes
0790 | 
0791 | different computational budgets
0792 | 
0793 | different absolute population scales
0794 | ```
0795 | 
0796 | But occupation of never-before-used territory is more contingent.
0797 | 
0798 | Especially under severe scarcity.
0799 | 
0800 | That is a much more interesting result than a fixed-size crystal would have been.
0801 | 
0802 | ---
0803 | 
0804 | ## Staying and Growing Are Not the Same Problem
0805 | 
0806 | Earlier versions implicitly treated all attachments as equivalent.
0807 | 
0808 | Chapter 20 already broke that assumption by separating:
0809 | 
0810 | ```text
0811 | first occupation
0812 | ```
0813 | 
0814 | from:
0815 | 
0816 | ```text
0817 | reoccupation
0818 | ```
0819 | 
0820 | Chapter 21 now shows why the distinction matters.
0821 | 
0822 | Under scarcity, reoccupation can remain relatively stable while first occupation changes much more strongly.
0823 | 
0824 | So:
0825 | 
0826 | ```text
0827 | STAYING
0828 | ≠
0829 | GROWING
0830 | ```
0831 | 
0832 | Not biologically.
0833 | 
0834 | Operationally.
0835 | 
0836 | The dynamics required to keep material traffic going are not identical to the dynamics required to expand into new territory.
0837 | 
0838 | And because the scheduling policy never knows whether a site is old or new, this distinction emerges from geometry and history rather than from a hard-coded biological category.
0839 | 
0840 | ---
0841 | 
0842 | ## What Does It Cost to Stay?
0843 | 
0844 | We can finally answer the chapter title.
0845 | 
0846 | Not with an energy unit.
0847 | 
0848 | Not with calories.
0849 | 
0850 | Not with ATP.
0851 | 
0852 | Not with a made-up digital metabolism.
0853 | 
0854 | In this substrate, the relevant cost is:
0855 | 
0856 | ```text
0857 | evaluation opportunity
0858 | ```
0859 | 
0860 | The crystal can only continue constructing where computation is actually spent.
0861 | 
0862 | Reduce the number of evaluated frontier sites and the scale of the process falls dramatically.
0863 | 
0864 | Change how those evaluations are allocated and the balance between reoccupation and first occupation changes.
0865 | 
0866 | So the bounded claim is not:
0867 | 
0868 | > The crystal has metabolism.
0869 | 
0870 | It is:
0871 | 
0872 | > **Continued material turnover in the lossy Digital Crystal depends strongly on finite computational opportunity, and the allocation of that opportunity changes whether construction tends toward reuse of lost material or occupation of new sites.**
0873 | 
0874 | That is a real computational constraint.
0875 | 
0876 | And it required no biological metaphor to define.
0877 | 
0878 | ---
0879 | 
0880 | ## Three Failures, One Better Model
0881 | 
0882 | Chapter 21 can be summarized as a sequence of rejected simplifications.
0883 | 
0884 | ```mermaid
0885 | flowchart TD
0886 |     V1[V1: Scheduling creates full two-sided allocation tradeoff] -->|FAILED| F1[Strong reoccupation side,<br/>weak first-occupation side]
0887 |     V2[V2: Some budget gives stationary population] -->|FAILED| F2[Turnover continues,<br/>but slope criterion missed]
0888 |     V3[V3: Full normalized process vector invariant] -->|FAILED| F3[Gross turnover stable,<br/>first occupation sensitive at B=48]
0889 | ```
0890 | 
0891 | ### V1
0892 | 
0893 | We predicted a strong two-sided allocation tradeoff.
0894 | 
0895 | High-support scheduling strongly increased reoccupation.
0896 | 
0897 | Low-support scheduling increased first occupation, but not enough to clear the frozen magnitude threshold.
0898 | 
0899 | ```text
0900 | FAILED
0901 | ```
0902 | 
0903 | ### V2
0904 | 
0905 | We predicted that some finite budget would produce approximately stationary population while turnover continued.
0906 | 
0907 | Every tested budget retained substantial turnover.
0908 | 
0909 | But none cleared the frozen population-slope criterion.
0910 | 
0911 | ```text
0912 | FAILED
0913 | ```
0914 | 
0915 | ### V3
0916 | 
0917 | We predicted that the entire normalized process vector would be invariant across starting sizes and budgets.
0918 | 
0919 | Most of it was.
0920 | 
0921 | First occupation under the harshest scarcity retained too much dependence on starting condition.
0922 | 
0923 | ```text
0924 | FAILED
0925 | ```
0926 | 
0927 | The failures progressively removed bad simplifications.
0928 | 
0929 | What remained was more precise.
0930 | 
0931 | ---
0932 | 
0933 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
0934 | 
0935 | Chapter 21 contained three formal hypotheses.
0936 | 
0937 | All three failed.
0938 | 
0939 | V1 did not establish the full two-sided allocation tradeoff at the predeclared magnitudes.
0940 | 
0941 | V2 did not establish a finite approximately stationary population regime.
0942 | 
0943 | V3 did not establish invariance of the complete normalized process vector across every tested starting size and budget.
0944 | 
0945 | Those failures remain failures.
0946 | 
0947 | But beneath them, several process-level regularities survived.
0948 | 
0949 | ### Scarce computation changed the scale of the process
0950 | 
0951 | The first result was immediate.
0952 | 
0953 | As computational evaluation budget fell, the size of the lossy crystal fell with it.
0954 | 
0955 | Approximate late populations under neutral scheduling ranged from:
0956 | 
0957 | ```text
0958 | B = 64
0959 | ~381
0960 | ```
0961 | 
0962 | to:
0963 | 
0964 | ```text
0965 | B = 1024
0966 | ~3513
0967 | ```
0968 | 
0969 | while the unlimited condition was of similar large scale.
0970 | 
0971 | So:
0972 | 
0973 | ```text
0974 | AVAILABLE COMPUTATIONAL OPPORTUNITY
0975 | ↓
0976 | PROCESS SCALE
0977 | ```
0978 | 
0979 | is not metaphorical.
0980 | 
0981 | It is measured.
0982 | 
0983 | The crystal can only attempt construction where evaluation opportunity is actually spent.
0984 | 
0985 | This gives us a new substrate-level constraint:
0986 | 
0987 | > **Finite computation limits the scale at which the material process can continue.**
0988 | 
0989 | That is not energy.
0990 | 
0991 | It is not metabolism.
0992 | 
0993 | It is simply computational scarcity.
0994 | 
0995 | ### Scheduling changed what the same budget produced
0996 | 
0997 | At the same budget, local scheduling changed the balance between reoccupation and first occupation.
0998 | 
0999 | High-support scheduling produced much greater reoccupation.
1000 | 
1001 | Low-support scheduling produced more first occupation.
1002 | 
1003 | The full V1 tradeoff failed because the exploration-side magnitude did not clear its frozen threshold.
1004 | 
1005 | But the measured allocation effect remains real.
1006 | 
1007 | So:
1008 | 
1009 | ```text
1010 | SAME COMPUTATIONAL BUDGET
1011 | ≠
1012 | SAME MATERIAL FUTURE
1013 | ```
1014 | 
1015 | and:
1016 | 
1017 | ```text
1018 | WHERE COMPUTATION IS SPENT
1019 | MATTERS
1020 | ```
1021 | 
1022 | The crystal does not know whether it is servicing old territory or new territory.
1023 | 
1024 | Yet geometry makes different scheduling rules allocate evaluation opportunity differently across those categories.
1025 | 
1026 | ### The Flux Principle became much stronger
1027 | 
1028 | V2 failed to find a truly stationary population.
1029 | 
1030 | But it exposed something more interesting.
1031 | 
1032 | Across the tested budget family, gross turnover remained close to:
1033 | 
1034 | ```text
1035 | 0.17 per update
1036 | ```
1037 | 
1038 | as a fraction of population.
1039 | 
1040 | V3 then measured this more carefully.
1041 | 
1042 | Late gross-turnover fractions were approximately:
1043 | 
1044 | ```text
1045 | B=48     0.17229
1046 | B=64     0.17150
1047 | B=80     0.17066
1048 | B=96     0.17147
1049 | B=128    0.17132
1050 | ```
1051 | 
1052 | The coefficient of variation across those budget means was only:
1053 | 
1054 | ```text
1055 | 0.0030
1056 | ```
1057 | 
1058 | and temporal drift in late gross turnover was also very small.
1059 | 
1060 | That gives us the strongest version yet of the **Flux Principle**:
1061 | 
1062 | > **The Digital Crystal can exhibit highly stable normalized material traffic even while absolute population and spatial scale remain different or drifting.**
1063 | 
1064 | ```mermaid
1065 | flowchart TD
1066 |     subgraph Stable Flows
1067 |     A[Loss / population] --> E[Stable]
1068 |     B[Attachment / population] --> E
1069 |     C[Reoccupation / population] --> E
1070 |     D[Gross turnover / population] --> E
1071 |     end
1072 |     subgraph Sensitive Flow
1073 |     F[First occupation / population] --> G[Sensitive to starting size<br/>and severe scarcity]
1074 |     end
1075 |     E --> H[Stable process traffic<br/>not stable body size]
1076 |     G --> H
1077 | ```
1078 | 
1079 | So:
1080 | 
1081 | ```text
1082 | STABLE SIZE
1083 | ≠
1084 | STABLE PROCESS
1085 | ```
1086 | 
1087 | The process can be statistically stable in flow without being stationary in body size.
1088 | 
1089 | ### Phenomenon record
1090 | 
1091 | **Phenomenon:** Stable normalized material flux
1092 | 
1093 | **Status:** **MEASURED**
1094 | 
1095 | **Current bounded description:**
1096 | 
1097 | > Across the tested budgets and starting sizes, normalized loss, attachment, reoccupation and gross material turnover were highly stable, while first occupation retained greater sensitivity to starting condition under severe computational scarcity.
1098 | 
1099 | This is narrower than calling the system homeostatic.
1100 | 
1101 | But it is also more precise.
1102 | 
1103 | The stable object may be process traffic rather than body size.
1104 | 
1105 | ### Continuation and expansion separated
1106 | 
1107 | The metric that broke V3 was:
1108 | 
1109 | ```text
1110 | first occupation / population
1111 | ```
1112 | 
1113 | especially at the harshest budget.
1114 | 
1115 | Meanwhile:
1116 | 
1117 | ```text
1118 | loss
1119 | attachment
1120 | reoccupation
1121 | gross turnover
1122 | ```
1123 | 
1124 | remained much more stable.
1125 | 
1126 | That exposes another structural decomposition:
1127 | 
1128 | ```text
1129 | CONTINUATION
1130 | =
1131 | ongoing loss / attachment / reuse traffic
1132 | 
1133 | EXPANSION
1134 | =
1135 | occupation of never-before-used territory
1136 | ```
1137 | 
1138 | The two are not the same process.
1139 | 
1140 | Under severe scarcity, continuation remains comparatively regular while expansion remains more dependent on starting history and scale.
1141 | 
1142 | So:
1143 | 
1144 | ```text
1145 | STAYING
1146 | ≠
1147 | GROWING
1148 | ```
1149 | 
1150 | and:
1151 | 
1152 | ```text
1153 | CONTINUATION
1154 | ≠
1155 | EXPANSION
1156 | ```
1157 | 
1158 | These are operational distinctions, not biological ones.
1159 | 
1160 | ### Phenomenon record
1161 | 
1162 | **Phenomenon:** Continuation–expansion separation
1163 | 
1164 | **Status:** **SUPPORTED**
1165 | 
1166 | **Current bounded description:**
1167 | 
1168 | > Under finite computational opportunity, the Digital Crystal's ongoing reuse and turnover dynamics are more stable than its expansion into never-before-occupied territory.
1169 | 
1170 | This result could become important later because it tells us not to treat every attachment as one undifferentiated activity.
1171 | 
1172 | Chapter 20 already separated first occupation from reoccupation.
1173 | 
1174 | Chapter 21 shows that those categories respond differently to scarcity.
1175 | 
1176 | ### A caution about the apparent turnover invariant
1177 | 
1178 | The striking stability around:
1179 | 
1180 | ```text
1181 | ~0.171
1182 | ```
1183 | 
1184 | should not yet be promoted into a deep emergent law.
1185 | 
1186 | The loss rate is frozen at:
1187 | 
1188 | ```text
1189 | δ = 0.08
1190 | ```
1191 | 
1192 | and rapid reoccupation is already known from Chapter 20.
1193 | 
1194 | So part of the observed gross-turnover stability may arise mechanically from:
1195 | 
1196 | ```text
1197 | expected losses
1198 | +
1199 | rapid replacement
1200 | ```
1201 | 
1202 | rather than from a new self-organized invariant.
1203 | 
1204 | That means the phenomenon is real:
1205 | 
1206 | ```text
1207 | stable normalized turnover
1208 | ```
1209 | 
1210 | but the explanation remains open.
1211 | 
1212 | A future audit should compare:
1213 | 
1214 | ```text
1215 | OBSERVED TURNOVER
1216 | -
1217 | MECHANICALLY EXPECTED TURNOVER
1218 | ```
1219 | 
1220 | before claiming a deeper substrate law.
1221 | 
1222 | This does not weaken the chapter.
1223 | 
1224 | It tells us exactly what remains to be explained.
1225 | 
1226 | ### Connection to the Interface Principle
1227 | 
1228 | Chapter 20 showed that loss creates new frontier.
1229 | 
1230 | Chapter 21 now shows that finite computation determines which frontier opportunities can actually be serviced.
1231 | 
1232 | So the interface story becomes:
1233 | 
1234 | ```mermaid
1235 | flowchart LR
1236 |     A[LOSS] --> B[CREATES FRONTIER]
1237 |     B --> C[FRONTIER CREATES OPPORTUNITY]
1238 |     C --> D[FINITE BUDGET SELECTS OPPORTUNITIES]
1239 |     D --> E[SCHEDULING CHANGES MATERIAL FUTURE]
1240 | ```
1241 | 
1242 | That is a much stronger substrate picture than simply saying the crystal has a boundary.
1243 | 
1244 | The relevant object is increasingly:
1245 | 
1246 | > **the dynamically generated set of construction opportunities together with the finite computation available to act on them.**
1247 | 
1248 | ### What this phenomenon does not establish
1249 | 
1250 | The surviving phenomena do **not** establish:
1251 | 
1252 | - metabolism,
1253 | - homeostasis,
1254 | - self-maintenance,
1255 | - energy use,
1256 | - resource sensing,
1257 | - active prioritization,
1258 | - a fixed sustainable body size,
1259 | - or life.
1260 | 
1261 | They establish something narrower:
1262 | 
1263 | > **Finite computational opportunity constrains the scale and allocation of Digital Crystal construction. Under those constraints, gross normalized turnover can remain strikingly stable while expansion remains more sensitive to history and scarcity.**
1264 | 
1265 | That belongs in the project-wide phenomenon record independently of the three failed primary hypotheses.
1266 | 
1267 | ---
1268 | 
1269 | ## What We Actually Earned
1270 | 
1271 | The strongest description of the Chapter 21 system is:
1272 | 
1273 | > **A lossy Digital Crystal under finite computational opportunity exhibits persistent material turnover whose gross normalized traffic is strikingly stable across budget, population scale and starting condition, while expansion into never-before-occupied territory remains more sensitive to history and scarcity.**
1274 | 
1275 | That statement is much narrower than:
1276 | 
1277 | ```text
1278 | homeostasis
1279 | ```
1280 | 
1281 | or:
1282 | 
1283 | ```text
1284 | metabolism
1285 | ```
1286 | 
1287 | or:
1288 | 
1289 | ```text
1290 | self-maintenance
1291 | ```
1292 | 
1293 | And that is exactly why it is useful.
1294 | 
1295 | The mechanism exists without those words.
1296 | 
1297 | ---
1298 | 
1299 | ## Another Ladder
1300 | 
1301 | The project now has another separation:
1302 | 
1303 | ```text
1304 | MATERIAL EXISTS
1305 | ↓
1306 | MATERIAL TURNS OVER
1307 | ↓
1308 | TURNOVER CONTINUES UNDER SCARCITY
1309 | ↓
1310 | NORMALIZED TURNOVER CAN BE STABLE
1311 | ↓
1312 | EXPANSION REMAINS HISTORY-SENSITIVE
1313 | ```
1314 | 
1315 | And another set of distinctions:
1316 | 
1317 | ```text
1318 | STABLE SIZE
1319 | ≠
1320 | STABLE PROCESS
1321 | 
1322 | NET GROWTH
1323 | ≠
1324 | GROSS TURNOVER
1325 | 
1326 | REOCCUPATION
1327 | ≠
1328 | FIRST OCCUPATION
1329 | 
1330 | CONTINUATION
1331 | ≠
1332 | EXPANSION
1333 | ```
1334 | 
1335 | We should keep all four.
1336 | 
1337 | They will matter later.
1338 | 
1339 | ---
1340 | 
1341 | ## Why We Stop Here
1342 | 
1343 | It would be easy to run V4.
1344 | 
1345 | We could relax the first-occupation CV threshold.
1346 | 
1347 | Remove `B=48`.
1348 | 
1349 | Change the starting sizes.
1350 | 
1351 | Wait longer.
1352 | 
1353 | Use a different late window.
1354 | 
1355 | None of those would ask a genuinely new question.
1356 | 
1357 | They would turn Chapter 21 into a search for a passing definition.
1358 | 
1359 | So we stop.
1360 | 
1361 | The chapter has already done its job.
1362 | 
1363 | It showed us that the Digital Crystal under loss and scarcity is not well described by a single scalar such as population.
1364 | 
1365 | The more stable object may be the flow itself.
1366 | 
1367 | And now a harder problem appears.
1368 | 
1369 | ---
1370 | 
1371 | ## Is There Actually a Thing Here?
1372 | 
1373 | Throughout Chapters 20 and 21 we have increasingly spoken about:
1374 | 
1375 | ```text
1376 | the process
1377 | ```
1378 | 
1379 | But what exactly is that process?
1380 | 
1381 | Is it one coherent entity?
1382 | 
1383 | Or are we looking at a large stochastic field whose local statistics happen to be stable?
1384 | 
1385 | A connected shape is not enough.
1386 | 
1387 | A stable turnover rate is not enough.
1388 | 
1389 | A persistent region is not enough.
1390 | 
1391 | If there is something individual-like here, we should be able to earn that claim experimentally.
1392 | 
1393 | So the next question is not:
1394 | 
1395 | > How does the crystal maintain itself?
1396 | 
1397 | We have not earned that.
1398 | 
1399 | It is:
1400 | 
1401 | > **Does this continuing process occupy a causally coherent region, or are we still looking at a field with no natural individual?**
1402 | 
1403 | That is the next boundary.
1404 | 
1405 | The crystal can grow.
1406 | 
1407 | It can be perturbed.
1408 | 
1409 | It can carry material history.
1410 | 
1411 | It can lose material.
1412 | 
1413 | It can reoccupy what vanished.
1414 | 
1415 | It can continue under computational scarcity.
1416 | 
1417 | Its gross material traffic can remain strikingly stable even while its size drifts.
1418 | 
1419 | But none of that tells us whether there is actually **one thing** there.
1420 | 
1421 | Chapter 22 will try to find out.
```

```markdown
0001 | +++

0003 | date = "2026-08-12T21:47:00+01:00"

0005 | description = "After finding stable turnover, causal locality and dynamically generated interfaces, Chapter 22 asks whether the Digital Crystal is best understood as a bounded thing or as a coherent process in space and time."
0006 | weight = 22
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Digital Crystal", "Causality", "Process", "Interfaces", "Flux", "Experiments"]
0009 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | Chapter 21 ended with a question that sounded obvious.
0013 | 
0014 | Is there actually one thing here?
0015 | 
0016 | For most of the book, we had spoken naturally about:
0017 | 
0018 | ```text
0019 | the crystal
0020 | ```
0021 | 
0022 | as though the noun had already been earned.
0023 | 
0024 | There was a connected occupied structure.
0025 | 
0026 | It grew.
0027 | 
0028 | It could be perturbed.
0029 | 
0030 | It could carry historical material.
0031 | 
0032 | It could lose material.
0033 | 
0034 | Lost sites could be reoccupied.
0035 | 
0036 | Under finite computational opportunity, large amounts of material could turn over while the process continued.
0037 | 
0038 | And in Chapter 21, normalized gross turnover became strikingly stable even while absolute population and scale changed.
0039 | 
0040 | That made the question harder, not easier.
0041 | 
0042 | A stable process is not automatically an individual.  
0043 | A connected shape is not automatically an individual.  
0044 | A region that persists is not automatically an individual.  
0045 | And a system with local causal relationships is not automatically an individual.
0046 | 
0047 | So Chapter 22 began with a very cautious question:
0048 | 
0049 | > **Does the continuing Digital Crystal occupy a causally coherent region that is meaningfully different from the surrounding field?**
0050 | 
0051 | That was already weaker than asking whether the crystal was an organism.
0052 | 
0053 | It was weaker than asking whether it had a self.
0054 | 
0055 | It was weaker than asking whether it was autonomous.
0056 | 
0057 | But after the experiments in this chapter, even that framing needs revision.
0058 | 
0059 | The most interesting object may not be a bounded region of occupied material at all.
0060 | 
0061 | It may be the process moving through it.
0062 | 
0063 | ---
0064 | 
0065 | ## The Temptation to Draw a Boundary
0066 | 
0067 | We have a strong habit of looking for boundaries.
0068 | 
0069 | If something is alive, we expect an inside and an outside.
0070 | 
0071 | A bacterium has a membrane.  
0072 | A cell has a boundary.  
0073 | An animal has skin.  
0074 | Even a machine usually has a chassis.
0075 | 
0076 | So when the Digital Crystal began to exhibit:
0077 | 
0078 | ```text
0079 | persistent turnover
0080 | local causal effects
0081 | history-dependent material
0082 | loss
0083 | reoccupation
0084 | scarce computation
0085 | ```
0086 | 
0087 | the natural question was:
0088 | 
0089 | ```text
0090 | where does the thing end?
0091 | ```
0092 | 
0093 | But that question already contains a hypothesis.
0094 | 
0095 | It assumes there is a privileged spatial boundary to discover.
0096 | 
0097 | The crystal may not work that way.
0098 | 
0099 | Chapter 18 had already shown that causally useful historical state lives near the active construction frontier.  
0100 | Chapter 20 showed that loss can create new frontier inside previously occupied material.  
0101 | Chapter 21 showed that finite computation determines which frontier opportunities are actually serviced.
0102 | 
0103 | So the active region is not a fixed shell.  
0104 | It is dynamically generated.
0105 | 
0106 | A site can be:
0107 | 
0108 | ```text
0109 | inert bulk
0110 | ```
0111 | 
0112 | at one moment and become:
0113 | 
0114 | ```text
0115 | active construction opportunity
0116 | ```
0117 | 
0118 | after nearby material disappears.
0119 | 
0120 | That should have made us suspicious of any definition based only on a centered radius.
0121 | 
0122 | But we tried one anyway.
0123 | 
0124 | ---
0125 | 
0126 | ## V1: Look for Predictive Coherence
0127 | 
0128 | The first Chapter 22 experiment asked a deliberately modest question.
0129 | 
0130 | Not:
0131 | 
0132 | > Is this region an individual?
0133 | 
0134 | But:
0135 | 
0136 | > **Does any predeclared spatial scale contain predictive information about its own future beyond what is already available from the surrounding lattice?**
0137 | 
0138 | The substrate was frozen:
0139 | 
0140 | ```text
0141 | Digital Crystal v1
0142 | loss rate δ = 0.08
0143 | neutral evaluation budget B = 96
0144 | ```
0145 | 
0146 | We tested five candidate scales:
0147 | 
0148 | ```text
0149 | R / R_eff
0150 | 
0151 | 0.30
0152 | 0.45
0153 | 0.60
0154 | 0.75
0155 | 0.90
0156 | ```
0157 | 
0158 | At each measurement point, we divided the system into:
0159 | 
0160 | ```text
0161 | S_t
0162 | candidate region
0163 | 
0164 | E_t
0165 | surrounding active environment
0166 | ```
0167 | 
0168 | and asked whether adding the current candidate-region state improved prediction of that region's later state.
0169 | 
0170 | The state representation was process-oriented.
0171 | 
0172 | It included measurements such as:
0173 | 
0174 | ```text
0175 | population
0176 | frontier density
0177 | recent attachment
0178 | loss
0179 | reoccupation
0180 | first occupation
0181 | gross turnover
0182 | angular process structure
0183 | ```
0184 | 
0185 | rather than occupancy alone.
0186 | 
0187 | The central quantity was:
0188 | 
0189 | ```text
0190 | Δ_self
0191 | =
0192 | prediction using S_t + E_t
0193 | -
0194 | prediction using E_t alone
0195 | ```
0196 | 
0197 | Then we compared that with an observer-only spatial null.
0198 | 
0199 | The hope was simple.
0200 | 
0201 | If one scale contained unusually strong information about its own future, perhaps we had found a candidate process boundary.
0202 | 
0203 | ```mermaid
0204 | flowchart TD
0205 |     A[Candidate region S(t)] --> B[Predict future state of S]
0206 |     C[Environment E(t)] --> B
0207 |     B --> D[Prediction using S + E]
0208 |     C --> E[Prediction using E alone]
0209 |     D - E --> F[Excess self-coherence Δ_self]
0210 |     F --> G[Compare with spatial null]
0211 | ```
0212 | 
0213 | ---
0214 | 
0215 | ## At First, V1 Looked Promising
0216 | 
0217 | The excess predictive-coherence values were:
0218 | 
0219 | ```text
0220 | R = 0.30    0.1691
0221 | R = 0.45    0.0447
0222 | R = 0.60    0.0611
0223 | R = 0.75    0.1666
0224 | R = 0.90    0.2906
0225 | ```
0226 | 
0227 | The largest value occurred at:
0228 | 
0229 | ```text
0230 | 0.90 R_eff
0231 | ```
0232 | 
0233 | and it was far above the frozen minimum effect of:
0234 | 
0235 | ```text
0236 | 0.02
0237 | ```
0238 | 
0239 | Looking only at the observed statistic, this seemed spectacular.
0240 | 
0241 | A large outer region appeared to contain substantial additional information about its own future.
0242 | 
0243 | But we had predeclared a family-level permutation test for exactly this reason.
0244 | 
0245 | We were allowed to look across all five frozen scales.
0246 | 
0247 | So the null had to preserve that search.
0248 | 
0249 | The observed family maximum was:
0250 | 
0251 | ```text
0252 | 0.2906
0253 | ```
0254 | 
0255 | The permutation-null mean was approximately:
0256 | 
0257 | ```text
0258 | 0.2569
0259 | ```
0260 | 
0261 | and its 95th percentile was approximately:
0262 | 
0263 | ```text
0264 | 0.2947
0265 | ```
0266 | 
0267 | The one-sided permutation result was:
0268 | 
0269 | ```text
0270 | p ≈ 0.0849
0271 | ```
0272 | 
0273 | So the formal result was:
0274 | 
0275 | ```text
0276 | FAILED
0277 | ```
0278 | 
0279 | The observed maximum did not beat the frozen family-level null at the required threshold.
0280 | 
0281 | We did not tune the radius.
0282 | 
0283 | We did not add more scales.
0284 | 
0285 | We did not increase decoder complexity.
0286 | 
0287 | The prediction had failed.
0288 | 
0289 | ---
0290 | 
0291 | ## A Large Statistic Can Still Be a Weak Boundary
0292 | 
0293 | This result is useful because the raw number looked so convincing.
0294 | 
0295 | A value near:
0296 | 
0297 | ```text
0298 | 0.29 excess R²
0299 | ```
0300 | 
0301 | feels large.
0302 | 
0303 | But the null also generated large apparent predictive coherence.
0304 | 
0305 | That tells us something important.
0306 | 
0307 | The Digital Crystal contains strong shared process structure.
0308 | 
0309 | Large regions of the system can predict later large-region state simply because they share:
0310 | 
0311 | ```text
0312 | growth phase
0313 | population scale
0314 | frontier geometry
0315 | turnover regime
0316 | global stochastic context
0317 | ```
0318 | 
0319 | Predictability alone does not isolate a thing.
0320 | 
0321 | It may only reveal that the field is structured.
0322 | 
0323 | So:
0324 | 
0325 | ```text
0326 | PREDICTIVE COHERENCE
0327 | ≠
0328 | INDIVIDUATION
0329 | ```
0330 | 
0331 | and even:
0332 | 
0333 | ```text
0334 | LARGE PREDICTIVE COHERENCE
0335 | ≠
0336 | PRIVILEGED BOUNDARY
0337 | ```
0338 | 
0339 | That was already enough to weaken the original framing.
0340 | 
0341 | But there was another problem.
0342 | 
0343 | ---
0344 | 
0345 | ## The V1 Audit
0346 | 
0347 | After running V1, we examined the experimental geometry more carefully.
0348 | 
0349 | Several issues made the test less clean than we wanted.
0350 | 
0351 | First, the candidate system was defined as a centered region.
0352 | 
0353 | But the earlier chapters increasingly suggest that the causally active object lives near dynamically generated interfaces rather than at the geometric center.
0354 | 
0355 | Second, the observer-null environment was not exactly the same geometry as the real annular environment.
0356 | 
0357 | That makes the real-versus-null comparison harder to interpret.
0358 | 
0359 | Third, the construction of the measurement support used future extent in part of the bookkeeping.
0360 | 
0361 | Even if that did not create the entire result, future-dependent geometry should not be allowed into a clean present-state predictor.
0362 | 
0363 | And fourth, the scrambled region was generated independently at different times, so the null did not preserve a stable temporal identity for the candidate region.
0364 | 
0365 | These are not reasons to rescue V1.
0366 | 
0367 | They are reasons to record it as:
0368 | 
0369 | ```text
0370 | PRIMARY PREDICTIVE HYPOTHESIS
0371 | FAILED
0372 | 
0373 | PROTOCOL
0374 | ALSO NOT CLEAN ENOUGH
0375 | TO SUPPORT A STRONG BOUNDARY CLAIM
0376 | ```
0377 | 
0378 | That distinction matters.
0379 | 
0380 | A failed experiment can still be informative while also teaching us how not to formulate the next one.
0381 |

0384 | ## V2: Stop Predicting and Perturb the Boundary

0416 | affected inner region more

0421 | affected outer region more

0475 | ```

0478 | 
0479 | ```text
0480 | 25
0481 | ```
0482 | 
0483 | produced usable matched interventions.

0486 | 
0487 | ```text
0488 | 0.260
0489 | ```
0490 | 
0491 | Seventy-one groups were skipped because the frozen matching conditions could not be satisfied.
0492 | 
0493 | That is a real limitation.
0494 | 
0495 | It means the confirmatory sample is much smaller than intended.
0496 | 
0497 | But it does not rescue the hypothesis.
0498 | 
0499 | Because the direction of the result was not merely weak.
0500 | 
0501 | It was opposite.

0515 | ```text
0516 | 0.04497
0517 | ```

0523 | =
0524 | -0.00724

0618 |

0622 | SPATIAL CAUSAL LOCALITY
0623 | ```
0624 | 
0625 | Perturbations preferentially affected nearby regions on the same side of either tested boundary.

0640 | 
0641 | It is not causal closure.

0646 |

0706 | ## The Interface Principle
0707 | 
0708 | The previous chapters now support a recurring principle.
0709 | 
0710 | > **In the Digital Crystal, causal relevance is concentrated around dynamically active interfaces where state changes can influence future construction.**
0711 | 
0712 | The interface is not merely the visual outside edge.
0713 | 
0714 | Chapter 20 destroyed that simplification.
0715 | 
0716 | Loss can create new empty sites inside the existing structure.
0717 | 
0718 | Those sites become active local boundaries.
0719 | 
0720 | So the interface is better described as:
0721 | 
0722 | > **the dynamically generated set of locations where the process currently has an opportunity to change material state.**
0723 | 
0724 | That definition does not care whether the opportunity is:
0725 | 
0726 | ```text
0727 | outside the old crystal
0728 | ```
0729 | 
0730 | or:
0731 | 
0732 | ```text
0733 | inside a vacancy created by loss
0734 | ```
0735 | 
0736 | It cares whether the process can act there.
0737 | 
0738 | ```mermaid
0739 | flowchart TD
0740 |     A[Occupied material] -->|loss| B[New empty site]
0741 |     B --> C[Local frontier opportunity]
0742 |     C -->|finite computation| D[Evaluation selection]
0743 |     D --> E[Construction event]
0744 |     E --> F[Interface changes again]
0745 |     F --> A
0746 | ```
0747 | 
0748 | ---
0749 | 
0750 | ## The Flux Principle
0751 |

0753 | 
0754 | A population might change by only:
0755 | 
0756 | ```text
0757 | +100
0758 | ```
0759 | 
0760 | while the same update contains:
0761 | 
0762 | ```text
0763 | +600 attachments
0764 | -500 losses
0765 | ```
0766 | 
0767 | Chapter 21 then showed that normalized gross material traffic can remain extremely stable even while:
0768 | 
0769 | ```text
0770 | population differs
0771 | scale differs
0772 | first occupation differs
0773 | absolute size drifts
0774 | ```
0775 | 
0776 | That gives us another principle:
0777 | 
0778 | > **The dynamically stable object may be the flow of construction and loss rather than the stock of occupied material.**
0779 | 
0780 | This matters enormously for Chapter 22.
0781 | 
0782 | If we define the system using:
0783 | 
0784 | ```text
0785 | occupied cells inside radius R
0786 | ```
0787 | 
0788 | we may be measuring accumulated residue rather than the active process.
0789 | 
0790 | The bulk is what remains.
0791 | 
0792 | The flux is what is happening.

0922 | ## A Thing or a Flow?
0923 | 
0924 | The title question can now be answered only partially.
0925 | 
0926 | Is the crystal a thing?
0927 | 
0928 | We have not established that.
0929 | 
0930 | Is it a flow?
0931 | 
0932 | We have strong evidence that flow is an important part of the correct description.
0933 | 
0934 | But even that can be overclaimed.
0935 | 
0936 | A stable statistical field is not automatically a coherent process.
0937 | 
0938 | A fluid can have stable local statistics without containing a natural individual.
0939 | 
0940 | A reaction-diffusion system can have persistent patterns without those patterns being autonomous entities.
0941 | 
0942 | So the new question is not:
0943 | 
0944 | ```text
0945 | IS THIS AN INDIVIDUAL?
0946 | ```
0947 | 
0948 | It is:
0949 | 
0950 | > **Can the causally active process itself be localized and tracked through space-time more successfully than a static occupied region can?**
0951 | 
0952 | That is a different experiment.
0953 | 
0954 | And it is the one Chapter 22 has now earned.
0955 |

1197 | ```

1222 | flowchart LR
1223 |     A[ACTIVE REGION at t] --> B[ACTIVE REGION at t+1]

1229 | The scientific question becomes:
1230 | 
1231 | > **Does active causal organization persist through space-time as a coherent process even when the material participating in it changes?**
1232 | 
1233 | That is much closer to the phenomena the previous chapters actually exposed.
1234 | 
1235 | And it avoids pretending we already know what the individual is.
1236 | 
1237 | ---
1238 | 
1239 | ## A Better Boundary Question
1240 | 
1241 | If a coherent active process is eventually found, boundaries can return later.
1242 | 
1243 | But then the boundary should be discovered from the process.
1244 | 
1245 | Not imposed as:
1246 | 
1247 | ```text
1248 | radius = 0.90
1249 | ```
1250 | 
1251 | A future boundary might be defined by where:
1252 | 
1253 | ```text
1254 | predictive influence falls
1255 | causal influence falls
1256 | event flux separates
1257 | local future becomes conditionally independent
1258 | ```
1259 | 
1260 | or some combination of those.
1261 | 
1262 | The important reversal is:
1263 | 
1264 | ```mermaid
1265 | flowchart TD
1266 |     subgraph Old
1267 |     O1[Choose region] --> O2[Ask if it behaves like a thing]
1268 |     O2 --> O3[Impose boundary]
1269 |     end
1270 |     subgraph New
1271 |     N1[Measure causal process] --> N2[Find coherent organization]
1272 |     N2 --> N3[Ask if boundary emerges]
1273 |     end
1274 | ```
1275 | 
1276 | ```text
1277 | OLD APPROACH
1278 | 
1279 | choose region
1280 | ↓
1281 | ask whether it behaves like a thing
1282 | ```
1283 | 
1284 | becomes:
1285 | 
1286 | ```text
1287 | NEW APPROACH
1288 | 
1289 | measure causal process
1290 | ↓
1291 | find coherent organization
1292 | ↓
1293 | only then ask whether a boundary emerges
1294 | ```
1295 | 
1296 | That is a much more defensible route.
1297 | 
1298 | ---
1299 | 
1300 | ## Where Chapter 22 Stops
1301 | 
1302 | It would be easy to build V3 immediately.
1303 | 
1304 | Choose a new interface thickness.
1305 | 
1306 | Choose a new activity threshold.
1307 | 
1308 | Choose a new field representation.
1309 | 
1310 | Run another experiment.
1311 | 
1312 | We should not do that yet.
1313 | 
1314 | The backfill changed the ontology of the problem.
1315 | 
1316 | Before another confirmatory run, the next experiment needs a genuinely new frozen object:
1317 | 
1318 | ```text
1319 | not occupied body
1320 | 
1321 | not centered radius
1322 | 
1323 | not hand-chosen boundary
1324 | 
1325 | but
1326 | 
1327 | spatiotemporal active process
1328 | ```
1329 | 
1330 | That design deserves to be specified separately.
1331 | 
1332 | So Chapter 22 ends with two failed boundary hypotheses and one much better question.
1333 | 
1334 | The crystal may not be a thing with a process inside it.
1335 | 
1336 | The process may be the thing we have been trying to see.
1337 | 
1338 | Not an organism.
1339 | 
1340 | Not yet an individual.
1341 | 
1342 | Not even necessarily one coherent entity.
1343 | 
1344 | But finally, perhaps, the right experimental object.
1345 | 
1346 | ```mermaid
1347 | flowchart TD
1348 |     A[MATERIAL] --> B[INTERFACE]
1349 |     B --> C[EVENTS]
1350 |     C --> D[FLUX]
1351 |     D --> E[CAUSAL LOCALITY]
1352 |     E --> F[SPATIOTEMPORAL PROCESS?]
1353 |     F -.-> G[?]
1354 | ```
1355 | 
1356 | That final question mark stays.
1357 | 
1358 | It has earned the right to.
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "23: What Does One Attachment Cause?"
0003 | date = "2026-08-13T00:35:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "After failing to find a propagating process field, Chapter 23 replaces correlation with intervention and asks what one additional Digital Crystal attachment actually causes."
0006 | weight = 23
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Digital Crystal", "Causality", "Cellular Automata", "Experimental Method"]
0009 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | At the end of Chapter 22, the Digital Crystal had stopped looking like a simple bounded thing.
0013 | 
0014 | We had looked for a privileged region whose future belonged especially to itself.  
0015 | We had not found one.
0016 | 
0017 | What survived instead was locality.
0018 | 
0019 | Change something here, and the consequences are stronger nearby than far away.
0020 | 
0021 | That left a new possibility.
0022 | 
0023 | Perhaps the important object was not the crystal as a body.
0024 | 
0025 | Perhaps it was the process occurring across its changing interface.
0026 | 
0027 | The obvious next question seemed to be:
0028 | 
0029 | > **Does that process move?**
0030 | 
0031 | That question would consume most of this chapter.
0032 | 
0033 | It would also turn out to be the wrong one.
0034 | 
0035 | Not useless.
0036 | 
0037 | Wrong in a productive way.
0038 | 
0039 | Because after four experiments, the Digital Crystal gave us something more precise than motion.
0040 | 
0041 | It gave us a causal quantity.
0042 | 
0043 | One additional attachment can change what happens next.
0044 | 
0045 | The question is how much.
0046 | 
0047 | ---
0048 | 
0049 | ## From Boundary to Process
0050 | 
0051 | The previous chapters had gradually changed what counted as interesting.
0052 | 
0053 | Chapter 18 found that persistent state mattered only while it remained coupled to active construction.  
0054 | Chapter 20 found that loss manufactured new construction opportunity.  
0055 | Chapter 21 found that finite computation rationed which opportunities could even be evaluated.  
0056 | Chapter 22 found spatial causal locality, but no privileged enclosing boundary.
0057 | 
0058 | A common object was beginning to appear:
0059 | 
0060 | ```text
0061 | CURRENT MATERIAL
0062 | ↓
0063 | ACTIVE CONSTRUCTION OPPORTUNITIES
0064 | ↓
0065 | EVALUATION
0066 | ↓
0067 | ATTACHMENT OR LOSS
0068 | ↓
0069 | NEW MATERIAL
0070 | ↓
0071 | NEW OPPORTUNITIES
0072 | ```
0073 | 
0074 | The material mattered.
0075 | 
0076 | But mostly because it changed what could happen next.
0077 | 
0078 | ```mermaid
0079 | flowchart LR
0080 |     A[Current material] --> B[Active construction opportunities]
0081 |     B --> C[Finite evaluation]
0082 |     C --> D[Attachment or loss]
0083 |     D --> E[New material]
0084 |     E --> F[New opportunities]
0085 |     F --> B
0086 | ```
0087 | 
0088 | So Chapter 23 began with a process-first hypothesis.
0089 | 
0090 | If activity was genuinely propagating through the crystal, then activity near one place at time `t` should predict activity farther away at later times.
0091 | 
0092 | Not just:
0093 | 
0094 | ```text
0095 | nearby things happen near nearby things
0096 | ```
0097 | 
0098 | but something more structured:
0099 | 
0100 | ```text
0101 | near distance
0102 | → early lag
0103 | 
0104 | farther distance
0105 | → later lag
0106 | ```
0107 | 
0108 | A moving ridge through space-time.
0109 | 
0110 | That was Experiment V1.
0111 | 
0112 | ---
0113 | 
0114 | ## V1 — Does Active Process Propagate?
0115 | 
0116 | We defined an active process field from material-changing events.
0117 | 
0118 | The first version pooled:
0119 | 
0120 | ```text
0121 | ATTACHMENT
0122 | +
0123 | LOSS
0124 | ```
0125 | 
0126 | into a single material-event field.
0127 | 
0128 | For an event at position `x` and time `t`, we measured future event density at distance `d` and lag `tau`.
0129 | 
0130 | Each event was compared with a matched non-event location sharing local geometric context.
0131 | 
0132 | A second control compared the source run against future event fields from another run at the same relative stage.
0133 | 
0134 | That cross-run null mattered.
0135 | 
0136 | If ordinary crystal development itself created a distance-lag trend, then an apparent travelling ridge could exist even without continuity from the original event.
0137 | 
0138 | The primary statistic looked for a shift in the lag at which positive excess activity was concentrated as distance increased.
0139 | 
0140 | The experiment failed.
0141 | 
0142 | The real ridge moved too little.
0143 | 
0144 | Its displacement over the cross-run null was too small.
0145 | 
0146 | The paired test did not clear the frozen significance gate.
0147 | 
0148 | Yet two broad shape statistics passed.
0149 | 
0150 | For a moment, that looked tantalizing.
0151 | 
0152 | Distance and ridge lag were positively associated.
0153 | 
0154 | Perhaps a weak process was travelling after all.
0155 | 
0156 | Then we looked at the surface.
0157 | 
0158 | ---
0159 | 
0160 | ## The Estimator Had Manufactured a Story
0161 | 
0162 | At distance one, the real event field showed a small positive excess at the first lag and negative excess afterwards.
0163 | 
0164 | The positive-weighted centroid therefore collapsed to:
0165 | 
0166 | ```text
0167 | lag = 1
0168 | ```
0169 | 
0170 | At farther distances, where the surface was mostly weak noise, the same positive weighting produced centroids near the middle of the lag grid.
0171 | 
0172 | The resulting statistic looked approximately like:
0173 | 
0174 | ```text
0175 | distance 1
0176 | → early lag
0177 | 
0178 | far distance
0179 | → later lag
0180 | ```
0181 | 
0182 | But there was no moving ridge.
0183 | 
0184 | There was:
0185 | 
0186 | ```text
0187 | one strongly anchored near-distance row
0188 | +
0189 | far-field noise centred by the estimator
0190 | ```
0191 | 
0192 | Had we frozen a slightly weaker threshold, this could have passed.
0193 | 
0194 | We might then have written a chapter about propagation that was actually caused by the geometry of the estimator.
0195 | 
0196 | That was the most important result of V1.
0197 | 
0198 | Not propagation.
0199 | 
0200 | A methodological warning:
0201 | 
0202 | > **An estimator can manufacture the shape of the phenomenon it was designed to detect.**
0203 | 
0204 | The strongest signal in the entire V1 surface was not positive.
0205 | 
0206 | It was a persistent negative band at short range.
0207 | 
0208 | And the positive-weighted ridge statistic had discarded it before inference.
0209 | 
0210 | So we did not tune V1.
0211 | 
0212 | We closed the propagation claim as failed.
0213 | 
0214 | Then we asked what that signed short-range structure meant.
0215 | 
0216 | ```mermaid
0217 | flowchart TD
0218 |     A[Event at x, t] --> B[Measure future event density by distance and lag]
0219 |     B --> C{Positive-weighted lag centroid moves with distance?}
0220 |     C -- Yes --> D[Travelling ridge]
0221 |     C -- No --> E[No propagation]
0222 |     E --> F[Check estimator: positive weighting<br/>can manufacture apparent movement]
0223 |     F --> G[Short-range signed structure remains]
0224 | ```
0225 | 
0226 | ---
0227 | 
0228 | ## V2 — Is the Interface a Source/Sink Field?
0229 | 
0230 | One tempting interpretation was that attachment consumed local interface while loss created it.
0231 | 
0232 | That gave a simple physical picture:
0233 | 
0234 | ```text
0235 | LOSS
0236 | → SOURCE
0237 | 
0238 | ATTACHMENT
0239 | → SINK
0240 | ```
0241 | 
0242 | Chapter 20 already gave strong independent reason to expect:
0243 | 
0244 | ```text
0245 | LOSS
0246 | ↓
0247 | empty site
0248 | ↓
0249 | new attachment opportunity
0250 | ↓
0251 | rapid reoccupation
0252 | ```
0253 | 
0254 | So V2 separated the pooled event field into transition channels.
0255 | 
0256 | Sources:
0257 | 
0258 | ```text
0259 | attachment
0260 | loss
0261 | ```
0262 | 
0263 | Targets:
0264 | 
0265 | ```text
0266 | attachment
0267 | loss
0268 | reoccupation
0269 | first occupation
0270 | ```
0271 | 
0272 | It also removed the positive centroid entirely.
0273 | 
0274 | All statistics remained signed.
0275 | 
0276 | Negative lags were added so that forward temporal structure could be separated from static geometric selection.
0277 | 
0278 | The experiment again failed to support the story we expected.
0279 | 
0280 | And this time the failure was more informative.
0281 | 
0282 | ---
0283 | 
0284 | ## The Zero-Distance Trap
0285 | 
0286 | The first interpretation of V2 suggested:
0287 | 
0288 | ```text
0289 | loss
0290 | → more future attachment
0291 | 
0292 | attachment
0293 | → more future attachment
0294 | ```
0295 | 
0296 | But the source and control states at distance zero were definitionally different.
0297 | 
0298 | At `d = 0`:
0299 | 
0300 | ```text
0301 | attachment source
0302 | = occupied
0303 | 
0304 | attachment control
0305 | = empty
0306 | ```
0307 | 
0308 | and:
0309 | 
0310 | ```text
0311 | loss source
0312 | = empty
0313 | 
0314 | loss control
0315 | = occupied
0316 | ```
0317 | 
0318 | Those differences automatically alter what events are possible at the same site later.
0319 | 
0320 | They are not neighbourhood dynamics.
0321 | 
0322 | Once `d = 0` was separated from the analysis, the neighbourhood result became much cleaner.
0323 | 
0324 | At distances one and two:
0325 | 
0326 | ```text
0327 | ATTACHMENT
0328 | → MORE nearby attachment
0329 | 
0330 | LOSS
0331 | → LESS nearby attachment
0332 | ```
0333 | 
0334 | The effect decayed rapidly with distance.
0335 | 
0336 | By roughly distance three, it was close to the scale of the remaining background structure.
0337 | 
0338 | The simple source/sink hypothesis was wrong.
0339 | 
0340 | But the reversal immediately suggested a simpler explanation.
0341 | 
0342 | ---
0343 | 
0344 | ## The Rule Already Contains Local Gain
0345 | 
0346 | The Digital Crystal attachment rule rewards occupied neighbours.
0347 | 
0348 | Schematically:
0349 | 
0350 | ```text
0351 | attachment score
0352 | =
0353 | base tendency
0354 | +
0355 | neighbor gain
0356 | +
0357 | signal effect
0358 | +
0359 | anisotropy
0360 | -
0361 | crowding
0362 | ```
0363 | 
0364 | The neighbour term is positive.
0365 | 
0366 | So if an empty frontier site `x` becomes occupied:
0367 | 
0368 | ```text
0369 | x attaches
0370 | ↓
0371 | nearby empty cells gain an occupied neighbour
0372 | ↓
0373 | their attachment probability can increase
0374 | ```
0375 | 
0376 | Likewise, if an occupied cell disappears:
0377 | 
0378 | ```text
0379 | x is lost
0380 | ↓
0381 | nearby candidates lose an occupied neighbour
0382 | ↓
0383 | their attachment probability can decrease
0384 | ```
0385 | 
0386 | That explanation was almost embarrassingly simple.
0387 | 
0388 | Which made it exactly the kind of explanation we needed to test.
0389 | 
0390 | The observational V2 result could still be confounded.
0391 | 
0392 | The sites that actually attached were not random frontier sites.
0393 | 
0394 | They may already have occupied a favourable local trajectory.
0395 | 
0396 | So V3 stopped observing naturally selected events.
0397 | 
0398 | It intervened.
0399 | 
0400 | ---
0401 | 
0402 | ## V3 — Force One Attachment
0403 | 
0404 | The new experiment began from the same checkpoint and the same eligible frontier cell.
0405 | 
0406 | Then the future split:
0407 | 
0408 | ```text
0409 | SAME CHECKPOINT
0410 | SAME CELL x
0411 | SAME ENVIRONMENT
0412 | SAME KEYED RANDOMNESS
0413 | 
0414 |         ┌──────────────┐
0415 |         │              │
0416 |      FORCE          PREVENT
0417 |    x attaches       x does not
0418 |         │              │
0419 |         └──────┬───────┘
0420 |                ↓
0421 |         compare futures
0422 | ```
0423 | 
0424 | The intervention site itself was excluded from every causal-gain measurement.
0425 | 
0426 | That mattered.
0427 | 
0428 | We were no longer asking whether two different states at `x` remained different.
0429 | 
0430 | We were asking what happened around `x` because the state had been changed.
0431 | 
0432 | ```mermaid
0433 | flowchart TD
0434 |     A[Same checkpoint<br/>same cell x<br/>same environment<br/>same keyed randomness] --> B[Force x attaches]
0435 |     A --> C[Prevent x from attaching]
0436 |     B --> D[Future A]
0437 |     C --> E[Future B]
0438 |     D --> F[Measure gain around x]
0439 |     E --> F
0440 | ```
0441 | 
0442 | Before observing the realized first future update, we also calculated what the frozen rule mechanically predicted.
0443 | 
0444 | Call that:
0445 | 
0446 | ```text
0447 | g_mech_1
0448 | ```
0449 | 
0450 | Then we measured the realized one-step neighbouring gain:
0451 | 
0452 | ```text
0453 | g1
0454 | ```
0455 | 
0456 | And finally the cumulative finite-horizon construction gain:
0457 | 
0458 | ```text
0459 | G_H
0460 | ```
0461 | 
0462 | over ten updates.
0463 | 
0464 | That separation was deliberate.
0465 | 
0466 | A causal effect should not automatically be called emergence.
0467 | 
0468 | If the local rule already predicts it, then the rule deserves the credit.
0469 | 
0470 | ---
0471 | 
0472 | ## The First-Step Effect Was Almost Entirely Mechanical
0473 | 
0474 | The V3 run found approximately:
0475 | 
0476 | ```text
0477 | mechanically expected one-step gain
0478 | g_mech_1 ≈ 0.105
0479 | 
0480 | realized one-step gain
0481 | g1 ≈ 0.115
0482 | ```
0483 | 
0484 | The discrepancy interval included zero and remained inside the frozen accounting tolerance.
0485 | 
0486 | So the immediate causal effect was real.
0487 | 
0488 | But it was not mysterious.
0489 | 
0490 | > **Forcing one frontier attachment caused additional next-update neighbouring construction, and the magnitude was consistent with the frozen local attachment mechanics at the tested precision.**
0491 | 
0492 | That was one of the cleanest results in the project.
0493 | 
0494 | For once we were not comparing a measured quantity against zero.
0495 | 
0496 | We were comparing it against what the mechanism already gave us for free.
0497 | 
0498 | And the mechanism survived.
0499 | 
0500 | ---
0501 | 
0502 | ## Then the Effect Kept Going
0503 | 
0504 | The ten-update cumulative gain was larger:
0505 | 
0506 | ```text
0507 | G_10 ≈ 0.58
0508 | ```
0509 | 
0510 | Only a small fraction of that appeared in the first update.
0511 | 
0512 | Later updates contributed additional construction differences.
0513 | 
0514 | At first this looked like a cascade.
0515 | 
0516 | Perhaps one attachment caused other attachments, which caused still more attachments.
0517 | 
0518 | The temptation was to compare the gain against the classical branching reference:
0519 | 
0520 | ```text
0521 | 1 additional event
0522 | per initiating event
0523 | ```
0524 | 
0525 | The ten-update interval sat below one.
0526 | 
0527 | But that interpretation contained a hidden assumption.
0528 | 
0529 | The forced cell remained in the lattice.
0530 | 
0531 | It was not merely an event that happened and finished.
0532 | 
0533 | It was a persistent state change.
0534 | 
0535 | And the lag profile had not obviously converged by ten updates.
0536 | 
0537 | So V3 had mixed two possibilities:
0538 | 
0539 | ```text
0540 | TRANSIENT CASCADE
0541 | 
0542 | and
0543 | 
0544 | CONTINUING CONSEQUENCE
0545 | OF A PERSISTENT OCCUPANCY DIFFERENCE
0546 | ```
0547 | 
0548 | Those are not the same phenomenon.
0549 | 
0550 | We needed one final decomposition.
0551 | 
0552 | ---
0553 | 
0554 | ## V4 — Persistent State Versus Transient Cascade
0555 | 
0556 | V4 repeated the force/prevent experiment on a fresh seed.
0557 | 
0558 | Ninety-six independent groups were used.
0559 | 
0560 | All 96 passed the coverage gates.
0561 | 
0562 | There were 384 interventions across four predeclared frontier-probability strata.
0563 | 
0564 | Capacity remained far from the hard lattice boundary.
0565 | 
0566 | The intervention timing was also corrected.
0567 | 
0568 | Force and prevent now occurred inside the canonical growth update.
0569 | 
0570 | Then the ordinary loss step was applied to every branch.
0571 | 
0572 | The forced cell therefore faced the same background loss rule as an ordinary newly attached cell.
0573 | 
0574 | Each probe created three futures:
0575 | 
0576 | ```text
0577 | PREVENT
0578 | x does not attach
0579 | 
0580 | PERSISTENT
0581 | x is forced to attach
0582 | and then remains under normal dynamics
0583 | 
0584 | TRANSIENT
0585 | x is forced to attach
0586 | it gets one full causal update
0587 | then x is removed
0588 | ```
0589 | 
0590 | The transient arm was the key.
0591 | 
0592 | It allowed the original attachment to influence its neighbours once.
0593 | 
0594 | Then the direct continuing support from `x` disappeared.
0595 | 
0596 | If the downstream process could sustain itself, the transient branch should continue to separate from prevent.
0597 | 
0598 | If not, its gain should die away.
0599 | 
0600 | The observation window was extended to thirty updates.
0601 | 
0602 | ```mermaid
0603 | flowchart TD
0604 |     A[Same checkpoint, same cell x] --> PREVENT[Prevent: x does not attach]
0605 |     A --> PERSISTENT[Persistent: x attaches,<br/>then remains under normal dynamics]
0606 |     A --> TRANSIENT[Transient: x attaches,<br/>gets one causal update,<br/>then x is removed]
0607 |     PREVENT --> B[Compare cumulative gains]
0608 |     PERSISTENT --> B
0609 |     TRANSIENT --> B
0610 | ```
0611 | 
0612 | ---
0613 | 
0614 | ## Immediate Gain Replicated
0615 | 
0616 | The mechanical one-step expectation in V4 was:
0617 | 
0618 | ```text
0619 | g_mech_1
0620 | = 0.0883
0621 | 95% CI
0622 | [0.0676, 0.1095]
0623 | ```
0624 | 
0625 | The realized neighbouring gain was:
0626 | 
0627 | ```text
0628 | g1
0629 | = 0.1016
0630 | 95% CI
0631 | [0.0677, 0.1380]
0632 | ```
0633 | 
0634 | and the discrepancy was:
0635 | 
0636 | ```text
0637 | g1 - g_mech_1
0638 | = 0.0132
0639 | 95% CI
0640 | [-0.0160, 0.0411]
0641 | ```
0642 | 
0643 | The frozen accounting verdict remained:
0644 | 
0645 | ```text
0646 | CONSISTENT WITH MECHANICS
0647 | ```
0648 | 
0649 | So the direct local causal effect had now replicated on a fresh experiment.
0650 | 
0651 | That part of the story was no longer tentative.
0652 | 
0653 | ---
0654 | 
0655 | ## The Transient Cascade Was Small
0656 | 
0657 | After thirty updates, the transient arm had accumulated:
0658 | 
0659 | ```text
0660 | G_transient(30)
0661 | = 0.198
0662 | 95% CI
0663 | [-0.026, 0.440]
0664 | ```
0665 | 
0666 | More important than the cumulative number was the late-time behaviour.
0667 | 
0668 | Across updates 21 through 30:
0669 | 
0670 | ```text
0671 | transient late gain
0672 | = -0.0081 per update
0673 | 
0674 | 95% CI
0675 | [-0.0201, 0.0039]
0676 | ```
0677 | 
0678 | That passed the frozen practical-convergence criterion.
0679 | 
0680 | The transient trajectory did not continue accumulating positive construction at a meaningful late rate.
0681 | 
0682 | Once the initiating occupancy was removed, the downstream effect became small and exhausted itself.
0683 | 
0684 | That is the cleanest answer Chapter 23 obtained.
0685 | 
0686 | > **The Digital Crystal supports local causal amplification, but under this protocol the transient cascade is small and converges.**
0687 | 
0688 | The thirty-update transient gain was also entirely below the descriptive reference value of one.
0689 | 
0690 | The experiment records that result as:
0691 | 
0692 | ```text
0693 | TRANSIENT_GAIN_BELOW_ONE_REFERENCE
0694 | ```
0695 | 
0696 | but deliberately does not call it a branching ratio or proof of subcriticality.
0697 | 
0698 | That distinction stays.
0699 | 
0700 | ---
0701 | 
0702 | ## Persistent State Was Different
0703 | 
0704 | The persistent arm told a very different story.
0705 | 
0706 | At thirty updates:
0707 | 
0708 | ```text
0709 | G_persistent(30)
0710 | = 1.164
0711 | 
0712 | 95% CI
0713 | [0.786, 1.542]
0714 | ```
0715 | 
0716 | while:
0717 | 
0718 | ```text
0719 | G_transient(30)
0720 | = 0.198
0721 | ```
0722 | 
0723 | The cumulative difference between the two arms was:
0724 | 
0725 | ```text
0726 | G_persistent(30)
0727 | -
0728 | G_transient(30)
0729 | 
0730 | = 0.966
0731 | 
0732 | 95% CI
0733 | [0.612, 1.333]
0734 | ```
0735 | 
0736 | The continuing state difference therefore contributed much more to the thirty-step causal consequence than the free-running transient cascade.
0737 | 
0738 | That gives us a distinction worth keeping:
0739 | 
0740 | ```text
0741 | PERSISTENT STATE CHANGE
0742 | ≠
0743 | TRANSIENT CAUSAL CASCADE
0744 | ```
0745 | 
0746 | ```mermaid
0747 | flowchart LR
0748 |     subgraph Transient
0749 |     A[Forced attachment] --> B[One causal update]
0750 |     B --> C[x removed]
0751 |     C --> D[Small downstream cascade<br/>G ≈ 0.198]
0752 |     end
0753 |     subgraph Persistent
0754 |     E[Forced attachment] --> F[Remains under dynamics]
0755 |     F --> G[Persistent state difference<br/>G ≈ 1.164]
0756 |     end
0757 |     D -.-> H[Most causal consequence comes<br/>from persistent state, not cascade]
0758 |     G -.-> H
0759 | ```
0760 | 
0761 | But V4 also killed another attractive interpretation.
0762 | 
0763 | ---
0764 | 
0765 | ## There Was No Permanent Positive Growth Offset
0766 | 
0767 | One concern after V3 was that the persistent arm might simply grow a little faster forever.
0768 | 
0769 | If that were true:
0770 | 
0771 | ```text
0772 | gain per update
0773 | ≈ constant positive c
0774 | ```
0775 | 
0776 | and cumulative gain would rise roughly linearly with the chosen horizon.
0777 | 
0778 | At thirty updates, that was not what we found.
0779 | 
0780 | The frozen late-window persistent gain was:
0781 | 
0782 | ```text
0783 | 0.0057 per update
0784 | 
0785 | 95% CI
0786 | [-0.0159, 0.0281]
0787 | ```
0788 | 
0789 | far below the predeclared positive-offset threshold and with an interval spanning zero.
0790 | 
0791 | The cumulative persistent trajectory instead rose early and then flattened into noisy variation:
0792 | 
0793 | ```text
0794 | H=1      0.156
0795 | H=5      0.539
0796 | H=10     0.839
0797 | H=17     1.008
0798 | H=22     1.190
0799 | H=30     1.164
0800 | ```
0801 | 
0802 | So the persistent effect was neither:
0803 | 
0804 | ```text
0805 | a freely propagating cascade
0806 | ```
0807 | 
0808 | nor:
0809 | 
0810 | ```text
0811 | a permanent constant-rate growth advantage
0812 | ```
0813 | 
0814 | It was a finite consequence of keeping one state difference around long enough for it to reshape later opportunities.
0815 | 
0816 | The frozen verdict was therefore:
0817 | 
0818 | ```text
0819 | TRANSIENT CASCADE
0820 | CONVERGES
0821 | 
0822 | PERSISTENT POSITIVE LATE OFFSET
0823 | NOT ESTABLISHED
0824 | ```
0825 | 
0826 | ---
0827 | 
0828 | ## Opportunity Is Not One Thing
0829 | 
0830 | V3 had contained one more striking clue.
0831 | 
0832 | The causal effect varied dramatically depending on which frontier cell was forced.
0833 | 
0834 | V4 made those strata explicit.
0835 | 
0836 | The lowest-probability probe typically sat in sparse geometry.
0837 | 
0838 | Its mean baseline attachment probability was about:
0839 | 
0840 | ```text
0841 | 0.372
0842 | ```
0843 | 
0844 | and it had almost exactly one occupied neighbour.
0845 | 
0846 | Forcing it promoted approximately:
0847 | 
0848 | ```text
0849 | 2.23
0850 | ```
0851 | 
0852 | new ring-one cells into the frontier.
0853 | 
0854 | The total frontier changed by approximately:
0855 | 
0856 | ```text
0857 | +1.23
0858 | ```
0859 | 
0860 | sites.
0861 | 
0862 | At the highest-probability probe, the geometry was almost the opposite.
0863 | 
0864 | Baseline attachment probability was about:
0865 | 
0866 | ```text
0867 | 0.798
0868 | ```
0869 | 
0870 | with roughly:
0871 | 
0872 | ```text
0873 | 4.07 occupied neighbours
0874 | ```
0875 | 
0876 | Forcing the site promoted almost no new frontier:
0877 | 
0878 | ```text
0879 | 0.031
0880 | ```
0881 | 
0882 | cells on average.
0883 | 
0884 | And total frontier changed by approximately:
0885 | 
0886 | ```text
0887 | -0.969
0888 | ```
0889 | 
0890 | sites.
0891 | 
0892 | The same action therefore meant different things in different local geometry.
0893 | 
0894 | ---
0895 | 
0896 | ## Sparse and Dense Interfaces
0897 | 
0898 | At a sparse interface:
0899 | 
0900 | ```text
0901 | one frontier site attaches
0902 | ↓
0903 | previously unsupported empty neighbours
0904 | gain their first occupied neighbour
0905 | ↓
0906 | new frontier is created
0907 | ```
0908 | 
0909 | At a dense interface:
0910 | 
0911 | ```text
0912 | one frontier site attaches
0913 | ↓
0914 | most nearby cells are already occupied
0915 | or already eligible
0916 | ↓
0917 | the attached site itself disappears
0918 | from frontier
0919 | ↓
0920 | little new frontier is created
0921 | ```
0922 | 
0923 | ```mermaid
0924 | flowchart TD
0925 |     subgraph Sparse
0926 |     A1[One frontier site attaches] --> A2[Unsupported empty neighbours gain support]
0927 |     A2 --> A3[New frontier created<br/>+1.23 total frontier]
0928 |     end
0929 |     subgraph Dense
0930 |     B1[One frontier site attaches] --> B2[Most nearby cells already occupied]
0931 |     B2 --> B3[Site disappears from frontier<br/>-0.969 total frontier]
0932 |     end
0933 | ```
0934 | 
0935 | The paired difference was enormous.
0936 | 
0937 | Low-probability probes created about:
0938 | 
0939 | ```text
0940 | 2.20
0941 | ```
0942 | 
0943 | more frontier sites than high-probability probes.
0944 | 
0945 | The 95% interval was approximately:
0946 | 
0947 | ```text
0948 | [1.99, 2.41]
0949 | ```
0950 | 
0951 | with:
0952 | 
0953 | ```text
0954 | p = 0.000125
0955 | ```
0956 | 
0957 | The same difference appeared in newly promoted neighbouring frontier sites.
0958 | 
0959 | This is now established.
0960 | 
0961 | > **Sparse and dense frontier locations respond very differently to the same one-cell attachment intervention.**
0962 | 
0963 | But one stronger idea did not survive.
0964 | 
0965 | ---
0966 | 
0967 | ## Geometry Did Not Yet Predict Long-Run Gain Reliably
0968 | 
0969 | The low-probability transient probe had a larger point estimate:
0970 | 
0971 | ```text
0972 | G_transient(30)
0973 | ≈ 0.677
0974 | ```
0975 | 
0976 | while the high-probability probe was:
0977 | 
0978 | ```text
0979 | ≈ 0.073
0980 | ```
0981 | 
0982 | That looks dramatic.
0983 | 
0984 | But the predeclared paired low-versus-high comparison was:
0985 | 
0986 | ```text
0987 | difference
0988 | = 0.604
0989 | 
0990 | 95% CI
0991 | [-0.031, 1.271]
0992 | 
0993 | p
0994 | = 0.0777
0995 | ```
0996 | 
0997 | The persistent comparison was even less convincing:
0998 | 
0999 | ```text
1000 | difference
1001 | = 0.156
1002 | 
1003 | p
1004 | = 0.810
1005 | ```
1006 | 
1007 | So the chapter must stop here.
1008 | 
1009 | We have established:
1010 | 
1011 | ```text
1012 | SPARSE GEOMETRY
1013 | ≠
1014 | DENSE GEOMETRY
1015 | ```
1016 | 
1017 | We have not established:
1018 | 
1019 | ```text
1020 | SPARSE GEOMETRY
1021 | →
1022 | RELIABLY HIGHER LONG-RUN CAUSAL GAIN
1023 | ```
1024 | 
1025 | The point estimates make that relationship interesting.
1026 | 
1027 | They do not make it true.
1028 | 
1029 | ---
1030 | 
1031 | ## Local Gain Is Not Global Gain
1032 | 
1033 | The finite evaluation budget also leaves a weak system-wide footprint.
1034 | 
1035 | Persistent local gain at thirty updates was:
1036 | 
1037 | ```text
1038 | 1.164
1039 | ```
1040 | 
1041 | but global gain excluding the intervention site was:
1042 | 
1043 | ```text
1044 | 1.036
1045 | ```
1046 | 
1047 | For the transient arm:
1048 | 
1049 | ```text
1050 | local
1051 | 0.198
1052 | 
1053 | global
1054 | 0.044
1055 | ```
1056 | 
1057 | The implied far-field differences were negative:
1058 | 
1059 | ```text
1060 | persistent
1061 | -0.128
1062 | 
1063 | transient
1064 | -0.154
1065 | ```
1066 | 
1067 | but their intervals still overlapped zero.
1068 | 
1069 | The candidate-selection sets nevertheless remained extremely similar between branches, typically overlapping by more than 99 percent.
1070 | 
1071 | So finite computation does introduce some non-local redistribution, but the intervention does not wholesale rewrite the global schedule.
1072 | 
1073 | Most of the measurable effect remains local.
1074 | 
1075 | ---
1076 | 
1077 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
1078 | 
1079 | Chapter 23 began with a hypothesis about motion.
1080 | 
1081 | That hypothesis failed.
1082 | 
1083 | What survived was more useful.
1084 | 
1085 | ### Predeclared claim
1086 | 
1087 | > Local process activity propagates through space-time as a reproducible distance-lag structure beyond ordinary geometry and developmental progression.
1088 | 
1089 | **Status: FAILED**
1090 | 
1091 | V1 did not establish a travelling process ridge.
1092 | 
1093 | The estimator itself was shown capable of turning a strong local signed feature plus far-field noise into apparent displacement.
1094 | 
1095 | ### Stronger interpretation
1096 | 
1097 | > The active interface behaves as a simple source/sink field in which loss creates interface and attachment consumes it.
1098 | 
1099 | **Status: FAILED**
1100 | 
1101 | After zero-distance eligibility effects were separated, the neighbourhood signs were opposite to that interpretation.
1102 | 
1103 | ### Surviving causal phenomenon
1104 | 
1105 | > Forcing one eligible Digital Crystal frontier attachment causes additional neighbouring construction during the next update.
1106 | 
1107 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1108 | 
1109 | The direct result replicated across V3 and V4.
1110 | 
1111 | ### Mechanistic accounting
1112 | 
1113 | > The immediate neighbouring causal gain is quantitatively consistent, at the tested precision, with the attachment probability changes mechanically implied by the frozen local rule.
1114 | 
1115 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1116 | 
1117 | V4 measured:
1118 | 
1119 | ```text
1120 | g_mech_1
1121 | ≈ 0.088
1122 | 
1123 | realized g1
1124 | ≈ 0.102
1125 | 
1126 | discrepancy
1127 | ≈ 0.013
1128 | CI includes zero
1129 | ```
1130 | 
1131 | ### Transient causal cascade
1132 | 
1133 | > After the initiating occupancy is removed following one causal update, the remaining construction cascade is small and practically converges over the frozen thirty-update observation window.
1134 | 
1135 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1136 | 
1137 | The late transient rate was indistinguishable from zero under the frozen criterion.
1138 | 
1139 | ### Persistent-state consequence
1140 | 
1141 | > Keeping the intervention-induced occupancy difference produces a substantially larger accumulated construction consequence than removing it after one causal update.
1142 | 
1143 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1144 | 
1145 | The thirty-update persistent-minus-transient difference was:
1146 | 
1147 | ```text
1148 | 0.966
1149 | 95% CI
1150 | [0.612, 1.333]
1151 | ```
1152 | 
1153 | ### Persistent positive late-rate offset
1154 | 
1155 | > The persistent branch retains a scientifically meaningful positive construction-rate offset at late times.
1156 | 
1157 | **Status: FAILED**
1158 | 
1159 | The frozen late-window mean was too small and its interval included zero.
1160 | 
1161 | ### Frontier-geometry heterogeneity
1162 | 
1163 | > Sparse and dense intervention sites differ strongly in how much frontier geometry one attachment creates or consumes.
1164 | 
1165 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1166 | 
1167 | The paired low-versus-high frontier difference was about `2.20` sites with a narrow interval and `p = 0.000125`.
1168 | 
1169 | ### Geometry determines long-run gain
1170 | 
1171 | > Sparse frontier geometry produces reliably greater thirty-update causal gain than dense frontier geometry.
1172 | 
1173 | **Status: FAILED / NOT ESTABLISHED**
1174 | 
1175 | The transient point estimate was larger in sparse regions, but the frozen paired comparison did not clear the significance gate.
1176 | 
1177 | ---
1178 | 
1179 | ## The Causal Opportunity Principle
1180 | 
1181 | The Digital Crystal now suggests a refinement of the Interface Principle.
1182 | 
1183 | The active interface is not simply a set of empty cells adjacent to occupied cells.
1184 | 
1185 | Its local causal structure depends on what an event does to future opportunity.
1186 | 
1187 | One attachment can:
1188 | 
1189 | ```text
1190 | remove one current frontier opportunity
1191 | ```
1192 | 
1193 | while simultaneously:
1194 | 
1195 | ```text
1196 | increase support for nearby candidates
1197 | ```
1198 | 
1199 | or:
1200 | 
1201 | ```text
1202 | create entirely new frontier sites
1203 | ```
1204 | 
1205 | depending on local geometry.
1206 | 
1207 | That means we need to distinguish:
1208 | 
1209 | ```text
1210 | OPPORTUNITY COUNT
1211 | 
1212 | from
1213 | 
1214 | OPPORTUNITY STRENGTH
1215 | 
1216 | from
1217 | 
1218 | REALIZED CONSTRUCTION
1219 | 
1220 | from
1221 | 
1222 | DOWNSTREAM CAUSAL GAIN
1223 | ```
1224 | 
1225 | Those quantities are not interchangeable.
1226 | 
1227 | A site can reduce the number of frontier locations while increasing expected realized construction.
1228 | 
1229 | A sparse site can manufacture frontier.
1230 | 
1231 | A dense site can consume frontier.
1232 | 
1233 | And a locally strong immediate causal effect can still fail to sustain a free-running cascade.
1234 | 
1235 | ```mermaid
1236 | flowchart TD
1237 |     A[Local attachment] --> B{Local geometry?}
1238 |     B -- Sparse --> C[Creates frontier<br/>increases opportunity count]
1239 |     B -- Dense --> D[Consumes frontier<br/>reduces opportunity count]
1240 |     C --> E[Immediate causal gain may be high]
1241 |     D --> F[Immediate causal gain may be low]
1242 |     E -.-> G[Long-run gain not reliably predictable<br/>from geometry alone]
1243 |     F -.-> G
1244 | ```
1245 | 
1246 | This is a much richer object than the static boundary we went looking for in Chapter 22.
1247 | 
1248 | ---
1249 | 
1250 | ## The Crystal Does Not Carry the Event Forward
1251 | 
1252 | The most important negative result may be the simplest.
1253 | 
1254 | The event itself does not seem to travel.
1255 | 
1256 | After the initiating state change is removed, the causal consequence fades.
1257 | 
1258 | There is local influence.
1259 | 
1260 | There is downstream consequence.
1261 | 
1262 | There is finite amplification.
1263 | 
1264 | But we did not find a self-sustaining propagating process.
1265 | 
1266 | So the progression is now:
1267 | 
1268 | ```text
1269 | LOCAL EVENT
1270 | ↓
1271 | LOCAL RULE CHANGES FUTURE PROBABILITIES
1272 | ↓
1273 | SHORT-RANGE CAUSAL GAIN
1274 | ↓
1275 | SOME DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE
1276 | ↓
1277 | ATTENUATION
1278 | ```
1279 | 
1280 | not:
1281 | 
1282 | ```text
1283 | LOCAL EVENT
1284 | ↓
1285 | TRAVELLING PROCESS
1286 | ↓
1287 | SELF-SUSTAINING CAUSAL FIELD
1288 | ```
1289 | 
1290 | That distinction matters enormously for the larger project.
1291 | 
1292 | The Digital Crystal can remember consequences in its material.
1293 | 
1294 | It can create and destroy construction opportunity.
1295 | 
1296 | One local change can alter later local construction.
1297 | 
1298 | But causal influence does not automatically organize itself into a persistent process.
1299 | 
1300 | Something else would be required.
1301 | 
1302 | ---
1303 | 
1304 | ## Maybe the Important State Is Opportunity
1305 | 
1306 | The crystal began this book as occupied cells.
1307 | 
1308 | Then morphology became insufficient.
1309 | 
1310 | Checkpoint state mattered.
1311 | 
1312 | History became lossy.
1313 | 
1314 | Frontier accessibility mattered.
1315 | 
1316 | Loss became construction opportunity.
1317 | 
1318 | Finite computation rationed opportunity.
1319 | 
1320 | Now intervention tells us that the same material change has different immediate geometric consequences depending on where it occurs.
1321 | 
1322 | That suggests a new candidate experimental object:
1323 | 
1324 | ```text
1325 | LOCAL CAUSAL OPPORTUNITY FIELD
1326 | ```
1327 | 
1328 | Not a biological field.
1329 | 
1330 | Not an energy field.
1331 | 
1332 | Not a hidden substance.
1333 | 
1334 | Just an observer-defined description of where a state change would have high or low causal leverage on future construction.
1335 | 
1336 | For a location `x` at time `t`, we might eventually want something like:
1337 | 
1338 | ```text
1339 | C(x,t)
1340 | =
1341 | {
1342 |     occupied-neighbour count,
1343 |     frontier creation potential,
1344 |     attachment probability,
1345 |     crowding,
1346 |     evaluation probability,
1347 |     transient causal gain
1348 | }
1349 | ```
1350 | 
1351 | The question would no longer be:
1352 | 
1353 | > Where is the crystal?
1354 | 
1355 | Or:
1356 | 
1357 | > Where is the wave?
1358 | 
1359 | It would be:
1360 | 
1361 | > **Where can one local change meaningfully alter what the process does next?**
1362 | 
1363 | That is a different kind of map.
1364 | 
1365 | And unlike the boundaries we drew first, this one can be derived from intervention.
1366 | 
1367 | ---
1368 | 
1369 | ## What This Does Not Establish
1370 | 
1371 | Chapter 23 does not establish:
1372 | 
1373 | ```text
1374 | a wave
1375 | an excitable medium
1376 | a Hawkes process
1377 | a branching process
1378 | a critical point
1379 | a phase transition
1380 | directed percolation
1381 | a self
1382 | an individual
1383 | autonomy
1384 | homeostasis
1385 | an organism
1386 | life
1387 | ```
1388 | 
1389 | The experiment explicitly records those as forbidden overclaims.
1390 | 
1391 | It also does not establish that sparse geometry causes larger long-run gain.
1392 | 
1393 | That remains a candidate relationship.
1394 | 
1395 | And it does not establish that a thirty-update transient gain below one is a universal property of the substrate.
1396 | 
1397 | The result is conditional on this model, these parameters, this intervention, this horizon and this definition of causal gain.
1398 | 
1399 | ---
1400 | 
1401 | ## What We Have Earned
1402 | 
1403 | We have earned something narrower and more useful.
1404 | 
1405 | > **A local Digital Crystal attachment has measurable causal leverage on subsequent construction. Its immediate effect is consistent with the frozen local attachment mechanics. When the initiating occupancy is removed after one causal update, the remaining cascade is small and converges over the tested horizon. Keeping the occupancy difference produces a substantially larger accumulated consequence, but no persistent positive late-rate offset was established. Sparse and dense frontier locations differ strongly in how an attachment changes future construction opportunity, although a corresponding difference in long-run causal gain remains unconfirmed.**
1406 | 
1407 | That is not life.
1408 | 
1409 | It is not individuality.
1410 | 
1411 | It is not even a coherent process yet.
1412 | 
1413 | But it is something we did not have before Chapter 23.
1414 | 
1415 | A measured causal leverage of local state.
1416 | 
1417 | ---
1418 | 
1419 | ## Next: Where Is Causal Gain Created?
1420 | 
1421 | The obvious next experiment is no longer a search for a boundary.
1422 | 
1423 | Nor should we immediately sweep a global parameter and announce a critical point.
1424 | 
1425 | The substrate has already shown us that local geometry matters.
1426 | 
1427 | So Chapter 24 should begin there.
1428 | 
1429 | Map the conditions under which an intervention has high or low transient causal gain.
1430 | 
1431 | Then ask whether high-gain regions are:
1432 | 
1433 | ```text
1434 | rare
1435 | common
1436 | 
1437 | isolated
1438 | clustered
1439 | 
1440 | momentary
1441 | persistent
1442 | 
1443 | disconnected
1444 | connected through space-time
1445 | ```
1446 | 
1447 | Only after that would it make sense to ask whether a change in global neighbour coupling or computational budget moves the system into a new collective regime.
1448 | 
1449 | The research path has changed again:
1450 | 
1451 | ```mermaid
1452 | flowchart TD
1453 |     A[MATERIAL] --> B[INTERFACE]
1454 |     B --> C[OPPORTUNITY]
1455 |     C --> D[LOCAL CAUSAL GAIN]
1456 |     D --> E[HIGH-GAIN REGIONS?]
1457 |     E --> F[PERSISTENT HIGH-GAIN REGIONS?]
1458 |     F --> G[CONNECTED CAUSAL ORGANIZATION?]
1459 |     G --> H[ONLY THEN:<br/>A NATURAL INDIVIDUAL?]
1460 | ```
1461 | 
1462 | Chapter 23 began by asking whether the process moved.
1463 | 
1464 | It did not find a travelling process.
1465 | 
1466 | It found something more basic.
1467 | 
1468 | A local event can change the future.
1469 | 
1470 | But whether that influence becomes organization depends on where the event happens, how long its state persists, and whether the consequences can survive after the original cause is gone.
1471 | 
1472 | That is the next frontier.
```
