0011 | 
0012 | Chapter 23 ended with a controlled causal effect.
0013 | 
0014 | Take the same Digital Crystal checkpoint.  
0015 | Take the same eligible frontier cell.  
0016 | Give both futures the same environment and the same cell-keyed randomness.  
0017 | Then force the cell to attach in one future and prevent it from attaching in the other.
0018 | 
0019 | ```text
0020 | SAME CHECKPOINT
0021 | SAME CELL
0022 | SAME FUTURE RANDOMNESS
0023 | 
0024 | FORCE x
0025 | vs
0026 | PREVENT x
0027 | 
0028 | ↓
0029 | MEASURE DIFFERENCE
0030 | ```
0031 | 
0032 | The intervention changed subsequent construction.
0033 | 
0034 | The immediate neighbouring effect was measurable.
0035 | 
0036 | A small downstream consequence could survive after the initiating cell was removed.
0037 | 
0038 | That gave us something real:
0039 | 
0040 | > **A local intervention can causally change the future of the Digital Crystal.**
0041 | 
0042 | Chapter 24 began with what seemed like the obvious next question.
0043 | 
0044 | > **Where is that causal gain created?**
0045 | 
0046 | Perhaps some frontier locations were intrinsically high-gain.
0047 | 
0048 | Perhaps sparse interface geometry amplified a perturbation while dense geometry suppressed it.
0049 | 
0050 | Perhaps the crystal contained a hidden causal field that could be mapped.
0051 | 
0052 | We spent several experiments trying to find it.
0053 | 
0054 | The first versions of Chapter 24 were built around that idea.
0055 | 
0056 | They were useful.
0057 | 
0058 | They were also wrong in important ways.
0059 | 
0060 | The final experiments changed the question.
0061 | 
0062 | The strongest result of Chapter 24 is no longer:
0063 | 
0064 | ```text
0065 | WHERE IS THE GAIN?
0066 | ```
0067 | 
0068 | It is:
0069 | 
0070 | ```text
0071 | WHERE DOES THE CAUSAL DIFFERENCE GO?
0072 | ```
0073 | 
0074 | And the answer leads directly to a digital-native constraint:
0075 | 
0076 | > **A finite global evaluation budget couples otherwise local construction processes by changing which frontier opportunities are allowed to be evaluated.**
0077 | 
0078 | That is the chapter.
0079 | 
0080 | ---
0081 | 
0082 | ## The First Mistake: Treating Gain as One Number
0083 | 
0084 | Chapter 23 had already warned us that several causal quantities were different.
0085 | 
0086 | A local intervention could change:
0087 | 
0088 | ```text
0089 | expected construction
0090 | realized construction
0091 | probability of path divergence
0092 | where construction occurs
0093 | total construction
0094 | ```
0095 | 
0096 | Those are not the same measurement.
0097 | 
0098 | But the first Chapter 24 experiments compressed them into one noisy quantity:
0099 | 
0100 | ```text
0101 | G_T(H)
0102 | ```
0103 | 
0104 | the finite-horizon FORCE-minus-PREVENT attachment difference.
0105 | 
0106 | That gave us a seductive picture:
0107 | 
0108 | ```text
0109 | LOCAL GEOMETRY
0110 | ↓
0111 | LOCAL CAUSAL GAIN
0112 | ↓
0113 | DOWNSTREAM CASCADE
0114 | ```
0115 | 
0116 | The problem was that `G_T(H)` mixes several mechanisms.
0117 | 
0118 | A perturbation can change the probability distribution without changing the signed expected count.
0119 | 
0120 | Two futures can diverge while their net attachment counts cancel.
0121 | 
0122 | A local increase can be offset by a distant decrease.
0123 | 
0124 | And under a finite evaluation budget, changing one part of the frontier can change which completely different cells are evaluated elsewhere.
0125 | 
0126 | So before asking where gain was stored, we needed to separate:
0127 | 
0128 | ```mermaid
0129 | flowchart LR
0130 |     A[CAUSAL SENSITIVITY] -.->|≠| B[PATH DIVERGENCE]
0131 |     B -.->|≠| C[SPATIAL REDISTRIBUTION]
0132 |     C -.->|≠| D[NET CONSTRUCTION GAIN]
0133 | ```
0134 | 
0135 | It took four versions of the experiment to get there.
0136 | 
0137 | ---
0138 | 
0139 | ## V1 — Frontier Creation Potential
0140 | 
0141 | The first attempt introduced a simple geometric observer.
0142 | 
0143 | For an eligible frontier site `x`:
0144 | 
0145 | ```text
0146 | FCP(x)
0147 | =
0148 | |frontier after forcing x occupied|
0149 | -
0150 | |frontier before forcing x|
0151 | ```
0152 | 
0153 | We called it **Frontier Creation Potential**.
0154 | 
0155 | If `FCP > 0`, occupying `x` created more frontier opportunities than it consumed.  
0156 | If `FCP = 0`, the frontier count stayed unchanged.  
0157 | If `FCP < 0`, the intervention consumed more frontier opportunity than it created.
0158 | 
0159 | The original hypothesis was:
0160 | 
0161 | > **Sites that create more frontier opportunity will produce greater transient causal gain.**
0162 | 
0163 | The first run looked promising but was badly designed for the effect size it claimed to test.
0164 | 
0165 | It used only 48 independent groups.
0166 | 
0167 | The achieved confidence interval around the high-minus-low transient gain was roughly:
0168 | 
0169 | ```text
0170 | +0.167
0171 | 95% CI [-0.078, +0.431]
0172 | ```
0173 | 
0174 | while the declared smallest meaningful effect was:
0175 | 
0176 | ```text
0177 | +0.15
0178 | ```
0179 | 
0180 | The interval was far too wide to distinguish an effect at that scale.
0181 | 
0182 | That is not a scientific failure of the hypothesis.  
0183 | It is an inconclusive experiment.
0184 | 
0185 | There was another problem.
0186 | 
0187 | For a frontier intervention:
0188 | 
0189 | ```text
0190 | FCP
0191 | =
0192 | promoted_frontier - 1
0193 | ```
0194 | 
0195 | identically.
0196 | 
0197 | The original analysis treated the agreement between those quantities as construct validation.  
0198 | It was not.  
0199 | It was a consistency check between two expressions of the same geometry.
0200 | 
0201 | That belongs in an assertion, not in the evidence ledger.
0202 | 
0203 | The first lesson of Chapter 24 was methodological:
0204 | 
0205 | > **A failed significance gate does not become a negative result unless the experiment had enough precision to resolve the effect it claimed mattered.**
0206 | 
0207 | ---
0208 | 
0209 | ## V2 — Exact Local Motifs
0210 | 
0211 | The second attempt asked whether FCP was simply too compressed.
0212 | 
0213 | A frontier cell on the hexagonal lattice has six immediate neighbours.  
0214 | Each can be occupied or empty.
0215 | 
0216 | So its ring can be represented as six bits:
0217 | 
0218 | ```text
0219 | b0 b1 b2 b3 b4 b5
0220 | ```
0221 | 
0222 | There are 64 raw patterns and far fewer once rotation and reflection are treated as equivalent.
0223 | 
0224 | Perhaps exact local arrangement mattered.
0225 | 
0226 | The experiment compared **cross-motif pairs** against **same-motif pairs** while matching several scalar properties.
0227 | 
0228 | That experiment was even less precise than V1.  
0229 | Its primary confidence interval had a half-width of roughly `0.50 attachments` against a declared meaningful effect of `0.20`.
0230 | 
0231 | So again: **inconclusive**, not **failed**.
0232 | 
0233 | The experiment did teach us something else.
0234 | 
0235 | Matching on baseline attachment probability could condition away part of the very mechanism geometry was allowed to influence.
0236 | 
0237 | The frozen attachment rule depends on local exposure geometry.
0238 | 
0239 | So:
0240 | 
0241 | ```text
0242 | LOCAL MOTIF
0243 | ↓
0244 | ATTACHMENT PROBABILITY
0245 | ```
0246 | 
0247 | can itself be part of the causal path.
0248 | 
0249 | Conditioning tightly on that probability asks a narrower question:
0250 | 
0251 | > Does motif have an additional residual effect after one of its consequences has been held fixed?
0252 | 
0253 | That was not the broad geometric question we thought we were asking.
0254 | 
0255 | ---
0256 | 
0257 | ## V3 — Recent Process History
0258 | 
0259 | The third attempt moved from geometry to process.
0260 | 
0261 | Two frontier sites can look the same now while having experienced different recent histories.
0262 | 
0263 | So V3 measured six recent updates of:
0264 | 
0265 | ```text
0266 | attachments
0267 | losses
0268 | reoccupations
0269 | first occupations
0270 | evaluations
0271 | ```
0272 | 
0273 | and defined:
0274 | 
0275 | ```text
0276 | RECENT TURNOVER
0277 | =
0278 | recent attachments
0279 | +
0280 | recent losses
0281 | ```
0282 | 
0283 | High-turnover and low-turnover sites were matched tightly on present local state.
0284 | 
0285 | The manipulation was large:
0286 | 
0287 | ```text
0288 | high - low recent turnover
0289 | ≈ +7.73 events
0290 | ```
0291 | 
0292 | Yet the transient gain difference was:
0293 | 
0294 | ```text
0295 | -0.065
0296 | 95% CI [-0.221, +0.096]
0297 | ```
0298 | 
0299 | The positive side of that interval genuinely excluded the predeclared `+0.15` effect.
0300 | 
0301 | But there was a deeper problem.
0302 | 
0303 | The substrate used for V3 had no independent causal memory state.  
0304 | Persistent material modification was disabled.
0305 | 
0306 | The operative dynamics were Markov in current occupancy, current input and keyed randomness.
0307 | 
0308 | So recent history could influence the future only through the present state it had already created.
0309 | 
0310 | V3 therefore did not test:
0311 | 
0312 | > Does history itself matter?
0313 | 
0314 | It tested:
0315 | 
0316 | > Does recent turnover proxy for something about current state that our matching failed to capture?
0317 | 
0318 | That is a useful calibration test.  
0319 | It is not evidence that history-dependent digital substrates cannot exist.
0320 | 
0321 | ---
0322 | 
0323 | ## Reset
0324 | 
0325 | At this point Chapter 24 could have become an endless feature search.
0326 | 
0327 | ```text
0328 | FCP
0329 | ↓
0330 | motif
0331 | ↓
0332 | history
0333 | ↓
0334 | bigger motif?
0335 | ↓
0336 | classifier?
0337 | ↓
0338 | another window?
0339 | ```
0340 | 
0341 | That would have violated the method of the book.
0342 | 
0343 | So we stopped.
0344 | 
0345 | Then we rebuilt the experiment from zero.
0346 | 
0347 | The reset kept the frozen Digital Crystal.  
0348 | It kept the FORCE/PREVENT intervention.  
0349 | But it changed the measurement stack.
0350 | 
0351 | Instead of beginning with the noisy realized cascade, V4 began with the rule itself.
0352 | 
0353 | ---
0354 | 
0355 | ## V4 — Measure the Mechanism Before the Outcome
0356 | 
0357 | The reset used an extreme frontier-geometry contrast.
0358 | 
0359 | Only sites satisfying:
0360 | 
0361 | ```text
0362 | HIGH:
0363 | FCP >= +2
0364 | 
0365 | LOW:
0366 | FCP <= -1
0367 | ```
0368 | 
0369 | were eligible.
0370 | 
0371 | Every pair therefore differed by at least:
0372 | 
0373 | ```text
0374 | ΔFCP = 3
0375 | ```
0376 | 
0377 | The pair design retained the same occupied-neighbour count and radial band.  
0378 | It deliberately stopped matching baseline attachment probability or local frontier density.  
0379 | Those quantities could be part of the pathway.
0380 | 
0381 | The full run used:
0382 | 
0383 | ```text
0384 | 384 independent groups
0385 | ```
0386 | 
0387 | and produced:
0388 | 
0389 | ```text
0390 | 275 usable groups
0391 | 471 extreme pairs
0392 | 71.6% coverage
0393 | ```
0394 | 
0395 | The result was precise enough to test the declared effects.
0396 | 
0397 | ---
0398 | 
0399 | ## Exact Expected Construction
0400 | 
0401 | Before drawing any lag-one Bernoulli outcomes, V4 calculated:
0402 | 
0403 | ```text
0404 | E1
0405 | =
0406 | Σ p_force(candidate)
0407 | -
0408 | Σ p_prevent(candidate)
0409 | ```
0410 | 
0411 | using the actual branch-specific evaluated candidate sets.
0412 | 
0413 | This is the conditional expected construction difference before thresholding probabilities into realized attachments.
0414 | 
0415 | That distinction matters.
0416 | 
0417 | A realized attachment is a single bit:
0418 | 
0419 | ```text
0420 | attach
0421 | or
0422 | do not attach
0423 | ```
0424 | 
0425 | But the rule gives us the full probability shift.
0426 | 
0427 | Why throw that information away?
0428 | 
0429 | The primary V4 result was the high-minus-low difference in expected local construction.
0430 | 
0431 | It was approximately:
0432 | 
0433 | ```text
0434 | ΔE1
0435 | = -0.0026
0436 | 
0437 | 95% CI
0438 | [-0.0395, +0.0333]
0439 | ```
0440 | 
0441 | The achieved one-sided 80% minimum detectable effect was about:
0442 | 
0443 | ```text
0444 | 0.047
0445 | ```
0446 | 
0447 | against a frozen smallest meaningful effect of:
0448 | 
0449 | ```text
0450 | +0.10
0451 | ```
0452 | 
0453 | This time the experiment really had the precision.
0454 | 
0455 | So we could finally say:
0456 | 
0457 | > **The extreme FCP contrast does not produce a scientifically meaningful positive difference of +0.10 or more in expected lag-one local construction under this protocol.**
0458 | 
0459 | That is a bounded negative.
0460 | 
0461 | The original V1 question was now properly resolved.
0462 | 
0463 | More frontier creation did not mean more net expected local construction.
0464 | 
0465 | But something else was happening.
0466 | 
0467 | ---
0468 | 
0469 | ## The Wrong Comparison
0470 | 
0471 | V4 initially tempted us toward another story.
0472 | 
0473 | High-FCP interventions appeared more likely to make the FORCE and PREVENT futures diverge.
0474 | 
0475 | But a fresh-seed V5 did not cleanly replicate that class difference.
0476 | 
0477 | The important result survived elsewhere.
0478 | 
0479 | The breakthrough came from decomposing the expected effect rather than comparing only its total.
0480 | 
0481 | ---
0482 | 
0483 | ## V5 — Causal Accounting
0484 | 
0485 | For every lag-one intervention, expected construction can be split into three terms:
0486 | 
0487 | ```text
0488 | E1
0489 | =
0490 | SHARED-CELL PROBABILITY SHIFT
0491 | +
0492 | FORCE-ONLY SELECTOR CONTRIBUTION
0493 | +
0494 | PREVENT-ONLY SELECTOR CONTRIBUTION
0495 | ```
0496 | 
0497 | The first term comes from cells evaluated in both branches.  
0498 | Their probability can change because local occupancy changed.
0499 | 
0500 | The other two terms come from candidate substitution.
0501 | 
0502 | A cell evaluated only in FORCE contributes `+p_force`.  
0503 | A cell evaluated only in PREVENT contributes `-p_prevent`.
0504 | 
0505 | ```mermaid
0506 | flowchart TD
0507 |     E1[E1<br/>Expected construction difference] --> A[Shared-cell probability shift<br/>cells evaluated in both branches]
0508 |     E1 --> B[Force-only selector contribution<br/>+p_force]
0509 |     E1 --> C[Prevent-only selector contribution<br/>-p_prevent]
0510 |     A --> MECH[Changes local occupancy<br/>mechanically predicted]
0511 |     B --> SEL[Candidate substitution<br/>due to frontier change]
0512 |     C --> SEL
0513 | ```
0514 | 
0515 | This decomposition exposed the actual mechanism.
0516 | 
0517 | ---
0518 | 
0519 | ## The Supported Regime Was Narrower Than We Thought
0520 | 
0521 | Every extreme V5 pair had:
0522 | 
0523 | ```text
0524 | occupied neighbours n = 1
0525 | ```
0526 | 
0527 | All:
0528 | 
0529 | ```text
0530 | 467 / 467 pairs
0531 | ```
0532 | 
0533 | were single-contact frontier sites.
0534 | 
0535 | That immediately narrows the claim.
0536 | 
0537 | Chapter 24 is not establishing a universal law over every frontier geometry.  
0538 | It is establishing a mechanism in the supported `n = 1` regime.
0539 | 
0540 | The baseline probability of the focal site was also identical across the two classes:
0541 | 
0542 | ```text
0543 | HIGH p ≈ 0.38041
0544 | LOW  p ≈ 0.38041
0545 | ```
0546 | 
0547 | This is explained by the hexagonal symmetry of the frozen rule for single-contact sites.
0548 | 
0549 | So we obtained an unusually clean contrast.
0550 | 
0551 | The focal site itself had the same immediate attachment probability.  
0552 | What differed was what occupying it did to the surrounding frontier.
0553 | 
0554 | ---
0555 | 
0556 | ## Two Geometries, Similar Local Effect
0557 | 
0558 | The absolute lag-one expected local effects were:
0559 | 
0560 | ```text
0561 | HIGH FCP
0562 | local E1 ≈ +0.159
0563 | 
0564 | LOW FCP
0565 | local E1 ≈ +0.128
0566 | ```
0567 | 
0568 | Their difference was only about `+0.031`, with an interval crossing zero.
0569 | 
0570 | This is the real compensation result.
0571 | 
0572 | The two geometry classes produced broadly similar positive local expected construction.  
0573 | But they produced it through radically different computational pathways.
0574 | 
0575 | | Term | HIGH FCP | LOW FCP |
0576 | |------|----------|---------|
0577 | | Shared-cell shift | ≈ +0.017 | ≈ +0.123 |
0578 | | Selector-swap term | ≈ +0.141 | ≈ +0.005 |
0579 | | **Local expected effect** | **≈ +0.159** | **≈ +0.128** |
0580 | 
0581 | The contrast is not:
0582 | 
0583 | ```text
0584 | one class has causal gain
0585 | the other does not
0586 | ```
0587 | 
0588 | It is:
0589 | 
0590 | ```text
0591 | SIMILAR LOCAL EFFECT
0592 | ↓
0593 | DIFFERENT COMPUTATIONAL PATHWAYS
0594 | ```
0595 | 
0596 | That is much more interesting.
0597 | 
0598 | ---
0599 | 
0600 | ## Some Things Are Assertions, Not Findings
0601 | 
0602 | The reset also forced us to separate code identities from scientific measurements.
0603 | 
0604 | At lag one, FORCE and PREVENT differ locally around `x`.
0605 | 
0606 | For any shared evaluated cell farther than one lattice step from `x`, the frozen local rule sees exactly the same ring-one occupancy in both branches.
0607 | 
0608 | Therefore:
0609 | 
0610 | ```text
0611 | shared_shift_far = 0
0612 | ```
0613 | 
0614 | is not an empirical discovery.  
0615 | It follows from the rule.
0616 | 
0617 | Likewise:
0618 | 
0619 | ```text
0620 | E1_far_exact
0621 | =
0622 | swap_total_far
0623 | ```
0624 | 
0625 | because the shared far-field term is zero and the accounting decomposition is exact.
0626 | 
0627 | Those are excellent correctness controls.  
0628 | They would catch a bug.  
0629 | But they do not belong in the scientific findings.
0630 | 
0631 | A useful standing rule emerges:
0632 | 
0633 | > **If a quantity has exactly zero variance across hundreds of independent groups because of the program structure, it belongs in an `assert`, not in a bootstrap confidence interval.**
0634 | 
0635 | ---
0636 | 
0637 | ## The Strong Result: Far-Field Redistribution
0638 | 
0639 | Now look at the lag-one far field.
0640 | 
0641 | For HIGH FCP:
0642 | 
0643 | ```text
0644 | ΔF = +2
0645 | 
0646 | far-field expected effect
0647 | ≈ -0.117
0648 | ```
0649 | 
0650 | For LOW FCP:
0651 | 
0652 | ```text
0653 | ΔF = -1
0654 | 
0655 | far-field expected effect
0656 | ≈ +0.063
0657 | ```
0658 | 
0659 | Both are outside the local nearest-neighbour causal cone.
0660 | 
0661 | No signal propagated there.  
0662 | No wave travelled across the lattice.  
0663 | The coupling came from the selector.
0664 | 
0665 | The evaluation budget remained fixed:
0666 | 
0667 | ```text
0668 | B = 96
0669 | ```
0670 | 
0671 | frontier opportunities could be evaluated.
0672 | 
0673 | If a local intervention changed the frontier, the selector had to choose a different set of candidates.
0674 | 
0675 | Some distant opportunities were dropped.  
0676 | Others were added.
0677 | 
0678 | The local action changed the global candidate population.
0679 | 
0680 | That is the mechanism.
0681 | 
0682 | ```mermaid
0683 | flowchart LR
0684 |     A[Local intervention<br/>changes frontier size ΔF] --> B[Global candidate population changes]
0685 |     B --> C[Fixed budget B selects different candidates]
0686 |     C --> D[Far-field expected construction changes]
0687 |     D --> E[Redistribution outside causal cone]
0688 | ```
0689 | 
0690 | ![Finite-budget redistribution in the Digital Crystal](/images/books/digital-life/ch24-finite-budget-redistribution.png)
0691 | 
0692 | ---
0693 | 
0694 | ## The Parameter-Free Ratio
0695 | 
0696 | The sharpest quantitative result of V5 does not require fitting a free coefficient.
0697 | 
0698 | The extreme classes have:
0699 | 
0700 | ```text
0701 | HIGH:
0702 | ΔF = +2
0703 | 
0704 | LOW:
0705 | ΔF = -1
0706 | ```
0707 | 
0708 | If the far-field selector effect follows:
0709 | 
0710 | ```text
0711 | far-field effect ∝ -ΔF
0712 | ```
0713 | 
0714 | then the predicted ratio is:
0715 | 
0716 | ```text
0717 | HIGH : LOW
0718 | =
0719 | -2 : +1
0720 | ```
0721 | 
0722 | The observed far-field effects were:
0723 | 
0724 | ```text
0725 | HIGH
0726 | -0.117
0727 | 
0728 | LOW
0729 | +0.063
0730 | ```
0731 | 
0732 | So:
0733 | 
0734 | ```text
0735 | observed ratio
0736 | =
0737 | -0.117 / +0.063
0738 | ≈ -1.86
0739 | ```
0740 | 
0741 | against:
0742 | 
0743 | ```text
0744 | predicted ratio
0745 | =
0746 | -2.00
0747 | ```
0748 | 
0749 | This is the cleanest evidence in the chapter.
0750 | 
0751 | No fitted slope is needed to obtain the ratio.  
0752 | No post-hoc threshold is required.  
0753 | The sign flips exactly as predicted.  
0754 | The magnitude ratio is close to the parameter-free expectation.
0755 | 
0756 | The core empirical statement is therefore:
0757 | 
0758 | > **Within the supported single-contact frontier regime at `B = 96`, the selector-mediated far-field effect follows the sign and approximate magnitude expected from the change in frontier size: creating two frontier opportunities produces roughly twice the opposite far-field effect of removing one.**
0759 | 
0760 | That is stronger than saying only that a far-field effect exists.  
0761 | It says the effect carries the quantitative signature of frontier dilution under fixed computational capacity.
0762 | 
0763 | ---
0764 | 
0765 | ## What the Budget Actually Conserves
0766 | 
0767 | It is tempting to say the budget conserves construction.
0768 | 
0769 | It does not.
0770 | 
0771 | What remains fixed is:
0772 | 
0773 | ```text
0774 | NUMBER OF EVALUATIONS
0775 | =
0776 | B
0777 | ```
0778 | 
0779 | not:
0780 | 
0781 | ```text
0782 | NUMBER OF ATTACHMENTS
0783 | ```
0784 | 
0785 | Expected attachments are:
0786 | 
0787 | ```text
0788 | Σ p(candidate)
0789 | ```
0790 | 
0791 | over whichever `B` cells happen to be selected.
0792 | 
0793 | Change the candidate set and that sum can change.
0794 | 
0795 | So the correct statement is:
0796 | 
0797 | > **Finite budget conserves evaluation capacity, not attachment count.**
0798 | 
0799 | That distinction explains the V5 local/global accounting.
0800 | 
0801 | For HIGH FCP:
0802 | 
0803 | ```text
0804 | local E1     ≈ +0.159
0805 | far E1       ≈ -0.117
0806 | ──────────────────────
0807 | global E1    ≈ +0.042
0808 | ```
0809 | 
0810 | Most of the positive local effect is offset by far-field suppression.
0811 | 
0812 | For LOW FCP:
0813 | 
0814 | ```text
0815 | local E1     ≈ +0.128
0816 | far E1       ≈ +0.063
0817 | ──────────────────────
0818 | global E1    ≈ +0.191
0819 | ```
0820 | 
0821 | Here the local and far-field effects reinforce.
0822 | 
0823 | A fixed number of evaluations does not imply zero net expected construction.
0824 | 
0825 | It implies competition over **which opportunities receive those evaluations**.
0826 | 
0827 | That is a very different kind of conservation law.
0828 | 
0829 | ---
0830 | 
0831 | ## Selector Dilution
0832 | 
0833 | A first-order approximation follows naturally.
0834 | 
0835 | Let:
0836 | 
0837 | ```text
0838 | F
0839 | ```
0840 | 
0841 | be frontier size and:
0842 | 
0843 | ```text
0844 | B
0845 | ```
0846 | 
0847 | the fixed evaluation budget.
0848 | 
0849 | Then an arbitrary frontier opportunity is evaluated at roughly:
0850 | 
0851 | ```text
0852 | B / F
0853 | ```
0854 | 
0855 | when:
0856 | 
0857 | ```text
0858 | B < F
0859 | ```
0860 | 
0861 | If a local intervention changes frontier size by:
0862 | 
0863 | ```text
0864 | ΔF
0865 | ```
0866 | 
0867 | then the global evaluation probability of distant opportunities shifts.
0868 | 
0869 | A first-order far-field approximation is:
0870 | 
0871 | ```text
0872 | E_far
0873 | ≈
0874 | -(ΔF / F)
0875 | ×
0876 | (B / F)
0877 | ×
0878 | Σ p_far
0879 | ```
0880 | 
0881 | The V5 approximation cleared its frozen aggregate residual tolerance.
0882 | 
0883 | But its per-intervention correlation was only moderate.
0884 | 
0885 | So we should not pretend the formula predicts every individual intervention.
0886 | 
0887 | The stronger claim is narrower:
0888 | 
0889 | > **The aggregate far-field effect is consistent with the expected sign and scale of fixed-budget selector dilution, and the parameter-free `-2:1` ratio provides the clearest confirmation in the tested extreme-FCP classes.**
0890 | 
0891 | That is enough.
0892 | 
0893 | Chapter 25 will test the approximation as a general law.
0894 | 
0895 | ---
0896 | 
0897 | ## The FCP = 0 Control We Have Not Yet Used
0898 | 
0899 | The Digital Crystal also contains frontier sites with:
0900 | 
0901 | ```text
0902 | FCP = 0
0903 | ```
0904 | 
0905 | There, the local intervention does not change total frontier size.
0906 | 
0907 | It can still change frontier composition:
0908 | 
0909 | ```text
0910 | x leaves
0911 | one other opportunity enters
0912 | ```
0913 | 
0914 | So the size-dilution term predicts:
0915 | 
0916 | ```text
0917 | 0
0918 | ```
0919 | 
0920 | while candidate composition can still produce substitutions.
0921 | 
0922 | That gives us a powerful next control:
0923 | 
0924 | ```mermaid
0925 | flowchart LR
0926 |     A[FCP = 0] --> B[SIZE EFFECT REMOVED]
0927 |     B --> C[COMPOSITION SUBSTITUTION REMAINS]
0928 |     C --> D[Separate size dilution<br/>from composition substitution]
0929 | ```
0930 | 
0931 | This is not needed to close Chapter 24.  
0932 | It belongs in the next budget experiment.
0933 | 
0934 | But it tells us exactly how to separate:
0935 | 
0936 | ```text
0937 | frontier-size dilution
0938 | ```
0939 | 
0940 | from:
0941 | 
0942 | ```text
0943 | frontier-composition substitution
0944 | ```
0945 | 
0946 | without inventing a new observer.
0947 | 
0948 | ---
0949 | 
0950 | ## What Happened to the Divergence Story?
0951 | 
0952 | V4 suggested that high-FCP interventions might mainly change:
0953 | 
0954 | ```text
0955 | P(PATH DIVERGES)
0956 | ```
0957 | 
0958 | rather than:
0959 | 
0960 | ```text
0961 | CASCADE SIZE GIVEN DIVERGENCE
0962 | ```
0963 | 
0964 | A fresh-seed V5 did not confirm that cleanly.
0965 | 
0966 | The realized lag-one divergence rates were approximately:
0967 | 
0968 | ```text
0969 | HIGH  0.212
0970 | LOW   0.206
0971 | ```
0972 | 
0973 | with a high-minus-low difference close to zero relative to the planned effect size.
0974 | 
0975 | Likewise:
0976 | 
0977 | ```text
0978 | P(G_T != 0)
0979 | ```
0980 | 
0981 | did not establish the expected class difference.
0982 | 
0983 | The conditional magnitude among nonzero cases also changed dramatically between seeds.
0984 | 
0985 | That is a calibration result.
0986 | 
0987 | Rare-event conditional summaries can look extremely compelling and still be unstable.
0988 | 
0989 | So Chapter 24 does not use them as the mechanism.
0990 | 
0991 | The mechanism is identified one level earlier:
0992 | 
0993 | ```text
0994 | FRONTIER CHANGE
0995 | ↓
0996 | GLOBAL SELECTOR CHANGE
0997 | ↓
0998 | EXPECTED FAR-FIELD REDISTRIBUTION
0999 | ```
1000 | 
1001 | That pathway is both cleaner and more reproducible.
1002 | 
1003 | ---
1004 | 
1005 | ## The Scientific Result
1006 | 
1007 | We can now state the Chapter 24 result without pretending we found a causal-gain field.
1008 | 
1009 | > **Within the tested single-contact Digital Crystal frontier regime at a fixed evaluation budget of `B = 96`, a local attachment can immediately change expected construction outside its nearest-neighbour causal cone by altering the globally selected set of frontier candidates.**
1010 | 
1011 | More specifically:
1012 | 
1013 | ```text
1014 | ΔF = +2
1015 | →
1016 | far-field expected effect ≈ -0.117
1017 | 
1018 | ΔF = -1
1019 | →
1020 | far-field expected effect ≈ +0.063
1021 | ```
1022 | 
1023 | giving:
1024 | 
1025 | ```text
1026 | observed ratio ≈ -1.86
1027 | predicted ratio = -2 : 1
1028 | ```
1029 | 
1030 | The local mechanism is local.
1031 | 
1032 | The coupling mechanism is global.
1033 | 
1034 | That distinction matters.
1035 | 
1036 | ---
1037 | 
1038 | ## P005 — Finite-Budget Redistribution
1039 | 
1040 | The phenomenon ledger can now promote a new entry.
1041 | 
1042 | **Finite-Budget Redistribution**
1043 | 
1044 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1045 | 
1046 | Operational statement:
1047 | 
1048 | > **Under a fixed global evaluation budget, a local change in frontier geometry can immediately alter which distant construction opportunities are evaluated, producing expected far-field construction differences outside the nearest-neighbour causal cone.**
1049 | 
1050 | Mechanism:
1051 | 
1052 | ```text
1053 | LOCAL FRONTIER CHANGE
1054 | ↓
1055 | FIXED-SIZE GLOBAL EVALUATION
1056 | ↓
1057 | CANDIDATE SUBSTITUTION
1058 | ↓
1059 | FAR-FIELD REDISTRIBUTION
1060 | ```
1061 | 
1062 | Current scope:
1063 | 
1064 | ```text
1065 | Digital Crystal v1
1066 | single-contact frontier sites
1067 | extreme FCP +2 versus -1
1068 | B = 96
1069 | lag 1
1070 | ```
1071 | 
1072 | Stronger approximation:
1073 | 
1074 | ```text
1075 | far-field effect
1076 | ∝
1077 | -ΔF
1078 | ```
1079 | 
1080 | **Status: SUPPORTED APPROXIMATION IN TESTED REGIME**
1081 | 
1082 | Not yet established:
1083 | 
1084 | ```text
1085 | generality across B
1086 | generality across n
1087 | linearity over all FCP values
1088 | behaviour near B ≈ F
1089 | unbounded-limit behaviour
1090 | long-term system organization
1091 | ```
1092 | 
1093 | Those are now experimentally accessible.
1094 | 
1095 | ---
1096 | 
1097 | ## What Chapter 24 Did Not Find
1098 | 
1099 | The chapter began looking for:
1100 | 
1101 | ```text
1102 | HIGH-GAIN LOCATIONS
1103 | ```
1104 | 
1105 | It did not establish a stable local causal-gain field.
1106 | 
1107 | But the reason is now more interesting than a null result.
1108 | 
1109 | The local causal consequence is partly determined by a computational allocation process that is not local.
1110 | 
1111 | A cell can matter not only because it changes its neighbours.  
1112 | It can matter because it changes the set from which the entire system spends its finite computational budget.
1113 | 
1114 | That means:
1115 | 
1116 | ```text
1117 | LOCAL RULE
1118 | +
1119 | GLOBAL COMPUTATIONAL CONSTRAINT
1120 | ↓
1121 | NON-LOCAL CAUSAL COUPLING
1122 | ```
1123 | 
1124 | without requiring:
1125 | 
1126 | ```text
1127 | non-local physics
1128 | message passing
1129 | waves
1130 | hidden signals
1131 | ```
1132 | 
1133 | The non-locality is in resource allocation, not in the transition rule.
1134 | 
1135 | ---
1136 | 
1137 | ## This Is a Digital-Native Constraint
1138 | 
1139 | Biological systems force us to think about:
1140 | 
1141 | ```text
1142 | energy
1143 | matter
1144 | transport
1145 | space
1146 | ```
1147 | 
1148 | The Digital Crystal has another scarce quantity:
1149 | 
1150 | ```text
1151 | evaluation
1152 | ```
1153 | 
1154 | Only a finite number of possible construction events are allowed to receive computation on each update.
1155 | 
1156 | So two spatially distant regions can interact without exchanging a signal.
1157 | 
1158 | They interact because:
1159 | 
1160 | ```text
1161 | both want access to the same B evaluations
1162 | ```
1163 | 
1164 | This is not metabolism.
1165 | 
1166 | It is not biological resource competition.
1167 | 
1168 | It is a substrate-specific computational constraint.
1169 | 
1170 | And it emerged because we refused to call the budget “energy” merely because it behaved like scarcity.
1171 | 
1172 | The correct object was already there:
1173 | 
1174 | ```text
1175 | FINITE COMPUTATION
1176 | ```
1177 | 
1178 | ---
1179 | 
1180 | ## What We Learned From Getting Chapter 24 Wrong
1181 | 
1182 | The V1→V5 sequence is worth keeping because it demonstrates the experimental method under pressure.
1183 | 
1184 | We made several mistakes:
1185 | 
1186 | ```text
1187 | weak contrast
1188 | underpowered SEI
1189 | identity treated as evidence
1190 | conditioning on a possible mediator
1191 | history tested in a memoryless substrate
1192 | rare-event mean used as one noisy outcome
1193 | ```
1194 | 
1195 | Then the reset changed the result.
1196 | 
1197 | The solution was not:
1198 | 
1199 | ```text
1200 | run more prompts
1201 | add more features
1202 | use a classifier
1203 | ```
1204 | 
1205 | It was:
1206 | 
1207 | ```text
1208 | identify the mechanism
1209 | ↓
1210 | measure the expectation directly
1211 | ↓
1212 | separate identities from findings
1213 | ↓
1214 | decompose the causal pathway
1215 | ↓
1216 | use a parameter-free prediction where possible
1217 | ↓
1218 | retain bounded conclusions
1219 | ```
1220 | 
1221 | That is exactly the scientific discipline this book is supposed to practice.
1222 | 
1223 | ---
1224 | 
1225 | ## The New Causal Ladder
1226 | 
1227 | Chapter 23 and Chapter 24 now give us a cleaner causal decomposition:
1228 | 
1229 | ```mermaid
1230 | flowchart TD
1231 |     A[INTERVENTION] --> B[LOCAL RULE CHANGES PROBABILITIES]
1232 |     B --> C[FRONTIER MEMBERSHIP CHANGES]
1233 |     C --> D[GLOBAL SELECTOR CHANGES]
1234 |     D --> E[EVALUATION LOCATIONS CHANGE]
1235 |     E --> F[EXPECTED CONSTRUCTION REDISTRIBUTES]
1236 |     F --> G[REALIZED FUTURES MAY DIVERGE]
1237 |     G --> H[DOWNSTREAM CASCADE MAY FOLLOW]
1238 | ```
1239 | 
1240 | Those stages should never again be compressed into one word like:
1241 | 
1242 | ```text
1243 | gain
1244 | ```
1245 | 
1246 | They are different objects.  
1247 | They have different estimators.  
1248 | They require different controls.  
1249 | And some of them are much easier to identify than others.
1250 | 
1251 | ---
1252 | 
1253 | ## Next: Vary the Constraint, Not the Crystal
1254 | 
1255 | The next question is now obvious.
1256 | 
1257 | If the far-field effect really comes from finite candidate selection, then varying the budget should change the effect predictably.
1258 | 
1259 | But there is an important experimental requirement.
1260 | 
1261 | We must **not** grow a different crystal at each budget.
1262 | 
1263 | That would confound:
1264 | 
1265 | ```text
1266 | budget
1267 | morphology
1268 | population
1269 | frontier size
1270 | history
1271 | ```
1272 | 
1273 | Instead:
1274 | 
1275 | ```text
1276 | SAME CHECKPOINT
1277 | SAME INTERVENTION
1278 | SAME FRONTIER
1279 | 
1280 | ↓
1281 | RECOMPUTE LAG-1 EXPECTATION
1282 | UNDER DIFFERENT B
1283 | ```
1284 | 
1285 | That isolates the computational constraint itself.
1286 | 
1287 | The useful control parameter is not a fixed list of arbitrary budgets.
1288 | 
1289 | It is:
1290 | 
1291 | ```text
1292 | B / F
1293 | ```
1294 | 
1295 | the fraction of the current frontier that can be evaluated.
1296 | 
1297 | A meaningful sweep is therefore approximately:
1298 | 
1299 | ```text
1300 | B/F =
1301 | 0.05
1302 | 0.10
1303 | 0.25
1304 | 0.50
1305 | 0.75
1306 | 1.00
1307 | ```
1308 | 
1309 | plus:
1310 | 
1311 | ```text
1312 | UNBOUNDED
1313 | ```
1314 | 
1315 | At:
1316 | 
1317 | ```text
1318 | B >= F
1319 | ```
1320 | 
1321 | there is no candidate subsampling.
1322 | 
1323 | Every frontier opportunity is evaluated.
1324 | 
1325 | Therefore selector-mediated outside-cone displacement must be:
1326 | 
1327 | ```text
1328 | exactly zero
1329 | ```
1330 | 
1331 | If it is not, the implementation is wrong.
1332 | 
1333 | That is a hard correctness control.
1334 | 
1335 | The linear dilution approximation should work best when:
1336 | 
1337 | ```text
1338 | B << F
1339 | ```
1340 | 
1341 | and must break as:
1342 | 
1343 | ```text
1344 | B → F
1345 | ```
1346 | 
1347 | because at full evaluation there is nothing left to dilute.
1348 | 
1349 | So Chapter 25 does not merely ask:
1350 | 
1351 | > Does redistribution get weaker with more computation?
1352 | 
1353 | It asks:
1354 | 
1355 | > **Where does finite-budget redistribution disappear, and how does the mechanism depart from the linear approximation as evaluation capacity approaches the whole frontier?**
1356 | 
1357 | That is a real control-parameter experiment.
1358 | 
1359 | ---
1360 | 
1361 | ## From Gain to Constraint
1362 | 
1363 | Chapter 24 began with:
1364 | 
1365 | ```text
1366 | WHERE IS CAUSAL GAIN CREATED?
1367 | ```
1368 | 
1369 | We expected to find a local property.
1370 | 
1371 | Instead we found a coupling.
1372 | 
1373 | The local intervention changes the frontier.  
1374 | The frontier changes the candidate population.  
1375 | The candidate population competes for a fixed number of evaluations.  
1376 | And distant expected construction changes immediately.
1377 | 
1378 | So the chapter ends somewhere different from where it began.
1379 | 
1380 | ```mermaid
1381 | flowchart LR
1382 |     A[LOCAL CAUSAL EFFECT] --> B[NOT A SIMPLE LOCAL GAIN FIELD]
1383 |     B --> C[FINITE COMPUTATIONAL ALLOCATION]
1384 |     C --> D[FAR-FIELD REDISTRIBUTION]
1385 | ```
1386 | 
1387 | The most important sentence is no longer:
1388 | 
1389 | > The effect exists but the location does not.
1390 | 
1391 | It is:
1392 | 
1393 | > **The effect is partly local, but the constraint that distributes it is global.**
1394 | 
1395 | And that gives us something better than the high-gain map we went looking for.
1396 | 
1397 | It gives us a measurable law of the substrate.

0011 | 
0012 | Chapter 24 ended somewhere we did not expect.
0013 | 
0014 | We began by looking for a local causal-gain field.
0015 | 
0016 | We found something else.
0017 | 
0018 | A local intervention changed the frontier.
0019 | 
0020 | The frontier changed which candidates entered a fixed global evaluation budget.
0021 | 
0022 | And distant expected construction changed immediately, even though the local transition rule could not propagate influence that far in one update.
0023 | 
0024 | That gave us a new candidate substrate law:
0025 | 
0026 | ```text
0027 | LOCAL FRONTIER CHANGE
0028 | ↓
0029 | FIXED GLOBAL EVALUATION BUDGET
0030 | ↓
0031 | CANDIDATE SUBSTITUTION
0032 | ↓
0033 | FAR-FIELD REDISTRIBUTION
0034 | ```
0035 | 
0036 | The mechanism looked real.
0037 | 
0038 | But Chapter 24 tested it at one budget:
0039 | 
0040 | ```text
0041 | B = 96
0042 | ```
0043 | 
0044 | That was not enough.
0045 | 
0046 | If finite computation really caused the non-local coupling, then the effect should move when we changed the amount of computation available.
0047 | 
0048 | The next experiment therefore held the crystal fixed and varied only one thing:
0049 | 
0050 | ```text
0051 | HOW MUCH OF THE FRONTIER
0052 | CAN BE EVALUATED?
0053 | ```
0054 | 
0055 | The important design decision was what **not** to do.
0056 | 
0057 | We did not grow a different crystal for each budget.
0058 | 
0059 | That would have changed:
0060 | 
0061 | ```text
0062 | morphology
0063 | population
0064 | frontier size
0065 | history
0066 | turnover
0067 | ```
0068 | 
0069 | at the same time as budget.
0070 | 
0071 | Instead we froze the checkpoint.
0072 | 
0073 | We froze the intervention.
0074 | 
0075 | We froze the environment.
0076 | 
0077 | We froze the geometry.
0078 | 
0079 | Then, at the very next update, we changed only the number of candidate frontier cells allowed to receive computation.
0080 | 
0081 | That turns Chapter 25 into a control-parameter experiment.
0082 | 
0083 | ---
0084 | 
0085 | ## The Digital Resource Is an Evaluation Slot
0086 | 
0087 | It is tempting to compare finite computation to biological energy.
0088 | 
0089 | We should not.
0090 | 
0091 | The Digital Crystal does not burn calories.
0092 | 
0093 | It does not consume ATP.
0094 | 
0095 | It does not transport nutrients.
0096 | 
0097 | The scarce quantity in this experiment is simpler:
0098 | 
0099 | ```text
0100 | AN EVALUATION SLOT
0101 | ```
0102 | 
0103 | At every update, the frontier may contain hundreds of eligible construction opportunities.
0104 | 
0105 | But only:
0106 | 
0107 | ```text
0108 | B
0109 | ```
0110 | 
0111 | of them are evaluated.
0112 | 
0113 | So when:
0114 | 
0115 | ```text
0116 | B < F
0117 | ```
0118 | 
0119 | where `F` is frontier size, the system cannot inspect every possible attachment site.
0120 | 
0121 | It has to choose.
0122 | 
0123 | That means two distant regions can interact without exchanging a signal.
0124 | 
0125 | They interact because both compete for access to the same finite set of evaluation slots.
0126 | 
0127 | The local transition rule remains local.
0128 | 
0129 | The allocation constraint does not.
0130 | 
0131 | ```mermaid
0132 | flowchart LR
0133 |     subgraph Local
0134 |     A[Local rule] --> B[Changes nearby probabilities]
0135 |     end
0136 |     subgraph Global
0137 |     C[Fixed evaluation budget] --> D[Which frontier sites are evaluated?]
0138 |     D --> E[Distant regions compete for slots]
0139 |     E --> F[Non-local coupling without signal exchange]
0140 |     end
0141 |     B --> D
0142 | ```
0143 | 
0144 | ---
0145 | 
0146 | ## The Frozen Experiment
0147 | 
0148 | For each independent checkpoint we selected supported single-contact frontier sites:
0149 | 
0150 | ```text
0151 | occupied neighbours = 1
0152 | ```
0153 | 
0154 | and classified them by Frontier Creation Potential:
0155 | 
0156 | ```text
0157 | FCP = -1
0158 |        0
0159 |       +1
0160 |       +2
0161 | ```
0162 | 
0163 | Then we performed the same FORCE/PREVENT intervention introduced in Chapter 23 and refined in Chapter 24.
0164 | 
0165 | ```text
0166 | SAME CHECKPOINT
0167 | SAME CELL x
0168 | SAME INPUT
0169 | SAME RANDOMNESS
0170 | 
0171 | FORCE x
0172 | vs
0173 | PREVENT x
0174 | ```
0175 | 
0176 | The intervention update itself used the ordinary frozen budget.
0177 | 
0178 | After that intervention had created the two lag-one states, we stopped evolving the system.
0179 | 
0180 | Now we varied only the lag-one evaluation fraction.
0181 | 
0182 | For each branch we measured:
0183 | 
0184 | ```text
0185 | B/F =
0186 | 0.05
0187 | 0.10
0188 | 0.25
0189 | 0.50
0190 | 0.75
0191 | 1.00
0192 | ```
0193 | 
0194 | plus an explicit:
0195 | 
0196 | ```text
0197 | UNBOUNDED
0198 | ```
0199 | 
0200 | arm.
0201 | 
0202 | The same checkpoint therefore generated all budget conditions.
0203 | 
0204 | The budget sweep did not create different crystals.
0205 | 
0206 | It created different computational allocations over the same crystal state.
0207 | 
0208 | ---
0209 | 
0210 | ## The Region That Cannot Be Reached Locally
0211 | 
0212 | The primary measurement was taken outside the ordinary one-step causal cone.
0213 | 
0214 | At lag one:
0215 | 
0216 | ```text
0217 | distance > 1
0218 | ```
0219 | 
0220 | cannot be affected by the local nearest-neighbour attachment rule.
0221 | 
0222 | That fact is structural.
0223 | 
0224 | It follows from the rule.
0225 | 
0226 | So if FORCE and PREVENT differ there after one update, the difference cannot have travelled through ordinary local propagation.
0227 | 
0228 | The only available pathway is:
0229 | 
0230 | ```text
0231 | LOCAL INTERVENTION
0232 | ↓
0233 | FRONTIER SET CHANGES
0234 | ↓
0235 | GLOBAL CANDIDATE SELECTION CHANGES
0236 | ↓
0237 | DISTANT EVALUATIONS CHANGE
0238 | ```
0239 | 
0240 | This gives us unusually clean causal identification.
0241 | 
0242 | The experiment measured:
0243 | 
0244 | ```text
0245 | far FORCE-only selected cells
0246 | far PREVENT-only selected cells
0247 | far symmetric difference
0248 | far selected-set overlap
0249 | 
0250 | exact expected far attachment difference
0251 | ```
0252 | 
0253 | before any Bernoulli attachment draw was made.
0254 | 
0255 | The primary quantity was therefore not a noisy realized count.
0256 | 
0257 | It was the exact expected construction difference induced by the changed selector.
0258 | 
0259 | ---
0260 | 
0261 | ## The Hardest Control in the Book
0262 | 
0263 | The strongest part of the experiment was also the simplest.
0264 | 
0265 | At:
0266 | 
0267 | ```text
0268 | B/F = 1.00
0269 | ```
0270 | 
0271 | every frontier cell is evaluated.
0272 | 
0273 | There is no subsampling.
0274 | 
0275 | Likewise in the explicit unbounded arm.
0276 | 
0277 | So outside the nearest-neighbour causal cone, FORCE and PREVENT must evaluate the same cells.
0278 | 
0279 | The script therefore asserted:
0280 | 
0281 | ```text
0282 | far FORCE-only count   = 0
0283 | far PREVENT-only count = 0
0284 | far symmetric diff     = 0
0285 | far expected effect    = 0
0286 | ```
0287 | 
0288 | for every intervention.
0289 | 
0290 | Not approximately.
0291 | 
0292 | Exactly, up to floating-point tolerance.
0293 | 
0294 | Across the full scientific run, the hard-zero control was checked:
0295 | 
0296 | ```text
0297 | 10,750 times
0298 | ```
0299 | 
0300 | and never failed.
0301 | 
0302 | That is the spine of Chapter 25.
0303 | 
0304 | Not because zero itself is surprising.
0305 | 
0306 | It is not.
0307 | 
0308 | The zero is required by the mechanism.
0309 | 
0310 | The important evidence is the pair:
0311 | 
0312 | ```text
0313 | PARTIAL EVALUATION
0314 | → reproducible outside-cone effect
0315 | 
0316 | REMOVE SUBSAMPLING
0317 | → exact disappearance
0318 | ```
0319 | 
0320 | That turns a correlation with budget into a mechanistic identification.
0321 | 
0322 | > **The outside-cone coupling is produced by finite candidate selection.**
0323 | 
0324 | ---
0325 | 
0326 | ## The Full Run
0327 | 
0328 | The full experiment used:
0329 | 
0330 | ```text
0331 | 384 independent checkpoints
0332 | ```
0333 | 
0334 | and measured:
0335 | 
0336 | ```text
0337 | 5,375 supported n=1 sites
0338 | ```
0339 | 
0340 | across all four FCP classes.
0341 | 
0342 | Each site was evaluated across seven budget conditions.
0343 | 
0344 | That produced:
0345 | 
0346 | ```text
0347 | 37,625 site × budget measurements
0348 | ```
0349 | 
0350 | The hard-zero controls passed for the exhaustive arms.
0351 | 
0352 | Now we could ask what happened under partial evaluation.
0353 | 
0354 | ---
0355 | 
0356 | ## The Low-Budget Law
0357 | 
0358 | Chapter 24 suggested a first-order relationship:
0359 | 
0360 | ```text
0361 | E_far
0362 | ≈
0363 | -(ΔF/F)
0364 | ×
0365 | (B/F)
0366 | ×
0367 | Σp_far
0368 | ```
0369 | 
0370 | where:
0371 | 
0372 | ```text
0373 | ΔF
0374 | ```
0375 | 
0376 | is the actual lag-one frontier-size difference between FORCE and PREVENT.
0377 | 
0378 | If:
0379 | 
0380 | ```text
0381 | B = fF
0382 | ```
0383 | 
0384 | then the expression simplifies approximately to:
0385 | 
0386 | ```text
0387 | E_far
0388 | ≈
0389 | -ΔF × f × p̄_far
0390 | ```
0391 | 
0392 | where `p̄_far` is the mean attachment probability carried by the far frontier.
0393 | 
0394 | That gives us a very specific prediction:
0395 | 
0396 | ```text
0397 | E_far ∝ -ΔF
0398 | ```
0399 | 
0400 | at each fixed partial-evaluation fraction.
0401 | 
0402 | The experiment tested that relation at:
0403 | 
0404 | ```text
0405 | f = 0.05
0406 | 0.10
0407 | 0.25
0408 | ```
0409 | 
0410 | using the actual lag-one frontier difference rather than the earlier checkpoint-level FCP label.
0411 | 
0412 | ---
0413 | 
0414 | ## The Aggregate Test Passed
0415 | 
0416 | The frozen aggregate criterion required the weighted mean residual to remain within:
0417 | 
0418 | ```text
0419 | 25%
0420 | ```
0421 | 
0422 | of the predicted magnitude.
0423 | 
0424 | The through-origin fits were:
0425 | 
0426 | ```text
0427 | f = 0.05
0428 | beta ≈ 0.0251
0429 | relative residual ≈ 12.6%
0430 | 
0431 | f = 0.10
0432 | beta ≈ 0.0571
0433 | relative residual ≈ 9.9%
0434 | 
0435 | f = 0.25
0436 | beta ≈ 0.1422
0437 | relative residual ≈ 2.6%
0438 | ```
0439 | 
0440 | All three cleared the frozen criterion.
0441 | 
0442 | So the predeclared aggregate hypothesis was:
0443 | 
0444 | ```text
0445 | SUPPORTED
0446 | ```
0447 | 
0448 | The important result is not the very high `R²` values from fitting three class means.
0449 | 
0450 | Three points through an origin are not a scientific triumph.
0451 | 
0452 | The result is the scaling itself:
0453 | 
0454 | > **Under partial evaluation, the expected outside-cone construction effect tracks the negative of the actual frontier-size difference.**
0455 | 
0456 | That relation became tighter as the evaluation fraction increased from `0.05` to `0.25`.
0457 | 
0458 | ---
0459 | 
0460 | ## Recovering the Probability Scale
0461 | 
0462 | The fitted coefficient carries more information.
0463 | 
0464 | From:
0465 | 
0466 | ```text
0467 | E_far
0468 | ≈
0469 | -ΔF × f × p̄_far
0470 | ```
0471 | 
0472 | we expect:
0473 | 
0474 | ```text
0475 | beta / f
0476 | ≈
0477 | p̄_far
0478 | ```
0479 | 
0480 | The experiment returned:
0481 | 
0482 | ```text
0483 | f       beta       beta/f
0484 | 
0485 | 0.05    0.0251      0.502
0486 | 0.10    0.0571      0.571
0487 | 0.25    0.1422      0.569
0488 | ```
0489 | 
0490 | Across a fivefold change in evaluation fraction, the latter two estimates converge near:
0491 | 
0492 | ```text
0493 | 0.57
0494 | ```
0495 | 
0496 | That is exactly the kind of quantity the mechanism says should appear.
0497 | 
0498 | We should be careful not to overstate this.
0499 | 
0500 | The chapter should measure the actual far-frontier probability mass directly before claiming an exact parameter recovery.
0501 | 
0502 | But the pattern is strong:
0503 | 
0504 | > **The budget coefficient behaves like the mean attachment probability carried by the far frontier, as predicted by the finite-selection model.**
0505 | 
0506 | The effect does not merely increase with more evaluation.
0507 | 
0508 | That increase was already in the frozen model.
0509 | 
0510 | The sweep recovered the expected scaling.
0511 | 
0512 | ---
0513 | 
0514 | ## One Result Did Not Generalize
0515 | 
0516 | Chapter 24 had produced a striking extreme-class ratio.
0517 | 
0518 | At `B = 96`:
0519 | 
0520 | ```text
0521 | FCP +2 → E_far ≈ -0.117
0522 | FCP -1 → E_far ≈ +0.063
0523 | ```
0524 | 
0525 | giving approximately:
0526 | 
0527 | ```text
0528 | -1.86
0529 | ```
0530 | 
0531 | against a simple:
0532 | 
0533 | ```text
0534 | -2 : +1
0535 | ```
0536 | 
0537 | frontier-size prediction.
0538 | 
0539 | Chapter 25 froze that as a calibration target across the low-budget sweep.
0540 | 
0541 | It did not survive cleanly.
0542 | 
0543 | Observed ratios were approximately:
0544 | 
0545 | ```text
0546 | B/F = 0.05    -4.15
0547 | B/F = 0.10    -3.54
0548 | B/F = 0.25    -2.21
0549 | ```
0550 | 
0551 | Only the `0.25` arm came within the frozen 25% tolerance around `-2`.
0552 | 
0553 | So the ratio result is:
0554 | 
0555 | ```text
0556 | UNRESOLVED
0557 | ```
0558 | 
0559 | and it stays that way.
0560 | 
0561 | We do not rescue it.
0562 | 
0563 | The failure taught us something important about the control variable.
0564 | 
0565 | ---
0566 | 
0567 | ## FCP Is Not the Same as the Frontier Seen by the Selector
0568 | 
0569 | FCP is measured from checkpoint geometry.
0570 | 
0571 | But the finite selector acts one update later.
0572 | 
0573 | Between those moments, ordinary intervention loss occurs.
0574 | 
0575 | So the actual lag-one frontier differences were closer to:
0576 | 
0577 | ```text
0578 | FCP +2 class:
0579 | actual ΔF ≈ +1.84
0580 | 
0581 | FCP -1 class:
0582 | actual ΔF ≈ -0.78
0583 | ```
0584 | 
0585 | Their actual magnitude ratio is therefore not:
0586 | 
0587 | ```text
0588 | 2.00
0589 | ```
0590 | 
0591 | but closer to:
0592 | 
0593 | ```text
0594 | 2.36
0595 | ```
0596 | 
0597 | The selector responds to the frontier that actually exists when it runs.
0598 | 
0599 | Not to the label we assigned one step earlier.
0600 | 
0601 | That distinction sharpens the mechanism:
0602 | 
0603 | ```text
0604 | CHECKPOINT FCP
0605 | ↓
0606 | upstream geometry descriptor
0607 | 
0608 | ACTUAL LAG-1 ΔF
0609 | ↓
0610 | state presented to selector
0611 | 
0612 | SELECTION DISPLACEMENT
0613 | ↓
0614 | proximal mediator
0615 | ```
0616 | 
0617 | The Chapter 24 ratio was useful.
0618 | 
0619 | It led us to the right experiment.
0620 | 
0621 | But Chapter 25 tells us to stop treating FCP as the final control parameter.
0622 | 
0623 | ---
0624 | 
0625 | ## The Negative-ΔF Class Is Less Clean
0626 | 
0627 | The aggregate low-budget scaling test passed.
0628 | 
0629 | That does not mean every class followed it equally well.
0630 | 
0631 | For `FCP = -1`, the per-class relative residuals were approximately:
0632 | 
0633 | ```text
0634 | f = 0.05   40%
0635 | f = 0.10   31%
0636 | f = 0.25    7%
0637 | ```
0638 | 
0639 | The positive-ΔF classes were much closer to the model across all three fractions.
0640 | 
0641 | So the scientifically honest statement is:
0642 | 
0643 | > **The preregistered aggregate low-budget scaling criterion was supported. The positive-ΔF classes followed the relation closely at all tested low-budget fractions, while the negative-ΔF class deviated beyond the 25% per-class scale at 5% and 10% evaluation.**
0644 | 
0645 | This asymmetry matters.
0646 | 
0647 | It tells us the scalar frontier-size model is not the most proximal description of the selector.
0648 | 
0649 | The next quantity is more exact.
0650 | 
0651 | ---
0652 | 
0653 | ## Selection Slots Are Conserved
0654 | 
0655 | When both branches are budget limited:
0656 | 
0657 | ```text
0658 | |S_force| = B
0659 | |S_prevent| = B
0660 | ```
0661 | 
0662 | Exactly the same number of candidates is selected in each branch.
0663 | 
0664 | Split those selected cells into:
0665 | 
0666 | ```text
0667 | NEAR
0668 | d <= 1
0669 | 
0670 | FAR
0671 | d > 1
0672 | ```
0673 | 
0674 | Then:
0675 | 
0676 | ```text
0677 | ΔN_selected_near
0678 | +
0679 | ΔN_selected_far
0680 | =
0681 | 0
0682 | ```
0683 | 
0684 | necessarily.
0685 | 
0686 | Therefore:
0687 | 
0688 | ```text
0689 | ΔN_selected_far
0690 | =
0691 | -ΔN_selected_near
0692 | ```
0693 | 
0694 | This is not an empirical law.
0695 | 
0696 | It is an accounting identity of fixed-size selection.
0697 | 
0698 | But it tells us what the selector actually conserves:
0699 | 
0700 | > **evaluation slots.**
0701 | 
0702 | Not attachments.
0703 | 
0704 | Not frontier size.
0705 | 
0706 | Not causal gain.
0707 | 
0708 | Slots.
0709 | 
0710 | The signed far-field construction effect is then approximately:
0711 | 
0712 | ```text
0713 | E_far
0714 | ≈
0715 | -p̄_displaced_far
0716 | ×
0717 | ΔN_selected_near
0718 | ```
0719 | 
0720 | This is a deeper formulation than:
0721 | 
0722 | ```text
0723 | E_far ∝ -ΔF
0724 | ```
0725 | 
0726 | because `ΔF` is upstream.
0727 | 
0728 | The selector does not directly consume Frontier Creation Potential.
0729 | 
0730 | It consumes a fixed number of slots.
0731 | 
0732 | Local frontier changes alter how many of those slots are used nearby.
0733 | 
0734 | The far field receives the exact opposite slot imbalance.
0735 | 
0736 | ```mermaid
0737 | flowchart TD
0738 |     subgraph SelectionBudgets
0739 |     A[FORCE branch] -->|"|S_force| = B"| C[Selected cells]
0740 |     B[PREVENT branch] -->|"|S_prevent| = B"| C
0741 |     end
0742 |     C --> D[Near selection difference]
0743 |     C --> E[Far selection difference]
0744 |     D --> F[ΔN_near = -ΔN_far]
0745 |     E --> F
0746 |     F --> G[Slot conservation identity]
0747 | ```
0748 | 
0749 | ---
0750 | 
0751 | ## Why Candidate Churn Is Not Enough
0752 | 
0753 | The `FCP = 0` arm gives us a beautiful control.
0754 | 
0755 | At `f = 0.50`:
0756 | 
0757 | ```text
0758 | FCP = 0
0759 | far symmetric difference ≈ 0.483
0760 | 
0761 | FCP = -1
0762 | far symmetric difference ≈ 0.446
0763 | ```
0764 | 
0765 | The amount of candidate churn is almost the same.
0766 | 
0767 | But the signed expected effects are very different:
0768 | 
0769 | ```text
0770 | FCP = 0
0771 | E_far ≈ -0.013
0772 | 
0773 | FCP = -1
0774 | E_far ≈ +0.213
0775 | ```
0776 | 
0777 | So simply changing many candidate identities does not guarantee a large signed construction effect.
0778 | 
0779 | What matters is the probability mass those substituted candidates carry.
0780 | 
0781 | This separates:
0782 | 
0783 | ```text
0784 | HOW MANY EVALUATION SLOTS MOVED
0785 | ```
0786 | 
0787 | from:
0788 | 
0789 | ```text
0790 | WHAT EXPECTED CONSTRUCTION
0791 | THOSE SLOTS REPRESENTED
0792 | ```
0793 | 
0794 | That distinction is essential.
0795 | 
0796 | > **Finite-budget redistribution is a redistribution of evaluation opportunity first, and only secondarily a redistribution of expected construction.**
0797 | 
0798 | Two interventions can move nearly the same number of slots while producing very different signed attachment effects.
0799 | 
0800 | ---
0801 | 
0802 | ## Partial Evaluation Is a Coupling Regime
0803 | 
0804 | Across the fraction sweep, the far-field effect grew in magnitude as more of the frontier was evaluated.
0805 | 
0806 | For example, the `FCP +2` class produced approximately:
0807 | 
0808 | ```text
0809 | B/F     E_far
0810 | 
0811 | 0.05   -0.049
0812 | 0.10   -0.110
0813 | 0.25   -0.261
0814 | 0.50   -0.492
0815 | 0.75   -0.715
0816 | 1.00    0
0817 | ```
0818 | 
0819 | The `FCP -1` class moved in the opposite direction:
0820 | 
0821 | ```text
0822 | 0.05   +0.012
0823 | 0.10   +0.031
0824 | 0.25   +0.118
0825 | 0.50   +0.213
0826 | 0.75   +0.294
0827 | 1.00    0
0828 | ```
0829 | 
0830 | That rise is not surprising.
0831 | 
0832 | The first-order model predicts it.
0833 | 
0834 | More evaluation slots means more opportunities for the difference between the two frontier populations to be expressed.
0835 | 
0836 | The interesting part is what happens near exhaustive evaluation.
0837 | 
0838 | ---
0839 | 
0840 | ## We Did Not Resolve the Saturation Layer
0841 | 
0842 | The coarse budget grid jumped from:
0843 | 
0844 | ```text
0845 | 0.75
0846 | ```
0847 | 
0848 | directly to:
0849 | 
0850 | ```text
0851 | 1.00
0852 | ```
0853 | 
0854 | At full evaluation, candidate subsampling disappears and the outside-cone effect becomes exactly zero.
0855 | 
0856 | But that does **not** mean the effect is mathematically discontinuous.
0857 | 
0858 | The final saturation transition may occupy only a few evaluation slots out of several hundred frontier cells.
0859 | 
0860 | The fractional width can therefore be far below one percent.
0861 | 
0862 | Our grid simply stepped over it.
0863 | 
0864 | So the correct conclusion is:
0865 | 
0866 | > **The coarse sweep shows redistribution persisting through 75% frontier evaluation and disappearing at exhaustive evaluation, but it does not resolve the narrow saturation layer where the selector ceases to subsample.**
0867 | 
0868 | That boundary is now experimentally interesting in its own right.
0869 | 
0870 | ---
0871 | 
0872 | ## The Better Coordinate Near Saturation
0873 | 
0874 | Fractions are convenient when the budget is small.
0875 | 
0876 | They are a poor coordinate when:
0877 | 
0878 | ```text
0879 | B ≈ F
0880 | ```
0881 | 
0882 | Near full evaluation, the meaningful quantity is:
0883 | 
0884 | ```text
0885 | g
0886 | =
0887 | F_ref - B
0888 | ```
0889 | 
0890 | the number of evaluation slots missing from exhaustive computation.
0891 | 
0892 | Then:
0893 | 
0894 | ```text
0895 | g = 0
0896 | ```
0897 | 
0898 | means full evaluation.
0899 | 
0900 | ```text
0901 | g = 1
0902 | ```
0903 | 
0904 | means exactly one frontier opportunity cannot be evaluated.
0905 | 
0906 | ```text
0907 | g = 2
0908 | ```
0909 | 
0910 | means two are omitted.
0911 | 
0912 | The near-saturation regime becomes discrete.
0913 | 
0914 | That is more natural for this substrate.
0915 | 
0916 | A useful next sweep is:
0917 | 
0918 | ```text
0919 | g ∈ {
0920 | 0,
0921 | 1,
0922 | 2,
0923 | 3,
0924 | 5,
0925 | 10,
0926 | 25
0927 | }
0928 | ```
0929 | 
0930 | on the same frozen checkpoints.
0931 | 
0932 | Now we can see the mechanism at integer resolution.
0933 | 
0934 | ---
0935 | 
0936 | ## The Saturation Law Should Be Piecewise
0937 | 
0938 | Suppose FORCE has a larger frontier.
0939 | 
0940 | Let:
0941 | 
0942 | ```text
0943 | F_force = F
0944 | F_prevent = F - d
0945 | B = F - g
0946 | ```
0947 | 
0948 | with:
0949 | 
0950 | ```text
0951 | d > 0
0952 | ```
0953 | 
0954 | When:
0955 | 
0956 | ```text
0957 | g < d
0958 | ```
0959 | 
0960 | the PREVENT branch is already fully evaluated while FORCE still has to omit some cells.
0961 | 
0962 | The expected far selection difference follows one expression.
0963 | 
0964 | When:
0965 | 
0966 | ```text
0967 | g >= d
0968 | ```
0969 | 
0970 | both branches are still subsampled.
0971 | 
0972 | The expression changes.
0973 | 
0974 | That means the saturation boundary is not one smooth low-budget line carried all the way to `B = F`.
0975 | 
0976 | It is a piecewise finite-combinatorial regime.
0977 | 
0978 | This is important because it tells us what Chapter 25 should do next.
0979 | 
0980 | Not another broad fraction sweep.
0981 | 
0982 | A narrow integer-slot experiment.
0983 | 
0984 | ---
0985 | 
0986 | ## What Chapter 25 Has Established
0987 | 
0988 | The strongest bounded claim is now:
0989 | 
0990 | > **Within the tested single-contact Digital Crystal regime, partial candidate evaluation creates an immediate outside-causal-cone construction effect whose signed magnitude tracks the actual frontier imbalance and evaluation fraction; when candidate evaluation becomes exhaustive, the outside-cone effect vanishes exactly.**
0991 | 
0992 | A more mechanistic version is:
0993 | 
0994 | > **Finite computation couples distant construction opportunities because a fixed number of evaluation slots must be redistributed when local frontier geometry changes.**
0995 | 
0996 | The local transition rule is still local.
0997 | 
0998 | The non-locality appears in the allocation of computation.
0999 | 
1000 | ---
1001 | 
1002 | ## P005 — Finite-Budget Redistribution
1003 | 
1004 | The phenomenon ledger can now strengthen its entry.
1005 | 
1006 | ### Finite-Budget Redistribution
1007 | 
1008 | **Status: SUPPORTED**
1009 | 
1010 | Operational statement:
1011 | 
1012 | > **When the Digital Crystal evaluates only part of its frontier, a local frontier change reallocates a fixed number of global evaluation slots, producing expected construction differences outside the nearest-neighbour causal cone. The effect disappears exactly when candidate evaluation becomes exhaustive.**
1013 | 
1014 | Mechanistic chain:
1015 | 
1016 | ```text
1017 | LOCAL FRONTIER CHANGE
1018 | ↓
1019 | NEAR SLOT EXCESS / DEFICIT
1020 | ↓
1021 | EXACT OPPOSITE FAR SLOT CHANGE
1022 | ↓
1023 | DISPLACED FAR PROBABILITY MASS
1024 | ↓
1025 | FAR EXPECTED CONSTRUCTION EFFECT
1026 | ```
1027 | 
1028 | Current scope:
1029 | 
1030 | ```text
1031 | Digital Crystal v1
1032 | n = 1 frontier regime
1033 | lag 1
1034 | partial evaluation
1035 | same-checkpoint budget sweep
1036 | ```
1037 | 
1038 | Supported quantitative behaviour:
1039 | 
1040 | ```text
1041 | low-budget E_far tracks
1042 | -evaluation_fraction × actual ΔF
1043 | 
1044 | full evaluation gives
1045 | exact outside-cone zero
1046 | ```
1047 | 
1048 | Not yet established:
1049 | 
1050 | ```text
1051 | exact site-level law across all geometry
1052 | near-saturation integer law
1053 | generality across n
1054 | longer-horizon redistribution
1055 | effect on causal amplification
1056 | effect on individuation
1057 | ```
1058 | 
1059 | ---
1060 | 
1061 | ## A Digital-Native Coupling
1062 | 
1063 | This result matters because it is not an imported biological metaphor.
1064 | 
1065 | We did not rename evaluation budget:
1066 | 
1067 | ```text
1068 | energy
1069 | ```
1070 | 
1071 | and declare metabolism.
1072 | 
1073 | We asked what finite computation itself does.
1074 | 
1075 | It creates a shared allocation constraint.
1076 | 
1077 | Two spatially distant regions can become causally coupled because they compete for execution slots.
1078 | 
1079 | That is native to the substrate.
1080 | 
1081 | A biological cell cannot usually skip chemistry because another cell on the opposite side of the organism used too much CPU time.
1082 | 
1083 | A Digital Crystal can.
1084 | 
1085 | Its scarcity is computational.
1086 | 
1087 | Its non-local coupling is computational.
1088 | 
1089 | Its conservation law is computational.
1090 | 
1091 | That is exactly the kind of property we hoped a substrate-first approach would reveal.
1092 | 
1093 | ---
1094 | 
1095 | ## The Cost of a Slot
1096 | 
1097 | There is another subtle point.
1098 | 
1099 | Fixed budget conserves:
1100 | 
1101 | ```text
1102 | NUMBER OF EVALUATIONS
1103 | ```
1104 | 
1105 | but not:
1106 | 
1107 | ```text
1108 | EXPECTED CONSTRUCTION
1109 | ```
1110 | 
1111 | because evaluation slots carry different attachment probabilities.
1112 | 
1113 | A slot spent on a candidate with:
1114 | 
1115 | ```text
1116 | p = 0.8
1117 | ```
1118 | 
1119 | is not equivalent in expected construction to a slot spent on:
1120 | 
1121 | ```text
1122 | p = 0.2
1123 | ```
1124 | 
1125 | So the selector creates two layers of dynamics:
1126 | 
1127 | ```text
1128 | ALLOCATION
1129 | which cells receive computation
1130 | 
1131 | and
1132 | 
1133 | PAYLOAD
1134 | how much expected construction
1135 | those cells carry
1136 | ```
1137 | 
1138 | The FCP=0 control exposed exactly this distinction.
1139 | 
1140 | Similar slot churn can produce radically different signed attachment effects.
1141 | 
1142 | This means future experiments should never collapse:
1143 | 
1144 | ```text
1145 | candidate displacement
1146 | ```
1147 | 
1148 | and:
1149 | 
1150 | ```text
1151 | construction displacement
1152 | ```
1153 | 
1154 | into one number.
1155 | 
1156 | ---
1157 | 
1158 | ## The Next Question Changes Again
1159 | 
1160 | Chapter 24 asked:
1161 | 
1162 | > Where is causal gain created?
1163 | 
1164 | Chapter 25 asked:
1165 | 
1166 | > How does finite computation redistribute causal opportunity?
1167 | 
1168 | The next question is harder:
1169 | 
1170 | > **Does that redistribution merely move construction around, or can it change causal amplification itself?**
1171 | 
1172 | Chapter 23 measured a finite downstream causal gain well below sustained amplification.
1173 | 
1174 | The crystal remained strongly dissipative.
1175 | 
1176 | That may explain several previous negative results:
1177 | 
1178 | ```text
1179 | no persistent propagating process
1180 | no stable active structure
1181 | no coherent causal boundary
1182 | no sustained cascade
1183 | ```
1184 | 
1185 | But budget is dangerous as an experimental variable.
1186 | 
1187 | Increasing `B` trivially evaluates more candidates.
1188 | 
1189 | More evaluations produce more expected attachments.
1190 | 
1191 | More attachments can produce more downstream descendants.
1192 | 
1193 | If we simply sweep budget and observe larger amplification, we will have learned almost nothing.
1194 | 
1195 | So Chapter 26 needs a stricter design.
1196 | 
1197 | ---
1198 | 
1199 | ## Match Construction Rate, Vary Allocation
1200 | 
1201 | The next experiment should separate:
1202 | 
1203 | ```text
1204 | HOW MUCH CONSTRUCTION HAPPENS
1205 | ```
1206 | 
1207 | from:
1208 | 
1209 | ```text
1210 | HOW CONCENTRATED COMPUTATIONAL SELECTION IS
1211 | ```
1212 | 
1213 | As `B` changes, adjust the attachment calibration so that:
1214 | 
1215 | ```text
1216 | B × p̄(B)
1217 | ≈ constant
1218 | ```
1219 | 
1220 | across arms.
1221 | 
1222 | Then compare causal amplification.
1223 | 
1224 | Include an exhaustive-evaluation arm with the same expected attachment rate.
1225 | 
1226 | Now the question becomes:
1227 | 
1228 | > **At matched expected construction rate, does stronger candidate subsampling change downstream causal amplification?**
1229 | 
1230 | If amplification is invariant, then finite-budget redistribution is a spatial allocation law and nothing more.
1231 | 
1232 | If amplification changes, then finite computation provides a route from allocation structure to system-level causal dynamics.
1233 | 
1234 | Either answer would matter.
1235 | 
1236 | ---
1237 | 
1238 | ## What We Learned by Varying the Constraint
1239 | 
1240 | The progression now looks like this:
1241 | 
1242 | ```mermaid
1243 | flowchart TD
1244 |     A[CHAPTER 21<br/>FINITE COMPUTATION EXISTS] --> B[CHAPTER 23<br/>LOCAL CAUSAL EFFECT EXISTS]
1245 |     B --> C[CHAPTER 24<br/>LOCAL INTERVENTION CAN REDISTRIBUTE<br/>DISTANT EXPECTED CONSTRUCTION]
1246 |     C --> D[CHAPTER 25<br/>FINITE CANDIDATE SELECTION<br/>IS THE CONTROL MECHANISM]
1247 |     D --> E[PARTIAL EVALUATION<br/>→ NON-LOCAL COUPLING]
1248 |     D --> F[FULL EVALUATION<br/>→ EXACT ZERO]
1249 | ```
1250 | 
1251 | The experimental object has become much clearer.
1252 | 
1253 | We are no longer asking whether the crystal resembles an organism.
1254 | 
1255 | We are discovering what finite computation does to causal organization.
1256 | 
1257 | And that gives us a result we did not import from biology:
1258 | 
1259 | > **A local digital process can become non-locally coupled through competition for execution slots, even when its transition rule remains strictly local.**
1260 | 
1261 | That is a genuine property of this computational substrate.
1262 | 
1263 | The next chapter asks whether that coupling merely redistributes activity—
1264 | 
1265 | or changes what causal activity can become.

0011 | 
0012 | Chapter 25 established a non-local effect in a system whose transition rule was local.
0013 | 
0014 | A perturbation at one frontier site changed which distant candidates received evaluation slots.
0015 | 
0016 | When candidate subsampling disappeared, the far-field effect disappeared with it.
0017 | 
0018 | The mechanism was:
0019 | 
0020 | ```text
0021 | LOCAL FRONTIER CHANGE
0022 | ↓
0023 | FINITE EVALUATION SLOTS
0024 | ↓
0025 | CANDIDATE SUBSTITUTION
0026 | ↓
0027 | FAR-FIELD REDISTRIBUTION
0028 | ```
0029 | 
0030 | That result answered one question.
0031 | 
0032 | It created another.
0033 | 
0034 | If finite selection changes **where** causal opportunity is expressed, does it also change **how much** causal consequence accumulates?
0035 | 
0036 | Or does it merely route the same perturbation through different computational pathways?
0037 | 
0038 | That distinction became Chapter 26.
0039 | 
0040 | And the eventual answer was more interesting than either alternative alone.
0041 | 
0042 | ---
0043 | 
0044 | ## Redistribution Is Not Amplification
0045 | 
0046 | The obvious experiment would have been to vary the evaluation budget.
0047 | 
0048 | But that experiment would have been confounded immediately.
0049 | 
0050 | A larger budget evaluates more candidates.
0051 | 
0052 | More evaluated candidates produce more expected attachments.
0053 | 
0054 | More attachments can create more downstream attachments.
0055 | 
0056 | So an apparent increase in causal amplification could reduce to:
0057 | 
0058 | ```text
0059 | MORE COMPUTATION
0060 | ↓
0061 | MORE CONSTRUCTION
0062 | ```
0063 | 
0064 | rather than:
0065 | 
0066 | ```text
0067 | DIFFERENT ALLOCATION
0068 | ↓
0069 | DIFFERENT CAUSAL AMPLIFICATION
0070 | ```
0071 | 
0072 | Chapter 26 therefore had to control construction quantity while changing allocation structure.
0073 | 
0074 | The primary scientific question became:
0075 | 
0076 | > **At matched expected background construction rate, does strong candidate subsampling produce a larger finite downstream causal consequence than true exhaustive evaluation?**
0077 | 
0078 | The stronger mechanistic question emerged only later:
0079 | 
0080 | > **If the downstream consequence does not change much, does finite selection nevertheless change the pathway through which the immediate causal effect is realized?**
0081 | 
0082 | ---
0083 | 
0084 | ## The Perturbation
0085 | 
0086 | As in the previous chapters, we started from the same checkpoint and the same frontier probe `x`.
0087 | 
0088 | Two branches were created:
0089 | 
0090 | ```text
0091 | FORCE
0092 | x is occupied
0093 | 
0094 | PREVENT
0095 | x remains empty
0096 | ```
0097 | 
0098 | Both branches used:
0099 | 
0100 | ```text
0101 | same checkpoint
0102 | same probe
0103 | same future environment
0104 | same cell-keyed randomness
0105 | ```
0106 | 
0107 | The intervention was transient.
0108 | 
0109 | After one continuation update, `x` was removed from FORCE if it remained occupied.
0110 | 
0111 | The finite-horizon outcome was:
0112 | 
0113 | ```text
0114 | G_T(H)
0115 | ```
0116 | 
0117 | with:
0118 | 
0119 | ```text
0120 | H = 12
0121 | ```
0122 | 
0123 | where `G_T` is the cumulative FORCE-minus-PREVENT realized construction difference within the chosen local horizon.
0124 | 
0125 | This is not a formal branching ratio.
0126 | 
0127 | It can contain overlapping pathways, substitutions, descendants of descendants, and branch-specific frontier changes.
0128 | 
0129 | So Chapter 26 calls it:
0130 | 
0131 | > **finite-horizon causal amplification**
0132 | 
0133 | and nothing stronger.
0134 | 
0135 | No criticality claim follows from it.
0136 | 
0137 | ---
0138 | 
0139 | ## The Allocation Arms
0140 | 
0141 | The continuation compared:
0142 | 
0143 | ```text
0144 | f = 0.10
0145 | f = 0.25
0146 | f = 0.50
0147 | f = 0.75
0148 | f = 1.00
0149 | unbounded
0150 | ```
0151 | 
0152 | where `f` controls the fraction of the PREVENT frontier used to determine the finite evaluation budget.
0153 | 
0154 | The true unbounded arm is different.
0155 | 
0156 | It evaluates the complete current frontier of each branch.
0157 | 
0158 | That distinction turned out to matter.
0159 | 
0160 | ```mermaid
0161 | flowchart LR
0162 |     subgraph Finite
0163 |     A[PREVENT frontier F_PREVENT] --> B[Budget B = f × F_PREVENT]
0164 |     B --> C[Same B used by FORCE]
0165 |     C --> D[Evaluation count matched across branches]
0166 |     end
0167 |     subgraph Unbounded
0168 |     E[PREVENT evaluates F_PREVENT] --> F[FORCE evaluates F_FORCE]
0169 |     F --> G[Coverage matched, not count]
0170 |     end
0171 | ```
0172 | 
0173 | But before we could interpret any amplification result, we first had to solve a harder control problem.
0174 | 
0175 | ---
0176 | 
0177 | ## V1 — We Matched a State, Not a Process
0178 | 
0179 | The first version of the experiment calibrated each allocation arm to the same expected construction rate at lag 1.
0180 | 
0181 | The natural reference policy was:
0182 | 
0183 | ```text
0184 | f = 0.10
0185 | offset = 0
0186 | ```
0187 | 
0188 | For broader evaluation arms, an additive score offset lowered individual attachment probabilities until the PREVENT branch matched the same expected attachment count.
0189 | 
0190 | At lag 1, the calibration worked extremely well.
0191 | 
0192 | It looked as if we had separated:
0193 | 
0194 | ```text
0195 | HOW MANY CANDIDATES ARE EVALUATED
0196 | ```
0197 | 
0198 | from:
0199 | 
0200 | ```text
0201 | HOW MUCH CONSTRUCTION IS EXPECTED
0202 | ```
0203 | 
0204 | But the offset was solved once.
0205 | 
0206 | Then the crystal evolved.
0207 | 
0208 | Different selected candidates produced different attachments.
0209 | 
0210 | Different attachments produced different morphologies.
0211 | 
0212 | Different morphologies produced different frontiers and different probability distributions.
0213 | 
0214 | The single calibration no longer represented the changing process.
0215 | 
0216 | The V1 audit showed exactly that.
0217 | 
0218 | ```text
0219 | LAG 1
0220 | matched expected construction
0221 | 
0222 | ↓
0223 | 
0224 | LAGS 2–12
0225 | construction rates drift apart
0226 | ```
0227 | 
0228 | The lesson was simple:
0229 | 
0230 | > **A controlled initial condition is not a controlled dynamical process.**
0231 | 
0232 | V1 remained part of the scientific record.
0233 | 
0234 | But it was not the experiment we intended.
0235 | 
0236 | So we built V2.
0237 | 
0238 | ---
0239 | 
0240 | ## V2 — Match the Trajectory
0241 | 
0242 | V2 recalibrated the background process at every continuation lag.
0243 | 
0244 | A dedicated PREVENT-only reference trajectory used the natural:
0245 | 
0246 | ```text
0247 | f = 0.10
0248 | offset = 0
0249 | ```
0250 | 
0251 | policy.
0252 | 
0253 | At each lag `τ`, that trajectory defined:
0254 | 
0255 | ```text
0256 | C_target(τ)
0257 | ```
0258 | 
0259 | the expected background construction target.
0260 | 
0261 | Then every allocation arm solved a fresh offset on its own current PREVENT state:
0262 | 
0263 | ```mermaid
0264 | flowchart TD
0265 |     A[For each lag τ] --> B[Reference PREVENT defines C_target(τ)]
0266 |     B --> C[Arm PREVENT state chooses its candidate set]
0267 |     C --> D[Solve offset such that expected PREVENT attachments = C_target(τ)]
0268 |     D --> E[Apply same offset to FORCE]
0269 |     E --> F[Execute both branches]
0270 |     F --> G[Next lag]
0271 |     G --> A
0272 | ```
0273 | 
0274 | FORCE was deliberately **not** calibrated independently.
0275 | 
0276 | That would have normalized away part of the causal response.
0277 | 
0278 | Instead:
0279 | 
0280 | ```text
0281 | PREVENT
0282 | defines background policy
0283 | 
0284 | FORCE
0285 | receives the same policy
0286 | and remains free to differ causally
0287 | ```
0288 | 
0289 | This gave us the control we actually wanted.
0290 | 
0291 | ---
0292 | 
0293 | ## The Calibration Itself Became Part of the Experiment
0294 | 
0295 | The manipulation was not merely:
0296 | 
0297 | ```text
0298 | same rule
0299 | different allocation
0300 | ```
0301 | 
0302 | That description is too loose.
0303 | 
0304 | Expected construction was held constant by trading:
0305 | 
0306 | ```text
0307 | FEW EVALUATED OPPORTUNITIES
0308 | with relatively high per-candidate probability
0309 | 
0310 | against
0311 | 
0312 | MANY EVALUATED OPPORTUNITIES
0313 | with much lower per-candidate probability
0314 | ```
0315 | 
0316 | The broader the evaluation policy, the more negative the calibration offset had to become.
0317 | 
0318 | Across the V2 trajectory, the approximate mean offsets were:
0319 | 
0320 | ```text
0321 | f=.10        0.000
0322 | f=.25       -1.59
0323 | f=.50       -2.49
0324 | f=.75       -2.96
0325 | f=1.00      -3.28
0326 | unbounded   -3.28
0327 | ```
0328 | 
0329 | The reference `f=.10` offset is zero by definition.
0330 | 
0331 | That is not a measurement.
0332 | 
0333 | It is an assertion about the reference policy.
0334 | 
0335 | The broader-arm offsets are measurements of how strongly the native attachment rule had to be suppressed to preserve the same PREVENT construction expectation.
0336 | 
0337 | The offset also moved over time.
0338 | 
0339 | For the broadest arms it became less negative as the trajectory evolved.
0340 | 
0341 | That is another reminder that:
0342 | 
0343 | > **Controlling a process requires a moving control when the state itself moves.**
0344 | 
0345 | ---
0346 | 
0347 | ## The Validity Gate Passed
0348 | 
0349 | The full V2 run used:
0350 | 
0351 | ```text
0352 | 192 independent groups
0353 | 768 probes
0354 | 4 probes per group
0355 | 12 continuation lags
0356 | 6 allocation arms
0357 | ```
0358 | 
0359 | with fresh seed:
0360 | 
0361 | ```text
0362 | 20260913
0363 | ```
0364 | 
0365 | The supported probe regime remained:
0366 | 
0367 | ```text
0368 | occupied_neighbors = 1
0369 | ```
0370 | 
0371 | The dynamic matching validity gate required:
0372 | 
0373 | ```text
0374 | >= 95% of group × probe × arm × lag records
0375 | within 2% of target
0376 | ```
0377 | 
0378 | and:
0379 | 
0380 | ```text
0381 | every population-level arm × lag mean
0382 | within ±2%
0383 | ```
0384 | 
0385 | Both gates passed.
0386 | 
0387 | The record-level pass fraction was:
0388 | 
0389 | ```text
0390 | 1.0
0391 | ```
0392 | 
0393 | and cross-arm PREVENT expected-construction dispersion was effectively numerical zero.
0394 | 
0395 | So V2 really did compare different allocation regimes under dynamically matched background construction.
