0398 | 
0399 | ## The Frozen Amplification Test
0400 | 
0401 | The primary contrast was:
0402 | 
0403 | ```text
0404 | G_T(f=.10)
0405 | -
0406 | G_T(unbounded)
0407 | ```
0408 | 
0409 | Strong candidate subsampling versus true exhaustive evaluation.
0410 | 
0411 | The predeclared smallest scientifically meaningful effect was:
0412 | 
0413 | ```text
0414 | ±0.15 attachments
0415 | ```
0416 | 
0417 | The result was:
0418 | 
0419 | ```text
0420 | mean difference
0421 | +0.00130
0422 | 
0423 | 95% CI
0424 | [-0.08984, +0.08854]
0425 | 
0426 | achieved MDE80
0427 | 0.11536
0428 | ```
0429 | 
0430 | The complete confidence interval lies inside:
0431 | 
0432 | ```text
0433 | [-0.15, +0.15]
0434 | ```
0435 | 
0436 | So the result is:
0437 | 
0438 | ```text
0439 | BOUNDED_NEAR_ZERO
0440 | ```
0441 | 
0442 | at the frozen effect scale.
0443 | 
0444 | This is stronger than a nonsignificant result.
0445 | 
0446 | It is also narrower than saying the two regimes are equivalent.
0447 | 
0448 | The experiment resolves the predeclared:
0449 | 
0450 | ```text
0451 | ±0.15
0452 | ```
0453 | 
0454 | scale.
0455 | 
0456 | It would have been:
0457 | 
0458 | ```text
0459 | UNRESOLVED
0460 | ```
0461 | 
0462 | under a:
0463 | 
0464 | ```text
0465 | ±0.10
0466 | ```
0467 | 
0468 | smallest-effect threshold.
0469 | 
0470 | That precision boundary matters.
0471 | 
0472 | The scientifically bounded sentence is:
0473 | 
0474 | > **At dynamically matched PREVENT background construction rate, strong candidate subsampling did not produce a mean twelve-step causal consequence differing from true exhaustive evaluation by the predeclared ±0.15 attachment scale.**
0475 | 
0476 | ---
0477 | 
0478 | ## The Same Mean Outcome Does Not Mean the Same Computation
0479 | 
0480 | The primary arm means were:
0481 | 
0482 | ```text
0483 | f=.10       0.1497
0484 | unbounded   0.1484
0485 | ```
0486 | 
0487 | Almost identical.
0488 | 
0489 | But the mechanism audit showed that these similar outcomes were **not** produced in the same way.
0490 | 
0491 | To understand why, we had to look inside the immediate ring-one causal effect.
0492 | 
0493 | ---
0494 | 
0495 | ## First Filter: Did the Perturbation Survive?
0496 | 
0497 | The FORCE intervention can disappear before the continuation even begins.
0498 | 
0499 | The intervention-step background loss rate is:
0500 | 
0501 | ```text
0502 | δ = 0.08
0503 | ```
0504 | 
0505 | If `x` is removed by that loss draw, FORCE and PREVENT collapse back to the same occupancy state.
0506 | 
0507 | Then:
0508 | 
0509 | ```text
0510 | FORCE = PREVENT
0511 | ↓
0512 | E1 = 0
0513 | G_T = 0
0514 | ```
0515 | 
0516 | structurally.
0517 | 
0518 | The realized survival fraction was:
0519 | 
0520 | ```text
0521 | 0.9141
0522 | ```
0523 | 
0524 | against the expected:
0525 | 
0526 | ```text
0527 | 0.92
0528 | ```
0529 | 
0530 | So roughly eight to nine percent of recruited probes were not weak causal responses.
0531 | 
0532 | The perturbation itself had been annihilated.
0533 | 
0534 | That is the first source of structural zero inflation.
0535 | 
0536 | ---
0537 | 
0538 | ## Second Filter: Did the Selector Expose the Difference?
0539 | 
0540 | Even when `x` survives, a finite selector may fail to evaluate any ring-one opportunity affected by the intervention.
0541 | 
0542 | For an affected frontier set of size `k`, frontier size `F`, and finite budget `B`, the without-replacement protocol expectation is:
0543 | 
0544 | ```text
0545 | P(any affected candidate selected)
0546 | =
0547 | 1 - C(F-k, B) / C(F, B)
0548 | ```
0549 | 
0550 | So the probability that an immediate ring-one causal effect can be expressed is approximately:
0551 | 
0552 | ```text
0553 | P(E1 active)
0554 | =
0555 | P(x survives)
0556 | ×
0557 | P(any affected ring-1 candidate selected)
0558 | ```
0559 | 
0560 | No fitted parameter is required.
0561 | 
0562 | The prediction matched the observed active-`E1` fraction closely:
0563 | 
0564 | ```text
0565 | arm        predicted    observed
0566 | 
0567 | f=.10       0.363        0.401
0568 | f=.25       0.679        0.698
0569 | f=.50       0.876        0.880
0570 | f=.75       0.914        0.913
0571 | f=1.00      0.918        0.910
0572 | unbounded   0.918        0.910
0573 | ```
0574 | 
0575 | The largest discrepancy was under the strongest subsampling arm.
0576 | 
0577 | By `f=.50` and above, prediction and observation were within about one percentage point.
0578 | 
0579 | This explains something that originally looked like an estimator problem.
0580 | 
0581 | At `f=.10`:
0582 | 
0583 | ```text
0584 | ~60% of probes
0585 | have effectively zero E1
0586 | ```
0587 | 
0588 | not because the causal system is simply noisy, but because the protocol often prevents the causal difference from becoming expressible.
0589 | 
0590 | That gives us a new hierarchy:
0591 | 
0592 | ```mermaid
0593 | flowchart LR
0594 |     A[PERTURBATION DELIVERED] --> B[PERTURBATION SURVIVES]
0595 |     B --> C[IMMEDIATE CAUSAL DIFFERENCE EXPRESSED]
0596 |     C --> D[DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE REALIZED]
0597 |     A -.->|≠| B
0598 |     B -.->|≠| C
0599 |     C -.->|≠| D
0600 | ```
0601 | 
0602 | The primary `f=.10` arm had:
0603 | 
0604 | ```text
0605 | E1 ≈ 0 for ~59.9% of probes
0606 | 
0607 | G_T = 0 for ~83.1% of probes
0608 | ```
0609 | 
0610 | So most delivered perturbations did not produce a realized twelve-step construction difference.
0611 | 
0612 | ---
0613 | 
0614 | ## Why the Immediate Mean Stayed Nearly Flat
0615 | 
0616 | Before the mechanism audit, the arm-level ring-one means looked almost invariant:
0617 | 
0618 | ```text
0619 | f=.10        0.11305
0620 | f=.25        0.10860
0621 | f=.50        0.10573
0622 | f=.75        0.10757
0623 | f=1.00       0.10810
0624 | unbounded    0.10824
0625 | ```
0626 | 
0627 | It was tempting to say that dynamic construction matching mathematically pinned the immediate causal input.
0628 | 
0629 | That was wrong.
0630 | 
0631 | We tested that hypothesis.
0632 | 
0633 | The simple probe-level law failed.
0634 | 
0635 | The apparent stability came from something more interesting.
0636 | 
0637 | There were **two causal channels** whose relative weights changed in opposite directions.
0638 | 
0639 | ---
0640 | 
0641 | ## Two Ways the Same Local Intervention Can Matter
0642 | 
0643 | For an `n=1` frontier probe, `x` has one occupied neighbour and five empty neighbours.
0644 | 
0645 | Some of those empty neighbours are not frontier cells before FORCE occupies `x`.
0646 | 
0647 | When `x` is present, they become new frontier candidates.
0648 | 
0649 | Those contribute through a:
0650 | 
0651 | ```text
0652 | FORCE-ONLY / PROMOTION CHANNEL
0653 | ```
0654 | 
0655 | Other empty neighbours were already frontier cells in PREVENT.
0656 | 
0657 | When `x` becomes occupied, their local neighbourhood changes.
0658 | 
0659 | Those contribute through a:
0660 | 
0661 | ```text
0662 | SHARED PROBABILITY-SHIFT CHANNEL
0663 | ```
0664 | 
0665 | The exact ring-one accounting is:
0666 | 
0667 | ```text
0668 | E1_ring1
0669 | =
0670 | FORCE-only contribution
0671 | +
0672 | PREVENT-only selector contribution
0673 | +
0674 | shared probability-shift contribution
0675 | ```
0676 | 
0677 | The equality itself is a code-level accounting identity.
0678 | 
0679 | We asserted it across:
0680 | 
0681 | ```text
0682 | 4,608 probe × arm rows
0683 | ```
0684 | 
0685 | to floating tolerance.
0686 | 
0687 | The scientific result is not that the sum equals itself.
0688 | 
0689 | The scientific result is how the channel weights change.
0690 | 
0691 | ---
0692 | 
0693 | ## The Causal Pathway Rotates with Evaluation Breadth
0694 | 
0695 | Conditioning on the 702 probes where `x` survived, the mean contributions were:
0696 | 
0697 | ```text
0698 |            FORCE-only      shared shift      total E1
0699 | 
0700 | f=.10        0.0694           0.0542           0.1237
0701 | f=.25        0.0433           0.0761           0.1188
0702 | f=.50        0.0361           0.0798           0.1157
0703 | f=.75        0.0337           0.0840           0.1177
0704 | f=1.00       0.0330           0.0853           0.1183
0705 | unbounded    0.0332           0.0853           0.1184
0706 | ```
0707 | 
0708 | That is the mechanism Chapter 26 was missing.
0709 | 
0710 | As evaluation becomes broader:
0711 | 
0712 | ```text
0713 | FORCE-ONLY / PROMOTION CONTRIBUTION
0714 | falls
0715 | 
0716 | while
0717 | 
0718 | SHARED PROBABILITY-SHIFT CONTRIBUTION
0719 | rises
0720 | ```
0721 | 
0722 | The two compensate.
0723 | 
0724 | The total immediate causal input stays near the same arm-level scale even though the computational route changes substantially.
0725 | 
0726 | ```mermaid
0727 | flowchart LR
0728 |     subgraph StrongSubsampling
0729 |     A[Finite selector] --> B[FORCE-only promotion dominates]
0730 |     A --> C[Shared probability shift weaker]
0731 |     end
0732 |     subgraph BroadEvaluation
0733 |     D[Broad selector] --> E[Shared probability shift dominates]
0734 |     D --> F[FORCE-only promotion weaker]
0735 |     end
0736 |     B & C --> G[Similar total E1]
0737 |     E & F --> G
0738 |     G --> H[Arm-level mean nearly stable]
0739 | ```
0740 | 
0741 | So the correct conclusion is not:
0742 | 
0743 | ```text
0744 | allocation does not change E1
0745 | ```
0746 | 
0747 | and not:
0748 | 
0749 | ```text
0750 | construction matching algebraically fixes E1
0751 | ```
0752 | 
0753 | It is:
0754 | 
0755 | > **Changing evaluation breadth reroutes the immediate causal effect between selector-mediated promotion and probability modification of already-shared opportunities. Those pathways compensate strongly enough that the arm-level mean ring-one effect remains nearly stable.**
0756 | 
0757 | That is a genuine mechanistic finding.
0758 | 
0759 | ---
0760 | 
0761 | ## Strong Subsampling Makes Selection Matter More
0762 | 
0763 | A compressed two-term model reinforces the same picture.
0764 | 
0765 | Conditioned on intervention survival, the fitted promotion proxy declines systematically as evaluation broadens, while the shared-shift proxy rises:
0766 | 
0767 | ```text
0768 | arm        promotion proxy    shared proxy
0769 | 
0770 | f=.10          0.580             0.379
0771 | f=.25          0.224             0.565
0772 | f=.50          0.121             0.608
0773 | f=.75          0.038             0.669
0774 | f=1.00         0.015             0.686
0775 | unbounded      0.017             0.686
0776 | ```
0777 | 
0778 | These coefficients are descriptive.
0779 | 
0780 | They are not literal attachment probabilities.
0781 | 
0782 | The exact selected-set decomposition is the mechanistic object.
0783 | 
0784 | But the progression is clear:
0785 | 
0786 | ```text
0787 | STRONG SUBSAMPLING
0788 | ↓
0789 | which opportunities receive evaluation
0790 | carries more of the causal effect
0791 | 
0792 | BROAD EVALUATION
0793 | ↓
0794 | probability changes on already-shared opportunities
0795 | carry more of the causal effect
0796 | ```
0797 | 
0798 | The same intervention can matter because:
0799 | 
0800 | ```text
0801 | a new opportunity receives computation
0802 | ```
0803 | 
0804 | or because:
0805 | 
0806 | ```text
0807 | an existing opportunity becomes more likely to construct
0808 | ```
0809 | 
0810 | Finite selection changes the mixture.
0811 | 
0812 | ---
0813 | 
0814 | ## Redistribution Still Exists
0815 | 
0816 | None of this removes the Chapter 25 result.
0817 | 
0818 | Under strong subsampling:
0819 | 
0820 | ```text
0821 | E1_far(f=.10)
0822 | ≈ -0.0387
0823 | ```
0824 | 
0825 | True unbounded evaluation has:
0826 | 
0827 | ```text
0828 | E1_far = 0
0829 | ```
0830 | 
0831 | by construction.
0832 | 
0833 | That zero is not an empirical finding.
0834 | 
0835 | When every far frontier candidate is evaluated in both branches and their far probabilities are identical, the expected selector-mediated far difference must be zero.
0836 | 
0837 | So:
0838 | 
0839 | ```text
0840 | unbounded E1_far = 0
0841 | ```
0842 | 
0843 | is a correctness assertion.
0844 | 
0845 | The experiment's scientific evidence comes from the contrast:
0846 | 
0847 | ```text
0848 | finite selection
0849 | → nonzero selector-mediated far redistribution
0850 | 
0851 | true exhaustive evaluation
0852 | → selector pathway absent
0853 | ```
0854 | 
0855 | The non-local allocation effect remains real.
0856 | 
0857 | ---
0858 | 
0859 | ## But Redistribution Did Not Become Additional Mean Amplification
0860 | 
0861 | Now we can interpret the frozen primary result more precisely.
0862 | 
0863 | Finite selection changed:
0864 | 
0865 | ```text
0866 | where evaluation slots were spent
0867 | how the ring-one effect was divided between causal channels
0868 | whether the immediate effect became expressible
0869 | ```
0870 | 
0871 | Yet the mean twelve-step causal consequence remained bounded near the exhaustive result at the predeclared scale.
0872 | 
0873 | A post-hoc analysis asked whether residual differences in immediate causal input could be masking an allocation effect.
0874 | 
0875 | At group level:
0876 | 
0877 | ```text
0878 | ΔG
0879 | =
0880 | α
0881 | +
0882 | β ΔE1
0883 | ```
0884 | 
0885 | gave:
0886 | 
0887 | ```text
0888 | α ≈ -0.0063
0889 | 
0890 | 95% bootstrap CI
0891 | [-0.0944, +0.0794]
0892 | ```
0893 | 
0894 | This does not replace the frozen primary test.
0895 | 
0896 | It is interpretive evidence.
0897 | 
0898 | And it points in the same direction.
0899 | 
0900 | So the stronger distinction is now:
0901 | 
0902 | ```text
0903 | CAUSAL REDISTRIBUTION
0904 | ≠
0905 | ADDITIONAL DOWNSTREAM AMPLIFICATION
0906 | ```
0907 | 
0908 | Finite selection can reroute causal influence without producing a scientifically meaningful additional mean downstream consequence at the tested scale.
0909 | 
0910 | ---
0911 | 
0912 | ## `f=1.00` and Unbounded Mean Different Things
0913 | 
0914 | In V2:
0915 | 
0916 | ```text
0917 | B = |PREVENT frontier|
0918 | ```
0919 | 
0920 | for the `f=1.00` arm at each lag.
0921 | 
0922 | So PREVENT is exhaustively evaluated.
0923 | 
0924 | But that same evaluation count is handed to FORCE.
0925 | 
0926 | If FORCE has a larger frontier, some FORCE opportunities still compete for a finite number of slots.
0927 | 
0928 | Thus `f=1.00` is not stale-budget V1 behaviour.
0929 | 
0930 | It is a different resource-allocation convention.
0931 | 
0932 | Finite arms conserve approximately:
0933 | 
0934 | ```text
0935 | EVALUATION COUNT ACROSS BRANCHES
0936 | ```
0937 | 
0938 | True unbounded evaluation instead conserves:
0939 | 
0940 | ```text
0941 | COVERAGE
0942 | ```
0943 | 
0944 | because each branch evaluates its own entire frontier:
0945 | 
0946 | ```text
0947 | B_PREVENT = F_PREVENT
0948 | B_FORCE   = F_FORCE
0949 | ```
0950 | 
0951 | That distinction appears directly in FORCE expected construction.
0952 | 
0953 | At lag 1:
0954 | 
0955 | ```text
0956 | FORCE expected surplus over target
0957 | 
0958 | f=.10        +0.041
0959 | f=.25        +0.045
0960 | f=.50        +0.048
0961 | f=.75        +0.049
0962 | f=1.00       +0.036
0963 | unbounded    +0.093
0964 | ```
0965 | 
0966 | The unbounded arm lets FORCE evaluate all of the extra opportunities created by the perturbation.
0967 | 
0968 | Finite arms hold the evaluation count to the PREVENT-defined budget.
0969 | 
0970 | So the `f=1.00` versus unbounded difference is best understood as a methodological contrast between two resource-allocation semantics:
0971 | 
0972 | ```text
0973 | FINITE POLICY
0974 | matches evaluation count
0975 | 
0976 | UNBOUNDED POLICY
0977 | matches evaluation coverage
0978 | ```
0979 | 
0980 | ---
0981 | 
0982 | ## What Happened to Common Random Numbers?
0983 | 
0984 | Every arm used the same keyed random numbers.
0985 | 
0986 | But pairing only reduces variance if the two arms tend to put the same cells on the same side of their probability thresholds.
0987 | 
0988 | The calibration offsets differ greatly.
0989 | 
0990 | So the same random uniforms are being compared against very different probabilities.
0991 | 
0992 | The group-level correlations with unbounded `G_T` were approximately:
0993 | 
0994 | ```text
0995 | f=.10       0.13
0996 | f=.25       0.05
0997 | f=.50       0.12
0998 | f=.75       0.44
0999 | f=1.00      0.82
1000 | ```
1001 | 
1002 | The closer the allocation/calibration policy gets to unbounded, the stronger the pairing becomes.
1003 | 
1004 | That explains why the primary contrast did not receive the dramatic variance reduction we might have expected from common random numbers.
1005 | 
1006 | Again, this does not invalidate the result.
1007 | 
1008 | It defines its precision.
1009 | 
1010 | The experiment resolved:
1011 | 
1012 | ```text
1013 | ±0.15
1014 | ```
1015 | 
1016 | not:
1017 | 
1018 | ```text
1019 | ±0.10
1020 | ```
1021 | 
1022 | ---
1023 | 
1024 | ## What Finite Selection Actually Controls
1025 | 
1026 | The picture is now more specific than the original Chapter 26 question.
1027 | 
1028 | Finite selection controls at least three things.
1029 | 
1030 | First:
1031 | 
1032 | ```text
1033 | SPATIAL ALLOCATION
1034 | ```
1035 | 
1036 | It creates outside-cone redistribution by making distant candidates compete for finite evaluation slots.
1037 | 
1038 | Second:
1039 | 
1040 | ```text
1041 | CAUSAL PATHWAY
1042 | ```
1043 | 
1044 | Under strong subsampling, selector-mediated promotion carries a larger share of the immediate local effect.
1045 | 
1046 | Under broad evaluation, shared-neighbour probability shifts carry more.
1047 | 
1048 | Third:
1049 | 
1050 | ```text
1051 | CAUSAL EXPRESSIBILITY
1052 | ```
1053 | 
1054 | A perturbation must survive loss and gain access to an affected evaluated opportunity before an immediate causal difference can appear at all.
1055 | 
1056 | What finite selection did **not** do, at the frozen resolution, was create a large additional mean twelve-step causal consequence.
1057 | 
1058 | That gives us a much better substrate statement:
1059 | 
1060 | > **Finite computational selection changes where causal influence is expressed, how that influence is routed through local computational pathways, and how often it becomes immediately expressible. Under dynamically matched background construction, those changes did not produce an additional mean twelve-step causal consequence of ±0.15 attachments or greater relative to true exhaustive evaluation.**
1061 | 
1062 | ---
1063 | 
1064 | ## Chapter 26 Status
1065 | 
1066 | ```text
1067 | CHAPTER 26
1068 | STATUS: COMPLETE
1069 | ```
1070 | 
1071 | Primary frozen result:
1072 | 
1073 | ```text
1074 | BOUNDED_NEAR_ZERO
1075 | at ±0.15 attachments
1076 | ```
1077 | 
1078 | Best bounded claim:
1079 | 
1080 | > **At dynamically matched PREVENT background construction rate, strong candidate subsampling did not produce a mean twelve-step causal consequence differing from true exhaustive evaluation by the predeclared ±0.15 attachment scale.**
1081 | 
1082 | Mechanistic finding:
1083 | 
1084 | > **Evaluation breadth changes the mixture of immediate causal pathways: strong subsampling increases the FORCE-only promotion contribution, while broader evaluation shifts causal weight toward probability changes on already-shared opportunities. The two pathways compensate strongly at the arm-average level.**
1085 | 
1086 | Protocol-level zero-inflation result:
1087 | 
1088 | > **Immediate causal expression is gated first by intervention survival and then by whether finite selection exposes an affected ring-one opportunity.**
1089 | 
1090 | Measured:
1091 | 
1092 | > **Finite candidate subsampling continues to produce selector-mediated far-field redistribution.**
1093 | 
1094 | Structural assertions:
1095 | 
1096 | ```text
1097 | ring-one channel accounting sums exactly to E1
1098 | unbounded E1_far = 0
1099 | reference f=.10 offset = 0
1100 | ```
1101 | 
1102 | Not established:
1103 | 
1104 | ```text
1105 | formal branching process
1106 | criticality
1107 | subcriticality
1108 | supercriticality
1109 | phase transition
1110 | self-sustaining propagation
1111 | coherent structure
1112 | individuality
1113 | organism
1114 | life
1115 | ```
1116 | 
1117 | No V3.
1118 | 
1119 | No further Chapter 26 audit.
1120 | 
1121 | ---
1122 | 
1123 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
1124 | 
1125 | The original hypothesis asked whether candidate subsampling amplified causality.
1126 | 
1127 | At the tested scale, it did not.
1128 | 
1129 | But the experiment revealed more than a null.
1130 | 
1131 | ```mermaid
1132 | flowchart TD
1133 |     A[FINITE SELECTION] --> B[Changes which opportunities receive computation]
1134 |     B --> C[Changes whether perturbation becomes expressible]
1135 |     C --> D[Changes mixture of local causal pathways]
1136 |     D --> E[Creates non-local redistribution]
1137 |     E --> F[Does not produce additional mean<br/>12-step causal consequence<br/>above ±0.15 scale]
1138 | ```
1139 | 
1140 | That gives us a clearer distinction than the chapter began with:
1141 | 
1142 | ```text
1143 | CAUSAL ROUTING
1144 | ≠
1145 | CAUSAL AMPLIFICATION
1146 | ```
1147 | 
1148 | And another:
1149 | 
1150 | ```text
1151 | PERTURBATION DELIVERED
1152 | ≠
1153 | PERTURBATION SURVIVES
1154 | ≠
1155 | CAUSAL DIFFERENCE EXPRESSED
1156 | ≠
1157 | DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE REALIZED
1158 | ```
1159 | 
1160 | Those are not biological categories imported into the model.
1161 | 
1162 | They came from the computational substrate itself.
1163 | 
1164 | ---
1165 | 
1166 | ## The Next Missing Ingredient Is History
1167 | 
1168 | Chapter 18 showed that persistent material state can alter later construction while it remains causally accessible.
1169 | 
1170 | Chapter 19 showed that different experiences can leave distinguishable persistent organization without establishing a meaningful common-challenge response.
1171 | 
1172 | Chapter 24 briefly attempted to use recent process history, but the tested substrate had no independent material-history state.
1173 | 
1174 | Now we can build the missing experiment deliberately.
1175 | 
1176 | The next chapter should hold constant:
1177 | 
1178 | ```text
1179 | present occupancy geometry
1180 | occupied-neighbour count
1181 | promoted-neighbour count
1182 | shared-neighbour count
1183 | allocation policy
1184 | background construction rate
1185 | perturbation
1186 | ```
1187 | 
1188 | while changing:
1189 | 
1190 | ```text
1191 | PERSISTENT MATERIAL STATE
1192 | ```
1193 | 
1194 | And the perturbation should survive its intended causal exposure **by design**, rather than recruiting probes and later discarding the roughly eight percent whose intervention is annihilated by loss.
1195 | 
1196 | Then the question becomes:
1197 | 
1198 | > **Can two states with the same visible geometry route the same perturbation differently because their material histories differ?**
1199 | 
1200 | That would be genuinely new.
1201 | 
1202 | Not history inferred from geometry.
1203 | 
1204 | Not a variable named `memory`.
1205 | 
1206 | A separate persistent state channel whose causal consequence can be measured.
1207 | 
1208 | If history changes the promotion channel, the shared probability-shift channel, the total immediate effect, or the downstream consequence under matched present geometry, then the past has become causally active.
1209 | 
1210 | If it does not, stored state remains storage without demonstrated use.
1211 | 
1212 | That is Chapter 27.
1213 | 
1214 | ---
1215 | 
1216 | ## Where We Are Now
1217 | 
1218 | The path from Chapters 24 through 26 has become unexpectedly coherent.
1219 | 
1220 | ```text
1221 | CHAPTER 24
1222 | A local intervention can alter distant expected construction
1223 | through a finite selector.
1224 | 
1225 | ↓
1226 | 
1227 | CHAPTER 25
1228 | The effect scales with finite allocation
1229 | and vanishes when subsampling disappears.
1230 | 
1231 | ↓
1232 | 
1233 | CHAPTER 26
1234 | Finite selection changes:
1235 | - spatial redistribution
1236 | - causal expressibility
1237 | - causal pathway mixture
1238 | 
1239 | but not additional mean downstream
1240 | causal consequence above ±0.15
1241 | under dynamically matched construction.
1242 | ```
1243 | 
1244 | We started by asking whether finite computation could make a perturbation grow.
1245 | 
1246 | Instead we learned how finite computation **routes** a perturbation.
1247 | 
1248 | That is a better answer.
1249 | 
1250 | And it gives us a clean next experiment:
1251 | 
1252 | > **What changes when the material itself can remember?**
```

```markdown
0001 | +++
0002 | title = "27: Can Stored Material History Redirect the Future?"
0003 | date = "2026-08-13T20:38:00+01:00"
0004 | draft = false
0005 | description = "Chapter 27 tests whether hidden material state can change the causal response of identical visible geometry, and whether that effect persists after the original trace has decayed."
0006 | weight = 27
0007 | categories = ["Programming", "Artificial Life"]
0008 | tags = ["Digital Life", "Digital Crystal", "Causality", "Finite Computation", "Experimental Method", "Cellular Automata"]
0009 | series = ["Digital Life From First Principles"]
0010 | +++
0011 | 
0012 | By the end of the previous chapters, the Digital Crystal had become harder to describe with ordinary biological language.
0013 | 
0014 | It could grow.  
0015 | It could lose material.  
0016 | It could rapidly reuse vacated sites.  
0017 | Finite computation could couple distant regions by redistributing evaluation slots.  
0018 | Local causal influence could be measured directly.
0019 | 
0020 | But none of those results required an organism.  
0021 | None required an individual.  
0022 | And none required memory.
0023 | 
0024 | That distinction mattered.
0025 | 
0026 | It would have been easy to look at a persistent alteration inside the crystal and call it memory simply because the present depended on something that had happened before.
0027 | 
0028 | Chapter 19 had already shown why that would be too fast.
0029 | 
0030 | Two different pasts could leave persistent, spatially distinguishable traces, yet those traces did not produce a scientifically meaningful common-challenge response beyond the erasure control.
0031 | 
0032 | A trace could persist without being usefully read.  
0033 | A past could leave structure without that structure functioning as a causal history channel.
0034 | 
0035 | So Chapter 27 asked a narrower question.
0036 | 
0037 | Not:
0038 | 
0039 | > Does the Digital Crystal have memory?
0040 | 
0041 | But:
0042 | 
0043 | > **Can two states with the same visible geometry respond differently to the same perturbation because they contain different hidden material state?**
0044 | 
0045 | That question is much more primitive.  
0046 | And much more testable.
0047 | 
0048 | ---
0049 | 
0050 | ## Same Shape, Different State
0051 | 
0052 | The experiment introduced a second kind of state into the crystal.
0053 | 
0054 | Visible occupancy remained the same.  
0055 | The occupied cells were identical.  
0056 | The probe geometry was identical.  
0057 | The future environment was identical.  
0058 | The random-number stream was identical.  
0059 | The allocation policy was identical.
0060 | 
0061 | But some occupied cells carried a decaying internal material value.
0062 | 
0063 | That value was invisible if we looked only at occupancy.
0064 | 
0065 | The important comparison was therefore:
0066 | 
0067 | ```text
0068 | SAME VISIBLE GEOMETRY
0069 | +
0070 | DIFFERENT MATERIAL STATE
0071 | ```
0072 | 
0073 | The material state did one simple thing.
0074 | 
0075 | For a frontier candidate \(y\), attachment probability depended not only on the ordinary Digital Crystal terms, but also on the material stored in neighbouring occupied cells.
0076 | 
0077 | Conceptually:
0078 | 
0079 | $$
0080 | \text{score}(y)
0081 | =
0082 | \text{ordinary crystal score}(y)
0083 | +
0084 | g_m \sum_{z \in N(y)} m(z)
0085 | $$
0086 | 
0087 | where:
0088 | 
0089 | - \(m(z)\) is the stored material value on neighbour \(z\),
0090 | - \(g_m = 0.30\),
0091 | - and the final attachment probability is obtained through the same logistic response used elsewhere in the crystal.
0092 | 
0093 | The material was not permanent.
0094 | 
0095 | Its half-life was frozen at six updates.  
0096 | The trace had already aged three updates before the test began.
0097 | 
0098 | Each stored cell therefore started the experiment with strength:
0099 | 
0100 | $$
0101 | 2^{-3/6}
0102 | =
0103 | 2^{-1/2}
0104 | \approx 0.707
0105 | $$
0106 | 
0107 | Two cells carried the trace.
0108 | 
0109 | The total starting material mass was therefore approximately:
0110 | 
0111 | $$
0112 | 2 \times 0.707
0113 | =
0114 | 1.414
0115 | $$
0116 | 
0117 | Newly attached cells did not inherit it.
0118 | 
0119 | The material did not propagate.
0120 | 
0121 | It simply decayed.
0122 | 
0123 | This was deliberately weak.
0124 | 
0125 | We were not building a memory system.
0126 | 
0127 | We were giving the crystal one hidden state variable and asking whether that variable could matter causally.
0128 | 
0129 | ---
0130 | 
0131 | ## Accessible and Remote History
0132 | 
0133 | The experiment used three material-state conditions.
0134 | 
0135 | ### Accessible
0136 | 
0137 | Two occupied cells close to the probe carried the decaying material trace.
0138 | 
0139 | The sole occupied neighbour of the probe cell was always included.
0140 | 
0141 | This guaranteed that the stored state was locally causally accessible.
0142 | 
0143 | ### Remote
0144 | 
0145 | The same number of occupied cells carried the same amount of material, but those carriers were placed beyond the twelve-step local causal reach of the probe.
0146 | 
0147 | ### Erased
0148 | 
0149 | No material state was present.
0150 | 
0151 | The primary comparison was:
0152 | 
0153 | $$
0154 | \text{ACCESSIBLE}
0155 | -
0156 | \text{REMOTE}
0157 | $$
0158 | 
0159 | not accessible versus erased.
0160 | 
0161 | The remote arm mattered because it separated:
0162 | 
0163 | > material exists somewhere
0164 | 
0165 | from:
0166 | 
0167 | > material is causally positioned to affect the probe.
0168 | 
0169 | ```mermaid
0170 | flowchart LR
0171 |     subgraph Accessible
0172 |     A[Probe x] --> B[Sole occupied neighbour<br/>carries material]
0173 |     B --> C[Locally exposed<br/>to perturbation]
0174 |     end
0175 |     subgraph Remote
0176 |     D[Probe x] --> E[No local material carrier]
0177 |     F[Material cells<br/>far beyond 12-step reach] --> G[Only global calibration<br/>pathway possible]
0178 |     end
0179 |     A & D --> H[Same visible geometry]
0180 |     B & F --> I[Same material mass<br/>different spatial placement]
0181 | ```
0182 | 
0183 | ---
0184 | 
0185 | ## What Went Wrong in V1
0186 | 
0187 | The first full experiment looked promising.
0188 | 
0189 | The immediate causal response differed strongly between accessible and remote material states.
0190 | 
0191 | The twelve-step causal consequence also appeared lower under accessible history.
0192 | 
0193 | But inspection of the implementation exposed a construct-validity failure.
0194 | 
0195 | The intended intervention was:
0196 | 
0197 | ```text
0198 | FORCE:
0199 | x is occupied for one causal exposure
0200 | 
0201 | PREVENT:
0202 | x is kept empty for that same exposure
0203 | ```
0204 | 
0205 | The implementation did something different.
0206 | 
0207 | `FORCE` inserted \(x\).
0208 | 
0209 | `PREVENT` merely began with \(x\) empty.
0210 | 
0211 | During the first growth update, the PREVENT branch was still allowed to attach \(x\) naturally.
0212 | 
0213 | That is not prevention.
0214 | 
0215 | And because the accessible material trace deliberately included \(x\)'s sole occupied neighbour, it changed the probability that \(x\) would attach.
0216 | 
0217 | The audit recovered that probability exactly.
0218 | 
0219 | Mean probability that PREVENT would naturally attach \(x\):
0220 | 
0221 | ```text
0222 | accessible   0.428
0223 | remote       0.377
0224 | erased       0.378
0225 | ```
0226 | 
0227 | The accessible treatment increased the probability of the supposedly prevented cell appearing by about five percentage points.
0228 | 
0229 | That contaminated the twelve-step intervention.
0230 | 
0231 | The formal V1 downstream result was therefore invalid.
0232 | 
0233 | This was not a statistical problem.  
0234 | It was not lack of power.  
0235 | It was not an inconvenient confidence interval.
0236 | 
0237 | It was an intervention that did not implement the experiment we thought we were running.
0238 | 
0239 | That distinction is worth preserving.
0240 | 
0241 | > **An empty cell at the start of a control branch is not the same thing as a cell being prevented from appearing.**
0242 | 
0243 | ---
0244 | 
0245 | ## Something Survived V1
0246 | 
0247 | The V1 failure did not destroy everything.
0248 | 
0249 | The immediate expected causal response had been calculated before realized growth occurred.
0250 | 
0251 | It therefore did not depend on whether \(x\) later attached in PREVENT.
0252 | 
0253 | That immediate quantity was:
0254 | 
0255 | $$
0256 | E_1
0257 | =
0258 | \text{expected FORCE attachment}
0259 | -
0260 | \text{expected PREVENT attachment}
0261 | $$
0262 | 
0263 | over the local ring around the probe.
0264 | 
0265 | Accessible material reduced that immediate causal response.
0266 | 
0267 | The accessible-minus-remote difference was approximately:
0268 | 
0269 | $$
0270 | \Delta E_1
0271 | \approx -0.0182
0272 | $$
0273 | 
0274 | with a narrow confidence interval entirely below zero.
0275 | 
0276 | That effect was real.
0277 | 
0278 | But why would a positive material term reduce causal response?
0279 | 
0280 | The material gain was positive.  
0281 | Material increased attachment probability.
0282 | 
0283 | It seemed at first that the response should therefore increase.
0284 | 
0285 | The mechanism audit showed the opposite.
0286 | 
0287 | ---
0288 | 
0289 | ## Stored State Can Reduce Sensitivity
0290 | 
0291 | The attachment function is logistic.
0292 | 
0293 | A candidate's probability does not increase linearly with score.
0294 | 
0295 | The derivative is:
0296 | 
0297 | $$
0298 | p(1-p)
0299 | $$
0300 | 
0301 | which means the same score increment produces different probability changes depending on where the candidate already sits on the sigmoid.
0302 | 
0303 | The accessible material raised the baseline attachment probability of shared frontier candidates.
0304 | 
0305 | Those candidates were therefore pushed toward a flatter part of the response curve.
0306 | 
0307 | Then the FORCE intervention added its own local causal input.
0308 | 
0309 | But because the candidate was already further along the sigmoid, the additional probability increase caused by FORCE became smaller.
0310 | 
0311 | ```mermaid
0312 | flowchart TD
0313 |     A[Accessible material] --> B[Higher baseline attachment probability]
0314 |     B --> C[Shared candidate moves toward saturation]
0315 |     C --> D[Same FORCE intervention produces smaller Δp]
0316 |     D --> E[Reduced immediate causal response]
0317 | ```
0318 | 
0319 | So:
0320 | 
0321 | ```text
0322 | material raises baseline probability
0323 | ↓
0324 | candidate moves toward saturation
0325 | ↓
0326 | same perturbation produces smaller Δp
0327 | ```
0328 | 
0329 | The candidate-level accounting made this mechanism unusually clean.
0330 | 
0331 | For accessible versus erased history, the shared-candidate saturation contribution was approximately:
0332 | 
0333 | $$
0334 | -0.01814
0335 | $$
0336 | 
0337 | while the total immediate difference was approximately:
0338 | 
0339 | $$
0340 | -0.01930
0341 | $$
0342 | 
0343 | Almost the entire immediate effect was explained by reduced sensitivity on the shared frontier opportunities.
0344 | 
0345 | This gave us a sharper statement than:
0346 | 
0347 | > history changes response.
0348 | 
0349 | The actual result was:
0350 | 
0351 | > **Stored material state changed the response function itself.**
0352 | 
0353 | More precisely:
0354 | 
0355 | > **Locally accessible material state raised baseline attachment probability and thereby reduced the incremental causal sensitivity of shared frontier opportunities to the same perturbation.**
0356 | 
0357 | That is not memory.
0358 | 
0359 | But it is hidden-state causal modulation.
0360 | 
0361 | ---
0362 | 
0363 | ## Remote State Was Not Automatically a Clean Null
0364 | 
0365 | The V1 audit uncovered another problem.
0366 | 
0367 | Remote material was physically beyond the local causal reach of the probe.
0368 | 
0369 | Yet remote and erased states still produced a tiny difference in local \(E_1\).
0370 | 
0371 | The reason was not material propagation.
0372 | 
0373 | It was calibration.
0374 | 
0375 | The protocol dynamically matched expected background construction.
0376 | 
0377 | If remote material changed expected construction somewhere else in the crystal, the calibration system compensated by changing a global score offset.
0378 | 
0379 | That offset applied everywhere.
0380 | 
0381 | So:
0382 | 
0383 | ```text
0384 | remote material
0385 | ↓
0386 | global expected construction changes
0387 | ↓
0388 | calibration offset changes
0389 | ↓
0390 | local probabilities change slightly
0391 | ```
0392 | 
0393 | The remote state's entire V1 local effect could be attributed to that calibration pathway.
0394 | 
0395 | This was another useful lesson.
0396 | 
0397 | > **A global compensator can create a causal channel between regions that are otherwise locally separated.**
0398 | 
0399 | That is not a property of the material state.
0400 | 
0401 | It is a property of the experimental controller.
0402 | 
0403 | For V2, the remote control therefore needed to be better matched.
0404 | 
0405 | ---
0406 | 
0407 | ## Correcting the Experiment
0408 | 
0409 | Chapter 27 V2 kept the material parameters frozen.
0410 | 
0411 | No gain was changed.  
0412 | No half-life was changed.  
0413 | No history age was changed.  
0414 | No horizon was changed.  
0415 | No effect threshold was changed.
0416 | 
0417 | The changes were construct-validity corrections.
0418 | 
0419 | The first correction was simple:
0420 | 
0421 | ```text
0422 | PREVENT explicitly blocks x during lag 1.
0423 | FORCE explicitly contains x during lag 1.
0424 | ```
0425 | 
0426 | After one causal growth exposure, \(x\) was removed from FORCE.
0427 | 
0428 | Both branches then continued normally.
0429 | 
0430 | The second correction improved the remote control.
0431 | 
0432 | Instead of choosing remote carriers simply because they were far away, remote material carriers were matched to accessible carriers on baseline frontier influence.
0433 | 
0434 | For each accessible carrier, the experiment measured:
0435 | 
0436 | - how many frontier cells it touched,
0437 | - and the total baseline attachment-probability mass of those adjacent frontier cells.
0438 | 
0439 | A remote carrier had to match the frontier count exactly and the probability mass within a frozen tolerance.
0440 | 
0441 | It also had to remain beyond the twelve-step local causal reach of the probe.
0442 | 
0443 | This produced a much cleaner remote control.
0444 | 
0445 | The remote-minus-erased immediate effect fell to approximately:
0446 | 
0447 | $$
0448 | 8.2 \times 10^{-5}
0449 | $$
0450 | 
0451 | effectively removing the calibration leakage that had complicated V1.
0452 | 
0453 | ---
0454 | 
0455 | ## The Primary Estimator Changed Too
0456 | 
0457 | The realized twelve-step attachment difference was noisy.
0458 | 
0459 | That was obvious in V1.
0460 | 
0461 | So V2 used a Rao-Blackwellized estimator as the primary quantity.
0462 | 
0463 | At every lag, before realized Bernoulli attachment decisions were drawn, the experiment calculated the expected local causal difference:
0464 | 
0465 | $$
0466 | \Delta_t
0467 | =
0468 | \sum_{y \in L}
0469 | p_{\text{FORCE}}(y,t)
0470 | -
0471 | \sum_{y \in L}
0472 | p_{\text{PREVENT}}(y,t)
0473 | $$
0474 | 
0475 | where \(L\) was the same local spatial support used for the realized outcome, and the intervention cell itself was always excluded.
0476 | 
0477 | The cumulative expected causal consequence was then:
0478 | 
0479 | $$
0480 | G_{\mathrm{RB}}
0481 | =
0482 | \sum_{t=1}^{12} \Delta_t
0483 | $$
0484 | 
0485 | This did not freeze the trajectory into expectation.
0486 | 
0487 | The FORCE and PREVENT branches still evolved through realized stochastic events.
0488 | 
0489 | Their states could diverge.  
0490 | Material could decay.  
0491 | Cells could be lost.  
0492 | Geometry could change.
0493 | 
0494 | The estimator merely removed the extra Bernoulli noise from measuring each lag's consequence.
0495 | 
0496 | The realized twelve-step result remained as a secondary outcome.
0497 | 
0498 | ```mermaid
0499 | flowchart LR
0500 |     subgraph RB Estimator
0501 |     A[At each lag, compute expected local difference Δt] --> B[Sum Δt over 12 lags]
0502 |     B --> C[G_RB: expected cumulative causal consequence]
0503 |     end
0504 |     subgraph Realized
0505 |     D[Actual Bernoulli draws at each lag] --> E[Realized attachment differences]
0506 |     E --> F[G_realized: secondary noisy outcome]
0507 |     end
0508 |     C -.->|compare| F
0509 | ```
0510 | 
0511 | ---
0512 | 
0513 | ## V2 Passed
0514 | 
0515 | The corrected experiment used 192 independent groups.
0516 | 
0517 | All 192 groups remained represented after the stricter remote-matching rule.
0518 | 
0519 | There were 564 supported probes.
0520 | 
0521 | Every major validity gate passed:
0522 | 
0523 | ```text
0524 | group coverage                     100%
0525 | dynamic matching records           100%
0526 | population matching gate           PASS
0527 | intervention assertions            PASS
0528 | remote carrier matching            PASS
0529 | ```
0530 | 
0531 | The corrected experiment was valid.
0532 | 
0533 | ---
0534 | 
0535 | ## The Immediate Effect Replicated
0536 | 
0537 | The immediate accessible-minus-remote causal difference was:
0538 | 
0539 | $$
0540 | \Delta E_1
0541 | =
0542 | -0.01499
0543 | $$
0544 | 
0545 | with 95% confidence interval approximately:
0546 | 
0547 | $$
0548 | [-0.01725,\,-0.01281]
0549 | $$
0550 | 
0551 | The sign matched V1.
0552 | 
0553 | The magnitude was slightly smaller, which was expected after removing control asymmetries.
0554 | 
0555 | But the effect survived.
0556 | 
0557 | This mattered.
0558 | 
0559 | The local sensitivity reduction was not an artifact of the V1 PREVENT bug.
0560 | 
0561 | It was not an artifact of the old remote-carrier placement rule.
0562 | 
0563 | The hidden material state genuinely changed the immediate causal response of identical visible geometry.
0564 | 
0565 | ---
0566 | 
0567 | ## The Downstream Effect Was Negative Too
0568 | 
0569 | The primary twelve-step Rao-Blackwellized comparison was:
0570 | 
0571 | $$
0572 | \Delta G_{\mathrm{RB}}
0573 | =
0574 | G_{\mathrm{accessible}}
0575 | -
0576 | G_{\mathrm{remote}}
0577 | =
0578 | -0.397
0579 | $$
0580 | 
0581 | with 95% confidence interval approximately:
0582 | 
0583 | $$
0584 | [-0.679,\,-0.119]
0585 | $$
0586 | 
0587 | The realized secondary result pointed in the same direction:
0588 | 
0589 | $$
0590 | \Delta G_{\mathrm{realized}}
0591 | \approx -0.357
0592 | $$
0593 | 
0594 | with 95% confidence interval approximately:
0595 | 
0596 | $$
0597 | [-0.673,\,-0.040]
0598 | $$
0599 | 
0600 | So both estimators agreed.
0601 | 
0602 | Accessible material state reduced the later causal consequence of the same perturbation.
0603 | 
0604 | But the frozen decision rule contained another requirement.
0605 | 
0606 | The predeclared smallest effect of interest was:
0607 | 
0608 | $$
0609 | \pm 0.15
0610 | $$
0611 | 
0612 | To call the magnitude **SUPPORTED**, the experiment required not only a confidence interval excluding zero, but enough precision to resolve the predeclared threshold.
0613 | 
0614 | The achieved MDE was still around:
0615 | 
0616 | $$
0617 | 0.357
0618 | $$
0619 | 
0620 | So the formal minimum-magnitude claim remained:
0621 | 
0622 | ```text
0623 | UNRESOLVED
0624 | ```
0625 | 
0626 | That does not mean the direction was unresolved.
0627 | 
0628 | It means two different questions had different answers.
0629 | 
0630 | ```text
0631 | Is the effect negative?
0632 | SUPPORTED
0633 | 
0634 | Can we establish with the frozen precision rule
0635 | that the mean effect is at least 0.15 in magnitude?
0636 | UNRESOLVED
0637 | ```
0638 | 
0639 | Those statements are compatible.
0640 | 
0641 | And keeping them separate is important.
0642 | 
0643 | ---
0644 | 
0645 | ## Did the Effect Simply Track the Material?
0646 | 
0647 | At this point Chapter 27 still had one unresolved mechanistic question.
0648 | 
0649 | The material trace decayed.
0650 | 
0651 | The downstream causal consequence accumulated.
0652 | 
0653 | Was the later effect merely proportional to the amount of material still present?
0654 | 
0655 | Or did the material alter the trajectory early, after which the changed trajectory continued under its own dynamics?
0656 | 
0657 | The V2 raw results already contained enough information to answer that descriptively.
0658 | 
0659 | No new experiment was needed.
0660 | 
0661 | ---
0662 | 
0663 | ## The Material Weakened. The Causal Difference Kept Growing.
0664 | 
0665 | The material began with total mass:
0666 | 
0667 | $$
0668 | M_0
0669 | \approx 1.414
0670 | $$
0671 | 
0672 | Half that value was:
0673 | 
0674 | $$
0675 | 0.707
0676 | $$
0677 | 
0678 | The accessible material mass fell below that threshold at lag 4.
0679 | 
0680 | By the previous lag, cumulative expected causal difference was only:
0681 | 
0682 | $$
0683 | -0.0995
0684 | $$
0685 | 
0686 | The final twelve-step difference was:
0687 | 
0688 | $$
0689 | -0.3972
0690 | $$
0691 | 
0692 | Therefore approximately:
0693 | 
0694 | $$
0695 | 75\%
0696 | $$
0697 | 
0698 | of the final causal difference accumulated after the material had already fallen below half of its initial mass.
0699 | 
0700 | The trace fell below one quarter of its starting mass around lag 8.
0701 | 
0702 | Even after that point, another approximately:
0703 | 
0704 | $$
0705 | -0.141
0706 | $$
0707 | 
0708 | of cumulative causal difference accrued.
0709 | 
0710 | That was about:
0711 | 
0712 | $$
0713 | 36\%
0714 | $$
0715 | 
0716 | of the final effect.
0717 | 
0718 | The material was disappearing.
0719 | 
0720 | The causal consequence was still accumulating.
0721 | 
0722 | ```mermaid
0723 | flowchart LR
0724 |     subgraph Timeline
0725 |     T0[Start<br/>material mass 1.414] --> T1[Lag 4<br/>mass below half<br/>cumulative diff -0.0995]
0726 |     T1 --> T2[Lag 8<br/>mass below quarter<br/>additional diff -0.141]
0727 |     T2 --> T3[Lag 12<br/>final diff -0.3972]
0728 |     end
0729 |     T1 -.->|75% of final effect<br/>occurs after this point| T3
0730 |     T2 -.->|36% of final effect<br/>occurs after this point| T3
0731 | ```
0732 | 
0733 | ---
0734 | 
0735 | ## Early, Middle and Late
0736 | 
0737 | Dividing the twelve-step continuation into three descriptive epochs made the pattern even clearer.
0738 | 
0739 | ```text
0740 | EARLY    lags 1–4     -0.120
0741 | MIDDLE   lags 5–8     -0.158
0742 | LATE     lags 9–12    -0.119
0743 | ```
0744 | 
0745 | The effect was not concentrated in the first few updates.
0746 | 
0747 | The middle epoch contributed more than the early epoch.
0748 | 
0749 | Even the late epoch, when mean accessible material mass had fallen to roughly:
0750 | 
0751 | $$
0752 | 0.183
0753 | $$
0754 | 
0755 | still contributed an average negative increment.
0756 | 
0757 | The late-period interval was wide enough to include zero, so this was not promoted as a separate confirmatory finding.
0758 | 
0759 | But descriptively the trajectory did not look like a direct material-dose response.
0760 | 
0761 | The system had already been redirected.
0762 | 
0763 | ---
0764 | 
0765 | ## Material Amount Did Not Predict the Causal Increment
0766 | 
0767 | The closeout analysis also asked whether more surviving material simply produced a larger causal effect.
0768 | 
0769 | It did not.
0770 | 
0771 | The pooled correlation between accessible material mass and the accessible-minus-remote causal increment was approximately:
0772 | 
0773 | $$
0774 | r \approx -0.001
0775 | $$
0776 | 
0777 | essentially zero.
0778 | 
0779 | At the group level, final causal difference was also only weakly related to average surviving material or to the difference in material mass between accessible and remote arms.
0780 | 
0781 | So the simplest dose model failed descriptively:
0782 | 
0783 | ```text
0784 | more material
0785 | ≠
0786 | larger downstream causal effect
0787 | ```
0788 | 
0789 | The more plausible sequence was:
0790 | 
0791 | ```text
0792 | material state
0793 | ↓
0794 | changes immediate local sensitivity
0795 | ↓
0796 | changes which construction events occur
0797 | ↓
0798 | changes later geometry and state
0799 | ↓
0800 | later causal response changes
0801 | even after original material weakens
0802 | ```
0803 | 
0804 | The material did not need to remain strong forever.
0805 | 
0806 | It only needed to alter the path.
0807 | 
0808 | ---
0809 | 
0810 | ## Material-State Trajectory Redirection
0811 | 
0812 | This gives us a new phenomenon.
0813 | 
0814 | Not memory.  
0815 | Not learning.  
0816 | Not adaptation.
0817 | 
0818 | A more primitive property.
0819 | 
0820 | We can state it operationally:
0821 | 
0822 | > **A locally accessible decaying material state can alter the causal sensitivity of otherwise identical visible geometry, and the resulting construction differences can redirect later system evolution so that additional causal consequences accumulate after the original material trace has substantially weakened.**
0823 | 
0824 | Call this **Material-State Trajectory Redirection**.
0825 | 
0826 | The name matters less than the distinction it captures.
0827 | 
0828 | A hidden state variable does not merely need to persist physically to matter.
0829 | 
0830 | Its effect can be converted into later geometry.
0831 | 
0832 | Once that happens, the consequences may continue after much of the original hidden state has disappeared.
0833 | 
0834 | This is one way a past can matter without the present containing a complete record of that past.
0835 | 
0836 | ```mermaid
0837 | flowchart TD
0838 |     A[Hidden material state] --> B[Changes immediate response function]
0839 |     B --> C[Changes local construction events]
0840 |     C --> D[Changes later geometry and state]
0841 |     D --> E[Later causal response changes]
0842 |     E --> F[Consequences accumulate after original material decays]
0843 |     F -.->|not memory| G[Trajectory redirection]
0844 | ```
0845 | 
0846 | ---
0847 | 
0848 | ## What This Is Not
0849 | 
0850 | The temptation now is obvious.
0851 | 
0852 | The system has hidden state.  
0853 | The hidden state changes later response.  
0854 | Its consequences outlive much of the original trace.
0855 | 
0856 | Why not call that memory?
0857 | 
0858 | Because the material was experimentally written.
0859 | 
0860 | The crystal did not acquire it from an endogenous experience encoder.
0861 | 
0862 | It did not decide what to store.  
0863 | It did not reconstruct past events.  
0864 | It did not use the state to choose among remembered alternatives.  
0865 | It did not demonstrate learning.  
0866 | It did not demonstrate adaptation.
0867 | 
0868 | What we have shown is more basic:
0869 | 
0870 | ```text
0871 | PAST-DEPENDENT HIDDEN STATE
0872 | ↓
0873 | CAUSAL RESPONSE MODULATION
0874 | ↓
0875 | TRAJECTORY REDIRECTION
0876 | ```
0877 | 
0878 | A memory system would need to build on that.
0879 | 
0880 | But this result does not yet earn the word.
0881 | 
0882 | ---
0883 | 
0884 | ## What Survived the Hypothesis?
0885 | 
0886 | The Chapter 27 evidence can be separated cleanly.
0887 | 
0888 | ### Immediate hidden-state modulation — SUPPORTED
0889 | 
0890 | With occupancy geometry held fixed, locally accessible material state changed the immediate expected causal response to the same perturbation.
0891 | 
0892 | ### Mechanism — SUPPORTED
0893 | 
0894 | The immediate reduction was primarily explained by shared frontier candidates being shifted toward a flatter region of the logistic attachment response.
0895 | 
0896 | ### Corrected downstream direction — SUPPORTED NEGATIVE
0897 | 
0898 | In V2, both expected and realized twelve-step causal consequences were lower under accessible material state than under matched remote material state.
0899 | 
0900 | ### Frozen \(\pm0.15\) minimum-magnitude claim — UNRESOLVED
0901 | 
0902 | The experiment did not achieve enough precision to establish the predeclared minimum meaningful magnitude under the frozen decision rule.
0903 | 
0904 | ### Trajectory-redirection interpretation — DESCRIPTIVELY SUPPORTED
0905 | 
0906 | Most of the cumulative expected causal difference accrued after the material trace had fallen below half its starting mass, and substantial additional difference accrued after it had fallen below one quarter.
0907 | 
0908 | ### Memory — NOT ESTABLISHED
0909 | 
0910 | The stored material state was experimentally written.
0911 | 
0912 | ---
0913 | 
0914 | ## The Broader Lesson
0915 | 
0916 | Chapter 27 began with a small question.
0917 | 
0918 | Can hidden state matter if visible geometry is the same?
0919 | 
0920 | The answer is yes.
0921 | 
0922 | But the more interesting result came afterward.
0923 | 
0924 | The hidden state did not merely bias one attachment decision.
0925 | 
0926 | It changed sensitivity.
0927 | 
0928 | That changed construction.
0929 | 
0930 | Changed construction altered later state.
0931 | 
0932 | And later state carried forward consequences after the original hidden trace had substantially decayed.
0933 | 
0934 | The causal chain was therefore not:
0935 | 
0936 | ```text
0937 | stored material
0938 | → persistent force
0939 | ```
0940 | 
0941 | It was:
0942 | 
0943 | ```text
0944 | stored material
0945 | → altered response
0946 | → altered events
0947 | → altered trajectory
0948 | ```
0949 | 
0950 | That distinction will matter later.
0951 | 
0952 | A digital system does not necessarily need a durable biological-style memory object to let the past shape the future.
0953 | 
0954 | It may need something more primitive:
0955 | 
0956 | > **a state difference that can alter the path strongly enough for the path itself to carry the consequence forward.**
0957 | 
0958 | That is what the Digital Crystal has now demonstrated.
0959 | 
0960 | The next question is no longer whether hidden material state can matter.
0961 | 
0962 | It can.
0963 | 
0964 | The harder question is whether those causal histories can become organized into something with a boundary of its own.
0965 | 
0966 | Not merely a process that has a past.
0967 | 
0968 | But a process whose internal causal structure becomes more strongly coupled to itself than to the rest of the world.
0969 | 
0970 | That is where individuality begins.
```
